summary.title: Multi-spectral Observations of Lunar Occultations: I. Resolving The Dust Shell Around AFGL 5440
summary.authors: Paul M. Harvey and Andrew Oldag
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents multi-spectral lunar occultation observations and radiative transfer modeling of the dust-enshrouded carbon star AFGL 5440 (also known as OH 06.86-1.5, IRAS 18036-2344), a member of the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) phase of stellar evolution. AGB stars are characterized by substantial mass loss that contributes heavy elements and solid particles to the interstellar medium, yet the underlying physical mechanisms—radiation pressure, stellar pulsation, and their coupling—remain not well understood. Studying the spatial structure of circumstellar mass-loss shells provides a key lever to clarify these processes, yet such studies require angular resolutions well under 1 arcsec to probe the inner regions. While previous speckle interferometry and adaptive optics observations achieved resolutions of about 0.1 arcsec, lunar occultations and multi-aperture interferometry have reached the milli-arcsecond level. The authors utilize the pMIRAS high-speed infrared spectrophotometer, a long/wide-slit instrument that disperses light from a slit using a NaCl prism onto a 32×100 pixel InSb array detector, to cover the entire 1–4µm spectral region with a time resolution of 8 msec and a plate scale of 0.4 arcsec/pixel. The observation of AFGL 5440 was performed as an immersion occultation on August 28, 2001, at an elevation of 36° with minimal cloud cover and a lunar phase of 0.72. The wide wavelength coverage allows simultaneous observation of the Fresnel fringe pattern of the obscured central star and the circumstellar dust emission from the warmest part of the dust distribution. AFGL 5440 is classified as a carbon-rich AGB star on the basis of its IRAS LRS spectrum; its distance is estimated to be 2.25 kpc, implying a luminosity of 1.4×10^4 L⊙. In addition to AFGL 5440, the authors modeled two calibration stars, IRC+00233 and HD 155292, which have no detectable dust shells based on near-infrared and IRAS colors. The analysis is grounded in the finding that the occultation fringes cannot be fit by any single-size model, motivating the use of the DUSTY radiative transfer code to model a circumstellar shell that fits both the observed occultation light curves and the spectral energy distribution. About 200 models were explored, varying dust optical depth, dust temperature at the inner radius, and radial density gradient; models that provided an approximate fit consistently had a maximum dust temperature of 950 K ± 50 K, a radial density gradient close to r^-2, and a best-fit optical depth at the fiducial wavelength of 5µm within the range 0.3–0.6. For the best-fit model, the physical inner radius is 3.7×10^14 cm, corresponding to an angular radius of 11 mas at the assumed distance of 2.25 kpc. A central finding is that the IRAS 60µm flux cannot be fit by any similar model without including graphite, which contrasts with general evidence against substantial graphite in stars like AFGL 5440, and suggests the 60µm flux may reflect a past higher mass-loss rate. The derived dust mass-loss rate is 6.5×10^-8 M⊙/yr, with a comparison gas-to-dust ratio of 600. The results resolve the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the circumstellar dust shell around AFGL 5440, and strongly constrain the inner radius and near-infrared optical depth.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents multi-spectral lunar occultation observations and radiative transfer modeling of the dust-enshrouded carbon star AFGL 5440 (also known as OH 06.86-1.5, IRAS 18036-2344), a member of the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) phase of stellar evolution. AGB stars are characterized by substantial mass loss that contributes heavy elements and solid particles to the interstellar medium, yet the underlying physical mechanisms—radiation pressure, stellar pulsation, and their coupling—remain not well understood. Studying the spatial structure of circumstellar mass-loss shells provides a key lever to clarify these processes, yet such studies require angular resolutions well under 1 arcsec to probe the inner regions. While previous speckle interferometry and adaptive optics observations achieved resolutions of about 0.1 arcsec, lunar occultations and multi-aperture interferometry have reached the milli-arcsecond level. The authors utilize the pMIRAS high-speed infrared spectrophotometer, a long/wide-slit instrument that disperses light from a slit using a NaCl prism onto a 32×100 pixel InSb array detector, to cover the entire 1–4µm spectral region with a time resolution of 8 msec and a plate scale of 0.4 arcsec/pixel. The observation of AFGL 5440 was performed as an immersion occultation on August 28, 2001, at an elevation of 36° with minimal cloud cover and a lunar phase of 0.72. The wide wavelength coverage allows simultaneous observation of the Fresnel fringe pattern of the obscured central star and the circumstellar dust emission from the warmest part of the dust distribution. AFGL 5440 is classified as a carbon-rich AGB star on the basis of its IRAS LRS spectrum; its distance is estimated to be 2.25 kpc, implying a luminosity of 1.4×10^4 L⊙. In addition to AFGL 5440, the authors modeled two calibration stars, IRC+00233 and HD 155292, which have no detectable dust shells based on near-infrared and IRAS colors. The analysis is grounded in the finding that the occultation fringes cannot be fit by any single-size model, motivating the use of the DUSTY radiative transfer code to model a circumstellar shell that fits both the observed occultation light curves and the spectral energy distribution. About 200 models were explored, varying dust optical depth, dust temperature at the inner radius, and radial density gradient; models that provided an approximate fit consistently had a maximum dust temperature of 950 K ± 50 K, a radial density gradient close to r^-2, and a best-fit optical depth at the fiducial wavelength of 5µm within the range 0.3–0.6. For the best-fit model, the physical inner radius is 3.7×10^14 cm, corresponding to an angular radius of 11 mas at the assumed distance of 2.25 kpc. A central finding is that the IRAS 60µm flux cannot be fit by any similar model without including graphite, which contrasts with general evidence against substantial graphite in stars like AFGL 5440, and suggests the 60µm flux may reflect a past higher mass-loss rate. The derived dust mass-loss rate is 6.5×10^-8 M⊙/yr, with a comparison gas-to-dust ratio of 600. The results resolve the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the circumstellar dust shell around AFGL 5440, and strongly constrain the inner radius and near-infrared optical depth.

Research Context
Mass loss from post-main-sequence stars provides a large fraction of the heavy element abundance. The mechanism(s) of mass loss during the AGB phase are not well understood. Studies of molecular emission lines have found periodic variations in mass-loss rates. These variations lead to the appearance of rings in the radial distribution of molecular emission lines. Studies of the nearby extreme IRC+10216 have found similar phenomena in the dust. Probing the inner regions of circumstellar shells requires angular resolutions well under 1 arcsec. Previous speckle and adaptive optics observations reached resolutions of about 0.1 arcsec. Lunar occultations have pushed angular resolutions to the milli-arcsecond level. Prior interferometric observations were typically made in one or two relatively broad bands. The multi-spectral approach aims to simultaneously see the central star and the dust.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether lunar occultation can resolve the inner regions of circumstellar shells. The study uses AFGL 5440 (OH 06.86-1.5, IRAS 18036-2344) as the primary target. AFGL 5440 is a carbon-rich AGB star. The central hypothesis is that the occultation fringes cannot be fit by any single-size model. A single-size uniform disk is used as the simplest baseline model. The predicted best-fit density gradient is expected to be r^-2. The predicted inner dust temperature is expected to be approximately 950 K. The best-fit model is expected to require the inclusion of graphite to fit the long-wavelength flux. The best-fit optical depth at 5µm is expected to be in the 0.3–0.6 range. The model is expected to provide a passable fit in the 2.5–3.2µm range with an 11 mas disk.

Methodological Details
The observations cover the entire 1–4µm spectral region. The observations were made over a continuous range of wavelengths with a high-speed spectrophotometer. The instrument is the pMIRAS spectrophotometer. The instrument is mounted on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope. The instrument uses a NaCl prism to disperse light onto a 32×100 InSb array detector. The plate scale is 0.4 arcsec/pixel. The time resolution is 8 msec. The detector is read out every 8 msec. The spectrometer is read-noise limited shortward of 2.5µm. The spectrometer is background-limited longward of 3µm. A typical observation consists of taking 5000 frames at a time. AFGL 5440 was observed during an immersion occultation on August 28, 2001. The elevation of the Moon was 36° and the Sun was 17° below the horizon. The position angle of the occultation was 54° and the lunar phase was 0.72. The slit width was set at about 5 arcsec for typical seeing of 1.5 arcsec. Two calibration stars, IRC+00233 and HD 155292, were also observed. IRC+00233 was observed on June 29, 2001, and HD 155292 on August 26, 2001. The resolving power varies from ~20 at the shortest wavelengths to ~100 at the long end. Data reduction uses a cross-correlation algorithm for alignment. Data reduction uses sky measurements on either side of the stellar spectrum for sky subtraction. The wavelength calibration is good to ±.01 λ throughout. No flux calibration was attempted due to variable instrumental efficiency and non-photometric sky conditions. The assumed distance to AFGL 5440 is 2.25 kpc. The inferred luminosity is 1.4×10^4 solar luminosities. The calibration stars have no detectable circumstellar dust shell based on near-infrared and IRAS colors.

Procedures And Architectures
The fringe pattern is a convolution of parameters blurring the point source fringe. Blurring parameters include aperture, integration time, bandwidth, and source size/structure. The fringe frequency is the speed of the lunar shadow, which must also be fit. The study used the DUSTY radiative transfer code for modeling. AFGL 5440 was modeled as a carbon-rich star with dust composed of amorphous carbon, silicon carbide, and graphite. The radiative transfer code computes model source images and the total energy distribution. The dust optical depth was varied to find the best fit to the energy distribution. The output source images were used to calculate expected occultation fringes. The dust temperature at the inner radius was held at order 950 K ± 50 K. The radial density gradient was assumed to be close to r^-2. Models with r^-2.2 could fit the energy distribution out to 20µm but had worse 60µm fits. Grain size distributions were sampled using the MRN slope and the KMH shape. Either grain size distribution provided reasonably good fits to the data. More than 200 models were explored. The outer radius of the dust shell was set to at least 100 times the inner radius. The inner radius was the only critical parameter not fixed to a single value.

Key Results
The occultation fringes could not be fit by any single-size model. The best-fit inner dust temperature is 950 K ± 50 K. The best-fit optical depth at 5µm is 0.5 ± 0.1. The best-fit radial density gradient is close to r^-2. A 11 mas uniform disk provides a passable fit in the mid-range of wavelengths. The best-fit size for IRC+00233 is between 4.5 and 5.0 mas. All uniform-disk models with a size less than about 3 mas fit HD 155292 reasonably well. A discrepancy appears around ~1.7µm for IRC+00233, where a substantially larger size would fit better. Electronic pickup at shorter wavelengths affects the observed fringe patterns of HD 155292. The dust mass-loss rate is 6.5×10^-8 M⊙/yr using the DUSTY optical constants. The gas mass-loss rate is 3.1×10^-5 M⊙/yr and the dust mass-loss rate is 5.1×10^-8 M⊙/yr. The inferred gas-to-dust mass ratio is 600. AFGL 5440's magnitude is consistent with the literature to within ±30%. A 11 mas disk produces fringes too sharp at the long end and too broadened at the short end.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Grains emitting in the 3–4µm region must be dense to produce the observed fringe blurring. The data constrain the dust density gradient in the innermost part of the circumstellar shell. Dust cooler than 900 K cannot emit sufficiently to produce the required 3–4µm emission. The physical inner radius is 3.7×10^14 cm, or 11 mas at the assumed distance of 2.25 kpc. The central star has an angular diameter of about 3 mas. The photosphere temperature of the central star is 2500 K ± 300 K. Models with only amorphous carbon and SiC failed to fit the 60µm flux by factors of 3. Including graphite is contrary to general evidence against substantial graphite in stars like AFGL 5440. A past higher mass-loss rate can explain the 60µm flux and contrast with recent high mass-loss rates. The 60µm-emitting dust is at order 1 to a few arcseconds from the star. For an assumed outflow velocity of 22 km s−1, this corresponds to 500–2000 years in the past. The findings are consistent with radiatively driven mass loss. A recent decrease in the mass-loss rate is suggested for the far-infrared flux. The derived dust mass-loss rate of order 5×10^-8 M⊙/yr is consistent with the data.

Contradictions And Limitations
There is no good explanation for the discrepancy in IRC+00233 around 1.7µm. Electronic pickup at shorter wavelengths affects the fringe patterns of HD 155292. The wavelength calibration is only good to ±.01 λ throughout. No flux calibration was attempted due to variable efficiency and non-photometric conditions. AFGL 5440's magnitude is consistent with literature only to within ±30%. Any similar model without graphite cannot fit the 60µm flux. Explaining the 60µm discrepancy is beyond the scope of our study. A uniform-disk fit with a size less than about 3 mas is consistent with data uncertainties. The 11 mas inner radius depends on the assumed distance of 2.25 kpc. The graphite conclusion is contrary to the large amount of evidence against graphite. The study lacks reported demographics, random seeds, or train/test split statistics. The inner radius of the dust shell is only constrained at wavelengths ≤4µm. The 60µm flux may require substantial modifications to the assumed density law. The study does not attempt to extract details of the stellar photosphere.

Claims
The occultation fringes cannot be fit by any single-size model for AFGL 5440. The model cannot fit the observed fringes with a single size. Models with the best-fit 11 mas disk fail at the short and long ends. An 11 mas disk provides a passable fit in the 2.5–3.2µm mid-range. The data suggests a central star and a circumstellar shell contribute together. The emission from the central star and a shell are combined.
The inner radius of the dust shell is strongly constrained. The inner dust temperature is 950 K ± 50 K. The optical depth at 5µm is 0.5 ± 0.1. The angular radius of the shell is 11 mas at 2.25 kpc. The 11 mas radius depends on the assumed distance of 2.25 kpc. The central star diameter is only about 3 mas. The inner edge location is fixed by the 3–4µm emission. The data constrain the recent dust mass-loss rate for AFGL 5440.
The IRAS 60µm flux requires the inclusion of graphite. Amorphous carbon and SiC alone fail to fit the flux by factors of 3. Graphite enabled a fit to the flat emissivity 10–50µm. The graphite conclusion is contrary to general evidence against graphite. The 60µm problem is beyond the scope of our study. The 60µm flux may reflect a past higher mass-loss rate. This time scale is 500–2000 years ago.
The observed density gradient is consistent with radiatively driven mass loss. The radial density gradient is close to r^-2. The 60µm flux is consistent with radiatively driven mass loss. The r^-1.8 gradient produced the IRAS 60µm flux but fit the 5–20µm range poorly. The r^-2.2 gradient fit the 20µm range but had worse 60µm fits. The far-infrared flux may imply a recent decrease in the mass-loss rate.

Data And Code Availability
The study employed the DUSTY radiative transfer code for radiative transfer modeling. No formal data or code availability statement is reported in the paper.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
About 200 models were explored to test the fit quality. A density gradient of r^-1.8 was tested. A density gradient of r^-2.2 was tested. The graphite-free model was compared to the best-fit model. Either the MRN or the KMH grain size distribution yielded reasonably good fits. The slit width was set to 5 arcsec for 1.5 arcsec seeing. The instrument is read-noise limited shortward of 2.5µm. The instrument is background-limited longward of 3µm. A typical observation uses 5000 frames at a time. The wavelength calibration accuracy is good to ±.01 λ.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows observed and model light curves for a 4.5 mas uniform disk. Figure 2 shows the χ2 and S/N as a function of wavelength. Figure 3 shows all uniform-disk models with a size less than about 3 mas. Figure 5 shows the observed light curves for AFGL 5440. Figure 6 shows the χ2 of the 11 mas uniform-disk model. Figure 7 shows the spectral energy distribution and occultation light curve fits. Figure 10 shows the spatial profiles of the best-fit model.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution resolves the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the circumstellar dust shell around AFGL 5440. 2. The strongest evidence is the inner dust temperature of 950 K ± 50 K and an optical depth of 0.5 ± 0.1 at 5µm. 3. The future path involves explaining the 60µm flux discrepancy that is beyond the scope of our study.

Executive Summary:
This paper reports multi-spectral lunar occultation observations of the dust-enshrouded carbon star AFGL 5440 (OH 06.86-1.5, IRAS 18036-2344), conducted over a continuous wavelength range from 1 to 4 µm using the pMIRAS high-speed infrared spectrophotometer on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope. AFGL 5440 is classified as a carbon-rich asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star based on its IRAS Low Resolution Spectrometer spectrum. The star's distance is estimated to be 2.25 kpc, and its luminosity is inferred to be 1.4×10^4 solar luminosities. The observation took place during an immersion occultation on August 28, 2001. The pMIRAS instrument uses a NaCl prism to disperse light onto a 32×100 InSb array detector, providing a time resolution of 8 msec, which corresponds to an effective angular resolution on the order of a couple milli-arcseconds. The wide spectral coverage simultaneously captures the Fresnel fringe pattern of the central star at shorter wavelengths and the circumstellar dust emission from the warmest part of the dust distribution. 

The analysis is grounded in the realization that a single-size source model cannot fit the observed occultation fringes across the entire band. Consequently, the authors employ the DUSTY radiative transfer code to build a circumstellar shell model and fit both the observed occultation light curves and the spectral energy distribution (SED) from the literature. For carbon-rich stars, the dust composition is modeled with amorphous carbon, silicon carbide (SiC), and graphite. About 200 models were explored, varying the dust optical depth, dust temperature at the inner radius, and radial density gradient. 

The models that provide an approximate fit consistently have a maximum dust temperature at the inner radius of approximately 950 K ± 50 K. Furthermore, the radial density gradient is close to r^-2, consistent with a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow. For the best-fit model, the optical depth at the fiducial wavelength of 5 µm is within the range 0.3–0.6. Two comparison stars, IRC+00233 and HD 155292, which have no detectable circumstellar dust shells based on near-infrared and IRAS colors, were also modeled. 

For AFGL 5440, a 11 mas uniform disk yields a passable fit in the 2.5–3.2 µm range but fringes that are too sharp at longer wavelengths and too broadened at the shortest wavelengths. The physical inner radius is constrained to 3.7×10^14 cm, corresponding to an angular radius of 11 mas at the assumed distance of 2.25 kpc. A key finding is that the IRAS 60 µm flux cannot be fit by any model without including graphite, which contrasts with the general evidence against substantial graphite in stars like AFGL 5440. This suggests a recent decrease in the mass-loss rate since the 60 µm-emitting dust was ejected. The derived dust mass-loss rate is 6.5 × 10^-8 M_solar/yr. The gas-to-dust mass ratio inferred from Groenewegen et al. is 600.

summary.executive_summary: The paper investigates gluon radiation during the hydrodynamic stage of the evolution of deconﬁned hot QCD matter (quark gluon plasma, QGP) by modeling the color charge transport as a nonlinear sigma model representing an ideal ﬁuid. Given that the RHIC ﬁreball is usually modeled as a relativistic ﬁuid undergoing hydrodynamic flow, the author develops a class of expanding soliton solutions within color ﬂuid to match the expanding nature of the fireball generated in RHIC experiments. Specifically, a single skyrmion solution is considered that expands in time, and a semiclassical approach is used to calculate the gluon radiation spectrum corresponding to the color current of these non-static configurations. The study assumes a hierarchy between the partonic coupling gY M and the effective coupling geff, allowing for a free parton picture where gluon self-interaction can be omitted. The key methodological step is the derivation of a semiclassical amplitude linking the classical current to a free quantum gluon field, resulting in analytical expressions for the density of states n and the radiation energy per unit momentum dE/dk. The main quantitative results are presented via figures showing the density of states and energy spectrum for three values of the small parameter λ = τ/R0 = 1/5, 2/15, 1/15. The text identifies three key spectral features: a fast fall-off in the UV side, a smooth peak dominating the intermediate energy, and a long tail in the IR. Comparison with prior literature is made: for small k, the paper finds an asymptotic number density proportional to 1/√k, which differs from the 1/k behavior found in prior work [6] because the prior work takes the medium size to be infinitely large whereas this work uses the finite soliton size R0. A distinction is also made between jet quenching radiation (scattering off static centers) and the medium-induced radiation characterized by the frequency ωC; the paper finds a hierarchy where ωC is significantly larger than the characteristic momentum 1/R0. The author acknowledges that the work was supported by a CUNY Collaborative Research Incentive grant and thanks V. P. Nair for mentoring. The paper concludes by opening possibilities to address the eccentricity of the elliptic flow either intrinsically or exogenously as a topic of follow-up work.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents three-particle azimuthal correlation results from the STAR experiment in high-energy heavy-ion collisions, specifically examining pp, d+Au, and Au+Au collisions at √sNN = 200 GeV. Heavy ion collisions create a medium that may be the quark gluon plasma (QGP), which can be studied through jets and jet-correlations, as jet properties can be calculated in vacuum with perturbative quantum chromodynamics (pQCD). Two-particle jet-like azimuthal correlations showed the away-side shape in central Au+Au to be broadened with respect to pp and peripheral Au+Au or even double-humped, consistent with mechanisms including large-angle gluon radiation, jets deflected by radial flow, path-length dependent energy loss, hydrodynamic conical flow from Mach-cone shock waves, and Cerenkov radiation. Three-particle correlations distinguish conical flow and Cerenkov radiation from other mechanisms, as both have characteristic conical emission. The associated particle pT dependence of the conical emission angle distinguishes hydrodynamic conical flow from simple Cerenkov radiation. The analysis treats events as a sum of jet-like correlated particles and background particles. The trigger particle is a charged particle with 3 < pT < 4 GeV/c and two associated particles with 1 < pT < 2 GeV/c. Combinatorial backgrounds (hard-soft and soft-soft) are subtracted. The hard-soft background is constructed from the 2-particle jet-like correlation folded with the normalized 2-particle background; the soft-soft background is from mixed events; the trigger flow background is added in triplet-wise; v4 is parameterized as v4 = 1.15v2^2. Backgrounds are normalized (with scale factor α) to the signal within 0.8 < |Δφ| < 1.2. The β factor accounts for non-Poisson multiplicity distributions. Results show an off-diagonal structure at about π ± 1.45 radians, consistent with conical emission, which increases with centrality and is prominent in the high-statistics ZDC-triggered 0-12% central Au+Au data. The Mach cone emission angle is expected to be independent of associated particle pT, while Cerenkov radiation predicts an angle sharply decreasing with pT. The off-diagonal peak angle is found to be consistent with constant as a function of associated particle pT. No strong pT dependence is observed, consistent with Mach cone emission.

Research Context
Heavy-ion collisions may create a medium known as quark-gluon plasma. Jets are good probes because their vacuum properties are calculable in pQCD. Prior two-particle correlations showed an away-side broadening or double-hump in central Au+Au. Several mechanisms have been proposed, including hydrodynamic Mach-cone flow. Cerenkov radiation and Mach cones both predict conical emission but differ in angular pT dependence.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether conical emission (Mach cones) exists in heavy-ion collisions. Three-particle correlations can differentiate conical flow from other mechanisms. Conical emission is hypothesized to appear as an off-diagonal structure at π ± 1.45 radians. The predicted outcome is that Mach cone angles are independent of pT, unlike Cerenkov radiation.

Methodological Details
The analysis treats events as a sum of jet-like correlated and background particles. Results are for charged trigger particles with 3 < pT < 4 GeV/c. Two associated charged particles have 1 < pT < 2 GeV/c. Data were taken in the STAR time projection chamber for pp, d+Au, and Au+Au at √sNN=200 GeV/c. Data covers pp, d+Au and Au+Au collisions at √sNN=200 GeV/c. The 2-particle background uses v2 from reaction plane and 4-particle cumulant methods. The v4 contribution uses the parameterization v4 = 1.15v2^2. The background is normalized within 0.8 < |Δφ| < 1.2. The β factor accounts for non-Poisson multiplicity distributions. The 2-particle jet-like correlation is folded with the normalized 2-particle background. Figure 1c shows the soft-soft background β²Binc3. Figure 1d shows the hard-soft background ν2 × αBinc2 + β²Binc,TF3. The analysis is performed on ZDC-triggered 0-12% Au+Au collisions at √sNN=200 GeV/c.

Procedures And Architectures
The 3-particle correlation method is described in reference 9. The trigger flow background is added in triplet-wise from mixed events. The hard-soft background results from one correlated and one uncorrelated associated particle. The soft-soft background combines minijets, other jets, and flow between associated particles. The v2 and v4 values are obtained the same way as for the 2-particle background. The normalization window was doubled to 0.6 < |Δφ| < 1.4. The normalization factor α is obtained by equating background pairs to squared signal pairs. A double Gaussian fit is used to locate the off-diagonal signals.

Key Results
The pp and d+Au results are similar. Peaks appear at the near-side (0,0), away-side (π,π), and one-each (0,π), (π,0). The away-side peak shows diagonal elongation consistent with kT broadening. Peripheral Au+Au shows additional on-diagonal elongation from deflected jets. The on-diagonal broadening persists into the more central Au+Au collisions. The off-diagonal structure is consistent with conical emission. The structure increases with centrality and is prominent in the high-statistics 0-12% ZDC data. Off-diagonal signals increase with centrality and significantly deviate from zero. The off-diagonal signals were found to be 1.45 radians from π. On-diagonal signals combine conical and deflected jet contributions. Figure 3 (right) shows the signal difference. The angle is constant as a function of associated particle pT. The angle is consistent with remaining constant as a function of centrality. The solid line at 1.46 is from a fit to a constant. No strong pT dependence of the angles on associated particle pT is observed.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Off-diagonal peaks consistent with conical emission are present in central Au+Au collisions. The on-diagonal difference may indicate contribution from deflected jets. The difference decreases with distance from (π,π). Mach cone angles are expected to be independent of associated particle momentum. The result is consistent with Mach cone emission.

Contradictions And Limitations
Major systematic errors come from elliptic flow measurement and normalization. The hard-soft and trigger flow variations cancel to first order in the sum. The signal is robust with respect to this change in normalization. Trigger flow from requiring a correlated particle adds 20% to trigger v2. Uncertainty in the v4 parameterization persists. Multiplicity bias effects on the soft-soft background remain a source.

Claims
Central Au+Au collisions exhibit an off-diagonal 3-particle structure consistent with conical emission. Off-diagonal structure at π ± 1.45 radians is consistent with conical emission. The structure increases with centrality and is prominent in the ZDC 0-12% central data. Off-diagonal signals increase with centrality and significantly deviate from zero in central Au+Au collisions. On-diagonal signals also show additional broadening, possibly from deflected jets. The off-diagonal structure supports the hydrodynamic conical flow interpretation.
Associated particle pT dependence of the cone angle favors Mach cone over Cerenkov radiation. The cone angle is constant as a function of associated particle pT. No strong pT dependence of the angles on associated particle pT is observed. The result is consistent with Mach cone emission. The Cerenkov model predicts an angle sharply decreasing with increasing pT. The finding reduces the role of simple Cerenkov radiation as the mechanism.

Data And Code Availability
The data were taken by the STAR experiment and are not publicly released. The 3-particle correlation method is described in reference 9.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The signal is robust with respect to the elliptic flow variation. The normalization window doubling preserves the signal.

Ethical Considerations
The data are from particle collisions; there are no human subjects.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows 2-particle and 3-particle correlations with background subtraction. Figure 2 shows background subtracted 3-particle jet-like correlations. Figure 3 shows centrality dependence of the average signal strengths. Figure 4 shows away-side projections of a strip of width 0.7 radians. Figure 5 shows emission angles from double Gaussian fits vs pT and centrality. Figure 6 shows systematic checks for v2 and normalization.

Three Takeaways
1. Core contribution: three-particle correlations show an off-diagonal structure in central Au+Au collisions. 2. The strongest evidence: a constant cone angle versus pT favors Mach cones over Cerenkov. 3. The future path: further systematic study of the pT dependence and flow harmonics.

summary.title: A schematic model of scattering in PT −symmetric Quantum Mechanics
summary.authors: Miloslav Znojil
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a schematic, one-dimensional scattering model within PT −symmetric quantum mechanics, which extends the conventional Schrödinger equation to a complex, PT −symmetric short-range potential V(x) = Z(x) + iY(x), where Z(−x) = Z(x) and Y(−x) = −Y(x). The central novelty resides not in the discretization itself, but in the 'complexification' of a potential-characterizing parameter, with the derivation of reflection and transmission coefficients realized through a Runge-Kutta-discretized version of the Schrödinger equation. Using a finite-difference approach, the Schrödinger operator is recast as a tridiagonal system of linear algebraic equations for potentials that vanish beyond a cutoff M, which yields a two-dimensional matrix inversion whose four corners encode all dynamical input via two functions α and β. The key analytical result is that the transmission and reflection coefficients, B and C, are expressed as rational functions of the real coupling constants (Z0, ..., ZM−1) and imaginary couplings (Y1, ..., YM−1), reducing the problem to the inversion of a (2M−1)-dimensional non-square matrix. The paper demonstrates that in both Hermitian and non-Hermitian (PT −symmetric) cases, the same form of transmission and reflection coefficients applies, with all differences captured solely by α and β, thereby encoding the 'dynamical input' information. Notably, the M=1 model is Hermitian, while PT −symmetry enters at M=2, and the computational complexity of the formulae escalates rapidly, represented by increasing product sums at M=4. The study situates itself within the broader literature of quasi-Hermitian Hamiltonians and PT −symmetry, noting a scarcity of scattering-specific work and suggesting a close formal parallelism between real-potential and complex-potential scattering treatments. Finally, the authors emphasize that the in/out state asymmetry, a distinguishing feature of PT −symmetric scattering, is merely formal and that the problem remains tractable by standard linear-algebraic techniques.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a schematic, one-dimensional scattering model within PT −symmetric quantum mechanics, which extends the conventional Schrödinger equation to a complex, PT −symmetric short-range potential V(x) = Z(x) + iY(x), where Z(−x) = Z(x) and Y(−x) = −Y(x). The central novelty resides not in the discretization itself, but in the 'complexification' of a potential-characterizing parameter, with the derivation of reflection and transmission coefficients realized through a Runge-Kutta-discretized version of the Schrödinger equation. Using a finite-difference approach, the Schrödinger operator is recast as a tridiagonal system of linear algebraic equations for potentials that vanish beyond a cutoff M, which yields a two-dimensional matrix inversion whose four corners encode all dynamical input via two functions α and β. The key analytical result is that the transmission and reflection coefficients, B and C, are expressed as rational functions of the real coupling constants (Z0, ..., ZM−1) and imaginary couplings (Y1, ..., YM−1), reducing the problem to the inversion of a (2M−1)-dimensional non-square matrix. The paper demonstrates that in both Hermitian and non-Hermitian (PT −symmetric) cases, the same form of transmission and reflection coefficients applies, with all differences captured solely by α and β, thereby encoding the 'dynamical input' information. Notably, the M=1 model is Hermitian, while PT −symmetry enters at M=2, and the computational complexity of the formulae escalates rapidly, represented by increasing product sums at M=4. The study situates itself within the broader literature of quasi-Hermitian Hamiltonians and PT −symmetry, noting a scarcity of scattering-specific work and suggesting a close formal parallelism between real-potential and complex-potential scattering treatments. Finally, the authors emphasize that the in/out state asymmetry, a distinguishing feature of PT −symmetric scattering, is merely formal and that the problem remains tractable by standard linear-algebraic techniques.

Research Context
The conventional approach to the one-dimensional quantum bound state problem uses a real potential well in the stationary Schrödinger equation. This conventional framework defines bound states at E < V(∞) ≤ +∞ and scattering states at E > V(∞) = 0 with fixed boundary conditions. Standard textbooks prescribe boundary conditions ψ(±∞) = 0 and switch to reflection and transmission coefficients B and C in the scattering regime. The quantum bound state problem has been generalized to many non-Hermitian Hamiltonians H ≠ H† that are merely quasi-Hermitian. Quasi-Hermiticity means these Hamiltonians are Hermitian only in the sense of a nontrivial metric operator Θ = Θ† > 0. The key ideas incorporate the so-called PT −symmetry of the Hamiltonians, summarized in the fresh review by Carl Bender. This new development has left the specific problem of scattering relatively unaddressed compared to bound states. Prior work covers analytically continued, singular, multidimensional, many-body, relativistic, and supersymmetric potentials.

Research Question And Hypothesis
We intend to investigate a very simple PT −symmetric scattering model where the potential takes the form V(x) = Z(x) + iY(x). The potential V(x) is assumed real-symmetric, Z(−x) = Z(x), and imaginary-antisymmetric, Y(−x) = −Y(x). The Schrödinger equation is replaced by its Runge-Kutta-discretized, difference-equation representation with lattice step h > 0. We hypothesize that the scattering coefficients can be expressed as rational functions of the real and imaginary coupling constants. We expect the form of transmission and reflection coefficients to remain the same as in the Hermitian case, differing only in the dynamical input. The key prediction is that the four corners of the inverse matrix encode all the dynamical input information via two functions α and β.

Methodological Details
The potential V(x) vanishes beyond a certain distance from the origin, V(x±j) = 0 for j = M, M+1, ... The Schrödinger equation is discretized into the finite-difference form −ψk−1 + (2 cos ϕ + Vk) ψk −ψk+1 = 0. The new energy variable ϕ is defined such that 2 cos ϕ = 2 −h2E, restricting the original energy to E ∈ (0, 4/h2). Discrete scattering boundary conditions set ψ(xm) = A ei m ϕ + B e−i m ϕ for m ≤ −(M −1) and ψ(xm) = C ei m ϕ for m ≥ M−1. The conventional choice of A = 1 is adopted to specify the reflection coefficient B and transmission coefficient C. The discretization uses a lattice step h > 0, which is taken independently from the cutoff M in order to achieve quickest convergence. The Runge-Kutta method disappears in the limit h → 0, removing the O(h4) discrepancy between difference and differential operators. Two comments note that O(h4) corrections are present and E ∈ (0, 4/h2) is reminiscent of relativistic spectra.

Procedures And Architectures
The scattering coefficients B and C are determined by the matrix-inversion of a finite-dimensional and tridiagonal non-square-matrix problem. The difference equation is written as a doubly infinite system of linear algebraic equations with Sk = 2 cos ϕ + Zk + iYk sign k for |k| < M. judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents the theory of QED⊗QCD resummation, an exact rearrangement of the perturbative series that allows simultaneous exponentiation of both QED and QCD radiative effects in a single, double-counting-free framework. Built upon the QCD resummation theory from the work of Ward and Yost (Ref [3]), which is grounded in the non-Abelian eikonal exponentiation proven by Ref [4], the QED⊗QCD theory is obtained by simultaneously exponentiating the large infrared (IR) terms in QCD and the exact IR divergent terms in QED. The resulting exact result is represented via YFS residuals that are free of all infrared singularities, making the theory suitable for contact with parton-shower Monte Carlo methods without double-counting or unnecessary averaging of effects. The authors illustrate the theory by calculating the cross-section ratios (rexp = σexp/σBorn) for single heavy gauge boson production (W and Z) at LHC and Tevatron energies. The key finding is that QED effects enter at the ~0.3% level, a magnitude that makes QED resummation necessary to achieve theoretical precision below 1.0% at the LHC, given that the required theoretical precision tag for luminosity processes is 0.67%. The paper also describes two approaches for shower/ME matching, a shower-subtracted residual approach which they claim to have implemented for the O(α) Bhabha process. However, the paper does not present a fully realized Monte Carlo implementation, stating that a Monte Carlo realization will appear elsewhere, and no quantitative comparison with HERWIG or PYTHIA is provided. The bibliography is omitted, and no quantitative data beyond the four rexp values are reported. The study is a theoretical framework paper rather than an experimental result.

Research Context
The imminent LHC environment requires an experimental luminosity precision tag at the 2% level. The required theoretical precision tag for corresponding luminosity processes should be 0.67%. Multiple gluon and photon radiative effects must be controlled to reach this precision. The prior QCD resummation theory was an exact rearrangement of the QCD perturbative series. Prior QED-only evolution of structure functions showed QED effects at the 0.3% level. The 0.3% effect is already almost half of the stated error budget. All these effects must be taken into account for a 1.0% theoretical precision tag.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how to simultaneously resum QCD and QED radiative effects without double-counting. The proposed QED⊗QCD resummation is an exact rearrangement of the full perturbative series. Hypothesis: QED⊗QCD resummation will maintain exactness to all orders in αs and α. Hypothesis: QED effects will enter at the level sufficient to impact 1.0% precision. Hypothesis: QED⊗QCD residuals will be free of all infrared singularities and usable with showers.

Methodological Details
The process studied is single heavy boson production: q + ¯q′ → V + n(g) + X → ¯ℓℓ′ + n(g) + X. The vector boson V is W ±, Z, and ℓ= e, µ, ℓ′ = νe, νµ(e, µ) for V = W +(Z). The cross section is expressed via an exact rearrangement of the QCD perturbative series. The QCD exponent is the N = 1 term in the exponent from non-Abelian eikonal exponentiation. The QED⊗QCD theory exponentiates QCD and QED terms simultaneously. The new residuals are defined as ˜¯βn,m with n hard gluons and m hard photons. The functions SUMIR(QCED) and DQCED are derived via substitutions. Structure functions used are from Ref [23], a semi-analytical approach. The Monte Carlo realization is deferred to a separate publication. The QED effect is evaluated at the 0.3% level for both LHC and Tevatron.

Procedures And Architectures
The QCD exponent SUMIR(QCD) and DQCD are defined in Ref [3]. The QED⊗QCD exponent is γQCED = (2Q^2/α_f + 2Cf/αs)Lnls. F_YFS and δ_YFS are the well-known YFS functions. Two shower/ME matching approaches are proposed: pT matching and shower-subtracted residuals. pT matching restricts the gluon emission to avoid double-counting. The shower-subtracted residuals can be used for the entire gluon pT phase space. The shower-subtracted residuals were previously realized for the O(α) Bhabha process.

Key Results
The ratio rexp = σexp/σBorn at LHC for QCED equals 1.1901. The ratio rexp at LHC for QCD alone equals 1.1872. The ratio rexp at Tevatron for QCED equals 1.1911. The ratio rexp at Tevatron for QCD alone equals 1.1879. The QED effect is at the .3% level at both LHC and FNAL. The QED effect is stable under scale variations. The QED effect is similar in size to structure function results from Refs [9–13].

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The simultaneous exponentiation removes double-counting and averaging of azimuthal distributions. The QCD dominant corrections happen an order of magnitude earlier than QED. The 0.3% QED effect is needed for predictions at ≲1% precision. The shower-subtracted residuals offer a systematic improvement over pT matching. This framework provides a firm theoretical basis for O(α^2_s, αα_s, α^2) results.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper does not present a fully realized Monte Carlo generator. The Monte Carlo implementation is deferred to another publication. No quantitative shower/ME matching results are provided for HERWIG or PYTHIA. The exactness is not explicit because there is no ordered exponential operator shown. The paper lacks a bibliography and cannot be verified via external citations.

Claims
QED⊗QCD exponentiation is an exact rearrangement of the perturbative series that allows simultaneous resummation without double-counting. The approach exponentiates large QCD IR terms and exact QED IR terms. The residuals are free of all infrared singularities. The approach is valid over the entire phase space. The exactness is not explicitly shown via an ordered exponential. A full Monte Carlo generator is not provided. The framework can be used with HERWIG and PYTHIA. QED is needed for LHC predictions at ≲1%.
QED effects are at the 0.3% level and are required for luminosity precision below 1%. QED is at the .3% level at LHC and FNAL. The 0.3% effect is needed for predictions below 1%. The required theoretical precision tag is actually 0.67%. This justifies the effort to include QED resummation.

Data And Code Availability
No code or data is made available by the authors. The Monte Carlo realization appears elsewhere, not this paper. The bibliography is omitted; citations cannot be verified.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The QED effect is stable under scale variations. The shower-subtracted residuals were tested on the Bhabha process. Scale dependence was tested, though no numbers were given.

Ethical Considerations
No ethical considerations are reported.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 presents the rexp values. Table 1 gives four values: 1.1901, 1.1872, 1.1911, 1.1879. Table 2 shows Feynman functions.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is an exact QED⊗QCD resummation theory. 2. The strongest evidence is the .3% QED effect, making QED resummation necessary. 3. The future path is the full Monte Carlo realization.

summary.executive_summary: A.M. Mathai and H.J. Haubold present a theoretical study of generalized entropy measures that reduce to Shannon entropy in the limit α → 1. The paper examines the recursivity postulate — a requirement that entropy behaves additively under product probability (PPP) — and argues that it automatically generates the logarithmic functional form of Shannon entropy. Because Shannon entropy is logarithmic, it gives rise to additivity when applied to product-probability situations. However, the authors contend that non-additivity is the natural state, relevant for statistical mechanics even when PPP holds, and that additivity is an artifact of the recursivity assumption rather than intrinsic statistical independence. They introduce a family of generalized entropies — including Rényi, Havrda-Charvát, Tsallis, and Mathai entropy — and show that they satisfy a joint decomposition Fm,n,α(P, Q) = Fm,α(P) + Fn,α(Q) + a(α)Fm,α(P)Fn,α(Q) where the interaction term a(α) vanishes only for additive cases. They also demonstrate that optimizing these entropies under moment-like constraints produces a variety of probability densities: for α < 1 they yield type-1 beta, for α > 1 type-2 beta, and for α →1 a stretched exponential form. The so-called pathway model recovers Tsallis statistics, Maxwell-Boltzmann, Gaussian, Weibull, and Wigner atomic moment distributions in special limits, with a differential equation g(x) = f(x)/c that reduces to the power law from Tsallis statistics for β = 1. In the continuous case, the authors recover the same bivariate decomposition and connect Mathai's entropy to Kerridge's directed divergence or inaccuracy measure. Notably, the work is entirely theoretical, providing no empirical data, code, or reproducibility benchmarks.

summary.title: The Return of a Static Universe and the End of Cosmology
summary.authors: Lawrence M. Krauss, Robert J. Scherrer
summary.executive_summary:
The authors, Lawrence M. Krauss and Robert J. Scherrer, present a conceptual theoretical analysis demonstrating that the ΛCDM model of the universe, when extrapolated forward in time, predicts an observational regime where all current foundations of modern cosmology—the Hubble expansion, the cosmic microwave background, and primordial element abundances—will vanish.

They argue that while present-day observations support a flat ΛCDM universe composed of approximately 30% matter and 70% dark energy, this arrangement is fundamentally unstable over cosmological timescales. In the far future, dark energy will dominate so thoroughly that the de Sitter metric with a cosmological constant Λ becomes the appropriate physical coordinate system for observers within bound gravitational systems. Specifically, the authors contend that galaxies outside the Local Group will be driven outside the de Sitter event horizon on a timescale of roughly 100 billion years, leaving a local observer with only a single, gravitationally bound merger product of the Milky Way and Andromeda. Within this horizon, dark energy density will exceed matter density by a factor of ρM/ρΛ ∼10⁻¹².

Furthermore, the cosmic microwave background radiation will redshift so much that its peak wavelength reaches approximately 1 meter, its frequency drops to about 300 MHz, and its intensity vanishes by about 12 orders of magnitude, rendering it unobservable even in principle. Simultaneously, the CMB will redshift below the plasma frequency of the interstellar medium (about 1 kHz) and be screened from observation. Because the inferred expanding nature of the universe depends on an assumption of isotropy and homogeneity that will no longer apply to future observers, general relativity provides no assistance in recovering a Big Bang conclusion. Even if future physicists could determine the finite age of their local system via stellar evolution, they cannot determine the nature of its beginning without primordial element abundances, which will be overwhelmed by stellar contamination to a helium mass fraction of roughly 0.6. The authors thus conclude that this current epoch is a unique 'cosmic coincidence' because it is the only time when both expansion and dark energy can be observationally verified. Ultimately, cosmology will effectively end and the universe will appear static to future observers.

The authors, Lawrence M. Krauss and Robert J. Scherrer, present a conceptual theoretical analysis demonstrating that the ΛCDM model of the universe, when extrapolated forward in time, predicts an observational regime where all current foundations of modern cosmology—the Hubble expansion, the cosmic microwave background, and primordial element abundances—will vanish.

In the far future, dark energy will dominate so thoroughly that the de Sitter metric with a cosmological constant Λ becomes the appropriate physical coordinate system for observers within bound gravitational systems. Specifically, the authors contend that galaxies outside the Local Group will be driven outside the de Sitter event horizon on a timescale of roughly 100 billion years, leaving a local observer with only a single, gravitationally bound merger product of the Milky Way and Andromeda. Within this horizon, dark energy density will exceed matter density by a factor of ρM/ρΛ ∼10⁻¹².

Furthermore, the cosmic microwave background radiation will redshift so much that its peak wavelength reaches approximately 1 meter, its frequency drops to about 300 MHz, and its intensity vanishes by about 12 orders of magnitude, rendering it unobservable even in principle. Simultaneously, the CMB will redshift below the plasma frequency of the interstellar medium (about 1 kHz) and be screened from observation. Because the inferred expanding nature of the universe depends on an assumption of isotropy and homogeneity that will no longer apply to future observers, general relativity provides no assistance in recovering a Big Bang conclusion. Even if future physicists could determine the finite age of their local system via stellar evolution, they cannot determine the nature of its beginning without primordial element abundances, which will be overwhelmed by stellar contamination to a helium mass fraction of roughly 0.6. The authors thus conclude that this current epoch is a unique 'cosmic coincidence' because it is the only time when both expansion and dark energy can be observationally verified. Ultimately, cosmology will effectively end and the universe will appear static to future observers.

Research Context
Modern cosmology is built on the integration of general relativity with three observational pillars that form the basis of the Big Bang model. Current ΛCDM cosmology is consistent with a flat universe composed of roughly 30% matter and 70% dark energy. The cosmological constant is currently understood to be equivalent to a vacuum energy density. A non-zero cosmological constant drives all cosmological models toward a de Sitter universe in the far future. Prior literature explored the practical significance of this asymptotic de Sitter expansion.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether far-future observers within a bound system can detect Hubble expansion or a Big Bang origin. The authors hypothesize that such observers will see a static 'island universe' with no evidence of an expanding universe or a hot Big Bang. Within the horizon, the dominant energy will be dark energy, with a matter-to-dark-energy ratio of ρM/ρΛ ∼10⁻¹². Dark energy is predicted to be undetectable even when ρΛ ≫ ρM inside the horizon. The study examines how the CMB, the element abundances, and general relativity fail to support an expanding-universe conclusion. Future observers are predicted to conclude their island has a finite future but not a finite beginning.

Methodological Details
The paper is a conceptual theoretical analysis with no participants, experiments, or data collection. The framework is rooted in general relativity, using the de Sitter metric with a cosmological constant. The authors analyze the far-future limit of the current ΛCDM universe rather than original data. The de Sitter metric takes a static form when modeled as a four-dimensional hyperboloid. The cosmological radius is defined as R2 = 3Λ−1. The coordinate transformations set the time-dependent scale factor to R(t) = exp(Ht). All models with a non-zero cosmological constant approach a de Sitter universe in the far future. The study draws on analytic and numerical calculations from existing literature rather than new simulations. No original calculations, statistical significance tests, or error bars were reported by the authors. No datasets, random seeds, or demographic information were reported. The conclusions are purely conceptual and lack quantitative uncertainty or robustness checks.

Procedures And Architectures
The universe is modeled as a four-dimensional hyperboloid embedded in five-dimensional Minkowski spacetime. The metric takes the static form ds²_s = (1 −r²_s/R²)dt²_s − dr²_s/(1 −r²_s/R²) − r²_s dΩ². The coordinate transformations set ξ0 to sinh, ξ1 to sin, ξ2 to sin, ξ3 to cos, and ξ4 to cosh. The cosmological horizon is defined at R = r_s. The metric only corresponds to de Sitter space within the cosmological horizon. The de Sitter model actually incorporated Einstein’s cosmological term. The cosmological constant Λ is understood to be equivalent to vacuum energy density. All cosmological models with a non-zero cosmological constant approach a de Sitter universe. The study extrapolates the current flat ΛCDM universe forward in time.

Key Results
The Local Group remains gravitationally bound despite accelerated Hubble expansion. More distant structures are driven outside the de Sitter event horizon in a timescale of roughly 100 billion years. Light from distant objects becomes exponentially redshifted so that they eventually become invisible. Inside the horizon, dark energy density dominates matter by a factor of ρM/ρΛ ∼10⁻¹². The Cosmic Microwave Background peak wavelength redshifts to approximately 1 meter at t ≈100 Gyr. At this epoch, the CMB frequency drops to roughly 300 MHz. The intensity of the CMB redshifts by about 12 orders of magnitude. The CMB becomes unobservable even in principle when its peak wavelength exceeds the horizon. The interstellar medium plasma frequency is about 1 kHz, screening the CMB. This expansion factor is reached when the universe is less than 50 times its present age. The present-day CMB corresponds to an expansion factor of about 108. The present-day cosmological constant density appears constant with time. The Local Group merger product will be a single galaxy.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Future observers will see a static 'island universe' with no evidence of expansion. They will infer their island has a finite future but not a finite beginning. They can determine a lower limit on the age of their system via stellar evolution. They can determine an upper limit on the age via stellar nucleosynthesis. They cannot detect primordial abundances because helium-4 will be contaminated to a mass fraction of 0.6. The 'smoking gun' deuterium abundance from Lyman-α absorption systems will be unavailable. Dark energy is undetectable both when ρΛ ≪ ρM and when ρΛ ≫ ρM. We live at the unique cosmic coincidence when dark energy and dark matter densities are comparable. At this special time, we can actually infer both the expansion and dark energy. The current epoch marks the end of cosmology and the return of a static universe. Observers more than an order of magnitude older will not know they live in an expanding universe.

Contradictions And Limitations
No experiments, simulations, or data were performed as this is a purely conceptual, theoretical paper. The results are extrapolated forward by 100 Gyr, which introduces cosmological uncertainty. No error bars, statistical significance, or uncertainties were reported by the authors. No random seed, train/test split, or demographic information were reported. The bibliography is missing, so the cited references cannot be verified. The conclusions rest on the assumed ΛCDM flat universe model. No code or data availability is reported, as this is a theoretical argument. The paper reports no figures or tables. No ethical considerations are discussed, and no human subjects were involved.

Claims
Far-future observers within a bound system will see a static 'island universe' and cannot infer a Hubble expansion or a Big Bang. The observed Hubble expansion law will be undetectable to a local observer in the far future. The Cosmic Microwave Background will redshift below the plasma frequency of the interstellar medium. Primordial element abundances will be overwhelmed by stellar nucleosynthesis. No direct counterevidence is offered as the predictions are theoretical. Executive Summary
This paper presents a theoretical investigation into the temperature and magnetic field dependence of Coulomb drag transresistivity between two parallel layers of two-dimensional electron gases (2DEGs) in the quantum Hall regime near half filling of the lowest Landau level (ν ≈ 1/2). The author utilizes the well-established Coulomb drag transresistivity formula, which relates transresistivity to the density-density polarizabilities of the layers, combined with the Composite Fermion (CF) approach and a Random Phase Approximation (RPA) treatment. The central problem addressed is explaining a striking experimental feature: that the Coulomb drag transresistivity is nearly insensitive to the interlayer spacing between the two DEGs. At the heart of the analysis, the transresistivity near ν = 1/2 is split into a ballistic contribution ρD0 (at ν = 1/2, effective magnetic field zero) and a correction δρD due to a nonzero effective magnetic field. The author derives analytical expressions for both terms and finds that the quadratic-in-Δν enhancement of drag, as well as the temperature-dependent curvature coefficient β−1, matches experimental results. To resolve the interlayer-spacing insensitivity, the author incorporates Fermi-liquid interactions among quasiparticles via a renormalized polarizability. The renormalization reduces the compressibility of the CF liquid, which increases the parameter α—the ratio of the Thomas–Fermi screening length in a single 2DEG at ν = 1/2 to the layer separation. When α > 1, intralayer interactions dominate over interlayer ones, explaining the low sensitivity to spacing. The work concludes that the reported independence of drag on interlayer separation is strong evidence for significant Fermi-liquid interactions in the CF system near ν = 1/2. The author uses experimental parameters from Lilly et al. [7] and Willett et al. [11], such as electron density n = 1.4 × 10^15 m−2 and a mean free path of 1.0 µm, to quantitatively verify the theory. The numerical results show good agreement with experimental data when the Fermi-liquid parameter A0 takes values on the order of 10 −100. A key prediction is that at larger interlayer distances, the transresistivity dependence on d could eventually be revealed.

Research Context
Coulomb drag is a phenomenon where momentum is transferred between close parallel 2DEGs via Coulomb forces. A current applied to one layer induces a measurable voltage in the nearby layer without current flow. The strength of this effect is characterized by the transresistivity ρD = −VD/I. At half filling of the lowest Landau level, transresistivity is predicted proportional to T^4/3. This is qualitatively different from the temperature dependence in the absence of a magnetic field. Experimental measurements near ν = 1/2 found transresistivity enhanced quadratically with the filling factor deviation ∆ν = ν − 1/2. However, experimental results appeared insensitive to both the sign of ∆ν and the interlayer distance d. The prior theory could not fully explain this distance insensitivity, motivating the present work.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is what mechanism explains the interlayer-spacing insensitivity of Coulomb drag near ν = 1/2. The study investigates temperature and magnetic field dependences of transresistivity near half filling. The hypothesis is that Fermi-liquid interactions among quasiparticles (CFs) could explain the phenomenon. Specifically, Fermi-liquid renormalization is predicted to reduce the compressibility of the CF liquid and increase the parameter α. The predicted outcome is that when α > 1, intralayer interactions dominate interlayer ones. The author expects the derived expressions to quantitatively match the experimental curvature and magnetic field dependence. The author predicts the dependence on d remains hidden at small spacings but could emerge at larger distances.

Methodological Details
The paper is a purely theoretical study with no experimental participants or instruments. It treats two identical layers with equal electron densities (n1 = n2 = n). The transresistivity is calculated near ν ≈ 1/2 of the lowest Landau level for both layers. The Composite Fermion (CF) approach provides the single-layer polarizability. A Random Phase Approximation (RPA) is adopted for the response function matrix. The bare intralayer and interlayer Coulomb potentials are Fourier components Vb(q) = 2πe2/ǫq and Ub(q) = (2πe2/ǫq)e−qd. The scaling temperature T0 is a material-dependent characteristic defined in the analysis. Experimental values adopted include an electron density n = 1.4 × 10^15 m−2 from [7]. A mean free path of the order of 1.0 µm is taken from the experiments of [11]. The parameter T0 is estimated from the Coulomb interactions of the layers and the compressibility of the ν = 1/2 state.

Procedures And Architectures
The author starts from the general formula for transresistivity in terms of layer polarizabilities. The 2 × 2 response function matrix Π−1 = (K0)−1 + C−1 couples CF response and Chern-Simons interaction. The CF conductivity components are calculated from a Boltzmann transport equation solution for the distribution function. A smooth passage to the Beff → 0 limit at finite q is required; previous results are not appropriate. Asymptotic expressions are derived in the nonlocal (ql ≫ 1) and high-frequency (ωτ ≫ 1) regimes. The variable δ = ω/qvF and the small parameter (qR)−1 drive the expansions for the conductivity. The leading term in transresistivity is ρD0, plus a correction δρD away from ν = 1/2. Fermi-liquid corrections are added to the polarizability via terms F(0) and F(1) in the Fermi-liquid expansion. The effective mass renormalization is included via 1/mb = 1/(m∗+ f1/(2π¯h^2)) = 1 + A1/m∗.

Key Results
The zeroth-order transresistivity ρD0 follows the established T^4/3 law. The leading-order magnetic-field correction is roughly 4/3 ρD0 times Δν, giving a quadratic-in-Δν enhancement. The correction includes a linear-in-Δν term, which creates an asymmetric plot shape. At low temperatures, the second term (T/T0)^(2/3) predominates over the linear term. The magnetic-field dependence of the transresistivity near ν = 1/2 matches experimental observations. The scaled drag plot at T = 0.6 agrees with the experimental data of [7]. For two interlayer distances d = 10 nm and d = 22.5 nm, the T0 values are 487 K and 587 K respectively. With RPA only, the compressibility estimates yield α ≈ 0.44, failing to explain distance insensitivity. Fermi-liquid renormalization requires α > 1 to explain the distance insensitivity. The theoretical agreement holds when A0 takes values of the order of 10 −100.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The parameter α measures the ratio of the single-layer Thomas–Fermi screening length to the layer separation. When α > 1, intralayer interactions screen so well that interlayer ones are suppressed. The observed distance insensitivity of the experiments is an indirect signature of strong Fermi-liquid interactions. The reduction in compressibility enhances the single-layer screening length in the CF liquid. Larger layer separations may eventually reveal the interlayer dependence of the transresistivity.

Contradictions And Limitations
Within RPA, the CF effective mass equals the single-electron band mass, underestimating the compressibility. The α ≈ 0.44 value is too small to explain distance insensitivity without Fermi-liquid interactions. The expression for a2 cannot be used as T → 0, requiring the condition (T kF l/µ)^(1/3) ≥ 1.5. The assumption of a mean free path of 1.0 µm is needed to justify a2 for low temperatures. Fermi-liquid parameters A0 and A1 are assumed to be in the range of 10 to 100 for reasonable agreement. Only two terms of the Fermi-liquid expansion are kept, which may limit the precision of the approximation.

Claims
Coulomb drag near ν = 1/2 is dominated by a ballistic transresistivity component, giving the T^4/3 temperature dependence and a quadratic-in-Δν field dependence. The zeroth-order transresistivity is predicted to scale as T^(4/3) via the γ(7/3)ζ(4/3) factor. The magnetic-field-induced correction enhances the drag nearly quadratically with Δν. The magnetic-field dependence near ν = 1/2 matches the observed experimental curvature. The linear-in-Δν term would technically cause asymmetry, though it is smaller than the second term. This confirms the ballistic nature of Coulomb drag at the lowest Landau level.
The experimental distance insensitivity of Coulomb drag near ν = 1/2 is explained by strong Fermi-liquid interactions reducing the CF compressibility. The RPA-only analysis yields α ≈ 0.44, which fails to explain the insensitivity. Renormalization yields α > 1 when the Fermi-liquid parameter A0 is on the order of 10 −100. When α > 1, intralayer interactions dominate, screening out interlayer forces. The distance-independent conclusion relies on the assumed magnitude of Fermi-liquid parameters. The experimental results serve as evidence of strong Fermi-liquid interactions in the CF system. Larger distances may eventually uncover the spacing dependence.

Data And Code Availability
The study is purely theoretical; no data or code is reported for release.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Fermi-liquid corrections are compared to the noninteracting case, justifying the renormalization requirement. The T → 0 limit is excluded by a validity criterion on the mean free path and the temperature. Different effective masses m∗ are considered, such as m∗ = 4mb for the best fit.

Ethical Considerations
This is a theoretical physics paper; no human participants or ethical approval is applicable.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows scaled drag resistivity versus ∆ν at T = 0.6, with an overlaid experimental curve. Figure 2 shows temperature dependence of β−1 for two layer spacings d = 10 nm and d = 22.5 nm. The experimental curvature of β−1 is summarized in the same panel as a comparison.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a theoretical explanation for the interlayer-spacing insensitivity of Coulomb drag near ν = 1/2 via Fermi-liquid renormalization. 2. The strongest evidence is the quantitative agreement between the derived transresistivity expressions and the experimental data from Lilly et al. [7]. 3. The future path is to probe larger interlayer distances where the transresistivity's dependence on spacing might finally emerge.

summary.executive_summary: This paper by Theo M. Nieuwenhuizen, an epl draft titled "Einstein vs Maxwell: Is gravitation a curvature of space, a field in flat space, or both?", investigates whether gravitation should be viewed as a curvature of space (Einstein's view) or a field in flat space (Maxwell's view), or both. The author argues that the two perspectives are complementary, describing the same physics from different angles. Starting from a field-theoretic approach in Minkowski space, the paper derives the gravitational energy-momentum tensor from the Einstein equations, expressing it as the acceleration tensor proportional to the total energy-momentum tensor. For flat-space cosmology, this tensor indicates that gravitational energy is negative and cancels the material energy, implying a zero-overall-energy universe. The author then introduces the relativistic theory of gravitation (RTG), a bimetric theory based on Rosen's ideas, where general coordinate invariance is broken by a bimetric coupling between the Riemann and Minkowski metrics. A positive cosmological constant is considered, which leads to a 'tachyon' graviton and unstable gravitational waves at the Hubble scale. A singularity-free version of the Schwarzschild black hole is solved analytically in harmonic coordinates. Inside the horizon, the metric functions decay rapidly but remain positive, so time retains its standard role and escape is, in principle, possible. The theory also covers the ΛCDM cosmological model, reproducing its best-fit observations and allowing for a positive curvature-type contribution from the ρ2 term. The author argues that because the field-theoretic and curved-space descriptions are equivalent, both views apply; however, the RTG extension's bimetrism favors a Maxwellian view (gravitation as a field in flat space) as the more natural description for the extended theory. The conclusion is that both views apply equally to the underlying physics, but RTG frames the description differently. No experimental data or code is provided; the work is purely analytical and conceptual, and the supplied text includes no bibliography.

summary.title: Differential recursion and differentially algebraic functions
summary.authors: Akitoshi Kawamura
summary.executive_summary:
Moore introduced a class of real-valued 'recursive' functions by analogy with Kleene's formulation of the standard recursive functions. While his concise definition inspired a new line of research on analog computation, it contains some technical inaccuracies. Focusing on Moore's 'primitive recursive' functions, the author pins down what is problematic and discusses possible attempts to remove the ambiguity regarding the behavior of the differential recursion operator on partial functions. It turns out that in any case the purported relation to differentially algebraic functions, and hence to Shannon's model of analog computation, fails.

The paper contextualizes these recursive functions within three theoretical models of real function computability: Computable Analysis, which uses approximation to bring real numbers into the framework of the standard computability theory; the Blum-Shub-Smale model, in which continuous quantities are treated as entities but the machine still works with discrete clock ticks; and analog computation, in which data are real-valued and the transition takes place in continuous time. One of the oldest models is Shannon's General Purpose Analog Computer (GPAC), which models the Differential Analyzer and, after refinements, was shown capable of generating all and only the differentially algebraic functions. Little is known about how such analog models relate to the standard digital computability.

Moore addressed this question for his new function classes that also try to express the power of GPAC-like computation, defining the classes as closures under operators that are supposed to be real-number versions of primitive recursion and minimization. Moore made claims relating real primitive recursive functions to differentially algebraic functions and real recursive functions to digital computation on integers. The author argues that Moore's work lacked formality and that the definition of the classes suffers from ambiguity. The paper reformulates Moore's theory up to the real primitive recursive functions in a mathematically sound way, and shows that even the most restrictive formulation of the class fails to support Claim 1. The author also discusses issues about classes other than the real primitive recursive functions, including Claim 2.
