judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper investigates two ways to embed KF-type Lorentz-symmetry violating electrodynamics into an N=1-supersymmetric framework. The authors work from the motivating perspective that Lorentz-symmetry and CPT invariance may be spontaneously broken in string theories via the vacuum condensation of a tensor field, and that this breaking should not be dissociable from supersymmetry even if SUSY breaking occurs earlier. In the Standard Model Extension (SME), Lorentz-violation is parametrized by backgrounds; for the fermion sector, two CPT-odd terms v\mu\psi\gamma^\mu\psi and b\mu\psi\gamma^5\gamma^\mu\psi are defined. The authors note that the breaking of Lorentz-symmetry signals the violation of supersymmetry, although the order of the two breakings is undecided. 

The study proceeds by considering the K\mu\nu\kappa\lambda tensor which has the symmetries K\mu\nu\kappa\lambda = K\mu\nu\kappa\lambda, K\mu\nu\kappa\lambda = K\kappa\lambda\mu\nu, K\mu\nu\mu\nu = 0, and is reducible via the ansatz K\mu\nu\kappa\lambda = 1/2(\eta\mu\kappa\sim\kappa\nu\lambda - \eta\mu\lambda\sim\kappa\nu\kappa + \eta\nu\lambda\sim\kappa\mu\kappa - \eta\nu\kappa\sim\kappa\mu\lambda) with \tilde{\kappa}\mu\nu = \kappa(\xi\mu\xi\nu - \eta\mu\nu\xi\alpha\xi\alpha/4) and \kappa = 4/3\tilde{\kappa}\mu\nu\xi\mu\xi\nu. The authors argue that supersymmetrizing the quadratic bosonic action S = -1/4\int d^4x K\mu\nu\kappa\lambda F^\mu\nu F^\kappa\lambda yields the K-type model. Instead of higher-spin components, there are two routes: first, using K\mu\nu\kappa\lambda given by the ansatz without the specific expression for \tilde{\kappa}\mu\nu, the background superfield must be chiral, carrying the chiral supermultiplet \Omega with a complex scalar S and a spin-1/2 SUSY partner. Second, using the vector superfield \Xi with full \theta-expansion, which reproduces the K-tensor. 

The chiral approach imposes the constraint \xi\mu = \partial\mu S, yielding a special form for K\mu\nu\kappa\lambda fixed by a complex scalar field. The vector approach reproduces the model exactly with K\mu\nu\kappa\lambda defined by the ansatz. The authors note that in both cases SUSY is broken by the background, and in the chiral case D is fixed to be non-trivial even without coupling to matter. They also mention that charged scalar particles may acquire a magnetic dipole moment and point out future work on whether background fermionic condensates could influence the spectrum and whether Lorentz-breaking might produce non-physical excitations like tachyons and ghosts. They also suggest the possibility of a contemporary breaking of SUSY and Lorentz-symmetry where a tensor field coupled to the superfield responsible for SUSY breaking acquires a non-trivial vacuum expectation value when SUSY spontaneously breaks, a direction they state they shall report elsewhere.

Research Context
The Standard Model Extension (SME) is the natural framework to study Lorentz-violation properties. Lorentz-symmetry and CPT invariance may be spontaneously broken in some string theories. CPT-violating neutrino mass-squared difference could be an order of magnitude less than the CPT bound on quarks and leptons. Lorentz-symmetry breaking may be triggered by the vacuum condensation of a given tensor field. Supersymmetry partners are present and SUSY imprints are not lost even if SUSY was already broken. Lorentz-symmetry violation cannot be dissociated from supersymmetry even when both are broken. Katz and Shadmi discuss vacuum expectation values as a possible way to realize SUSY breaking by F- and D-terms in the MSSM. The gauge sector has proposed a supersymmetric minimal extension for the Chern-Simons-like term. The CPT-even part is represented by the tensor K\mu\nu\kappa\lambda with the same symmetries as the Riemann tensor. The authors state they do not have elements to decide whether SUSY breaking occurs before Lorentz-symmetry violation.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether KF-type Lorentz-symmetry violation can be accommodated in an N=1 supersymmetric framework. The authors hypothesize that Lorentz-symmetry breaking cannot be dissociated from supersymmetry because it may originate at a more fundamental level. They predict that Lorentz-symmetry violation signals the violation of supersymmetry even if the order of the breakings is undecided. The authors predict that supersymmetrizing the quadratic action K\mu\nu\kappa\lambda\times F\mu\nu\times F^\kappa\lambda yields the KF-type model. Two routes for supersymmetrization are hypothesized: one using a chiral superfield and one using a vector superfield. In the chiral route, the background superfield must be chiral, carrying a spin-1/2 component-field. In the vector route, a vector superfield is used to accommodate the background vector \xi\lambda. The vector superfield approach is predicted to reproduce the model exactly and the chiral approach to impose the constraint \xi\mu = \partial\mu S. They hypothesize that in either case SUSY is broken by the background and the breaking of Lorentz-symmetry does not support exact SUSY.

Methodological Details
The authors study two venues to embed KF-type Lorentz-symmetry breaking in N=1 supersymmetry. The background signals Lorentz-symmetry breaking and the K-tensor is expressed in terms of the background superfield. The fermionic partners of the background that determine K\mu\nu\kappa\lambda are presented in detail. The K-tensor is CPT-even, meaning it does not violate CPT-symmetry. The authors assume a chiral supermultiplet \Omega as the source of the K-tensor in the first proposal. This imposes the constraint \xi\mu = \partial\mu S where S is a complex scalar. The chiral superfield is a spin-1/2 component-field partnering a spinless dimensionless scalar field. The authors use a minimal extension of the quadratic action S = \kappa\int d^4x d^2\theta d^2\bar{\theta} (D\alpha\Omega)W\alpha(D\dot{\alpha}\Omega)W\dot{\alpha} + h.c. The vector supermultiplet W\alpha is the superfield strength of the gauge supermultiplet in the Wess-Zumino gauge. The vector superfield \Xi is used in the second proposal and its full \theta-expansion is taken. A Wess-Zumino gauge cannot be taken for \Xi as it is a fixed background and not a gauge super-potential. No random seed or train/test split is reported; the work is a theoretical superspace formulation.

Procedures And Architectures
The authors adopt a covariant superspace-superfield formulation to implement the Lorentz-symmetry-violating actions. The supersymmetric extension of the K-type model is pursued in two ways. In the chiral approach, a chiral supermultiplet Ω provides the background. The vector superfield approach uses a real vector supermultiplet. The covariant derivatives Da = \partial\partial\theta_a + i\sigma^\mu_a\dot{a}\bar{\theta}_\dot{a}\partial_\mu and D\dot{a} = -\partial\partial\bar{\theta}_\dot{a} - i\theta_a\sigma^\mu_a\dot{a}\partial_\mu are used. The superfield strength Wa is expanded in terms of the gauge superfield components. The SUSY-covariant derivatives act on the gauge superfields to produce the component-wise action. The vector supermultiplet is expanded as \Xi = C + \theta\chi + \bar{\theta}\bar{\chi} + \theta^2M + \bar{\theta}^2M^* + \theta\sigma^\mu\bar{\theta}\xi^\mu + \theta^2\bar{\theta}\bar{\psi} + \bar{\theta}^2\theta\psi + \theta^2\bar{\theta}^2B. The component-wise action is obtained by integrating out the superfields and using the chiral-superfield expansion. The auxiliary field D is fixed to be non-trivial even when the gauge potential superfield V is not coupled to matter. Charged scalar particles may acquire a magnetic dipole moment given in terms of v = \nabla S.\times\nabla S^*. The vector-superfield approach uses the full \theta-expansion and does not exploit a second way of working out the supersymmetrisation.

Key Results
The chiral approach gives a special form for the K-tensor fixed by a complex scalar field. In the chiral case, the K-tensor depends exclusively on the scalar component S. No \zeta-condensate and no G-dependence appear in the K-tensor in the chiral case. The K-tensor depends exclusively on the gradient of S. A constant \partial\mu S ensures the constancy of the K-tensor. The auxiliary field D is given by D = -8\kappa i\partial\mu S\partial\nu S^* F^\mu\nu / 16 + 32\kappa\partial\mu S\partial\mu S^*. The vector-superfield approach reproduces the K-tensor defined by the ansatz. In the vector case, the K-tensor depends on \xi^\lambda\neq 0 and gives a richer background. The vector approach includes richer background and fermion condensates that mix \chi and \Psi. The chiral approach does not couple charged scalar particles to the gauge field, whereas the vector approach does. The authors do not provide numerical data, as this is a theoretical work. In both cases, Lorentz-symmetry violation does not support exact supersymmetry.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The authors state that the K-tensor is CPT-even and its non-zero vacuum expectation value breaks Lorentz-symmetry. The fact that K\mu\nu\kappa\lambda is CPT-even shows that CPT-violation implies Lorentz-invariance violation but the reverse is not necessarily true. The K-tensor symmetries are inherited from the Riemann tensor and the ansätze are derived from irreducible representations of SO(1,3). The chiral approach gives the K-tensor fixed by a complex scalar field. In both cases, SUSY is broken by the background, indicating that Lorentz-symmetry breaking is not compatible with exact SUSY. The chiral approach may raise questions about the photon-photino mass splitting when the fermionic condensate is non-vanishing. The background fermionic condensates may clarify the role of the background when propagator poles are identified. The question of non-physical excitations like tachyons and ghosts should be investigated to set restrictions on the background. The authors could construct a model such that SUSY spontaneous breaking leads simultaneously to Lorentz-symmetry spontaneous breakdown.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors state they do not have elements to decide whether SUSY breaking occurs before Lorentz-symmetry violation. The authors admit that their models do not commit to any specific SUSY-breaking mechanism. The second vector-superfield route is formulated but not exploited. The order of SUSY and Lorentz-symmetry breakings is undecided, and the authors acknowledge they treat the latter. The paper does not contain numerical results, as it is a theoretical work. No bibliography is provided in the text, making influential citations untraceable. The analysis of non-physical excitations like tachyons and ghosts is deferred to future work. The authors note that their backgrounds are not invariant under SUSY, and they do not state they break both simultaneously.

Claims
Lorentz-symmetry and CPT invariance may be spontaneously broken at the Planck scale via tensor field vacuum condensation in some string theories. This motivates the consideration of supersymmetry because SUSY imprints are not lost even if SUSY was broken. Lorentz-symmetry breaking may be triggered by the vacuum condensation of a given tensor field. The order of the two breakings is undecided, and there is no commitment to a specific SUSY-breaking mechanism. The authors propose to build a model that couples a tensor field to the SUSY-breaking superfield.
The KF-type K-tensor can be accommodated in N=1 supersymmetry using either a chiral supermultiplet or a vector supermultiplet as the background. The chiral approach gives the K-tensor fixed by a complex scalar field. The vector approach reproduces the model exactly with the K-tensor defined by the ansatz. In either case, Lorentz-symmetry breaking does not support exact supersymmetry. The second vector-superfield route is formulated but not exploited in this paper. Future work could include propagator poles and whether background fermionic condensates clarify the role of the background.

Data And Code Availability
The work is purely theoretical and reports no data, code, or random seed.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The vector superfield approach uses the full theta-expansion and does not exploit a Wess-Zumino gauge. The second vector-superfield route is formulated but not exploited in this paper.

Ethical Considerations
The paper contains no ethical considerations or IRB approval as it is a theoretical work.

Key Figures Tables
The paper contains equations (1) to (30) but no figures or tables are reported.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: Two ways to embed KF-type Lorentz-symmetry breaking in N=1 supersymmetry using either a chiral or a vector superfield. 2. The strongest evidence: A constant grad(S) in the chiral case fixes the K-tensor and a constant xi^\lambda in the vector case reproduces the ansatz. 3. The future path: Identifying whether non-physical excitations arise and whether SUSY and Lorentz-symmetry can break simultaneously.

summary.title: B-Mode auto-bispectrum due to matter bounce
summary.authors: Rahul Kothari and Debottam Nandi
summary.executive_summary: The paper investigates the CMB B-mode auto-bispectrum arising from the matter bounce Universe, a bouncing cosmology alternative to inflation. B-modes are generated only by tensor perturbations (gravity waves). The authors derive an analytical expression for the matter bounce B-mode auto-bispectrum, numerically evaluate it, and compare it to the standard slow-roll inflationary bispectrum. They find that while the power spectrum is identical in both paradigms, the perturbations freeze outside the horizon in inflation but grow during matter bounce, leading to distinct higher-order correlation function behaviors. For tensor-to-scalar ratio r = 0.01, the inflation bispectrum peaks at ~6 × 10^-11 at multipoles (2, 15, 16), while the matter bounce bispectrum peaks at ~5 × 10^-23 at the same point, making the bounce signal approximately 10^-12 times smaller than inflation. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for r = 0.01 and l_max = 100 is ~10^-5 for inflation and ~10^-18 for matter bounce, which is ~10^-13 times smaller. The authors also develop numerical techniques including a Rasch algorithm, a binary search method for n-tuple storage, and the use of fgsl and wigxjpf software to handle Wigner 3j and 9j symbols, reducing computation to 1/6 due to symmetries.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The paper investigates the CMB B-mode auto-bispectrum arising from the matter bounce Universe, a bouncing cosmology alternative to inflation. B-modes are generated only by tensor perturbations (gravity waves). The authors derive an analytical expression for the matter bounce B-mode auto-bispectrum, numerically evaluate it, and compare it to the standard slow-roll inflationary bispectrum. They find that while the power spectrum is identical in both paradigms, the perturbations freeze outside the horizon in inflation but grow during matter bounce, leading to distinct higher-order correlation function behaviors. For tensor-to-scalar ratio r = 0.01, the inflation bispectrum peaks at ~6 × 10^-11 at multipoles (2, 15, 16), while the matter bounce bispectrum peaks at ~5 × 10^-23 at the same point, making the bounce signal approximately 10^-12 times smaller than inflation. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for r = 0.01 and l_max = 100 is ~10^-5 for inflation and ~10^-18 for matter bounce, which is ~10^-13 times smaller. The authors also develop numerical techniques including a Rasch algorithm, a binary search method for n-tuple storage, and the use of fgsl and wigxjpf software to handle Wigner 3j and 9j symbols, reducing computation to 1/6 due to symmetries.

Research Context
CMB radiation is a relic of the early Universe, and primordial fluctuations leave imprints. The CMB is generally assumed to be statistically isotropic and gaussian. All statistical information is contained in two-point correlations due to Wick's Theorem. Inflation is the remarkable inflationary paradigm of the standard model of cosmology. Inflation solves the horizon and flatness problems via nearly scale-invariant spectra. Bouncing cosmologies represent the universe contracting to a minimum then expanding. Matter bounce produces scale-invariant power spectra and varies as eta squared. Using only the power spectrum, it is difficult to distinguish inflation from matter bounce.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study asks whether the B-mode auto-bispectrum can distinguish matter bounce from slow-roll inflation. The hypothesis is that perturbations grow outside the horizon in matter bounce unlike inflation. This difference is encoded in the higher order correlation functions. Only higher order Galileons can boost tensor bispectra in generalized slow-roll inflation. The B-mode auto-bispectrum is predicted to be smaller for matter bounce than for inflation. The B-mode auto-bispectrum is predicted to be undetectable in future experiments.

Methodological Details
The B-mode auto-bispectrum is defined in terms of the three point correlations of harmonic coefficients. The CMB field is characterized via Stokes' parameters I, Q, and U. I represents temperature while Q and U represent linear polarization. Q and U are described in terms of spin 2 spherical harmonics. The transfer functions were obtained from the CAMB1 software. The analysis used Planck 2018 cosmological parameters. Only permutations where the sum of multipoles is odd give a nonzero bispectrum. The bispectrum is nonzero only when all multipoles l1, l2, l3 are different. The study calculated the bispectrum for ∑li = 33. This implies 114 possibilities for the triple of multipoles. Symmetry reduces the computation to 1/6. Numerical integration used the trapezoidal and rectangular methods.

Procedures And Architectures
The bispectrum expression contains Wigner 3j symbols which are summed over angular integrations. The procedure required four integrations over one x and three ki variables. Separable forms are evaluated as a single integral. Inseparable forms are integrated via Laplace's transform with variable y. Integrals were stored in an array; retrieval used a binary search method for tuples. Two theorems ensure the certainty of the binary search. Wigner symbols were computed with the Rasch Algorithm. The Rasch method employs 36 out of 72 symmetries. fgsl was used for Wigner symbols, but it gives segmentation faults at large l. wigxjpf was used for larger values of l. wigxjpf calculates symbols using prime number factorization. The flowchart summarizes the numerical algorithm in Figure 2.

Key Results
For inflation with r = 0.01, the bispectrum peaks at (2, 15, 16) with value ~6 × 10^-11. For matter bounce with r = 0.01, the bispectrum peaks at (2, 15, 16) with value ~5 × 10^-23. The matter bounce bispectrum is ~10^-12 times smaller than the inflation bispectrum. For inflation r = 0.01 and l_max = 100, SNR is ~10^-5. For matter bounce r = 0.01 and l_max = 100, SNR is ~10^-18. The matter bounce SNR is ~10^-13 times smaller than inflation. The shape functions exhibit stark differences across squeezed, folded, and equilateral limits. The shape function for inflation peaks at a higher normalized value. The power spectrum is the same for inflation and matter bounce.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The bispectrum distinguishes the two paradigms even when the power spectrum cannot. The growing perturbations outside the horizon in matter bounce drive the difference. Higher order Galileons are required to boost tensor bispectra in generalized slow-roll inflation. The small signal-to-noise ratio implies matter bounce is difficult to detect with future experiments. The numerical techniques developed can be applied in contexts beyond bispectrum calculation. The Rasch algorithm can be coupled with wigxjpf to improve computation speed.

Contradictions And Limitations
The fgsl software gives segmentation faults at larger values of l, necessitating wigxjpf. The analytical form is an approximation valid only in a specific regime. The exact coefficient C ~10^-26 is given only via Eq. (B9) and not explicitly stated. The full bibliography is not provided in the paper. The source code for Rasch algorithm is on GitHub, but other code links vary.

Claims
The matter bounce B-mode auto-bispectrum can distinguish it from slow-roll inflation via higher-order correlations. The bispectrum peaks are different for inflation and bounce at (2, 15, 16). The matter bounce bispectrum value is ~5 × 10^-23. The shape functions exhibit stark differences. The power spectrum is identical between the two paradigms. Only higher-order non-gaussianities break the degeneracy between models. The degeneracy cannot be broken by power spectrum measurements.
The matter bounce signal is practically undetectable in future CMB experiments. The bounce SNR is ~10^-18 for r = 0.01 and l_max = 100. The bounce signal is ~10^-13 times smaller than the inflation signal. The inflation SNR is ~10^-5. No actual experimental exclusion of matter bounce is claimed. Future experiments will not be able to detect the matter bounce signal. This may necessitate much longer or more sensitive future experiments.

Data And Code Availability
The Rasch algorithm source code is on GitHub. Rasch algorithm is on https://github.com/ramanujakothari/RaschAlgo. Source code links are referenced but not all are active or described.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The binary search method certainty is ensured by two theorems. Numerical convergence was checked via trapezoidal and rectangular integration. The exact Wigner 3j computation used 36 out of 72 symmetries.

Ethical Considerations
No ethical considerations or human subjects are discussed.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the matter bounce and inflation B-mode power spectra. Figure 2 is a flowchart of the bispectrum numerical algorithm. Figure 3 shows SNR as a function of l_max for different r. Figure 4 compares the bispectra for inflation and bounce. Figure 5 compares normalized shape functions.

Three Takeaways
1. The matter bounce B-mode auto-bispectrum differs from inflation's at higher-order correlations. 2. The matter bounce signal is orders of magnitude smaller and practically undetectable. 3. The numerical algorithm reduces bispectrum computation to 1/6 using Rasch and symmetries.

summary.title: Comparative Performance Analysis of Image De-noising Techniques
summary.authors: Vivek Kumar, Pranay Yadav, Atul Samadhiya, Sandeep Jain, and Prayag Tiwari
summary.type_of_paper: Survey and comparative study / technical report
summary.executive_summary: This paper provides a comprehensive survey and comparative analysis of image denoising techniques. The authors argue that noise is a critical degradation factor that reduces image quality and appearance, and therefore denoising must remove noise while preserving textural information and structural features. The objective of the paper is to present a brief account of types of noises, their classification, and various noise removal algorithms. In the first section, noises are categorized into additive and multiplicative natures. The second section presents a precise classification and analysis of different potential image denoising algorithms. The paper concludes with a comparative study of all these algorithms in the context of performance evaluation, followed by several promising directions for future research. The authors emphasize that selecting the appropriate denoising algorithm is application-dependent and requires knowledge of the specific noise present in the image. The work spans types of noise from Gaussian, salt and pepper, speckle, to Brownian, and classifies denoising methods into spatial filtering (linear and nonlinear) and transform domain filtering (spatial-frequency and wavelet domain). Within the wavelet domain, further distinctions are made between linear, non-linear coefficient thresholding, non-orthogonal wavelet transforms, and wavelet coefficient modeling. The paper uses the Lena gray-scale image at 90% noise density to evaluate the algorithms using PSNR and IEF metrics, reporting PSNR values ranging from 6.5759 to 17.9865 and IEF values from 1.1712 to 16.2066. The comparative results support the MDBUTMF filter as a strong performer, and the conclusion highlights future research paths. The overall work serves as a foundational survey for practitioners and researchers in the field of image restoration, establishing a grounded reference for noise classification and algorithm comparison.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper provides a comprehensive survey and comparative analysis of image denoising techniques. The authors argue that noise is a critical degradation factor that reduces image quality and appearance, and therefore denoising must remove noise while preserving textural information and structural features. The objective of the paper is to present a brief account of types of noises, their classification, and various noise removal algorithms. In the first section, noises are categorized into additive and multiplicative natures. The second section presents a precise classification and analysis of different potential image denoising algorithms. The paper concludes with a comparative study of all these algorithms in the context of performance evaluation, followed by several promising directions for future research. The authors emphasize that selecting the appropriate denoising algorithm is application-dependent and requires knowledge of the specific noise present in the image. The work spans types of noise from Gaussian, salt and pepper, speckle, to Brownian, and classifies denoising methods into spatial filtering (linear and nonlinear) and transform domain filtering (spatial-frequency and wavelet domain). Within the wavelet domain, further distinctions are made between linear, non-linear coefficient thresholding, non-orthogonal wavelet transforms, and wavelet coefficient modeling. The paper uses the Lena gray-scale image at 90% noise density to evaluate the algorithms using PSNR and IEF metrics, reporting PSNR values ranging from 6.5759 to 17.9865 and IEF values from 1.1712 to 16.2066. The comparative results support the MDBUTMF filter as a strong performer, and the conclusion highlights future research paths. The overall work serves as a foundational survey for practitioners and researchers in the field of image restoration, establishing a grounded reference for noise classification and algorithm comparison.

Research Context
Image restoration is a very large portion of digital image processing. Image restoration is defined as the removal or reduction of degradations occurring during image acquisition. Degradations stem from blurring and noise due to electronic and photometric sources. Blurring is caused by imperfect image formation, including relative camera motion and out-of-focus optical systems. Aerial photographs are degraded by atmospheric turbulence and relative motion between camera and ground. Images are also corrupted by noise introduced during transmission, measurement, and quantization for storage. Every element in the imaging chain, such as lenses, film, and digitizers, contributes to degradation. Image denoising is applied in photography, astronomy, medical imaging, and forensic science. Denoising is necessary because the optimal algorithm depends on the specific noise present in the image. Prior works establish that noise must be removed while preserving textural information and structural features.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central objective is to account for types of noises, their classification, and noise removal algorithms. The paper hypothesizes that denoising algorithms can be classified into two basic approaches: spatial filtering and transform domain filtering. It is predicted that the appropriate denoising algorithm depends on the noise type and the specific application. The authors hypothesize that wavelet domain techniques outperform spatial filtering in noisy contexts. A specific prediction is that MDBUTMF will outperform traditional filters in PSNR and IEF at 90% noise density.

Methodological Details
The paper is a survey and comparative study, not a primary experiment with a novel sample. No original dataset or participants are recruited; existing denoising algorithms are reviewed. Digital images are represented as 2-dimensional arrays s(x, y). Binary images store only two values: black at 0 and white at 1. Gray-scale images contain no color and up to 256 brightness levels. Color images are three band RGB images with 24 bits/pixel. Noise is classified into additive and multiplicative natures. Gaussian noise has a bell-shaped probability distribution. Salt and pepper noise is an impulse type of noise with two values, pepper at 0 and salt at 255. Speckle noise is multiplicative and follows a gamma distribution. Brownian noise falls under fractal or 1/f noise and is obtained by integrating white noise. The evaluation uses the gray-scale image of Lena. The noise density is set at 90%. Performance is measured by PSNR and IEF, with MSE standing for mean square error.

Procedures And Architectures
The classification branches into spatial filtering and transform domain filtering. Spatial filtering includes linear and non-linear filters, removing noise via low-pass filtering on pixel groups. Non-linear median types include weighted median, rank conditioned rank selection, and relaxed median. Linear filters include the mean filter and the Wiener filter, which optimal for Gaussian noise in MSE. The Wiener filter requires spectra information of noise and signal and works only if the signal is smooth. Transform domain filtering is subdivided by data-adaptive and non-adaptive functions. Spatial-frequency filtering uses FFT with frequency smoothing and cut-off frequency adaptation. Wavelet domain filtering uses linear filters like Wiener and non-linear coefficient thresholding. Wavelet-domain spatially adaptive FIR Wiener filtering filters only within each scale. Non-linear coefficient thresholding exploits the fact that wavelet transform maps white noise to white noise. Hard thresholding removes small coefficients, while soft thresholding shrinks coefficients above the threshold. Non-adaptive thresholds include VISU Shrink, depending only on number of data points. Adaptive thresholds include SURE Shrink, Bayes Shrink, and Cross Validation. Non-orthogonal wavelet transforms like UDWT are shift invariant and avoid pseudo-Gibbs artifacts. Multiwavelets combine shift invariance and multiple scaling functions for higher order vanishing moments. Wavelet coefficient modeling is deterministic, creating a tree structure of wavelet coefficients. Statistical modeling focuses on multi-scale and local correlation between neighborhood coefficients. The comparative study applies these filters to the Lena image at 90% noise.

Key Results
The comparison applies several denoising filters to the gray-scale Lena image at 90% noise density. The PSNR and IEF are the primary quantitative performance measures. MF achieved the lowest PSNR of 6.5759 and IEF of 1.1712. AMF achieved a PSNR of 8.0603 and IEF of 1.6499. PSMF achieved a PSNR of 6.7847 and IEF of 1.2257. DBA achieved a PSNR of 17.1205 and IEF of 13.2768. MDBA achieved a PSNR of 17.2242 and IEF of 13.5976. MDBUTMF achieved the highest PSNR of 17.9865 and IEF of 16.2066. The relative improvement of MDBUTMF over MF in PSNR is 173.6% and in IEF is 1303.8%. The absolute PSNR improvement from MF to MDBUTMF is 11.4106 and IEF is 15.0354. The table lists these five filters: MF, AMF, PSMF, DBA, MDBA, MDBUTMF. The paper concludes with promising directions for future research work.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Spatial filters remove noise via low-pass filtering, assuming noise occupies higher frequency regions. Linear filters blur edges and destroy lines, and perform poorly with signal-dependent noise. Donoho and Johnstone proposed wavelet denoising to overcome Wiener filtering weaknesses. Wavelet coefficient thresholding separates signal and noise by concentrating signal energy into fewer coefficients. Hard thresholding generates spurious blips, which are known as artifacts. VISU Shrink is known to yield overly smoothed images because its threshold choice can be unwarrantedly large. Cross validation replaces coefficients with a weighted average of neighbors to minimize GCV. The shift-invariant property of UDWT avoids visual artifacts like the pseudo-Gibbs phenomenon. Deterministic wavelet modeling treats wavelet coefficients as a tree structure of scales. Statistical modeling aims at perfect in the exact modeling of image data. The study implies denoising algorithm selection must be application-dependent and noise-aware. The comparative study implies wavelet-based methods are generally more robust for high noise density.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper is a survey and comparative study, not an empirical experiment with a novel sample. No new data, participants, or original experimental dataset are introduced. There is no reported random seed, train/test split, or hyperparameters for the reviewed filters. The noise density is fixed at 90% for the comparative study, limiting cross-density generalization. Only the gray-scale Lena image is used, omitting color image evaluation. There are no ablation studies, sensitivity analyses, or calibration checks for the filters. The text uses informal notation like [Ma68], which is not fully specified in the paper. The classification of denoising filters is presented, but specific filter designs for MDBUTMF are not detailed. There is no explicit reporting of whether each hypothesis was supported, refuted, or nuanced. The paper relies on published filter designs rather than reproducing them in a controlled setting.

Claims
Wavelet domain thresholding techniques outperform spatial filtering methods for image denoising. Donoho and Johnstone proposed wavelet denoising to overcome Wiener filtering weaknesses. The wavelet transform separates signal and noise by concentrating signal energy into fewer coefficients. MDBUTMF achieved the highest PSNR of 17.9865 among the compared filters. The relative improvement of MDBUTMF over MF in PSNR is 173.6%. Non-linear median type filters have been developed to overcome blurring drawbacks. VISU Shrink is known to yield overly smoothed images due to large threshold choices. Wavelet techniques should be preferred for applications with high noise density. Appropriate denoising selection must consider noise type and application requirements.

summary.executive_summary:
We study the time-dependent dynamical phase of fractional quasiparticles in quantum Hall states using Ramsey interferometry. A Ramsey two-pulse voltage modulation generates an interference term in the current noise of a quantum point contact oscillating with the dynamical phase. We show that the interference pattern probes the Green’s function of the fractional quasiparticles in the time domain and reveals the fractional charge. We address both the case of a point-like tunnel junction and the case of momentum-resolved tunneling which also provides information on the speed of those quasiparticles propagating along the edge. For the 5/2 fractional quantum Hall case, the Ramsey signal can differentiate between the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states.

The edge states are described by a chiral Luttinger liquid effective theory which illustrates the emergence of fractional quasiparticles due to electron-electron interactions in quantum Hall states. Ramsey interferometry has been suggested to probe mesoscopic electron systems and strongly correlated systems such as one-dimensional quasicondensates, spin ensembles, and Rydberg atoms. We study Ramsey interferometry in the Abelian and 5/2 non-Abelian fractional quantum Hall states at the edges through the quantum Hall bar geometry. A small constriction induces a coupling between the counter-propagating edge states; a quantum point contact leads to tunneling. A Ramsey voltage modulation composed of two short pulses involves tunneling during the pulses, and Ramsey interference oscillates with the time delay t0 between the pulses.
We consider Laughlin states with filling factor ν = 1/(2n+1), where n is an integer. The fractional quasiparticle creation operator is expressed by bosonic chiral fields φR/L(x). An electron is composed of ν−1 fractional quasiparticles. A quantum point contact can be designed in two geometries: a Hall bar constriction (tunneling Laughlin quasiparticles) and two separated droplets (electrons tunnel). Tunneling via QPC is described by a Hamiltonian involving the dynamical phase ϕ(t). Current noise is the Fourier transform of the current-current correlation function, calculated to second order in D using the Keldysh formalism. For a dc voltage, the noise yields the Schottky formula, but time-dependent voltage modulations require the stationary phase approximation. The pulse durations are treated as Dirac delta functions, and the cross-pulse contributions yield Ramsey interference at frequency ω − qVdc.
The charge appearing in this formula is the dressed charge: the Laughlin quasiparticle charge for Fig. 1a and the electron charge for Fig. 1b. For Laughlin states, the Green's function involves hyperbolic functions, and in the high temperature limit the amplitude decays exponentially as exp(−2πνTt0), while in the low temperature limit it follows a power law (t₀/τ)−2ν. Comparing fractional quasiparticle and electron noise reveals that fractionalization manifests in the prefactor (qD)², the Green's function, and the dynamical phase qVdc. For the 5/2 filling factor, the Pfaffian state (α = 0) and anti-Pfaffian state (α = 1) differ. The anti-Pfaffian is the particle-hole conjugate, and recent experiments support the particle-hole Pfaffian for the ν = 5/2 state. Ramsey interferometry cannot distinguish between the Pfaffian and the particle-hole Pfaffian because the Majorana field moves in the opposite direction. We suggest probing the time-dependent dynamical phase and Green's function by generalizing Ramsey interferometry to quantum Hall edge states, which could be generalized to superconductors.

Edge states of fractional quantum Hall systems are described by a chiral Luttinger liquid theory. The fractional quantum Hall effect is characterized by excitations with fractional charge and statistics.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether Ramsey interferometry can probe the Abelian and 5/2 non-Abelian fractional quantum Hall states at the edges. We hypothesize that the interference pattern probes the Green's function of the fractional quasiparticles in the time domain. We predict that it reveals the fractional charge of these quasiparticles. Specifically, the noise oscillates with the delay time t0 at frequency ω − qVdc. We predict the crossover between two decay regimes as temperature is tuned. Methodological Details
We consider Laughlin states with filling factor ν = 1/(2n+1), where n is an integer. The fractional quasiparticle creation operator is expressed by bosonic chiral fields φR/L(x). summary.title: An algorithm for stress and mixed control in Galerkin based FFT homogenization
summary.authors: S. Lucarini and J. Segurado
summary.field_subfield: Computational Mechanics / FFT Homogenization / Continuum Mechanics
summary.executive_summary: This work introduces a new algorithm to impose macroscopic stress or mixed stress/deformation gradient control within the framework of non-linear Galerkin-based Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) homogenization. Computational homogenization typically simulates material mechanical response by solving a boundary problem on a periodic representative volume element (RVE), traditionally using finite element (FE) methods that allow any load history by combining strain and stress control. FFT methods are an increasingly popular alternative, replacing differential operators with Fourier counterparts, making them ideal for complex geometries with millions of degrees of freedom; however, imposing macroscopic stress or mixed loading paths is not a direct task in FFT. Existing strain-control FFT schemes handle stress-controlled cases by imposing the full macroscopic strain tensor and iteratively correcting it, which significantly increases the number of iterations per step. An alternative for classical schemes uses projection tensors to account for load control with a Krylov solver, which is more efficient than iterative approaches but still requires a reference medium. In contrast, Galerkin-based FFT homogenization derives the problem from a weak formulation, making direct use of material tangents and avoiding a reference medium, yet it was originally formulated only for deformation gradient history. The authors extend this variational algorithm for finite strains to incorporate stress and mixed control by modifying the projection operator, preserving the original method's computational performance. The method works by redefining the null frequencies to enforce either stress or strain control for each component of the macroscopic first Piola stress or the deformation gradient, which is solved exactly as the original variational method without additional iterations in the linear solver or Newton scheme. Efficiency is demonstrated via numerical examples of a polycrystal and a particle-reinforced hyperelastic material, where cases of stress and mixed control follow the same paths as full strain control but with different strain increments. In the particle-reinforced hyperelastic RVE with 643 voxels and volume fraction 0.2, three loading cases share an endpoint, but transverse responses differ; stress and mixed control yield zero transverse stress while strain control develops small compressive stresses. The polycrystal benchmark, discretized in 643 voxels with around 200 grains, reveals that a pseudo-uniaxial strain-control test produces non-zero transverse stresses that grow with strain, suggesting such emulation can lead to inaccurate results. Performance comparisons show the proposed stress and mixed controls take approximately the same number of conjugate-gradient iterations as full strain control, and for the polycrystal, the purely elastic fast steps compensate global time, making case (2) faster overall; normalization shows nearly identical simulation times across cases when using fixed time steps. The study concludes that the new algorithm allows mixed boundary conditions without extra computational effort, sustaining FFT advantages.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This work introduces a new algorithm to impose macroscopic stress or mixed stress/deformation gradient control within the framework of non-linear Galerkin-based Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) homogenization. Computational homogenization typically simulates material mechanical response by solving a boundary problem on a periodic representative volume element (RVE), traditionally using finite element (FE) methods that allow any load history by combining strain and stress control. FFT methods are an increasingly popular alternative, replacing differential operators with Fourier counterparts, making them ideal for complex geometries with millions of degrees of freedom; however, imposing macroscopic stress or mixed loading paths is not a direct task in FFT. Existing strain-control FFT schemes handle stress-controlled cases by imposing the full macroscopic strain tensor and iteratively correcting it, which significantly increases the number of iterations per step. An alternative for classical schemes uses projection tensors to account for load control with a Krylov solver, which is more efficient than iterative approaches but still requires a reference medium. In contrast, Galerkin-based FFT homogenization derives the problem from a weak formulation, making direct use of material tangents and avoiding a reference medium, yet it was originally formulated only for deformation gradient history. The authors extend this variational algorithm for finite strains to incorporate stress and mixed control by modifying the projection operator, preserving the original method's computational performance. The method works by redefining the null frequencies to enforce either stress or strain control for each component of the macroscopic first Piola stress or the deformation gradient, which is solved exactly as the original variational method without additional iterations in the linear solver or Newton scheme. Efficiency is demonstrated via numerical examples of a polycrystal and a particle-reinforced hyperelastic material, where cases of stress and mixed control follow the same paths as full strain control but with different strain increments. In the particle-reinforced hyperelastic RVE with 643 voxels and volume fraction 0.2, three loading cases share an endpoint, but transverse responses differ; stress and mixed control yield zero transverse stress while strain control develops small compressive stresses. The polycrystal benchmark, discretized in 643 voxels with around 200 grains, reveals that a pseudo-uniaxial strain-control test produces non-zero transverse stresses that grow with strain, suggesting such emulation can lead to inaccurate results. Performance comparisons show the proposed stress and mixed controls take approximately the same number of conjugate-gradient iterations as full strain control, and for the polycrystal, the purely elastic fast steps compensate global time, making case (2) faster overall; normalization shows nearly identical simulation times across cases when using fixed time steps. The study concludes that the new algorithm allows mixed boundary conditions without extra computational effort, sustaining FFT advantages.

Research Context
Computational homogenization simulates material response via a boundary problem on a periodic RVE. Finite element methods traditionally solve these boundary value problems. FE methods allow imposing any macroscopic load history combining strain and stress control. FFT-based homogenization is a popular alternative to FE. FFT methods replace differential operators with Fourier counterparts. FFT is ideal for complex geometries with millions of degrees of freedom. Imposing macroscopic stress or mixed loading is not a direct task in FFT. Obtaining material response for any generic loading path is fundamental. FFT homogenization was first proposed by Moulinec and Suquet. Classical FFT schemes require a reference medium. In classical schemes, load is introduced via the full macroscopic strain tensor. Stress control requires iterative approaches that increase iterations per step. Kabel et al. proposed an alternative using projection tensors and a Krylov solver. Galerkin-based FFT uses a weak formulation and avoids a reference medium. The Galerkin framework can use any complex non-linear constitutive equation. The Galerkin variational approach was still formulated for deformation gradient history.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how to impose stress or mixed control in Galerkin-based FFT without extra cost. The authors extend the finite-strain variational algorithm to stress and mixed control. The hypothesis is a direct method using a modified projection operator can work. It is hypothesized that this preserves computational performance of the original method. The prediction is that it does not require additional iterations in the linear solver or Newton scheme. It is predicted that the algorithm has the same convergence rate as the original scheme.

Methodological Details
The RVE is discretized into nx by ny by nz voxels. Linear momentum balance is imposed in its weak form in the reference configuration. Test functions are virtual deformation gradients premultiplied by a projector. The discrete linear momentum balance is given by G(P(F, α)) = 0. P is the first Piola-Kirchhoff stress. F is the deformation gradient field. G is a linear map defined in R raised to the power of 9 nx nx ny nx nz. The unknown is the deformation gradient at each voxel F. F is decomposed into average value and fluctuation, eF. In strain control, the value of F average is given. The resulting problem is finding the fluctuations of the deformation gradient. Non-linear behavior is solved by splitting deformation gradient into n increments. The Newton scheme linearizes the stress around the last iteration. The linear system is solved using the conjugate gradient method. If rate-dependent, the velocity gradient L is included. The macroscopic strain history is divided into n time increments. The projection operator is a fourth-order tensor. It enforces compatibility via convolution in the real space. A tensor field is decomposed into curl-free, divergence-free, and average components. The Fourier-space projection omits null and Nyquist frequencies. The projector is a zero fourth-order tensor at the null frequency. The null frequency projects the average part into itself as the fourth-order identity. Under stress control, the input is the target macroscopic stress, P. Under stress control, the correction δF includes a mean value. The first benchmark is a non-linear elastic composite. The uniaxial test reaches an elongation of lambda_end = 0.2. The load is divided into 100 load increments. The load increments use a pseudo-time t and are defined by ramps. Case (1) is a mixed control ramp in x with stress-free terms. Case (2) is full stress control, a linear ramp from 0 to P(1)_end. Case (3) is full strain control via a linear ramp to F(1)_end. The second benchmark is a polycrystal. The polycrystal RVE has 643 voxels and around 200 grains. Each grain follows crystal plasticity elasto-visco-plastic behavior. The polycrystal test imposes a final elongation of 0.02 in 200s. The polycrystal time is discretized into 20 regular increments. Four loading conditions are studied. The fourth case is pseudo-uniaxial strain control. The convergence criterion is the L2 norm of the residual. Tolerances are 10^-8 for the linear solver and 10^-6 for Newton. Case (1) of the polycrystal is identical to the previous section. Case (4) is an isochoric deformation at the final stage.

Procedures And Architectures
The projection operator bG is defined through the Helmholtz decomposition. The projection acts identically on a zero average tensor. The new operator bG* projects into compatible and mean parts. The stress-controlled equilibrium is G*(P - P_avg) = 0. The stress-controlled correction is G*(K:δF) = −G*(P - P). The stress-controlled δF includes the mean deformation gradient. Mixed control sets P_IJ for stress-imposed components and F_ij for strain-imposed. Mixed control is imposed by modifying the null-frequency projection. For mixed control, the null frequency is the identity for stress-controlled terms. For mixed control, the null frequency is zero for strain-controlled terms. For mixed control, the null frequency is zero for Nyquist. The Newton scheme is used to solve the non-linear system. The first Piola stress is P = ⟨P⟩ + eP. The average stress appears only through the zero-frequency projection. The input data is the target macroscopic stress P. The target macroscopic stress is set to the average stress ⟨P⟩. The deformation gradient is split into n increments for the solver. Each Newton iteration implies several linear solver iterations.

Key Results
The hyperelastic and polycrystal RVEs both have 643 voxels. The hyperelastic matrix and particles have shear moduli 28 Pa and 46.67 Pa. The particles are 10 times stiffer than the matrix. The uniaxial test reaches an elongation of 0.2. The load is divided into 100 load increments. Stress and mixed controlled cases share the same path. The transverse stress is zero under stress and mixed control. Strain control develops small compressive transverse stresses. Macroscopic and microscopic endpoint results are the same for all cases. The polycrystal contains around 200 grains. The polycrystal test imposes an elongation of 0.02 in 200s. Case (1) of the polycrystal matches the previous section's loading. Case (4) is a pseudo-uniaxial strain control. Pseudo-uniaxial strain control yields non-zero transverse stresses. Strain control emulation can lead to inaccurate results for plastic materials. The hyperelastic stress and mixed simulations used approximately the same number of iterations. The polycrystal plastic regime requires more iterations. The hyperelastic simulations needed nearly identical times for every condition. For the polycrystal, case (2) is faster than others. Elastic fast steps compensate the plastic steps for global time. Fixed time steps require similar simulation times across all cases. The convergence criterion is the L2 norm of the residual. The Newton convergence tolerance is 10^-6.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Stress control is implemented via the null-frequency projection. The mean stress appears as an identity projection, enforcing ⟨P⟩ = P. Stress control correction adds a mean deformation term. Equilibrium is reached as δF goes to zero, restoring target stress. The algorithm preserves the convergence rate of the original scheme. Stress control paths match strain control paths but with different increments. Strain control develops compressive transverse stress in plastic materials. Pseudo-uniaxial strain control is a poor approximation for uniaxial stress. Mixed control enables combined stress and strain boundary conditions.

Contradictions And Limitations
The exact numerical value of the deformation gradient correction is not reported. Exact strain-rate-dependence for the polycrystal is not reported. Specific grain sizes and orientations are not reported. The paper omits exact random seeds or train/test splits. Exact shear and bulk moduli units and values are preserved. The polycrystal stress values are in Pa, but no absolute peak. The exact number of conjugate-gradient iterations is not reported. Normalization of simulation times is relative to case (3). The exact time step size is not reported. The Newton solver maximum deformation gradient correction is not reported. Numerical accuracy limits are not specified. The exact number of voxels is 643 for both RVEs.

Claims
The proposed stress-control algorithm requires no extra iterations compared to strain control. The method is solved exactly as the original variational method. It does not require additional iterations in the linear solver. It does not require additional iterations in the Newton scheme. Stress and mixed controls took approximately the same number of iterations. The algorithm has the same convergence rate. The polycrystal case (2) shows a few steps requiring much higher iterations. Case (2) of the polycrystal is clearly faster, not identical. Stress control can be added without extra computational effort. FFT methods can sustain their computational advantages.
Strain-controlled pseudo-uniaxial tests inaccurately emulate uniaxial stress in plastic materials. The polycrystal response is very different from a real uniaxial tensile test. Compressive transverse stresses are not zero and grow with strain. Strain control emulation can lead to inaccurate results. Case (1) of the polycrystal matches the previous section. Strain control must be used cautiously to emulate stress tests.
The algorithm works for both hyperelastic and crystal-plasticity constitutive models. The approach can be used for two types of constitutive models. The algorithm can be used for any material. It follows a Saint Venant-Kirchhoff hyperelastic model. The polycrystal uses crystal plasticity elasto-visco-plastic behavior. The exact crystal plasticity parameters are not reported. The approach is generalizable to diverse constitutive behaviors.

Data And Code Availability
The paper provides numerical examples but not an external code repository. No external code availability is explicitly reported.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Robustness is demonstrated across two material models and multiple control schemes. Three loading cases are compared for each model. Convergence rates are comparable for hyperelastic stress and mixed controls. The polycrystal elastic-plastic steps are balanced globally. Case (2) of the polycrystal is faster, illustrating sensitivity to plasticity.

Ethical Considerations
The study is computational; no ethical considerations are reported.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1(a) shows the particle-reinforced RVE structure. Figure 1(b) shows the longitudinal stress for three loading cases. Figure 1(c) shows the transverse stress for three loading cases. Figure 2(a) shows the polycrystalline RVE structure. Figure 2(b) shows the longitudinal stress for four loading cases. Figure 2(c) shows the transverse stress for four loading cases. Figure 3(a) shows iteration counts versus time for the hyperelastic RVE. Figure 3(b) shows iteration counts versus time for the polycrystal. Figure 3(c) shows normalized simulation time across all cases.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a stress-controlled Galerkin-based FFT algorithm that preserves the convergence rate and requires no extra iterations. 2. The strongest evidence is that stress and mixed controls achieve nearly identical iteration counts to full strain control in hyperelastic RVEs. 3. The future path lies in applying this mixed-control framework to more complex loading paths and rate-dependent materials.

summary.title: Nonlinearity in the dark: Broadband terahertz generation with extremely high eﬃciency
summary.authors: Ming Fang, Nian-Hai Shen, Wei E.I. Sha, Zhixiang Huang, Thomas Koschny, and Costas M. Soukoulis
summary.executive_summary: This work introduces a novel concept for high-efficiency broadband terahertz (THz) generation by combining a resonant dark-state metasurface with a metallic nano-resonator configuration designed to eliminate linear radiation damping. The authors identify that the principal loss channel limiting nonlinear metasurface efficiency is dissipative and radiative damping due to linear scattering, which restricts the near-field amplitude available for nonlinear conversion. To circumvent this, the study proposes a perfect absorbing metasurface where linear radiation from asymmetric metallic split-ring resonators (SRRs) is forced into destructive interference in the far field, while the nonlinear second-harmonic components add constructively. This is realized by using a resonant dark bound state in a thin silicon film to concentrate electromagnetic field energy into a high-quality-factor mode that drives the SRRs. By tuning the electric and magnetic sheet conductivities (σ(e) and σ(m)) of the metasurface to match the wave impedance (ζσ(e)=ζ−1σ(m)=2), the incident pump energy is channeled almost entirely into the dark mode and metallic dissipation, achieving nearly 94% absorption. A self-consistent finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) calculation, built upon the hydrodynamic model of electron gas nonlinearity, was used to simulate the response under a temporal optical pulse with τ = 140 fs (spectral width ∼3.2 THz) and peak amplitude E0 = 2 × 10^7 V/m. The resulting enhancement, quantified as ηdark/ηSRR, exceeds 120-fold in THz emission power compared to a reference 40 nm-thick SRR metasurface that matched the conversion efficiency of 0.2 mm-thick optimal ZnTe crystals. Furthermore, the effective second-order nonlinear susceptibility χ(2) was evaluated at ≈2.4 × 10^11 m/V, one order of magnitude greater than the reference χ(2) of ≈1.7 × 10^12 m/V (consistent with 1.6 × 10^12 m/V). The study thus establishes a paradigm for tunable, high-efficiency nonlinear meta-devices, demonstrating that radiating and non-radiating components can be separated and controlled independently to break the fundamental efficiency limits of nonlinear metasurfaces.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This work introduces a novel concept for high-efficiency broadband terahertz (THz) generation by combining a resonant dark-state metasurface with a metallic nano-resonator configuration designed to eliminate linear radiation damping. The authors identify that the principal loss channel limiting nonlinear metasurface efficiency is dissipative and radiative damping due to linear scattering, which restricts the near-field amplitude available for nonlinear conversion. To circumvent this, the study proposes a perfect absorbing metasurface where linear radiation from asymmetric metallic split-ring resonators (SRRs) is forced into destructive interference in the far field, while the nonlinear second-harmonic components add constructively. This is realized by using a resonant dark bound state in a thin silicon film to concentrate electromagnetic field energy into a high-quality-factor mode that drives the SRRs. By tuning the electric and magnetic sheet conductivities (σ(e) and σ(m)) of the metasurface to match the wave impedance (ζσ(e)=ζ−1σ(m)=2), the incident pump energy is channeled almost entirely into the dark mode and metallic dissipation, achieving nearly 94% absorption. A self-consistent finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) calculation, built upon the hydrodynamic model of electron gas nonlinearity, was used to simulate the response under a temporal optical pulse with τ = 140 fs (spectral width ∼3.2 THz) and peak amplitude E0 = 2 × 10^7 V/m. The resulting enhancement, quantified as ηdark/ηSRR, exceeds 120-fold in THz emission power compared to a reference 40 nm-thick SRR metasurface that matched the conversion efficiency of 0.2 mm-thick optimal ZnTe crystals. Furthermore, the effective second-order nonlinear susceptibility χ(2) was evaluated at ≈2.4 × 10^11 m/V, one order of magnitude greater than the reference χ(2) of ≈1.7 × 10^12 m/V (consistent with 1.6 × 10^12 m/V). The study thus establishes a paradigm for tunable, high-efficiency nonlinear meta-devices, demonstrating that radiating and non-radiating components can be separated and controlled independently to break the fundamental efficiency limits of nonlinear metasurfaces.

Research Context
THz technology has advanced in sensing, imaging and communication since quantum-cascade lasers and ultrafast photoconductive switches emerged. Natural nonlinear materials such as inorganic crystals are limited by narrow bandwidth, phase-matching constraints, and low emission intensity. Subwavelength building blocks in metamaterials and metasurfaces enable versatile functions by designing custom sub-scale atoms. Resonant nonlinearity coupled with local field enhancement in designed meta-atoms offers an alternative route for high-efficiency nonlinear devices. A 40 nm-thick SRR metasurface recently generated broadband gapless THz emission up to 4 THz, matching ZnTe crystal efficiency. Despite this, the nonlinear optical response of such metasurface devices remains fairly weak and needs fundamental improvement. A fundamental limit of conversion efficiency in nonlinear metasurfaces exists and requires a novel circumventing concept.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is: what fundamental limitation constrains conversion efficiency in nonlinear metasurfaces? Hypothesis 1: dissipative and radiative damping due to linear scattering govern the near-field amplitude and THz emission intensity. Hypothesis 2: because dissipative loss is fixed by materials, targeting the radiative loss channel is the key to breaking the efficiency limit. Predicted outcome: a perfect absorbing metasurface combined with a dielectric dark element should eliminate linear radiation damping while driving high Q-factor local field enhancement. A dark mode is used to separate resonant local field enhancement from the topology necessary for non-vanishing second-order nonlinearity. Hypothesis: combining a dark-mode-assisted metasurface with destructive interference of radiating linear moments will yield giant THz efficiency.

Methodological Details
The proposed emitter is a dark-mode-assisted perfect absorbing metasurface consisting of two asymmetric SRRs sitting on a thin silicon film. The metallic SRRs are gold (thickness tm), oriented in the same direction and asymmetrically positioned on both sides of the film. The silicon film slab has a sub-wavelength thickness h, punctuated by metal walls of width 2a to quantize the modes of the dielectric slab. A second quantized mode on the lowest dispersion branch, TE2,0, is selected to give an anti-symmetric electric field profile. The unit cell geometric parameters are set to length L = 800 nm, width W = 240 nm, and thickness h = 100 nm. The operation wavelength is tuned to around 1.5 µm, within the high-speed telecommunications range. The SRR thickness is set to tm = 50 nm. Coupling is designed by balancing equivalent electric and magnetic effective surface susceptibilities in the metasurface. Scanning step size for sheet conductivity calculation was 5 nm to balance resolution and simulation cost. The optimal configuration was identified at positions ∆x1 ~ 70 nm and ∆x2 ~ 470 nm. The wave impedance is denoted ζ, and the wave impedance condition for ideal perfect absorption is ζσ(e) = ζ−1σ(m) = 2. THz emission is driven by the electron gas in the SRRs, modeled by a hydrodynamic model of second-order nonlinearity.

Procedures And Architectures
The device architecture uses two SRRs as bridges coupling incident radiation into the dark element of the Si slab. Coupling is implemented via non-resonant weak SRR scatterers creating equivalent electric and magnetic effective surface susceptibilities. The dark mode is a TE2,0 mode giving an anti-symmetric electric field profile that cannot couple directly to the incident plane wave. The dark-state mode allows concentration of electromagnetic field energy to create a high Q-factor strong local field enhancement. Impedance matching is achieved by balancing the electric (σ(e)s) and magnetic (σ(m)s) sheet conductivities of the two SRR polarization currents. Critical coupling is selected to eliminate the linear transmitted field, channeling incident pump energy into the dark resonant state and metallic dissipation. A self-consistent FDTD calculation combines the hydrodynamic model and Maxwell's equations. The temporal optical pulse was applied with Ey(t) = E0 exp[-2ln(2)(t − t0)2/τ 2] cos(ω0t). The driving frequency equals the resonant frequency of the dark mode (ω0 = ωdark). The pulse duration was set to τ = 140 fs with a spectral width of ∼3.2 THz. The peak amplitude was set to E0 = 2 × 10^7 V/m. Both linear and nonlinear dynamics of the electron gas under infrared light excitation were fully considered in the simulation.

Key Results
The optimal metasurface reached absorption as high as 94%. The optimal sheet conductivity values were ζ|σ(e)s| = ζ−1|σ(m)s| = 1.8. The dark-mode THz emission power showed more than 120-fold enhancement compared to the reference SRR metasurface. The effective second-order nonlinear susceptibility was evaluated at χ(2) ≈ 2.4 × 10^11 m/V. The reference traditional SRR metasurface χ(2) was ≈1.7 × 10^12 m/V, consistent with 1.6 × 10^12 m/V in prior work. The proposed scheme has a χ(2) more than one order of magnitude larger than the regular SRR metasurface. The THz signal amplitude increases linearly with the pump pulse intensity. The THz spectrum peak is at ω = 2/τ with a bandwidth ΔωFWHM ≈ 2.31/τ. The design enables nearly two-order enhanced THz emission under the same conditions as the reference. The reference SRR metasurface conversion efficiency matched 0.2 mm-thick optimal ZnTe crystals.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The separation of local field enhancement from the non-radiating nonlinearity topology is the primary mechanism for decoupling radiation damping from local field strength. By balancing electric and magnetic moments, linear radiation damping is reduced through destructive interference of the linear electric and magnetic dipoles. Simultaneously, the second-order DFG and second-harmonic currents add constructively in the far field because the sign of currents does not matter for second order nonlinearity. The convection term of the electron gas hydrodynamic model plays the crucial role for the second-order nonlinearities. Eliminating linear radiation damping and driving high Q-factor local field enhancement simultaneously break the common efficiency limit. The concept is general and applicable to other nonlinear processes, paving the way to reversible nanoscale nonlinear devices. THz enhancements are inversely proportional to linear radiation damping, meaning optimal suppression maximizes performance.

Contradictions And Limitations
The model assumes a spatially infinite surface under plane-wave illumination, making it less suitable to predict practical absolute numbers observed in an actual experiment. The THz conversion efficiency depends on many factors such as pump power, polarization, pulse duration, and focusing conditions, limiting the model's predictive power. The dissipation loss is hard to minimize and is essentially given by the available constituent materials. Thermal damage threshold was estimated, but actual thermal effects in the simulation are not quantified. No random seed or specific numerical mesh parameters for the FDTD solver were reported, limiting reproducibility of the exact simulation values.

Claims
A dark-mode-assisted metasurface eliminates linear radiation damping and enhances local near-field to yield giant THz efficiency. The optimal metasurface reached absorption as high as 94%. The THz emission power showed more than 120-fold enhancement compared to the reference SRR metasurface. The scheme has a χ(2) more than one order of magnitude larger than the regular SRR metasurface. The model assumes a spatially infinite surface under plane-wave illumination, which is less suitable for predicting practical numbers. THz conversion efficiency depends on many factors such as pump power, polarization, and pulse duration. This opens up the opportunities for not only revolutionary THz technologies but also high efficiency on-chip nonlinear nano-optical devices. The concept is general and applicable to other nonlinear processes.

Data And Code Availability
The paper provides self-consistent FDTD calculations based on the hydrodynamic model and Maxwell's equations. Detailed numerical results, dispersion diagrams, and performance maps are presented as figures. No statement on public code or data repository availability is provided.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Tunable linear radiation damping was verified as each scatterer is shifted along the unit cell. The THz enhancement for different configurations is inversely proportional to linear radiation damping. A side-by-side comparison was made with a conventional, not radiation-managed SRR metasurface from prior work.

Ethical Considerations
Work was supported by US DOE (Ames Laboratory) and ERC grants (PHOTOMETA) and Chinese funding bodies. The authors thank Peng Zhang, Liang Luo and Xu Yang for fruitful discussions. No explicit statement on conflict of interest or ethics approval is provided.

Figure 1(a) shows the schematic unit of the designed metasurface THz emitter. Figure 1(b) shows the dispersion diagram of the composite system. Figure 3 reports the wave impedance ζ and the condition for ideal perfect absorption.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a dark-mode-assisted perfect absorbing metasurface that decouples local near-field enhancement from linear radiation damping. 2. The Leidenfrost temperature is influenced by surface roughness, surface structure, and the impact Weber number.

Reducing the droplet contact time—bounded by the Rayleigh scale for an inviscid droplet on a superhydrophobic surface—is critical for anti-icing, self-cleaning, corrosion resistance, and maintaining surface dryness. The study adopts the term 'residence time' instead of contact time because the droplet only visually contacts the substrate in the film boiling regime, separated by a vapor layer. In the nucleate boiling regime, the droplet sticks to the hot surface and evaporates, with residence time strongly influenced by substrate temperature. In the film boiling regime, the vapor layer acts as a lubricant film, and the droplet, with sufficient kinetic energy, may bounce from the substrate after the recoil; thus the droplet residence time can be approximated as the period of a freely oscillating droplet.

The authors identify a mode of droplet bouncing, the bouncing-with-spray mode, caused by the burst of vapor bubbles, that dramatically reduces residence time compared to the retraction-bouncing mode. This heat-induced approach is reliable, avoids surface degradation, and is easy to achieve by avoiding complex fabrication of surface microstructures or surface modification. A theoretical model, based on energy balance and a bubble radius approximately equal to the minimum film thickness at maximum expansion, gives a scaling law that agrees well with the experimental data.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Droplet impact on heated surfaces is a ubiquitous phenomenon, important for industrial applications such as spray cooling, painting, inkjet printing, and fuel-spray impingement in internal combustion engines.
