They also demonstrate canalized chiral valley surface states on all surfaces ((100), (010), and (001)), revealing a flat isofrequency contour and a right-hand-thumb rule where the direction of VCVs and the circulating propagation direction of the surface states are coupled. The surface states propagate diffractionlessly in the +y direction (Wx−), and they show valley-locking through a sharp bend with high transmission. The work is measured at frequencies near 14.6 GHz, and the authors note the framework extends to higher frequencies, including THz and optical ranges. Overall, the work is the first to show robust canalized valley surface states on all surfaces of a 3D photonic topological insulator.

Research Context
Valley photonics exploits the valley degree of freedom to control the flow of light beyond amplitude, phase, polarization, and frequency. Traditionally a 2D valley photonic crystal contains a single pair of valleys at the corners of the 2D Brillouin zone. Bloch modes near these valleys are described by two-band massive Dirac models related by time-reversal symmetry. Two contrasting phenomena relate to valley-contrasting physics: vortex states with valley-locked chirality and edge states protected by valley Chern number. Valley photonics is more experimentally feasible than Chern insulators or topological insulators as it requires only inversion symmetry reduction rather than breaking time-reversal symmetry. All previous valley photonics studies were limited to 2D systems with nontopological confinement along the third dimension. Full confinement of light with any polarization in 3D requires a complete photonic bandgap. Achieving this complete bandgap is a significant challenge, motivating the proposed 3D framework.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central RQ is whether 3D topological valley photonics with a complete bandgap can be realized. The hypothesis is that a 3D inversion-symmetry-broken photonic crystal hosts triple pairs of valleys instead of a single pair. These valleys should be characterized by vectorial rather than scalar valley Chern numbers. The hypothesis predicts the existence of vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral valley surface states. It is predicted that the valley Chern vectors and surface state circulation are governed by the right-hand-thumb rule. The predicted outcomes are 3D directional radiation and imaging applications.

Methodological Details
The 3D photonic crystal has a lattice constant a = 20 mm. Lattice vectors are a1 = (a/2, a/2, 0), a2 = (0, a/2, a/2), and a3 = (a/2, 0, a/2). The structure is a photonic diamond with PEC spheres and rods. Each fcc cell contains two spheres of diameters D1 and D2. Nearest-neighbor PEC rods have diameter B1 = 2.4 mm. Next-nearest-neighbor rods have diameter B2 = 1.2 mm to suppress high-order modes. The symmetry-preserving case has D1 = D2 = 5 mm (∆D = 0). The inversion-symmetry-broken case sets D1 = 6.4 mm and D2 = 3.6 mm. Six valleys are located at (±π/a, 2π/a, 0), (0, ±π/a, 2π/a), and (2π/a, 0, ±π/a). The effective Hamiltonian is derived near each valley via the k⋅p method. The four sources of the vectorial chiral array are at (0, 0, 0), (−a/2, −a/2, 0), (−a/2, 0, −a/2), and (0, −a/2, −a/2). For Wy±, relative phase delays are (0, π/2, π, 3π/2) for Wy− and (0, −π/2, −π, −3π/2) for Wy+. The boundary condition parameters are h = 6.25 mm and D3 = 4 mm. Measurements are performed near 13.8 GHz and 14.6 GHz.

Procedures And Architectures
The band topology is manifested by the local Berry curvature Ω = (Ωx, Ωy, Ωz) around each valley. The valley Chern vector is defined by the integral of Berry curvature over a planar region. The Hamiltonian mass term m = (ω1 − ω2)/2 is induced by breaking inversion symmetry. Boundary condition θV is tuned to π/2 with a metallic plate and varying D3/h. The vectorial chiral source array selectively excites chiral Bloch modes via phase winding. Pump-probe measurement verifies the vectorial valley-contrasting Berry curvature. Outcoupling fields are measured in the y-z plane at the (001) surface. The chiral surface states propagate diffractionlessly along +y corresponding to Wx−. Surface dispersion is independent of the wavevector vertical to propagation. Surface field distributions and Fourier-transformed spectra are mapped on the surfaces. Isofrequency contours are measured before and after a bend.

Key Results
The symmetry-preserving crystal (∆D = 0) hosts nodal lines at Wα± − X. Breaking inversion symmetry gaps the nodal lines into a complete photonic bandgap. Six valleys at Wα± form triple pairs grouped by time-reversal symmetry. Eigenstates at Wz± show opposite vortex chirality as required by time-reversal symmetry. Berry curvature at Wz± has only a nonzero component in the kx-ky plane. The VCV values are (±1/2, 0, 0), (0, ±1/2, 0), and (0, 0, ±1/2). Outcoupling fields at 13.8 GHz show −32.9° and +32.9° directions for Wy− and Wy+. Without phase winding, the direction is 0°, corresponding to X. Radiated beams are single-directional in 3D space unlike the 2D case. Surface transmission remains high within the complete photonic bandgap. The surface states propagate diffractionlessly along +y in a canalized fashion. Surface dispersion is nearly linear as confirmed by Fourier-transformed spectrum. The right-hand-thumb rule links VCVs to surface state circulation. The surface states pass smoothly through a sharp corner with high transmission.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The 3D valley states carry orbital moments that control the angular momentum of light. Directional outcoupling can serve as a mechanism for narrow-beam antennae. Canalized valley chiral surface states may inspire 3D topological photonic devices for guiding and trapping light. The right-hand-thumb rule is an intrinsic relation determined by the bulk Hamiltonian. Canalization stems from flat isofrequency contours that are intrinsic properties of the surface states. The framework extends to THz and optical ranges, which have been extensively studied.

Contradictions And Limitations
Demonstration is at lower frequencies (near 14.6 GHz). A full range of materials and frequencies is not exhaustively reported. No specific random seed or train/test split is mentioned for numerical simulations. Experimental characterization of all possible shapes and symmetries is not shown.

Claims
The 3D VPC framework realizes a complete bandgap and vectorial valley states with triple pairs of valleys. The crystal supports a complete photonic bandgap when ∆D≠ 0. It hosts six valleys grouped into triple pairs by time-reversal symmetry. The valley Chern vectors are (±1/2, 0, 0), (0, ±1/2, 0), and (0, 0, ±1/2). Berry curvature at Wz± has a nonzero component only in the kx-ky plane. Previous studies were limited to 2D systems with scalar valley Chern numbers. This enables a vectorial valley-contrasting physics that supports directional radiation and imaging.
Robust, canalized valley surface states persist on all surfaces and obey the right-hand-thumb rule. Chiral valley surface states propagate diffractionlessly along +y. Surface transmission remains high within the complete photonic bandgap. The surface states pass through a sharp corner with high transmission. The VCV and the circulating direction obey the right-hand-thumb rule. Existing 3D topological insulators only support surface states on certain surfaces. Canalization offers opportunities for imaging and lensing devices. The right-hand-thumb rule is an intrinsic property determined by the bulk Hamiltonian.

Data And Code Availability
The paper describes numerical band structure simulations. Specific code or raw data repositories are not cited in the text.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Next-nearest-neighbor rods B2 = 1.2 mm suppress high-order modes. The boundary condition h = 6.25 mm and D3 = 4 mm satisfy the θV = π/2 condition. The canalization phenomenon has been confirmed both experimentally and numerically.

Ethical Considerations
The paper is a theoretical and experimental materials science study; human participants are not involved.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the 3D VPC structure and vectorial Berry curvatures. Figure 2 shows the four-source array and measured outcoupling fields at 13.8 GHz. Figure 3 shows the canalized surface states on the modified (001) surface. Figure 4 illustrates the right-hand-thumb rule and the sharp corner bend.

Three Takeaways
The core contribution is a 3D framework of topological valley photonics with a complete bandgap, triple pairs of valleys, and vectorial valley Chern vectors. The strongest evidence is the right-hand-thumb rule connecting VCVs to circulating surface states, verified through sharp-corner bends and 13.8/14.6 GHz measurements. The future path is extending the 3D valley concept to higher frequencies (THz and optical) and building directional antennae or imaging devices.

summary.title: From Words to Wheels: Automated Style-Customized Policy Generation for Autonomous Driving
summary.authors: Xu Han, Xianda Chen, Zhenghan Cai, Pinlong Cai, Meixin Zhu, Xiaowen Chu
summary.field_subfield: Autonomous driving / reinforcement learning / natural language processing
summary.executive_summary: Words2Wheels is a framework that automatically generates style-customized driving policies from natural language user commands for autonomous vehicles, addressing the limitations of uniform driving styles. Current AVs face criticisms for uniform behaviors (e.g., 52.46% of AV crashes were rear-ended, 1.6 times the rate of conventional vehicles) and struggle to align driving style metrics with user preferences. Traditional methods rely on manually designed, expert-input driving styles (cumbersome, subjective) or data-driven IRL/clustering approaches that require behavior data hard to obtain in Robotaxi scenarios and cannot generalize to new commands. Foundation models (LLMs) can process instructions but often adjust only specific behaviors like speed/lane changes, not the overall style policy, and raise reliability/efficiency concerns by involving the foundation model in most decision loops. Words2Wheels introduces a Style-Customized Reward Function to bridge user input and a Style-Customized Driving Policy, leveraging LLMs and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with a Driving Style Database to retrieve, adapt, and generalize driving styles. It includes a Driving Style Database storing Style Rewards (code), Style Policies (pre-trained neural networks), and analytical data (e.g., jerk during braking), and a Statistical Evaluation module that uses a reserved test set to compare policies against natural driving behavior statistics. The framework is RAG-based, employing GPT-4o-2024-08-06 with temperature 0.3, selecting top k=3 relevant style rewards, and generating m new functions based on the best match. Results show Words2Wheels outperforms existing methods in accuracy, generalization, and adaptability, demonstrating strong style adaptation to commands like 'Drive aggressively' or 'Safety first.' Human-in-the-loop comparisons with 10 volunteers over 1000 tested events show participants preferred Words2Wheels over IDM in 72% of events. Case studies across 40 commands show high performance (97.5% analysis, 95% decision-making), with isolated failures in Cases 19, 26, and negative-value cases. Fuzzy memory recall succeeds in all but one case. The framework is extensible for fuzzy memory and could incorporate a Feedback and Reflection module. Code is available at https://yokhon.github.io/Words2Wheels/.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Words2Wheels is a framework that automatically generates style-customized driving policies from natural language user commands for autonomous vehicles, addressing the limitations of uniform driving styles. Current AVs face criticisms for uniform behaviors (e.g., 52.46% of AV crashes were rear-ended, 1.6 times the rate of conventional vehicles) and struggle to align driving style metrics with user preferences. Foundation models (LLMs) can process instructions but often adjust only specific behaviors like speed/lane changes, not the overall style policy, and raise reliability/efficiency concerns by involving the foundation model in most decision loops. Words2Wheels introduces a Style-Customized Reward Function to bridge user input and a Style-Customized Driving Policy, leveraging LLMs and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with a Driving Style Database to retrieve, adapt, and generalize driving styles. It includes a Driving Style Database storing Style Rewards (code), Style Policies (pre-trained neural networks), and analytical data (e.g., jerk during braking), and a Statistical Evaluation module that uses a reserved test set to compare policies against natural driving behavior statistics. The framework is RAG-based, employing GPT-4o-2024-08-06 with temperature 0.3, selecting top k=3 relevant style rewards, and generating m new functions based on the best match. Results show Words2Wheels outperforms existing methods in accuracy, generalization, and adaptability, demonstrating strong style adaptation to commands like 'Drive aggressively' or 'Safety first.' Human-in-the-loop comparisons with 10 volunteers over 1000 tested events show participants preferred Words2Wheels over IDM in 72% of events. Case studies across 40 commands show high performance (97.5% analysis, 95% decision-making), with isolated failures in Cases 19, 26, and negative-value cases. Fuzzy memory recall succeeds in all but one case. The framework is extensible for fuzzy memory and could incorporate a Feedback and Reflection module. Code is available at https://yokhon.github.io/Words2Wheels/.

Research Context
Autonomous driving foundation models improve interactivity but AVs suffer from uniform driving styles. 52.46% of AV crashes were rear-ended, 1.6 times the rate of conventional vehicles. Gentler braking styles are needed to improve user experience. Early driving style approaches relied on classification or calibration of predefined styles. Manual styles depend on expert input, making the process cumbersome and subjective. Data-driven approaches use clustering and IRL to derive policies from natural behavior. Data-driven approaches require small behavior data hard to obtain in Robotaxi scenarios. Existing methods cannot customize style based on user needs, limiting generalization. Foundation models adjust specific behaviors like speed but fall short at the style level. Foundation models in most decision loops raise reliability and efficiency concerns.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can a framework automatically generate style-customized driving policies from natural language user commands? Hypothesis: Words2Wheels can bridge user input and policy via a Style-Customized Reward Function. Hypothesis: RAG and LLMs enable generalizing to new commands without user behavior data. Hypothesis: A Statistical Evaluation module can objectively align generated styles with user commands. Hypothesis: Words2Wheels will outperform existing methods in accuracy, generalization, and adaptability.

Methodological Details
The framework is applied to the car-following scenario, a significant portion of driving behavior. The experiment used the HighD dataset collected by a 4K resolution drone camera. Data extraction and kinematic model were based on FollowNet. 15% of data was reserved as a test set to ensure objectivity of the Statistical Evaluation module. User commands were categorized into three levels of directness in Table I. The base model was GPT-4o-2024-08-06 with temperature set to 0.3. k = 3 was used for selecting relevant styles; n = 2 in Statistical Evaluation. The Driving Style Database initially contained 8 styles (data-driven and human-designed). RL training used Proximal Policy Optimization ran 5 times with different seeds. The database contains Style Rewards (code), Style Policies (pre-trained neural networks), and analytical data. Style Reward functions are programming codes; policies are pre-trained neural networks. Statistical metrics include speed, time headway, relative speed, acceleration, jerk, spacing.

Procedures And Architectures
The workflow follows the RAG-based pipeline shown in Fig. 3. Upon receiving a command, the LLM selects top k relevant style rewards from the database. If a matched command exists, Words2Wheels uses its Style Policy (fuzzy memory). If no match, the LLM generates m new reward functions based on the best match. New reward functions produce Style Policies via parallelized RL training. The Statistical Evaluation module determines if new policies outperform the temporary one. The database stores rewards, policies, and stats, which can be embedded as high-dimensional vectors. Statistics of natural behavior are provided to the LLM as a baseline. Statistical Evaluation follows Chain-of-Thought reasoning. RL training selects the Style Policy with the highest reward.

Key Results
Words2Wheels outperforms existing methods in accuracy, generalization, and adaptability. In 72% of events, participants preferred the generated style over IDM. In 18.8% of events, both models were considered equally effective. IDM was preferred in only 9.2% of events. The human-in-the-loop experiment used 10 volunteers with licenses over 1000 tested events. The generalization case study analyzed 40 commands across three levels. Overall generalization performance: analysis 97.5%, decision-making 95%, generation 92.5%, retrieval 85%. The aggressive style showed higher speeds and greater acceleration. The conservative style maintained a larger gap and relative speed. Fuzzy memory recalled all but one case (snowing and visibility decreased).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The Style-Customized Reward Function acts as a policy index to bridge preferences and behavior. LLM zero-shot generation enables style customization without prior user behavior data. RAG reduces reliance on RL by retrieving pre-trained styles directly. Human preferences are more consistent than direct quantification in RL with human feedback. Words2Wheels is the first framework to automatically customize style-aware driving policies via natural language. The Driving Style Database enables continuous enrichment of styles, expanding style range.

Contradictions And Limitations
The aggressive style had a larger time headway, unlike expected behavior. The normal style showed higher jerk, likely because the LLM did not prioritize metrics. The LLM sometimes selected the Style Reward with the highest jerk as a counterexample (Case 26). The LLM misinterpreted Case 19: 'You are allowing a large gap with the vehicle in front.' When acceleration and jerk values were negative, the LLM's understanding conflicted with human intuition. The Statistical Evaluation module was limited to the car-following scenario. The Statistical Evaluation module was reserved but the train/test split details are not explicitly reported.

Claims
Words2Wheels automatically generates and adapts driving policies from natural language commands, outperforming manual and data-driven baselines. In 72% of events, participants preferred the generated style over IDM. The aggressive style showed higher speeds and greater acceleration. Words2Wheels can generate driving styles that align with user commands rather than simply selecting. The aggressive style had a larger time headway, diverging from expectations. In 18.8% of events, both models were considered equally effective. The framework improves user experience through style customization in AVs. Words2Wheels enables the system to respond to a broader range of natural language instructions.
The Driving Style Database and Statistical Evaluation module allow objective, zero-shot customization and continual enrichment. With LLMs' zero-shot capabilities, Words2Wheels can generalize to new commands without user behavior data. The fuzzy memory function allows the system to match fuzzy inputs to existing memories. One fuzzy memory case involving snowing and visibility decreased was not recalled. Continuous updates expand the database, reducing reliance on RL. The Statistical Evaluation module prevents overfitting and provides benchmarks for evaluating policies.

Data And Code Availability
Code and demo available at https://yokhon.github.io/Words2Wheels/. Experimental records are available at https://bit.ly/4giYhB7.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Each command was run 5 times and outcomes averaged to ensure robustness. The Style Policy with the highest reward was selected from 5 RL training runs. The generation experiment limited initial styles to 4 for demonstration. The Statistical Evaluation module used a reserved test set to prevent overfitting.

Ethical Considerations
The authors state the paper is a preprint version.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1 illustrates the Style-Customized Reward Function workflow. Fig. 2 shows the workflow, Style Database, and Statistical Evaluation module. Fig. 3 displays an example of automated Style Policy generation. Fig. 4 illustrates the Statistical Evaluation module simplified example. Fig. 5 compares customized policies over style-aware metrics. Fig. 6 evaluates generated policies when no aligned styles provided. Fig. 7 shows the user interface for comparing driving style alignment. Table I categorizes user commands into three levels. Table II shows human preferences on driving style alignment. Table III presents case studies across all command levels. Table IV evaluates fuzzy memory function with similar commands.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: A framework that automatically generates style-customized driving policies from natural language user commands via a Style-Customized Reward Function and a Driving Style Database. 2. The strongest evidence: Human-in-the-loop testing with 10 volunteers over 1000 events showed participants preferred the generated style over IDM in 72% of cases. 3. The future path: Expanding the framework to complex scenarios beyond car-following, refining Statistical Evaluation, and incorporating a Feedback and Reflection module.

summary.title: Dense-TSNet: Dense Connected Two-Stage Structure for Ultra-Lightweight Speech Enhancement
summary.authors: Zizhen Lin (Sichuan University), Yuanle Li (Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications), Junyu Wang (Tianjin University), Ruili Li (Tohoku University)
summary.executive_summary:
Speech enhancement aims to improve speech quality and intelligibility in noisy environments, which is vital for applications like voice calls, video recording, and automatic speech recognition. Recent advancements have concentrated on deep neural networks, particularly employing the Two-Stage (TS) architecture for deep feature extraction, inspired by TSTNN. This architecture reshapes and partitions spectral data to address spectral distribution characteristics and features an encoder-decoder with a dilated dense block that improves information flow stability and enhances local and large-scale feature dependency. However, the complexity and size of these models remain significant, which limits their applicability in resource-constrained scenarios, and designing models suitable for edge devices presents its own set of challenges. Narrow lightweight models often encounter performance bottlenecks due to uneven loss landscapes, and advanced operators such as Transformers or Mamba may lack the practical adaptability and efficiency that convolutional neural networks (CNNs) offer in real-world deployments. Consequently, developing ultra-lightweight models is essential for practical applications in edge devices such as smartphones and cameras, and research on single-channel speech enhancement models with around 10k parameters is still limited. This gap underscores the need for innovative approaches to develop effective models at this scale.

The authors propose Dense-TSNet, an ultra-lightweight speech enhancement network that employs a novel Dense Two-Stage (Dense-TS) architecture, which, compared to the classic Two-Stage architecture, ensures more robust refinement of the objective function in the later training stages and leads to improved final performance by addressing the early convergence limitations of the baseline model. They also introduce the Multi-View Gaze Block (MVGB), which enhances feature extraction by incorporating global, channel, and local perspectives through convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and discuss how the choice of loss function impacts perceptual quality. Dense-TSNet demonstrates promising performance with a compact model size of around 14K parameters, making it well-suited for deployment in resource-constrained environments. The model inputs only the magnitude spectrum and performs time-frequency feature extraction through the Dense-TS structure with the TS-MVGB. The Dense-TSNet model has a size of only 14K, the first to achieve a speech enhancement model with approximately 10k parameters, and the authors explore loss functions through comparative experiments and propose Consistency Magnitude Loss to reconstruct speech signals, as relying on Metric Loss to improve objective perceptual metrics may negatively impact subjective perception.

The proposed Dense-TSNet is evaluated on the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset, with speech samples segmented into two-second intervals for short-time Fourier transform using an FFT size of 400, a window length of 400, and a hop length of 100. The training used a batch size of 2, the AdamW optimizer, and was carried out for up to 1,000,000 steps, with evaluation based on PESQ and MOS-based metrics ranging from -0.5 to 4.5. Ablation studies show that removing the Large Kernel Extractor, Channel Attention, or Learnable-Sigmoid Gate degrades performance, and Consistency Magnitude Loss was favored over Metric Loss due to perceptual distortions and training failure at high weights.

Speech enhancement aims to improve speech quality and intelligibility in noisy environments, which is vital for applications like voice calls, video recording, and automatic speech recognition. Recent advancements have concentrated on deep neural networks, particularly employing the Two-Stage (TS) architecture for deep feature extraction, inspired by TSTNN. This architecture reshapes and partitions spectral data to address spectral distribution characteristics and features an encoder-decoder with a dilated dense block that improves information flow stability and enhances local and large-scale feature dependency. Narrow lightweight models often encounter performance bottlenecks due to uneven loss landscapes, and advanced operators such as Transformers or Mamba may lack the practical adaptability and efficiency that convolutional neural networks (CNNs) offer in real-world deployments. Consequently, developing ultra-lightweight models is essential for practical applications in edge devices such as smartphones and cameras, and research on single-channel speech enhancement models with around 10k parameters is still limited. judge_context:
Executive Summary
This work addresses the challenge of modeling high-dimensional, complex probability distributions and cross-feature dependencies in time series forecasting—a gap left by standard recurrent or transformer models which, despite their ability to capture temporal dependencies, are constrained by simple differentiable probability families in their output layers. The authors argue that generative models (diffusion, flow, SGM) can capture sophisticated distributions but suffer from scalability issues because model size scales with both window length and feature dimension. The paper proposes a new framework: Recurrent Interpolants for Probabilistic Time Series Prediction. This method blends the computational efficiency of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with the high-quality probabilistic modeling of stochastic interpolants. Key insights include: 1) Stochastic interpolants extend the theory of stochastic mapping to arbitrary joint distributions through a conditional generation framework with extra control features; 2) A conditional stochastic interpolants (SI) module is used for sequential modeling, where an RNN encodes a large context window into a history prompt, and the velocity and score functions perform conditional generation; and 3) Empirical results on synthetic (Circles, Moons, Rings, Swissroll, 8gaussians) and real-world multivariate datasets (Solar, Exchange, Traffic, Wiki) show SI is a strong candidate for conditional generation, outperforming or matching SGM and DDPM across most datasets and beating the RNN-based Vec-LSTM, indicating that modeling the probability distribution explicitly is critical for large-dimension forecasting. The work is grounded in stochastic interpolants theory (Albergo et al., 2023b), score-based generative models, flow matching, and DDPMs, validated by Wasserstein distance and CRPS-sum metrics.

Research Context
Time series forecasting has relied on autoregressive models like RNNs and transformers to capture dependencies across diverse domains. While probabilistic outputs can provide uncertainty via parametric models, the probability family is simple and differentiable. Generative models like diffusion and flow-based methods can capture sophisticated distributions but face scalability issues. Generative procedure quality improves when starting from a distribution proximate to the terminal distribution. Time series data is continuous with strong correlations between neighboring points, suggesting a close distribution.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can a recurrent-generative framework combine RNN efficiency with diffusion-quality probabilistic modeling for large-scale forecasting? Hypothesis: Mapping the future distribution from the current time point is straightforward and improves quality. Hypothesis: A recurrent network can encode longer temporal dependency as guidance for the generative model. Hypothesis: Condition stochastic interpolants can generalize to arbitrary joint distributions with extra control features. Hypothesis: The framework will be more computational-friendly than window-scaled generative predictors.

Methodological Details
The method is framed as a conditional generation task given a context window and a prediction window. The joint density learned is p(x_next, x_curr | context), matching marginals ρ₀ = ρ₁. A RNN encodes the context window xt−P :t−1 into a history prompt ht. Training uses a tuple of three components: target, current, and history context. Importance sampling uses a Beta distribution to handle high loss at the ends of diffusion time. Synthetic datasets: Circles, Moons, Rings, Swissroll, 8gaussians. Real-world datasets: Solar, Exchange, Traffic, Wiki. Evaluation metrics: CRPS-sum, NRMSE, and ND. Code and preprocessing follow Salinas et al., 2019 and the gluonts package. Metrics are computed using the gluonts package.

Procedures And Architectures
DDPM defines forward Gaussian noise at scales β₁ < β₂ < ... < β_N. The generative model predicts noise added to clean data from noisy data. Flow matching learns a conditional vector field us(x|x₁) generating ps(x|x₁) from p0=N(0,I) to p1=N(x₁,σ²I). Stochastic interpolants construct xs = α(s)x₀ + β(s)x₁ + γ(s)z with s ∈ [0, 1], z ∼ N(0,I). The velocity b(s,x) and score s(s,x) model the drift and the score function separately. Schedules: α(0)=1, α(1)=0, β(0)=0, β(1)=1; γ(0)=γ(1)=0. Example schedules: α(s) = √(1−γ²(s)cos(1/2πs)), β(s) = √(1−γ²(s)sin(1/2πs)), γ(s) = √(2s(1−s)). The velocity and score depend on the condition ξ: b(s,xs,ξ) and s(s,xs,ξ). Inference runs a forward SDE to transport xt to the target distribution. Multiple-step prediction is recursive.

Key Results
On synthetic datasets, all models capture the true distribution across different metrics. Table 1: Wasserstein distances are low across datasets (e.g., Circles ~0.12–0.32). Table 1: SGM has highest Wasserstein on Circles (1.10) vs SI (0.52). On real-world datasets, a smaller CRPS-sum indicates better performance. On Solar: SI (0.359) is the best, beating SGM (0.364) and DDPM (0.359). Table 2: SI (0.080) beats SGM (0.084) and FM (0.090) on Solar CRPS. SI outperforms FM and SGM on three out of four datasets. On Traffic, FM is the only model that achieves better performance than SI. On Wiki, FM cannot capture the data distribution, leading to failure. Our model (SI) and SGM/DDPM beat the RNN-based Vec-LSTM on most datasets.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Explicitly modeling the probability distribution is critical for large-dimension forecasting. The method merges RNN efficiency with diffusion-quality probabilistic modeling. Theorem 1 extends stochastic interpolants to arbitrary joint distributions. The score function is optimized via a simple quadratic objective. SI is established as a strong candidate for conditional generation and multivariate probabilistic forecasting.

Contradictions And Limitations
FM cannot capture the distribution on Wiki, and a hyperparameter search on FM was unsuccessful. Only FM outperforms SI on the Traffic dataset. Loss values become larger when s is close to two ends, necessitating importance sampling. The analysis avoids characteristic functions for continuous-time interpretation but is detailed in the appendix. Hyperparameter search for FM was conducted but could not yield satisfying results.

Claims
The stochastic interpolant framework generalizes to arbitrary joint distributions and is a natural extension of generative models for conditional generation. The velocity and score functions can be conditioned on extra features ξ. The joint density matches ρ₀ = ρ₁ so that marginals align. The theorem formalizes arbitrary joint distributions under a conditional framework. SDEs enable conditional generation from the conditional density ρ(x1|x0). On Wiki, the flow-matching baseline fails to capture the data distribution. On Traffic, FM beats SI, indicating SI isn't the best in all scenarios. SI is a strong candidate for multivariate probabilistic forecasting. The explicit modeling of the distribution yields better large-dimension performance.
Recurrent networks can encode long-range context as guidance while preserving RNN efficiency, which SI exploits via a history prompt. The recurrent neural network is used to encode the context. The prediction of the next value relies on the history prompt ht. This framework inherits RNN efficiency while enjoying diffusion quality. The RNN encodes xt−P :t−1 into a history prompt ht, which is then passed to the generative model. The RNN-based baseline Vec-LSTM performs worse than the generative baselines. The hybrid architecture avoids window-length-scaled model sizes.

Data And Code Availability
The code will be made publicly available in the camera-ready version. Code is cited as coming from the camera-ready release.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors test different gamma-schedules: sqrt, quad, and trig. Most gamma-interpolant combinations achieve good results on the target distribution. The method is tested on varying data sizes, model sizes, and training lengths.

Ethical Considerations
The authors do not explicitly discuss ethics; the field uses public datasets.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1: Wasserstein distance between generated samples and true data across datasets. Table 2: CRPS-sum metric on multivariate probabilistic forecasting (Solar, Exchange, Traffic, Wiki). Figure 1: α(s), β(s), γ(s) interpolant schedules. Figure 2: Model architecture showing the recurrent and diffusion components. Figure 3: Sample generated data from different models (DDPM, SGM, FM, SI). Figure 4: Forecast paths on the Solar dataset with median and CI. Figure 5: The full Time-Grad conditional prediction pipeline.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a hybrid framework blending RNN efficiency with high-quality stochastic interpolant modeling for multivariate time series. 2. The strongest evidence is that SI matches or beats SGM and DDPM on three out of four real datasets while beating Vec-LSTM. 3. The future path lies in expanding the conditional generation framework and applying SI to more complex control features.

summary.title: The properties of highly concentrated aqueous CH3COOK/Na binary electrolyte and its use in sodium-ion batteries
summary.authors: Shahid Khalid (University of Milan-Bicocca); Nicolò Pianta (University of Milan-Bicocca); Simone Bonizzoni (University of Milan-Bicocca); Piercarlo Mustarelli (University of Milan-Bicocca); Riccardo Ruffo (University of Milan-Bicocca)
summary.executive_summary: Highly concentrated aqueous binary electrolytes based on potassium acetate (CH3COOK) and sodium acetate (CH3COONa) are explored as high-performance aqueous electrolytes for sodium-ion batteries, addressing the safety and cost limitations of conventional lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) using non-flammable organic carbonate electrolytes. These conventional electrolytes suffer from low flashpoints, high melting points, high viscosities at low temperatures, and the thermally unstable LiPF6 salt that decomposes into HF in the presence of moisture. To extend the narrow thermodynamic electrochemical stability window (ESW) of water (1.23 V) toward the 3 V window achieved by organic electrolytes, the authors investigate the water-in-salt electrolyte (WISE) concept (LiTFSI in water up to 21 mol kg -1), which leverages the low water activity and subnanometer water clusters at super-concentrations. Because the fluorinated salts needed for WISE have oral/dermal toxicity and high cost, the study turns to cost-effective, soluble, and widely available salts: NaAc and KAc, which were combined in a binary system. The authors fix the KAc concentration at 20 mol kg -1 and vary the NaAc concentration across four electrolytes (1, 2.5, 5, 7 mol kg -1 NaAc), plus a 1 M NaAc comparison. The most concentrated solution (7N20K) is the preferred WISE candidate, achieving a compromise between transport and electrochemical stability. Key results: The 7N20K electrolyte shows a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm -1 at 25°C and an electrochemical stability window up to 3 V in flooded three-electrode cells with small surface area/highly electrocatalytic electrodes. A carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 NASICON electrode demonstrates reversible Na + intercalation at ~ -0.7 V vs. SHE, with first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g -1 (104 mAh g -1 in specific capacity context, see discrepancy noted), average charge efficiency of 96% (99% at high current), and 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles. Impedance spectroscopy reveals a low charge transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV, and diffusion coefficient ~ 10 -13 cm2 s -1, suggesting strong kinetic-thermal coupling and that the aqueous electrolyte improves ion diffusion inside the NASICON structure. The paper uses DSC, rheology (VTF/Arrhenius), conductivity (EIS), and LSV to characterize the solutions, and GCPL with impedance to evaluate the NASICON/electrolyte interface, concluding that these acetate systems support the WISE approach for rechargeable alkaline-ion batteries.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Highly concentrated aqueous binary electrolytes based on potassium acetate (CH3COOK) and sodium acetate (CH3COONa) are explored as high-performance aqueous electrolytes for sodium-ion batteries, addressing the safety and cost limitations of conventional lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) using non-flammable organic carbonate electrolytes. These conventional electrolytes suffer from low flashpoints, high melting points, high viscosities at low temperatures, and the thermally unstable LiPF6 salt that decomposes into HF in the presence of moisture. To extend the narrow thermodynamic electrochemical stability window (ESW) of water (1.23 V) toward the 3 V window achieved by organic electrolytes, the authors investigate the water-in-salt electrolyte (WISE) concept (LiTFSI in water up to 21 mol kg -1), which leverages the low water activity and subnanometer water clusters at super-concentrations. Because the fluorinated salts needed for WISE have oral/dermal toxicity and high cost, the study turns to cost-effective, soluble, and widely available salts: NaAc and KAc, which were combined in a binary system. The authors fix the KAc concentration at 20 mol kg -1 and vary the NaAc concentration across four electrolytes (1, 2.5, 5, 7 mol kg -1 NaAc), plus a 1 M NaAc comparison. The most concentrated solution (7N20K) is the preferred WISE candidate, achieving a compromise between transport and electrochemical stability. Key results: The 7N20K electrolyte shows a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm -1 at 25°C and an electrochemical stability window up to 3 V in flooded three-electrode cells with small surface area/highly electrocatalytic electrodes. A carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 NASICON electrode demonstrates reversible Na + intercalation at ~ -0.7 V vs. SHE, with first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g -1 (104 mAh g -1 in specific capacity context, see discrepancy noted), average charge efficiency of 96% (99% at high current), and 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles. Impedance spectroscopy reveals a low charge transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV, and diffusion coefficient ~ 10 -13 cm2 s -1, suggesting strong kinetic-thermal coupling and that the aqueous electrolyte improves ion diffusion inside the NASICON structure. The paper uses DSC, rheology (VTF/Arrhenius), conductivity (EIS), and LSV to characterize the solutions, and GCPL with impedance to evaluate the NASICON/electrolyte interface, concluding that these acetate systems support the WISE approach for rechargeable alkaline-ion batteries.

Research Context
The study targets the safety and cost limitations of conventional non-aqueous organic carbonate electrolytes used in LIBs. The conventional LiPF6 electrolyte is thermally unstable and can degrade to form corrosive HF in the presence of moisture. Aqueous electrolytes are proposed to alleviate these challenges because they are non-flammable, less toxic, and cost-effective. A major limitation of aqueous electrolytes is the narrow thermodynamic electrochemical stability window (ESW) of water at 1.23 V. The water-in-salt electrolyte (WISE) concept was developed to extend the ESW to 3 V via super-concentration. Enhanced ESW in WISE stems from low water activity at high concentrations where ions outnumber water molecules. Wider ESW electrolytes are typically made from per-fluorinated sulfonyl imide salts like LiTFSI, NaOTF, KOTF, etc. However, fluorinated salts carry unresolved environmental/economic concerns: oral/dermal toxicity and very high cost. Finding suitable cost-effective, soluble salts that satisfy the WISE condition is the main challenge for new formulations. Cost-effective alternatives include LiCl, NaAc, and KAc, with KAc being investigated for potassium-ion batteries and supercapacitors.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study asks whether KAc/NaAc binary electrolytes can be engineered into a water-in-salt electrolyte for sodium-ion batteries. The central research question addresses the physicochemical properties of these binaries at a constant 20 mol kg -1 KAc and variable NaAc. Hypothesis: Increasing NaAc concentration will expand the electrochemical stability window of the aqueous electrolyte. Hypothesis: The most concentrated solution (7N20K) will provide the best compromise between transport and stability. Predicted: Higher salt concentration shifts glass transition to higher temperatures, correlating to stronger ion-solution interactions. Predicted: Transport and rheological mechanisms (VTF/Arrhenius) will correlate with the glass transition behavior. The work intends to prove that a carbon-coated NASICON electrode can reversibly insert Na + in this WISE electrolyte. A prediction is that Na + ions will be preferentially introduced into the NASICON anode in a mixed-cation electrolyte.

Methodological Details
Four binary electrolytes were prepared: NaAc plus KAc at 1, 2.5, 5, and 7 mol kg -1 NaAc, all with 20 mol kg -1 KAc. An additional 1 M NaAc solution was prepared as a diluted comparison. Salts were 99% purity from Alfa Aesar and dissolved in high-quality Milli-Q water (sigma = 6.7 umS cm -1) under sonication. Electrolytes were stored and used at room conditions. Carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 NASICON (CLTP) was synthesized via a one-pot sol gel route. Phosphate precursor NH4H2(PO4)3 (1.78 g) dissolved in 40 ml ethanol with Ti(OC4H9)4 (3.51 g) as Ti source. CH3COOLi (0.52 g) and C6H12O6 (0.58 g) added as lithium and carbon sources, then stirred 4 h at 55 deg C. Temperature raised to 80 deg C to yield a gel; dried under vacuum at 100 deg C; then calcined at 800 deg C for 6 h under argon. The calcination ramp rate was 5 deg C min -1 with gas flow at 50 ml min -1. Pristine LiTi2(PO4)3 (LTP) was synthesized without glucose. XRD was performed using Rigaku Miniflex 600 (Cu Kalpha) over 10-80 degrees, step size 0.02, scan speed 1 deg min -1. SEM used Zeiss Gemini SEM 450. Viscosity measured with MCR Rheometer 102 (Anthon Paar) using parallel plates (50 mm) at shear rates 10-300 s -1. Temperature measurements for viscosity at 10, 20, 30, and 40 deg C. Thermal analysis with Mettler Toledo DSC 1Star, sample range -120 to 90 deg C. DSC cooling at 1 deg C min -1 from 30 to -120 deg C; 5 min isotherm; heating at 1 deg C min -1 to 90 deg C. Conductivity measured via EIS in a dip probe cell with two platinum foils; cell factor 1.04 cm -1; range 1 Hz to 200 kHz; amplitude 25 mV. Samples degassed with nitrogen; measured under N2 flux over 5 to 70 deg C in a climatic chamber. For benchmarking, CLTP/LTP were characterized in organic electrolytes with PVDF:carbon-black in 8:1:1 wt ratio and NMP solvent. Active material loads were ~2.4, ~2.7, and ~1.7 mg cm -2 for Li, Na, K-based cells; ~6 mg cm -2 for aqueous-coated cells. ESW measured in flooded three-electrode cells: glassy carbon working, Pt mesh counter, double junction SCE reference. GCPL at various current rates; 1C corresponds to 136 mA g -1 for insertion of two alkaline ions. EIS at 1 kHz to 100 kHz; voltage 50 mV; under N2 in flooded three-electrode; in a Faraday cage.

Procedures And Architectures
Electrolyte samples: four binaries plus 1 M NaAc, all dissolved in Milli-Q under sonication. DSC: samples equilibrated at 30 deg C for 30 min to ensure fully liquid state; structure-making salt behavior. Conductivity: bulk ohmic resistance via x-axis intercept of high-frequency side of Nyquist plots. Rheology: VTF equation fits; viscosity follow Arrhenius behavior due to limited temp range. Walden plot: molar vs. fluidity (eta -1) at 25 deg C; Kohler-Laux law at 25 deg C. LSV: decomposition threshold 0.1 mA cm -2; quasi-ideal electrocatalytic electrode with small surface area. GCPL for electrochemical stability: starting at 0.1 C for 10 cycles, then increasing to 0.5, 1, 5, 10 C, then reducing. Charge transfer kinetics: EIS at temperature steps 20-70 deg C; R CT,inf charge transfer resistance at infinite temperature. Diffusion coefficient: calculated from Warburg coefficient; gas constant R, Faraday's constant F; n=1.7 ions; concentration 12930 mol cm -3; sigma W.

Key Results
DSC shows Tg below -70 deg C, Tc below -20 deg C, Tm around 0 deg C; Tg shifts higher with concentration. 7N20K electrolyte shows a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm -1 at 25 deg C (Table 2). 7N20K stability window reaches up to 3 V in flooded three-electrode conditions with small surface area. 7N20K cathode/anode capacity: first cycle anodic capacity 85 mAh g -1; 104 mAh g -1 in specific context. Average charge efficiency 96% at low current; 99% at high current (C-rate 1C at 136 mA g -1). Capacity retention 90% after 60 cycles in WISE; 68 mAh g -1 average anodic capacity at 1C. 7N20K capacity is ~2.85 times higher than potassium in mixed-cation context (from capacity values comparison). Diluted solution: cathodic/anodic capacities 96/36 mAh g -1 with 40% efficiency (decreased). Activation energy for charge transfer is low: 0.12 eV (impedance/temperature data). Diffusion coefficient at room temp ~ 10 -13 cm2 s -1; diffusion easily improved by temperature. 7N20K follows Kohlrausch's law for strong electrolytes at 25 deg C. Cathodic decomposition (hydrogen evolution) strongly suppressed as concentration increases; anodic less so. 7N20K liquidus is well below room temperature, preventing salt crystallization during long cycling.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Tg increase correlates to stronger ion-water interactions; solution transitions from salt-in-water to water-in-salt. Ionic conductivity decreases with concentration due to increased viscosity from Tg shift. T0 (vanishing mobility temperature) agrees with DSC Tg; suggests formation of internal water-salt structures. Water-salt structures limit anion (CH3COO -) solvation, modifying local hydrogen bonding. Viscosity rises with concentration, following Arrhenius behavior rather than Stokes-Einstein. OAc systems are structure-making salts: no viscosity decrease with concentration. Reduced water activity reduces water solvation, ordering cations and acetate anions. Quasi-ideal electrolytes: high temperature improves ideality. Kohlrausch law predicts complete salt dissociation even at highest concentrations (Lambda_0 = 52.90 ohm -1 cm2 mol -1). Suppressed hydrogen evolution (cathodic suppression) confirms reduced water activity. NASICON rhombohedral (R-3c) structure, JCPDS: 35-0754; carbon content doesn't affect crystal. Sodium preferred over potassium in the anode in mixed-cation electrolyte. Aqueous electrolyte improves ion diffusion inside electrode structure.

Contradictions And Limitations
7N20K capacity listed 85 mAh g -1 vs 104 mAh g -1 (Figure 7); discrepancy exists. LSV threshold 0.1 mA cm -2 may overestimate limits due to small surface area electrode. Only four binary electrolytes plus comparison; sparse coverage of other salt/concentration combinations. Electrode preparation: carbon-loaded cells have higher load (~6 mg cm -2) vs benchmark (~2.4 mg cm -2); load effect. No random seed reported; temperature range limited by instrumental constraints affecting VTF fit. Charge transfer activation energy from impedance 0.12 eV vs 0.48 eV for diffusion improvement discrepancy. Supporting information referenced but not fully accessible to verify all claims. Only NASICON (LiTi2(PO4)3) tested; no other active materials or cathode systems.

Claims
Highly concentrated KAc/NaAc binary electrolytes (especially 7N20K) exhibit superior electrochemical stability window and ionic conductivity compared to diluted systems, enabling water-in-salt battery operation. 7N20K conductivity 21.2 mS cm -1 at 25 deg C. Stability window up to 3 V in flooded conditions. Reduced water activity suppresses hydrogen evolution. Viscosity follows Arrhenius, classifying acetate as structure-making. Molar conductivities follow quasi-ideal and Kohlrausch behavior. LSV limits may be overestimated due to small surface area. Anodic expansion less significant than cathodic. KAc/NaAc systems could displace perfluorinated salts in WISE electrolytes. Sodium-ion batteries could use these for safer, cheaper, alkaline-ion energy storage.
Carbon-coated NASICON electrodes couple with the 7N20K electrolyte to enable reversible sodium intercalation with good kinetics and capacity. First cycle anodic capacity 85 mAh g -1 in 7N20K. 104 mAh g -1 (specific capacity) in 7N20K. 99% charge efficiency at 1C; 90% capacity retention at 60 cycles. Low charge-transfer activation energy 0.12 eV. Aqueous electrolyte improves diffusion inside structure. Sodium preferred over potassium in mixed-cation context. Diluted solution capacity significantly lower: 96/36 mAh g -1. Carbon coating is essential to lower NASICON conductivity and permit good performance. Aqueous electrolytes could facilitate better ion transport inside NASICON.

Data And Code Availability
Supporting Information available for free: shear-stress-vs-shear-rate curves, XRPD patterns, SEM images, thermal analysis, additional electrochemical characterization in organic electrolytes. The paper provides the full dataset but does not explicitly state a code repository for analysis.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
VTF and Arrhenius behavior observed across concentration and temperature. Viscosity, conductivity, and Tg mechanisms are internally consistent. Control: 1 M NaAc solution prepared for comparison. Ablation: pristine LTP synthesized without glucose.

Ethical Considerations
No ethics statement or statement of ethical approval.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: DSC thermograms showing Tg, Tc, Tm shifting with concentration. Figure 2: Ionic conductivity vs. temperature (VTF behavior) and concentration. Figure 3: Viscosity vs. temperature (Arrhenius behavior) and concentration. Figure 4: Walden plot (molar vs. fluidity); quasi-ideal electrolytes; Kohlrausch law at 25 deg C. Figure 5: ESW vs. SHE profiles with 0.1 mA cm -2 threshold. Table 2: molar conductivity, activation energies, ionic conductivities, T0, and Tg values. Table 3: cathodic and anodic decomposition potentials. Figure 7: Na intercalation in carbon-coated NASICON in 7N20K and 1M NaAc. Figure 8: EIS spectra for charge transfer and diffusion.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: A highly concentrated aqueous KAc/NaAc binary electrolyte, particularly the 7N20K solution, can combine ~21 mS cm -1 conductivity with a 3 V electrochemical stability window, enabling water-in-salt sodium-ion batteries. 2. The strongest evidence: Carbon-coated NASICON reversibly inserts Na + at ~ -0.7 V vs. SHE with 85 mAh g -1 anodic capacity, 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles, and a low charge-transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV. 3. The future path: The low charge-transfer and diffusion activation energies suggest these interfaces could be engineered for alkaline-ion batteries in the water-in-salt approach, pending wider exploration of anode/electrolyte pairings.

summary.executive_summary: This methodological publication expands upon a previously reported proof-of-concept freeze-float selection platform designed to identify ice-nucleating entities in droplets, now re-engineered for high-throughput screening and increased accuracy. In the prior iteration, a 1 cm² cuvette geometry accommodated up to 50 × 1 μL droplets but was severely hampered by the low thermal conductivity of the silicone oil, which prevented footprint expansion without introducing significant thermal lag, and by the difficulty of running more than 5–10 cuvettes simultaneously, leading to inter-cuvette temperature variations of a few degrees. To scale this technology, the authors integrated three core improvements: (a) automated droplet generation via a robotic liquid transfer system to replace manual repeat pipetting; (b) a controlled-rate freezer to ensure uniform cooling and mitigate the cell-to-cell thermal gradient; and (c) a semi-automated droplet detection program. For high-throughput droplet-based assays, polydispersity is detrimental because freezing temperature scales with the logarithm of droplet radius, causing a predicted ~0.09 °C dispersion at this scale. The droplet polydispersity was measured at 9.2%, confirming sufficient uniformity. Throughput was expanded by replacing the 50-droplet cuvette with 48 cryovials of 40 droplets each, yielding 1920 droplets—a 38-fold throughput increase. Statistical rigor was established by concluding that more than 30 droplets are sufficient for reliable freezing temperature observation. Controlled-rate cooling lowered the cell-to-cell thermal delay from p = 4.4 × 10⁻⁷ in a commodity freezer at -28 °C to p = 0.31 in an Asymptote VIA freezer at a constant linear rate of -0.25 °C/min, despite a widening of freezing-time range (47.4 and 50.6 min). In the Asymptote freezer, droplets with ice nucleators (1 mg/mL Snomax) froze at -7.1 ± 0.59 °C, compared to -7.5 ± 0.97 °C in the commodity freezer; droplets without INA froze only at -12.3 °C. The Asymptote system improved well-to-well freezing uniformity (p = 0.83, standard deviation 0.73) against the commodity system (p = 0.31, standard deviation 1.6), reducing dispersion by 36%. A critical limitation emerged: during transport between laboratories, static electricity friction caused droplet coalescing, precluding a fully combined droplet-generation system. Overall, the system increases efficiency and accuracy, demonstrating that while automated generation and controlled cooling improve screening, droplet stability remains transport-sensitive.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This methodological publication expands upon a previously reported proof-of-concept freeze-float selection platform designed to identify ice-nucleating entities in droplets, now re-engineered for high-throughput screening and increased accuracy. In the prior iteration, a 1 cm² cuvette geometry accommodated up to 50 × 1 μL droplets but was severely hampered by the low thermal conductivity of the silicone oil, which prevented footprint expansion without introducing significant thermal lag, and by the difficulty of running more than 5–10 cuvettes simultaneously, leading to inter-cuvette temperature variations of a few degrees. To scale this technology, the authors integrated three core improvements: (a) automated droplet generation via a robotic liquid transfer system to replace manual repeat pipetting; (b) a controlled-rate freezer to ensure uniform cooling and mitigate the cell-to-cell thermal gradient; and (c) a semi-automated droplet detection program. For high-throughput droplet-based assays, polydispersity is detrimental because freezing temperature scales with the logarithm of droplet radius, causing a predicted ~0.09 °C dispersion at this scale. The droplet polydispersity was measured at 9.2%, confirming sufficient uniformity. Throughput was expanded by replacing the 50-droplet cuvette with 48 cryovials of 40 droplets each, yielding 1920 droplets—a 38-fold throughput increase. Statistical rigor was established by concluding that more than 30 droplets are sufficient for reliable freezing temperature observation. Controlled-rate cooling lowered the cell-to-cell thermal delay from p = 4.4 × 10⁻⁷ in a commodity freezer at -28 °C to p = 0.31 in an Asymptote VIA freezer at a constant linear rate of -0.25 °C/min, despite a widening of freezing-time range (47.4 and 50.6 min). In the Asymptote freezer, droplets with ice nucleators (1 mg/mL Snomax) froze at -7.1 ± 0.59 °C, compared to -7.5 ± 0.97 °C in the commodity freezer; droplets without INA froze only at -12.3 °C. The Asymptote system improved well-to-well freezing uniformity (p = 0.83, standard deviation 0.73) against the commodity system (p = 0.31, standard deviation 1.6), reducing dispersion by 36%. A critical limitation emerged: during transport between laboratories, static electricity friction caused droplet coalescing, precluding a fully combined droplet-generation system. Overall, the system increases efficiency and accuracy, demonstrating that while automated generation and controlled cooling improve screening, droplet stability remains transport-sensitive.

Research Context
In the prior study, a first proof-of-concept freeze-float selection system was reported. This system identified ice-nucleation events in droplets containing ice-nucleating entities. The geometry accommodated up to 50 × 1 μL droplets at once. Low thermal conductivity of the silicone oil limited container footprint. Thermal lag prevented increasing droplet counts without temperature uniformity loss. Multiple cuvettes gave non-uniform results with degree variations. High-throughput screening was originally developed for drug discovery. 3456-well plates enable >100,000 assays per day. Droplet-based assays reduce reagent use a million fold. Droplet-based assays yielded 300-folds increase in throughput.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can automated dispensing and controlled cooling increase throughput and accuracy? The freezing behavior follows a stochastic random nucleation process. Freezing spectra show inherent distributions with spread temperatures. Ice nucleators accelerate freezing in the presence of INA. A larger vessel capacity is predicted to boost throughput by a factor of 38. Controlled cooling should produce a more uniform temperature distribution. Linear cooling rates are predicted to improve uniformity.

Methodological Details
The system introduced the Biomek 3000 for automated droplet generation. The design uses a 96 deep well plate for high throughput. Each well received 30 × 1 μL droplets. Dispensing operated at a rate of 1 droplet per 2 seconds. A single pipetting arm generated 40 droplets in 96 wells. Up to ~3800 droplets could be generated at once. Droplets were made of silicone oil and fluorescein dye. Fluorescence was captured on a 12 well plate with ChemiDoc MP. Droplet radii polydispersity was measured using Matlab circle detection code. The droplets' standard deviation of the radii was 9.2%. A large-scale assay uses 48 cryovials of 40 droplets each. The assay contains 1920 droplets in total. Samples contained 1 mg/mL Snomax marked with fluorescein. The controlled-rate freezer is an Asymptote VIA instrument. Each vial held 1 mL silicone oil with 1% surfactant. A metal cooling plate achieved homogeneous vial-to-vial cooling. The system was equipped with a custom-made glass lid. The detection was done with a generic digital camera.

Procedures And Architectures
The Biomek 3000 replaced manual repeat pipetting. A standard dispensing rate was 1 droplet per 2 seconds. The Biomek was purged of static electricity before dispensing. An ion pump removed the charge from the Biomek. Wet filter paper minimized static electricity during movement. Droplets were made of silicone oil and INA. Droplet dispersion was analyzed by circle detection. Freezing distributions were compared with KStest.ipynb. The KS-test yielded the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test p-values. Samples were placed in 48 cryovials of 40 droplets each. Cryovials held 50 μL of HFE-7500 cushion. Each vial contained 1 mL of silicone oil. The freezer cooled at a constant rate. The instrument was equipped with a custom lid.

Key Results
Droplet polydispersity was confirmed at 9.2%. Constant cooling at -28 °C gave a very low p-value. Linear cooling raised the p-value to 0.31. Freezing times in the cells varied (47.4 and 50.6 min). INA-containing droplets froze at -7.1 0.59 °C. INA-free droplets froze only at -12.3 °C. The commodity freezer gave -7.5 0.97 °C. The Asymptote freezer gave a p-value of 0.83. Asymptote freezing showed a standard deviation of 0.73. Asymptote freezing had 36% lower dispersion. The throughput increased by the factor of 38. The controlled-rate freezer improves detection of INA.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Freezing follows a stochastic freezing behavior model. Constant rate cooling improves temperature uniformity. The controlled-rate freezer improves detection of INA. The controlled-rate cooling lowered the cell-to-cell thermal delay.

Contradictions And Limitations
Static electricity friction caused droplet coalescing during transport. Coalescence of the droplets hindered the combined system. Droplet stability was not sufficient for transport. The droplets coalescing precluded a combined system. The system failed to combine generation and screening. Low thermal conductivity still limits the cuvette footprint. The formula is an approximation (y = ln(x) -26.8). The polydispersity of the droplets can directly influence accuracy.

Claims
Automated dispensing enables large-scale uniform droplets, increasing throughput and reducing polydispersity. The Biomek 3000 generated droplets in a 96 deep well plate. Throughput increased by the factor of 38. Droplet polydispersity was confirmed at 9.2%. Static electricity caused by frictions. Coalescence of the droplets hindered the system. The system can be implemented to the high throughput system.
Controlled cooling improves temperature uniformity and ice-nucleation detection accuracy. Linear cooling raised the p-value to 0.31. The Asymptote freezer had 36% lower dispersion. The controlled-rate cooling improved detection of INA. It significantly increased the range of freezing time. Controlled cooling rate provided better detection of INA.

Data And Code Availability
Source Code S1 implements circle detection. Source Code S3 computes the KStest. KStest.ipynb compares freezing temperature distributions. Droplet_Dispersion.m is the Matlab circle detection program. Matlab automated circle detection is available as code.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Constant cooling used a constant temperature of -28 °C. Linear cooling operated at -0.25 °C/min. A p-value of 4.4×10 -7 was observed for constant cooling. A p-value of 0.31 was observed for linear cooling. Static electricity was discharged by an ion pump. An ion pump model is Ion Pump (#19500, Charles Water, MA). A wet filter paper reduced static electricity.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 A-B shows robotic droplet dispensing by Biomek 3000. Figure 1C shows fluorescence imaging of the 12-well plate. Figure 1 D-E shows Matlab automated circle detection. Figure 2 validates the freeze-float system behaviour. Figure 3 compares constant and linear cooling distributions. Figure 4 shows Asymptote controlled-rate freezing temperatures. Figure 5 compares well-to-well freezing distributions. Figure 6 shows a 36% reduction in dispersion.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the factor of 38 throughput increase. 2. The strongest evidence is the 36% lower dispersion. 3. The future path faces static electricity causing coalescence.

summary.executive_summary: This study reports a continuous flow protocol for the radical cation-initiated dimerization of electron-rich alkenes using organophotoredox catalysis, providing a convenient synthetic route to carbazole cyclobutane materials and styrene-based natural products. By merging homogeneous small-molecule, sustainable organophotoredox catalysis with a commercial off-the-shelf continuous flow platform, the authors performed a batch versus continuous flow study that demonstrates higher chemical yields and significantly reduced reaction times compared to traditional batch conditions. The method was applied to synthesize the cyclobutane dimer t-DCzCB, a host material for blue electrophosphorescence and PhOLEDs, as well as a series of novel functional analogues and the lignan natural product magnosalin. The key advantage is the ability to deliver cyclobutane dimers under flow at a very low catalyst loading of only 0.1 mol%, nearing the efficiencies of Ru- and Ir-photoredox systems while bypassing the excessive reaction times and cryogenic requirements often seen with prior organophotoredox dimerizations. The scope was expanded to bromocyclobutane building blocks, showing improved isolated yields over batch and the ability to functionalize the products via Suzuki-Miyaura crosscoupling. The methodology also produced a new family of cyclobutane carbazoles bearing functionality for materials exploitation and delivered a scalable synthesis of the lignan natural product magnosalin without needing cryogenic temperatures. Key limitations include the problematic synthesis and low-yield isolation of the 15a substrate, which gave no cyclobutane product, and the reversal of selectivity in entry 17b where batch outperformed flow. The study concludes that continuous flow provides scalability, reproducibility, and efficiency benefits for photoredox dimerizations, opening new routes to both synthetic functional materials and natural products.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports a continuous flow protocol for the radical cation-initiated dimerization of electron-rich alkenes using organophotoredox catalysis, providing a convenient synthetic route to carbazole cyclobutane materials and styrene-based natural products. By merging homogeneous small-molecule, sustainable organophotoredox catalysis with a commercial off-the-shelf continuous flow platform, the authors performed a batch versus continuous flow study that demonstrates higher chemical yields and significantly reduced reaction times compared to traditional batch conditions. The method was applied to synthesize the cyclobutane dimer t-DCzCB, a host material for blue electrophosphorescence and PhOLEDs, as well as a series of novel functional analogues and the lignan natural product magnosalin. The key advantage is the ability to deliver cyclobutane dimers under flow at a very low catalyst loading of only 0.1 mol%, nearing the efficiencies of Ru- and Ir-photoredox systems while bypassing the excessive reaction times and cryogenic requirements often seen with prior organophotoredox dimerizations. The scope was expanded to bromocyclobutane building blocks, showing improved isolated yields over batch and the ability to functionalize the products via Suzuki-Miyaura crosscoupling. The methodology also produced a new family of cyclobutane carbazoles bearing functionality for materials exploitation and delivered a scalable synthesis of the lignan natural product magnosalin without needing cryogenic temperatures. Key limitations include the problematic synthesis and low-yield isolation of the 15a substrate, which gave no cyclobutane product, and the reversal of selectivity in entry 17b where batch outperformed flow. The study concludes that continuous flow provides scalability, reproducibility, and efficiency benefits for photoredox dimerizations, opening new routes to both synthetic functional materials and natural products.

Research Context
Cyclobutane dimers are formed via a radical cation-mediated [2+2]-cycloaddition of electron-rich alkenes. Prior synthetic routes required heavy metal oxidation with Fe(III) or Ce(IV) salts. Organophotoredox catalysis is a metal-free sustainable alternative to metal-based catalysts. Prior organophotoredox dimerizations used loadings typically near 3 mol%. Prior Ru- and Ir-photoredox systems achieved loadings as low as 0.025%. Photoredox dimerizations often required excessive reaction times and cryogenic conditions. Continuous flow technology improves irradiation efficiency and can raise conversion. A metal-free, polymeric carbon-nitride flow process was reported for magnosalin.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether continuous flow can deliver cyclobutane materials with low loading and reduced time. The hypothesis is that flow reduces catalyst loading to 0.1 mol% and reaction times compared to batch. It was expected that flow would provide a convenient synthetic route to t-DCzCB. The authors anticipated the protocol would be convenient and environmentally beneficial over conventional batch chemistry. Flow was expected to deliver scalability advantages for host materials and natural products.

Methodological Details
The starting material for flow optimization was commercial vinyl carbazole (VCZ). The reference batch conditions used an organophotoredox catalyst at 3 mol%. The batch conditions required deoxygenated acetone, cryogenic temperatures, and extended reaction times. The flow platform was a commercial, off-the-shelf, continuous flow platform. Optimization used HPLC-analysis with p-terphenyl as an internal standard. Optimal flow conditions used 2 mol% catalyst and irradiation at 450 nm. Flow rate for entry 1 was 0.5 mL.min -1 with tau = 20 min. Substrates 12a-24a were synthesized via the method of Obora and coworkers. Solubility issues required reducing concentration to 0.2 M in acetone. Dimerizations were performed at a 10 mmol scale of 2. For styrenes, an electron relay (anthracene) was added at 0.25 eq. HPLC and NMR were used for analysis; 1 H NMR detected entry 15b. The catalyst was a pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst.

Procedures And Architectures
Optimal synthesis realized at flow rate of 0.5 mL.min -1 with tau = 20 min. Catalyst loading of 2 mol% and irradiation at 450 nm define the reference. Entry 2 increased catalyst loading to 4.5 mol%. Entry 3 lowered catalyst loading to 1 mol%. Entry 4 lowered flow rate from 5 mL.min -1 to 2 mL.min -1. Entry 6 reduced flow rate to 0.1 mL.min -1 with tau = 100 min. Two further wavelengths were probed at 405 nm and 420 nm. The dimerizations required only 0.1 mol% of 10 at 0.5 mL.min -1 for entry 11. Entry 11 was performed at a 10 mmol scale. Concentrations were reduced from 0.4 M to 0.2 M in acetone.

Key Results
Batch synthesis provided t-DCzCB in 82% isolated yield. Flow entry 1 (optimal conditions) gave 98% isolated yield. Increasing catalyst loading to 4.5 mol% reduced yield to 90%. Lowering catalyst loading to 1 mol% yielded 93%. Lowering flow rate to 2 mL.min -1 reduced yield to 79%. Flow at 2 mL.min -1 with 1 mol% catalyst gave 82% yield. Flow at 0.1 mL.min -1 (tau = 100 min) dropped yield to 53%. Entry 11 at 0.1 mol% loading gave 79% isolated yield. Dimerization 12b gave 64% yield from flow vs 48% from batch. Dimerization 13b gave 71% from flow vs 31% from batch. 13b flow was completed in a considerably shorter time-period. 14b flow gave improved isolated yields over batch. 15a yielded no cyclobutane product in flow or batch. 16b gave 65% isolated yield under continuous flow. 2,7-dibromo-9vinylcarbazole 17b favored batch over flow. 2-chloro-9vinylcarbazole dimerized to 18b in 61% yield. 2-methoxy-9vinylcarbazole dimerized to 19b in 45% yield. 2-hydroxycarbazole dimerization to 21b gave 25% yield. 4-fluoroarylated cyclobutane 22b gave 65% yield. Tetra-alkyl cyclobutyl dimer 23b gave 57% yield. Bisarylated cyclobutane 24b gave 50% yield. Suzuki coupling of 13b gave cyclobutane 25 in 75% yield. Borylation gave cyclobutane 26 in 36% yield. 4-methoxystyrene dimerized to 28 in 44% isolated yield. Styrene with diethylaniline gave pellucidin A in 22% yield. E-aserone gave magnosalin 4 in 40% isolated yield.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The mechanism is a radical cation-mediated [2+2]-cycloaddition. Formation of carbazole stemmed from background oxidation by oxygen. Flow-rate dependence signals reversibility of the dimerization reaction. Continuous flow is scalable and reduces times and loading. Flow offers a path to novel host materials and natural products. The protocol sidesteps cryogenic conditions and long reaction times.

Contradictions And Limitations
15a was difficult to isolate and gave very low yields. 15a gave no observed cyclobutane product. Substrate 17b favored batch dimerization over continuous flow. Solubility in acetone was challenging at 0.4 M. No data was provided on catalyst recovery or recycling. The comparison of loading to Ru-systems remains illustrative.

Claims
Continuous flow drastically reduces reaction times and catalyst loadings for cyclobutane formation. Reaction times were reduced significantly compared to traditional batch. Batch required cryogenic temperatures and extended times. Flow entry 11 used only 0.1 mol% catalyst at 0.5 mL.min -1. Flow entry 11 gave 79% isolated yield. Entry 17b favored batch over continuous flow. Entry 15a gave no cyclobutane product in either mode. Flow provides a scalable and reproducible route. Lower loadings make organophotoredox competitive with metal systems. Reduced time and cold-free conditions improve practicality.
The protocol delivers a broad scope of substituted carbazoles and styrenes as cyclobutane dimers. Bromides 12b, 13b, 16b were dimerized with improved yields. 18b, 19b, 22b, 23b, 24b were dimerized in flow. Styrenes 28, 29, 4 were dimerized in flow. New functionality can be exploited as materials. 15a proved very challenging and gave no cyclobutane. The range of substrates was not systematically fully screened. The method enriches the carbazole host material library. Functional handles enable post-modification and polymerization.
Flow delivers a scalable synthesis of the natural product magnosalin. Magnosalin was made on a 10 mmol scale. Magnosalin gave 40% isolated yield. Flow did not require cryogenic temperatures. 40% is a modest yield for the natural product. Flow enables scalable natural product synthesis. This showcases flow benefits over batch for biocatalysis.

Data And Code Availability
No data or code availability was stated in the paper.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Reversibility was probed by lowering flow rate from 5 mL.min -1 to 2 mL.min -1. The yield dropped from 82% to 79% when flow rate was reduced. Extreme flow reduction (0.1 mL.min -1) reduced yield to 53%. Wavelength sensitivity was tested at 405 nm and 420 nm. These wavelengths gave yields comparable to 450 nm.

Ethical Considerations
No ethics statements were provided.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 presents the continuous flow optimization study across catalyst loadings and flow rates. Table 1 shows optimal yield was 98% at 2 mol% catalyst loading. Table 1 shows yields for 1 mol% (93%), 4.5 mol% (90%), and 0.1 mol% (79%). Schemes 1-7 present the synthetic routes and reaction profiles.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a continuous flow, organophotoredox protocol delivering cyclobutane dimers. 2. The strongest evidence is the 0.1 mol% catalyst loading giving 79% isolated yield in flow. 3. The future path lies in novel functional host materials and scalable natural products.
