summary.executive_summary: This computational study explores how molecular-scale nanoparticle morphology tunes the dielectric response of nanocomposite materials, specifically silver (Ag) inclusions in a magnesium oxide (MgO) matrix. The authors motivate the work by the increasing demand for high-permittivity dielectric materials for energy storage, computing power, and quantum devices, noting that traditional single-phase materials like Si/SiO2 reach limits when miniaturized to few-nanometer scales where current leakage and tunneling dominate. Nanocomposite (NC) materials, which combine standard dielectric matrices with mid- and high-kappa or even conducting inclusions, offer highly tunable dielectric and mechanical properties. The authors use a silver cluster of 8 atoms (Ag8) as a reference, which provides a range of unique features: insulating, no band structure, and lower percolation thresholds than traditional metallic nanoparticles. Molecular nanoparticles (mNPs) are source of highly polarizable electron density whose quantum behavior requires quantum mechanical treatments. Prior work by this group using the modern theory of polarization and Car-Parinello Molecular Dynamics (CPMD) found that significant interfacial effects between an Ag8 inclusion and the MgO matrix produced greater-than-expected polarization response. In this follow-up study, the authors model the polarization of Ag mNPs in MgO, considering trends in nanoparticle size, shape (rod-like and disk-like inclusions), and orientation relative to the applied field. They find that at mNP scales of fewer than 30 atoms the size, shape, and orientation of the inclusion greatly alter how the inclusion electrons behave and affect atomic-scale polarization. Dielectric permittivity enhancements of 30–100% were observed with inclusion sizes varying from 8 to 32 atoms, considering both rod-like and disk-like inclusions, with alignment either parallel or perpendicular to the external field. For Ag/MgO NCs with rod-like and disk-like inclusions, the multi-layer disks (disks 332, 432, and 442) exhibited more than 70% enhancement in dielectric constant over the matrix permittivity at similar volume loading, while a single spherical Ag8 inclusion produced a ~30% increase at ~4% volume ratio. The authors note that the calculated values are volume averages and do not capture surface charge or edge effects, and inclusion loading ratios were kept between 3–5% to preserve sufficient matrix separation. They also address a quantum of polarization effect where electron polarization shifts by nxboxlength, equivalent to creating a distortion of the simulation cell as described by Spaldin. Key results show that perpendicular orientation produces a much larger depolarization field around the nanoparticle that never decays to normal bulk values, lowering the average dielectric constant, while parallel orientation enhances induced polarization at the interface. Born effective charge maps visualize the local electrostatic fields, showing that the shape influences the reach and strength of induced polarization. The authors conclude that interfacial effects of these nanoparticles are the most important, as they can isolate the interfacial effect because nanoparticles are encapsulated by the matrix. Future work would expand into other matrix materials like SiO2 and HfO2, and other transition metal inclusions like Cu, Co, and Fe.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This computational study explores how molecular-scale nanoparticle morphology tunes the dielectric response of nanocomposite materials, specifically silver (Ag) inclusions in a magnesium oxide (MgO) matrix. The authors motivate the work by the increasing demand for high-permittivity dielectric materials for energy storage, computing power, and quantum devices, noting that traditional single-phase materials like Si/SiO2 reach limits when miniaturized to few-nanometer scales where current leakage and tunneling dominate. Nanocomposite (NC) materials, which combine standard dielectric matrices with mid- and high-kappa or even conducting inclusions, offer highly tunable dielectric and mechanical properties. The authors use a silver cluster of 8 atoms (Ag8) as a reference, which provides a range of unique features: insulating, no band structure, and lower percolation thresholds than traditional metallic nanoparticles. Molecular nanoparticles (mNPs) are source of highly polarizable electron density whose quantum behavior requires quantum mechanical treatments. Prior work by this group using the modern theory of polarization and Car-Parinello Molecular Dynamics (CPMD) found that significant interfacial effects between an Ag8 inclusion and the MgO matrix produced greater-than-expected polarization response. In this follow-up study, the authors model the polarization of Ag mNPs in MgO, considering trends in nanoparticle size, shape (rod-like and disk-like inclusions), and orientation relative to the applied field. They find that at mNP scales of fewer than 30 atoms the size, shape, and orientation of the inclusion greatly alter how the inclusion electrons behave and affect atomic-scale polarization. Dielectric permittivity enhancements of 30–100% were observed with inclusion sizes varying from 8 to 32 atoms, considering both rod-like and disk-like inclusions, with alignment either parallel or perpendicular to the external field. For Ag/MgO NCs with rod-like and disk-like inclusions, the multi-layer disks (disks 332, 432, and 442) exhibited more than 70% enhancement in dielectric constant over the matrix permittivity at similar volume loading, while a single spherical Ag8 inclusion produced a ~30% increase at ~4% volume ratio. The authors note that the calculated values are volume averages and do not capture surface charge or edge effects, and inclusion loading ratios were kept between 3–5% to preserve sufficient matrix separation. They also address a quantum of polarization effect where electron polarization shifts by nxboxlength, equivalent to creating a distortion of the simulation cell as described by Spaldin. Key results show that perpendicular orientation produces a much larger depolarization field around the nanoparticle that never decays to normal bulk values, lowering the average dielectric constant, while parallel orientation enhances induced polarization at the interface. Born effective charge maps visualize the local electrostatic fields, showing that the shape influences the reach and strength of induced polarization. The authors conclude that interfacial effects of these nanoparticles are the most important, as they can isolate the interfacial effect because nanoparticles are encapsulated by the matrix. Future work would expand into other matrix materials like SiO2 and HfO2, and other transition metal inclusions like Cu, Co, and Fe.

Research Context
The demand for new high-κ dielectric materials is increasing for energy storage and computing devices. Traditional single-phase materials reach a limit when miniaturized to few-nanometer sizes. Nanocomposite materials offer highly tunable dielectric and mechanical properties. Previous Si/SiO2 gate manufacturing gave way to higher-permittivity materials. Effective medium approximations are suitable for macroscale mixtures only. Classical atomistic approaches do not encompass the quantum response. A complete treatment of the quantum polarization of the mixed material has not been attempted until recently. Prior work by this group used the modern theory of polarization to model mNP NCs. A previous Ag8/MgO model found significant interfacial effects produced greater-than-expected polarization. There is a background gap in understanding how nanoparticle morphology alters induced charge.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how the size, shape, and orientation of mNP inclusions alter atomic-scale polarization. The hypothesis is that smaller mNPs behave as molecules and tune dielectric response without bulk metallic properties. The prediction is that alignment parallel to the field enhances permittivity, while perpendicular alignment lowers it. Larger inclusions and asymmetric shapes are predicted to yield non-linear enhancements relative to volume ratios. Interfacial effects between inclusion and matrix are hypothesized to dominate the response. A size threshold at which exponential growth changes as inclusion behaves more metallic is predicted. The predicted outcomes include 30-100% permittivity enhancement across varying sizes and shapes. The hypothesis extends to other transition metal inclusions and other matrix materials. The study assumes that the volume occupied by an inclusion atom equals matrix ion volume. It is hypothesized that the induced field's reach depends on electron dynamics at the interface.

Methodological Details
The study models molecular-scale silver inclusions in a magnesium oxide matrix. MgO is an inert material with a bulk dielectric constant of 8-9.8 and bandgap of 7.8 eV. MgO has a cubic crystal structure and isotropic polarization. Models were built using the Avogadro software. The study considered three rod-like and five disk-like inclusions. Inclusions were built on an ideal Ag fcc lattice and optimized in CPMD. The matrix extended 2 Mg-O layers beyond the inclusion edge in each direction. The CPMD method was implemented in the Quantum Espresso code. The Quantum Espresso versions used were 6.0 and 6.6. A plane wave-basis set was built using the LDA functional. Mg atoms were described using Bachelet-Hamann-Schluter norm-conserving pseudopotentials. O and Ag were described using ultra-soft pseudopotentials from MaterialsCloud. The total energy convergence criteria was set to 10^-8. A force threshold of 10^-4 was used. A wavefunction cutoff of 50-60 Ry and charge density cutoff of 560 Ry were used. Electron masses were increased from 300 a.u. to 450 a.u. All calculations were done with periodic boundary conditions. The Brillouin zone was sampled at the Γ point. A thermostat was not applied and temperatures were not controlled. A static field of 0.001 a.u. was applied along the z-axis. The %loading ratios of inclusions to matrix were kept between 3-5%.

Procedures And Architectures
Relaxed atomic and electronic structure was found using CPMD in optimization steps. Steps included electron minimization with Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization and damped dynamics. An additional step relaxed lattice vectors to remove stress on the cell. The process consists of two major stages: structure relaxation and polarization. The dielectric constant is calculated according to Equation 1. Equation 1 is ε_r = 1 + 4π(P_ε_damped - P_ε_relax) / ε_field. Damped dynamics gave the ionic polarization, and relaxed electronic structure gave electronic polarization. Reference polarization was calculated for the cell without an applied field. Electronic polarization couples to ionic positions in the clamped-ion step. Full relaxation was achieved by releasing ionic clamps while applying the field. The Born effective charge was calculated as the difference in force between zero-field and polarization. Forces were normalized to the bulk matrix to highlight the NP effect. A smeared BEC plot visualized the forces on each atom. The polarization was calculated using the Umari and Pasquarello method.

Key Results
The Ag8/MgO single inclusion gave ~30% permittivity increase at ~4% volume ratio. Asymmetric rod- and disk-like inclusions further enhanced the dielectric response. Disk inclusions with 332, 432, and 442 showed >70% dielectric constant enhancement. Disk442 had twice the x,y dimensions of Rod223 but >twice the polarization increase. Rod-shaped inclusions with polarization along the z-axis showed a greater increase at 9.23. Rod-like inclusions increased polarization from bulk at 12.48. The polarization field was enhanced adjacent to the NP poles along the applied field. A depolarization field arose in the equatorial region where the ionic charge decreased. Perpendicular polarization gave a much larger depolarization field around the nanoparticle. The perpendicular depolarization area affected only the interfacial atoms. Disk nanoparticles showed direction and shape effects to an increased degree. The 3D nanoparticles showed a higher polarization than similarly sized rods. 2D nanoparticles showed a decrease in polarization relative to the bulk in both directions. Induced field reach was further physically and stronger when oriented parallel to the field. The perpendicular BEC converged to +2, -2 values of the matrix over a short distance. Dielectric permittivity enhancements of 30-100% were observed with inclusion sizes 8-32 atoms. The induced field always appeared perpendicular to the direction of polarization. When direction effects dominate, the calculated dielectric constant was lower than for pure matrix.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Molecular-scale inclusions behave as molecules and not bulk metal, enabling electron dynamics modeling. Induced fields at the matrix-inclusion interface arise from the polarization of mNPs. Interfacial effects are the most important, as inclusion encapsulates the nanoparticle. Increasing atoms aligned to the field increases charge density and effective polarizability. The shape influences the reach and strength of the induced polarization. The perpendicular response can dominate, lowering the overall calculated dielectric constant. Induced fields at the nanoscale enable understanding of quantum materials as they miniaturize.

Contradictions And Limitations
The calculated ε_r is a volume average and not a true material dielectric constant. The volume-averaged values omit surface charge and edge effects of the periodic material. Dielectric constants in real materials are volume and %loading dependent. The inclusion loading was kept between 3-5% to preserve matrix separation. Wannier functions for nanoparticles >8 atoms were unable to converge due to delocalization. The distortion of the inclusion extended only to around 3 angstroms from the edge. DFT performance should be compared to nanoparticles rather than bulk materials. Computational constraints limit the study to mNPs up to a threshold. The inclusion volume was reported in numbers of atoms, not real volume. The exact value of nxboxlength for polarization jumps is not reported. A random seed for simulation reproduction is not reported. The training and test split for any model is not reported.

Claims
Molecular-scale silver inclusions in MgO tune the dielectric constant via shape and orientation. Rod- and disk-like inclusions gave 30-100% permittivity enhancement. Disk442 gave more than 70% dielectric enhancement over the matrix. Asymmetric inclusions enhance response beyond what volume ratios alone predict. Disk nanoparticles showed higher polarization than similarly sized rods. A spherical Ag8 inclusion produced only ~30% enhancement. The perpendicular response can lower the calculated dielectric constant. Interfacial effects isolate the nanoparticle-induced response. Future work could use these findings to explore other transition metals and matrices.
Quantum of polarization effects arise in periodic systems with distorted inclusion lattices. The calculated polarization shifts by nxboxlength equal to Spaldin. The matrix is deformed by larger, unsymmetrical inclusions. More polarization corrections were needed as the matrix is deformed. The high-symmetry previous model did not suffer distortion effects. Correcting for these jumps is required to obtain reliable effective polarization.
The Born effective charge maps visualize the local induced polarization and depolarization fields. The polarization field was enhanced adjacent to the NP poles. A depolarization field arose in the equatorial region. The perpendicular depolarization field affected only the interfacial atoms. The depolarization field never decays to normal bulk values. BEC maps are useful tools for spatial manipulation of induced fields.

Data And Code Availability
Methods are implemented in the Quantum Espresso code. No explicit code or data repository is cited in the text.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
DFT bandgap is generally lower than experimental values with LDA. Density of states near the Fermi level is populated by NP states. Wannier functions did not converge for nanoparticles larger than 8 atoms.

Ethical Considerations
No ethical approval or conflict of interest is reported.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the Ag12 inclusion in the MgO matrix. Table 1 presents dielectric constants for rod- and disk-like inclusions. Figure 4 shows the electronic structure and polarization steps. Figure 5 illustrates the QuantumEspresso polarization steps. Figure 6 shows the mathematical corrections for polarization jumps. Figure 9 shows the smeared BEC plot of forces.

Three Takeaways
1. Molecular-scale silver inclusions in MgO can enhance the dielectric constant by 30–100% through shape and size. 2. Asymmetric, disk-like inclusions outperform spherical ones and rod-like inclusions at similar volume loading. 3. Perpendicular orientation creates a non-decaying depolarization field that lowers the calculated dielectric constant.

summary.title: Learning design rules for selective oxidation catalysts from highthroughput experimentation and artificial intelligence
summary.authors: Lucas Foppa; Christopher Sutton; Luca M Ghiringhelli; Sandip De; Patricia Löser; Stephan A Schunk; Ansgar Schäfer; Matthias Scheffler
summary.field_subfield: Catalysis / Materials science with machine learning / AI
summary.type_of_paper: Research article reporting a methodology and results
summary.executive_summary: The design of heterogeneous catalysts is challenged by the complexity of materials and processes that govern reactivity and by the fact that the number of good catalysts is very small compared to the number of possible materials. Here, we show how the subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence approach can be applied to an experimental plus theoretical data set to identify constraints on key physicochemical parameters, the so-called SG rules, which exclusively describe materials and reaction conditions with outstanding catalytic performance. By using high-throughput experimentation, 120 SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten and phosphorus were synthesized and tested in the catalytic oxidation of propylene. As candidate descriptive parameters, the temperature and ten parameters related to the composition and chemical nature of the catalyst materials, derived from calculated freeatom properties, were offered. The temperature, the phosphorus content, and the composition-weighted electronegativity are identified as key parameters describing high yields towards the value-added oxygenate products acrolein and acrylic acid. The SG rules not only reflect the underlying processes particularly associated to high performance but also guide the design of more complex catalysts containing up to five elements in their composition. The SG rules derived from three-component materials were applied to four- and five-component materials, capturing a five-component catalyst with ruthenium, tungsten, phosphorus, tellurium, and tantalum that presents an oxygenate yield more than twice as large as any observation in the training data set. Further SGD analysis on the four- and five-component HTE data identified a rule-based subgroup constraining three parameters: temperature, a coordination-weighted distance, and electron-affinity-based electronegativity, with higher thresholds compared to the three-component case. The approach circumvents explicit modelling of the full catalytic progression by using product yield as the target and avoids extensive experimental characterization by using first-principles-calculated free-atom properties as candidate descriptors. Overall, the SGD-HTE-&-theory approach enables the discovery of interpretable, chemically meaningful, and complex patterns associated with exceptional performance and suggests generalizable rules for designing complex, high-performance, multi-element catalysts.

As candidate descriptive parameters, the temperature and ten parameters related to the composition and chemical nature of the catalyst materials, derived from calculated freeatom properties, were offered. The temperature, the phosphorus content, and the composition-weighted electronegativity are identified as key parameters describing high yields towards the value-added oxygenate products acrolein and acrylic acid. The SG rules not only reflect the underlying processes particularly associated to high performance but also guide the design of more complex catalysts containing up to five elements in their composition. The SG rules derived from three-component materials were applied to four- and five-component materials, capturing a five-component catalyst with ruthenium, tungsten, phosphorus, tellurium, and tantalum that presents an oxygenate yield more than twice as large as any observation in the training data set. Further SGD analysis on the four- and five-component HTE data identified a rule-based subgroup constraining three parameters: temperature, a coordination-weighted distance, and electron-affinity-based electronegativity, with higher thresholds compared to the three-component case. The approach circumvents explicit modelling of the full catalytic progression by using product yield as the target and avoids extensive experimental characterization by using first-principles-calculated free-atom properties as candidate descriptors. Overall, the SGD-HTE-&-theory approach enables the discovery of interpretable, chemically meaningful, and complex patterns associated with exceptional performance and suggests generalizable rules for designing complex, high-performance, multi-element catalysts.

120 SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten and phosphorus were synthesized and tested. Similar SG rules are obtained when training is performed with 90% of the data. Yield-based SG rules are insensitive to varying data thresholds. The SGD-HTE-&-theory approach extracts interpretable, chemically meaningful, and complex design rules from hybrid experimental and theoretical data. summary.title: Mechanochemical synthesis of eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell (calcite) and KH2PO4
summary.authors: Roger Borges; Amanda Soares Giroto; Rodrigo Klaic; Fernando Wypych (Universidade Federal do Paraná); Caue Ribeiro
summary.field_subfield: Materials chemistry and agrochemical engineering / green chemistry
summary.executive_summary: The present study reports a mechanochemical synthesis of calcium phosphate bioceramics from eggshell waste and monobasic potassium dihydrogen phosphate, positioned as an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective route within the concept of reverse logistics for a circular economy. Eggshells are major food industry wastes, disposed in landfills with no pretreatment and producing odors. The study aims to synthesize potassium calcium phosphate phases as smart release fertilizers that delay the bioavailability of phosphorus and potassium while improving calcium solubility when applied to soil, particularly at pH ~ 5 where many country soils reside. Using a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste and KH2PO4, the research produces K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4 phases. The process is solvent-free and produces no unwanted subproducts, offering huge savings in the production process. The precursors are reacted via solid-state activation using friction and impact forces to form a new structure. The synthesized bioceramics, composed of fertilizer components (HPO42-, PO43-, Ca2+, K+), were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) magic-angle spinning (MAS), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). Solubility and release behavior were assessed in citric acid (wt 2%) and in soil. The products exhibited slower release of potassium and phosphorus than the precursor KH2PO4 in both citric acid and soil assays, while calcium release was accelerated. In soil, potassium release mirrored the precursor at 30 days, but phosphorus release was significantly delayed, recovering only 15% at 30 days compared to 40% from the precursor. Radial phosphorus diffusion for the 2 h/600 rpm sample reached a value of 1.99 cm, intermediate between struvite (slow) and KH2PO4 (fast). Calcium release increased to 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days, about 8% recovery, which corroborated the citric acid results and indicated hydroxyapatite formation, further delaying phosphorus and calcium release in acidic soil. The authors report this as a new, eco-friendly route that avoids hydroxyapatite synthesis from phosphoric acid and produces potassium calcium phosphates with potassium as a main component. Limitations include characterization described only in supplementary material, no controlled pH assays, characterization of only one soil type (sandy soil), a release assay at a single citric acid concentration (2 wt%), and the lack of a code repository or random seed. The method relies on the literature-reported pseudo-second order model for kinetic fitting.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The present study reports a mechanochemical synthesis of calcium phosphate bioceramics from eggshell waste and monobasic potassium dihydrogen phosphate, positioned as an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective route within the concept of reverse logistics for a circular economy. Eggshells are major food industry wastes, disposed in landfills with no pretreatment and producing odors. The study aims to synthesize potassium calcium phosphate phases as smart release fertilizers that delay the bioavailability of phosphorus and potassium while improving calcium solubility when applied to soil, particularly at pH ~ 5 where many country soils reside. Using a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste and KH2PO4, the research produces K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4 phases. The process is solvent-free and produces no unwanted subproducts, offering huge savings in the production process. The precursors are reacted via solid-state activation using friction and impact forces to form a new structure. The synthesized bioceramics, composed of fertilizer components (HPO42-, PO43-, Ca2+, K+), were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) magic-angle spinning (MAS), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). Solubility and release behavior were assessed in citric acid (wt 2%) and in soil. The products exhibited slower release of potassium and phosphorus than the precursor KH2PO4 in both citric acid and soil assays, while calcium release was accelerated. In soil, potassium release mirrored the precursor at 30 days, but phosphorus release was significantly delayed, recovering only 15% at 30 days compared to 40% from the precursor. Radial phosphorus diffusion for the 2 h/600 rpm sample reached a value of 1.99 cm, intermediate between struvite (slow) and KH2PO4 (fast). Calcium release increased to 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days, about 8% recovery, which corroborated the citric acid results and indicated hydroxyapatite formation, further delaying phosphorus and calcium release in acidic soil. The authors report this as a new, eco-friendly route that avoids hydroxyapatite synthesis from phosphoric acid and produces potassium calcium phosphates with potassium as a main component. Limitations include characterization described only in supplementary material, no controlled pH assays, characterization of only one soil type (sandy soil), a release assay at a single citric acid concentration (2 wt%), and the lack of a code repository or random seed. The method relies on the literature-reported pseudo-second order model for kinetic fitting.

Research Context
Eggshells are a major food industry biowaste produced in millions of tons worldwide. These eggshells are disposed in landfills with no pretreatment and produce odors. Reverse logistics is an instrument of economic and social development that enables waste restitution. This instrument is perfectly applied in the agriculture context. The goal is to synthesize calcium and potassium phosphates from any source of calcium carbonate. These phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers, delaying nutrient bioavailability. Previous hydroxyapatite synthesis typically used a phosphoric acid solution instead of powder phosphate salts. As far as the authors know, no such mechanochemical process has been reported for this product type.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a free-solvent mechanochemical process can produce potassium calcium phosphates from eggshells and KH2PO4. The primary hypothesis is that solid-state activation initiates a new chemical structure. It is predicted that K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 will be the main products. The products are hypothesized to delay the bioavailability of phosphorus and potassium. They are also expected to improve the bioavailability of calcium. These materials are predicted to be a useful source at pH ~ 5.

Methodological Details
Eggshells were collected by the authors, washed with water and dried at room temperature. They were presented with a diameter between 1 and 10 mm before grinding. Milling was performed with a high-energy Fritsch Pulverisette 7 ball mill. The mill used a 250 ml zirconia bowl and 5 zirconia balls. A weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4 was used. Essays were performed at 600 rpm and across multiple time intervals from 15 min to 24 h. Speed sweeps were performed at 100, 200, 400 and 600 rpm for 2 h. The mixture corresponded to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. Milled samples were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD). Further characterization included NMR, TGA, and DSC. Details of each characterization are described in Supplementary Material. Nutrient content was obtained by acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 at 250 °C. Before release essays, the material was pelletized at a pressure of 5 bar. The pellets were standardized to 100 mg/L of P. One single pellet was used in each assay in triplicate. The release assay used 300 mL of 2% citric acid solution. Soil assays used Petri dishes of diameter of 8.6 cm. Each dish contained 78 g of dry and sieved 2.0 mm mesh soil. The soil was adjusted to a desired density of 1.2 g.cm -3. To reach 70% water retention, 15 mL of deionized water were added. Images were analyzed with GNU Image Manipulation Program. Soil release assays were carried out under 75% water saturation. Soil samples used 50 g of sandy soil. Nutrient extraction used HCl at 0.05 Mol/L and KCl at 1 Mol/L. Phosphorus was extracted using the Mehlich 1 method. Calcium and potassium were quantified by flame atomic absorption spectroscopy. The FAAS used a PerkinElmer PinAAcle 900T instrument.

Procedures And Architectures
XRD patterns were registered in the angular range of 3-40°. Analysis used a Cu Kα incident beam with a scanning speed of 2°. Data was collected at 30 kV voltage and 40 mA current. DSC used a refrigerated cooling system with the TA Q100 Controller. Samples were thermally degraded in the 25°C -600°C range. DSC analysis used an air flow of 60 mL.min -1. TGA used a range of ~20 to 900 °C at 10°C.min -1. The TGA was operated at a flow rate of 60/40 mL/min. NMR analysis used a Bruker Avance III HD instrument. Samples were rotated at 10KHz using the sequence HPDEC. The chemical shift reference was ADP at 0.8 ppm. The Citric acid release assay was closed with a PVC film. Aliquots of 1.2 mL were collected to evaluate the release. The release kinetics were fitted with multiple models.

Key Results
XRD confirmed a mixture of phosphates produced after milling. The main phase formed was K3CaH(PO4)2. A secondary phase was possibly CaKPO4. K3CaH(PO4)2 matched PDF database n° 22-1218. CaKPO4 matched PDF database n° 33-1002. Bellow 2 h/400 rpm, only the reactants diffraction patterns were found. The KH2PO4 residual mass was 89%. The theoretical KPO3 residual was 87%. The eggshell residual mass was 56%. The theoretical CaCO3 residue was 59%. Milled samples showed mass losses at 280 °C, 420 °C and 710 °C. The 600 rpm samples showed similar thermal decomposition. NMR of KH2PO4 gave a single signal at δ = 3.74 ppm. The precursor signal is characteristic of monosubstituted phosphate. The 2 h/600 rpm samples shifted to δ = 3.28 ppm. The disubstituted phosphate signal appeared at δ = 0.74 ppm. A pyrophosphate dimer signal appeared at δ -5 ppm. Phosphorus and potassium correlated best with the pseudo-second order model. KH2PO4 released 107 mg/kg after 3 days of soil release. The precursor accounted for 40% of total P released. The 2 h/600 rpm sample released 45 mg/kg after 30 days. The sample accounted for 15% of total P recovered. P radial diffusion for the sample reached a value of 1.99 cm. Precursor P radial diffusion reached 2.62 cm. Calcium release reached 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days. This corresponded to around 8% of calcium recovery. Hydroxyapatite matched PDF database n° 9-432. Hydroxyapatite was identified from 3 until 30 days in soil. Calcium release was accelerated compared to the eggshell.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The potassium calcium phosphates are smart release fertilizers. The delayed P and K supply is attributed to phosphate phases. Calcium release is accelerated by the newly formed phosphates. Hydroxyapatite formation is linked to slow-release calcium and phosphorus. Hydroxyapatite becomes systematically soluble under natural soil pH acidification. The product is an important long-term slow release fertilizer. The concept plays on the solubility of Ca, K and P.

Contradictions And Limitations
Characterization details are contained only in the Supplementary Material. No controlled soil pH assays were performed in the study. The soil release assays were conducted only in sandy soil. A single citric acid concentration (wt 2%) was used for release. The study did not report a random seed or train-test split. The study did not provide a code repository or data access.

Claims
Free-solvent mechanochemistry produces potassium calcium phosphate bioceramics from eggshells as smart release fertilizers. K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4 are formed. The products correlate with the pseudo-second order model. NMR signals shifted from monosubstituted to calcium phosphate forms. Only a minimal energy initiates the reaction. Milling bellow thresholds recovers only reactants. The materials are an excellent alternative in nutrient management. They avoid hydroxyapatite synthesis from phosphoric acid.
The milled products delay potassium and phosphorus release compared to the precursor.  The products showed a slower release character. The 2 h/600 rpm sample released 15% of total P. The precursor released 40% of total P. Calcium release was accelerated rather than delayed. Potassium release mirrored the precursor at 30 days. These materials improve calcium bioavailability. The mechanism is linked to phosphate dimerization.
Hydroxyapatite forms in soil conditions and slows calcium and phosphorus release. Hydroxyapatite was identified in soil assays. The phase appeared from 3 until 30 days in soil. Hydroxyapatite is an important slow release fertilizer. Calcium release increased to 8% recovery at 30 days. Fast release can be obtained with nanocomposites. Hydroxyapatite is systematically soluble under acidification. Nanocomposites could be used for faster release.

Data And Code Availability

summary.title: Environmentally friendly and roll-processed flexible organic solar cells based on PM6:Y6
summary.authors: Marcial Fernández Castro; Jean Truer; Espíndola Rodríguez; Jens Wenzel
summary.executive_summary:
This paper reports on the fabrication and optimization of environmentally friendly, roll-process compatible flexible organic solar cells (OSCs) based on the PM6:Y6 non-fullerene acceptor system, achieving power conversion efficiencies of 6.3% (binary) and 7.2% (ternary). The central objective was to close the "lab-to-fab gap"—the performance difference between lab-scale devices made on small active areas (<0.1 cm²) and industrially-compatible large-area devices. Spin-coating, the conventional lab method, produces substantial material waste and cannot be upscaled. To address this, the authors adopted slot-die coating on flexible, lightweight substrates, which is compatible with roll-to-roll manufacturing, to minimize waste and allow large-scale production. For the environmentally friendly upscaling, o-xylene (O-XY) was used as a green solvent without additives.

The PM6:Y6 system was chosen because the non-fullerene acceptors allow energy-level tuning and wider absorption, with PM6 matching the solar spectrum's peak irradiance and Y6 complementing the red part. However, the PM6 material exhibits temperature-dependent aggregation (TDA), requiring the slot-die head and related components to be heated to keep it liquid throughout the coating procedure. To overcome this, the authors implemented a "hot slot-die" approach, matching the flexible substrate temperature with that of the hot slot-die head at 100 °C.

The study optimized three key processing parameters: coating temperature, active layer thickness, and acceptor composition. Coating temperatures were screened from 60 to 120 °C, with the optimum fixed at 100 °C to maximize PCE by reducing bimolecular recombination. The active layer thickness was explored via four concentrations (12 to 28 mg/mL), leading to an optimal thickness around 217 nm (24 mg/mL), which yielded the highest PCE of 6.3%. Finally, a small amount of a fullerene acceptor (PC61BM) was added to form ternary blends at ratios of 1:1:0.2 and 1:1.1:0.1, raising the champion efficiency to 7.2% and increasing the short-circuit current density to up to 20 mA/cm².

A key mechanistic insight was gained from recombination analysis: the S value closest to unity (0.978) at 100 °C and the high slope values (higher than kT/q) indicate that while bimolecular recombination was minimized at the optimal temperature, trap-assisted recombination dominated, consistent with open-air processing without cleanroom conditions. Efficiency improvements were quantified via dissociation and collection probabilities, with ternary blends significantly improving both. Stability tests under the ISOS-D-1 protocol showed over 1500 hours of dark storage with >97% PCE retention for binary devices and 99.4% for ternary devices. The work demonstrates a scalable path toward commercializing high-performance, flexible, green-solvent processed OSCs.

Executive Summary
This paper reports on the fabrication and optimization of environmentally friendly, roll-process compatible flexible organic solar cells (OSCs) based on the PM6:Y6 non-fullerene acceptor system, achieving power conversion efficiencies of 6.3% (binary) and 7.2% (ternary). The central objective was to close the "lab-to-fab gap"—the performance difference between lab-scale devices made on small active areas (<0.1 cm²) and industrially-compatible large-area devices. Spin-coating, the conventional lab method, produces substantial material waste and cannot be upscaled. To address this, the authors adopted slot-die coating on flexible, lightweight substrates, which is compatible with roll-to-roll manufacturing, to minimize waste and allow large-scale production. For the environmentally friendly upscaling, o-xylene (O-XY) was used as a green solvent without additives.

The PM6:Y6 system was chosen because the non-fullerene acceptors allow energy-level tuning and wider absorption, with PM6 matching the solar spectrum's peak irradiance and Y6 complementing the red part. However, the PM6 material exhibits temperature-dependent aggregation (TDA), requiring the slot-die head and related components to be heated to keep it liquid throughout the coating procedure. To overcome this, the authors implemented a "hot slot-die" approach, matching the flexible substrate temperature with that of the hot slot-die head at 100 °C.

The study optimized three key processing parameters: coating temperature, active layer thickness, and acceptor composition. Coating temperatures were screened from 60 to 120 °C, with the optimum fixed at 100 °C to maximize PCE by reducing bimolecular recombination. The active layer thickness was explored via four concentrations (12 to 28 mg/mL), leading to an optimal thickness around 217 nm (24 mg/mL), which yielded the highest PCE of 6.3%. Finally, a small amount of a fullerene acceptor (PC61BM) was added to form ternary blends at ratios of 1:1:0.2 and 1:1.1:0.1, raising the champion efficiency to 7.2% and increasing the short-circuit current density to up to 20 mA/cm².

A key mechanistic insight was gained from recombination analysis: the S value closest to unity (0.978) at 100 °C and the high slope values (higher than kT/q) indicate that while bimolecular recombination was minimized at the optimal temperature, trap-assisted recombination dominated, consistent with open-air processing without cleanroom conditions. Efficiency improvements were quantified via dissociation and collection probabilities, with ternary blends significantly improving both. Stability tests under the ISOS-D-1 protocol showed over 1500 hours of dark storage with >97% PCE retention for binary devices and 99.4% for ternary devices. The work demonstrates a scalable path toward commercializing high-performance, flexible, green-solvent processed OSCs. 

Research Context
Organic Solar Cells (OSCs) have reached their highest lab-scale efficiencies on devices far below 0.1 cm². This tends to widen the so-called lab-to-fab gap between lab and industrial production. The conventional spin-coating fabrication technique has poor upscaling potential and causes waste. Blade or slot-die coating are suitable for roll-to-roll manufacturing, unlike silicon cells. Only few studies report OSCs using these industrial fabrication techniques. Environmentally friendly upscaling requires non-hazardous green solvent systems. Slot-die coating of PM6:Y6 with o-xylene without additives was chosen. There is still a need to transfer PM6:Y6 devices to roll-processing on flexible substrates. The PM6 material exhibits temperature-dependent aggregation behavior that needs heated coating. The PM6:Y6 material is a good candidate for minimizing the gap between processes.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can high-efficiency PM6:Y6 devices be made via roll-processing on flexible substrates? PM6:Y6 material is expected to be a good candidate for minimizing the gap. PM6 requires heated coating because it exhibits temperature-dependent aggregation behavior. OSCs can be manufactured using large-scale compatible processes on flexible lightweight substrates. High efficiencies using scalable techniques bring the technology to the edge of commercialization. The PM6 absorption matches well the highest spectral irradiance point of the solar spectrum. Y6 complements the absorption in the red part of the spectrum. We hope to contribute to reducing the lab-to-fab gap.

Methodological Details
The PM6:Y6 material combination is a good candidate for minimizing the gap. The materials involved in this study were used directly without purification. PM6 (batch YY19260CH100) and Y6 (batch DW7038S) were purchased from 1-Material Inc. PB61BM (batch M111) was purchased from Ossila. The ZnO Electron Transport Layer was made from ZnO nanoparticle ink (Sigma-Aldrich). MoO3 pellets were purchased from Kurt J. Lesker Co. The flexible substrate was pre-patterned ITO-coated polyethylene terephthalate (PET). Silver for the back electrode was pure silver bought from Sigma-Aldrich. Silver paste for printing was a heat-curing paste (DuPont 5025). The green solvent was O-XY with a ≥ 98% purity. The ETL and active layer are coated using a homemade roll-coater. A syringe pump controlled the flow rate of the inks. A hot tube was used to bring the AL from the syringe to the slot-die head. The ZnO nanoparticle ink ETL was coated at a substrate temperature of 75 °C. ZnO was coated at a 0.06 mL/min flow rate and a drum speed of 1.08 m/min. ZnO was then annealed in an oven at 100 °C for 10 min in air. The AL PM6:Y6 (ratio 1:1) was coated at different temperatures and concentrations. Temperatures were screened from 60 to 120 °C with the head, drum, tube at the same temperature. The drum speed was kept at 1.5 m/min and flow at 0.12 mL/min. 10 nm of MoO3 (HTL) and 150 nm of Ag were thermally evaporated. Evaporation was done at a base pressure of 2 x 10 -5 mbar. Different parts of the one-meter-long AL were selected to fabricate solar cells. Up to 24 solar cells are fabricated per evaporation. At least 8 devices are then encapsulated. The devices have an approximate active area of 0.8 cm 2. Activation used a reverse bias current (-5 V with a maximum current of 100 mA). Encapsulation used an epoxy-based glue, EPXR. Curing was made under UV light for approximately 5 min. Curing temperature reaches 66 ± 0.5 °C during the process. J-V curves were measured with a Keithley 2400 source meter. The simulator was calibrated to 1000 W/m 2 with a reference cell. Measurements were taken under AM1.5G illumination. A shadow mask (E2002A1) defined an aperture area of 0.3996 cm 2. Averages include statistics of eight devices. EQE and absorbance measurements were done with a QEX10 system. Measurements spanned from 300 to 1100 nm with a 5 nm step size. Intensity was increased from 62.14 mW/cm 2 to 147.33 mW/cm 2. Thickness measurements used a DS95-50 AFM instrument. The dimension of the scans is a 5 × 5 µm 2 surface.

Procedures And Architectures
The device follows an inverted geometry: ITO/ZnO/PM6:Y6/MoO3/Ag. The ZnO ETL and AL were coated using a homemade roll-coater. A syringe pump controlled the ink flow rate. A hot tube brought the AL from the syringe to the slot-die head. ZnO ETL was coated at substrate temperature of 75 °C, then annealed. AL was coated at the slot-die head temperature, matching the drum and tube. The donor and acceptor packing were influenced by the coating temperature. Recombination was analyzed through light intensity dependence of current and voltage. The bimolecular recombination was investigated using Jsc ∝ Pin S. The S value closest to unity (S = 0.978) was at 100 °C. Open-circuit recombination mechanism was extracted from the slope of VOC versus In(Pin). The slope was compared to kT/q to identify recombination type. Trap-assisted recombination is the dominant mechanism when slopes exceed kT/q. Four different AL thicknesses were investigated across a concentration range. The maximum absorption of the donor is at 625 nm. The maximum of the acceptor is at 820 nm. Ternary blends were tested at [1:1:0.2] and [1:1.1:0.1] PC61BM ratios. The PC61BM amount was reduced by half for the [1:1.1:0.1] ratio. A 12% higher JSC was obtained from the [1:1:0.2] ternary blend. Dissociation and collection probabilities were calculated from Jsc/Jsat and Jmax/sat. The dissociation probability is 93.7% for the binary device. The collection probability is improved from 69.6% for the binary device. Trap-assisted recombination was attributed to non-cleanroom, open-air processing. The ISOS-D-1 protocol was used for dark stability testing. Ternary PCE retained 99.4% after 1050 hours of dark storage. Binary devices retained more than 97% after more than 1500 hours.

Key Results
Coating temperature was optimized from 60 °C to 120 °C. The PCE improved towards higher temperature but saturated around 100 °C. At 100 °C the average PCE was slightly higher than at 120 °C. The lowest average FF of 42.2% was for devices coated at 120 °C. High-temperature drying induced aggregation on both edges of the AL. The S value closest to unity (S = 0.978) was at 100 °C. All obtained slope values are higher than kT/q, indicating trap-assisted recombination. The average PCE increases as the AL thickness increases from 101 nm. Short-circuit current reaches its maximum at 154 nm (17.3 mA/cm 2 ) of AL thickness. The FF improved from 42.0% for the thinnest AL to 47.1% for 116 nm of AL. The highest PCE in the thickness optimization is 6.3% with an FF of 49.0%. The average PCE for that AL thickness is 5.8%. A 12% higher JSC was obtained from the [1:1:0.2] ternary blend. The ternary devices achieved average PCEs of 6.6% and 6.7%. The ternary [1:1.1:0.1] blend had an average higher FF of 49.1%. Short-circuit current reached up to 20 mA/cm 2 in the ternary blends. The dissociation probability is 93.7% for the binary device. The collection probability improved from 69.6% for the binary device. The ternary device retained 99.4% of the average initial PCE after 1050 hours. Binary devices retained more than 97% after more than 1500 hours. The champion efficiency was 7.2% for the ternary PM6:Y6:PCBM devices.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Higher coating temperatures induce better carrier collection and a higher current. Rapid drying induces material aggregation on the AL edges, hurting fill factor. Thermal annealing improves devices coated at low temperatures via crystallinity. Adding PCBM enhances the dissociation probability and charge collection efficiency. PC61BM has a LUMO between -3.7 and -3.9 eV, creating an energy cascade. The energy cascade effect enhances both the short-circuit current and open-circuit voltage.

Contradictions And Limitations
The average FF remains around 45% with a 42.2% low at 120 °C. High-temperature processing may create inhomogeneities that hurt the fill factor. Devices were not prepared in a cleanroom or inside a glovebox. There is not a clear tendency in the S values. Trap-assisted recombination is high in open-air processed flexible devices. The paper uses PM6:Y6 in a configuration whose optimal conditions were not yet known.

Claims
Slot-die coating on roll-platform is feasible for PM6:Y6 OSCs on flexible substrates in open-air and green solvent. The ZnO ETL and AL were coated using a homemade roll-coater. Slot-die coated flexible devices based on PM6:Y6 were fabricated in open-air. The fabrication and optimization were done through slot-die coating on a roll-platform. Only few studies report OSCs using these fabrication techniques. This paves the way for upscaling the production of OSCs based on PM6:Y6.
Matching the substrate and head temperature at 100 °C maximizes PCE by reducing bimolecular recombination. The S value closest to unity (S = 0.978) is obtained by coating at 100 °C. The PCE shows a clear improvement trend towards higher coating temperature. The optimal temperature was fixed at 100 °C. The devices fabricated at 100 °C and 120 °C do not improve after annealing. Higher temperature processing may impact favorably molecular packing and texture.
Introducing a small fullerene acceptor enhances dissociation probability and collection efficiency in OSCs on flexible substrates. The dissociation probability is 96.3% and 95.7% for ternary devices. The collection probability is improved from 69.6% for the binary device. A 12% higher JSC is obtained from the [1:1:0.2] ternary blend. The EQEs do not show any specific photocurrent maximum at a specific wavelength. Better charge extraction can be achieved with a small acceptor fullerene amount.
Open-air, green-solvent processing maintains high stability over 1500 hours under ISOS-D-1 protocol. The ternary device retained 99.4% of the average initial value. Binary devices retained more than 97% after more than 1500 hours. The stability under dark storage follows the ISOS-D-1 protocol. Some devices showed improved performance after storage time. This supports a practical, environmentally friendly and stable path toward OSC commercialization.

Data And Code Availability
The paper does not report a specific data or code availability statement.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
AL coating temperature was screened from 60 to 120 °C matching the drum and tube. The D/A ratio was fixed at 1:1 throughout the study. The amount of PC61BM was reduced by half to [1:1.1:0.1] for optimization. The thickness optimization was performed across four different concentrations. The thickness optimization was performed across four different concentrations.

Ethical Considerations
No specific ethics approval or ethical oversight is reported.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 presents average PV parameters extracted from J-V curves. Table 2 summarizes PV parameters of PM6:Y6 -based solar cells. Table S2 reports average ternary device values. Table S3 reports ηdiss and ηcoll from Jsc/Jsat and Jmax/sat. Figure S2 shows absorption measurements of dried blend films. Figure S5 shows JSC and VOC for thickness optimization. Figure S6a investigates bimolecular recombination via Jsc ∝ Pin S. Figure S6b reports the trap-assisted recombination as dominant. Figure 1 shows PM6 and Y6 absorption spectra. Figure 7 compares binary and ternary PV parameters in a box plot.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first slot-die coated flexible PM6:Y6 devices in open-air with green solvent. 2. The strongest evidence is the 6.7% ternary PCE and 99.4% PCE retention over 1050 hours. 3. The future path is to upscale production via roll-to-roll slot-die coating on flexible substrates.

    *executive_summary draft:*
    This paper reports on the fabrication and optimization of environmentally friendly, roll-process compatible flexible organic solar cells (OSCs) based on the PM6:Y6 non-fullerene acceptor system, achieving power conversion efficiencies of 6.3% (binary) and 7.2% (ternary). The central objective was to close the "lab-to-fab gap"—the performance difference between lab-scale devices made on small active areas (<0.1 cm²) and industrially-compatible large-area devices. Spin-coating, the conventional lab method, produces substantial material waste and cannot be upscaled. To address this, the authors adopted slot-die coating on flexible, lightweight substrates, which is compatible with roll-to-roll manufacturing, to minimize waste and allow large-scale production. For the environmentally friendly upscaling, o-xylene (O-XY) was used as a green solvent without additives.

    The PM6:Y6 system was chosen because the non-fullerene acceptors allow energy-level tuning and wider absorption, with PM6 matching the solar spectrum's peak irradiance and Y6 complementing the red part. However, the PM6 material exhibits temperature-dependent aggregation (TDA), requiring the slot-die head and related components to be heated to keep it liquid.

    The study optimized three key processing parameters: coating temperature, active layer thickness, and acceptor composition. Coating temperatures were screened from 60 to 120 °C, with the optimum fixed at 100 °C. The active layer thickness was explored via four concentrations (12 to 28 mg/mL), leading to an optimal thickness around 217 nm (24 mg/mL), giving the highest PCE of 6.3%. Finally, a small amount of a fullerene acceptor (PC61BM) was added to form ternary blends at ratios of 1:1:0.2 and 1:1.1:0.1, raising the champion efficiency to 7.2% and increasing short-circuit current to up to 20 mA/cm².

    A key mechanistic insight was gained from recombination analysis: the S value closest to unity (0.978) at 100 °C and the high slope values (higher than kT/q) indicate that while bimolecular recombination was minimized at the optimal temperature, trap-assisted recombination dominated, consistent with open-air processing without cleanroom conditions. Efficiency improvements were quantified via dissociation and collection probabilities, with ternary blends significantly improving both. Stability tests under the ISOS-D-1 protocol showed over 1500 hours of dark storage with >97% PCE retention for binary and 99.4% for ternary devices.

summary.title: Stable open-shell aromatic nitric acid radicals: accessing highly efficient photothermal conversion with restricted radiative decay
summary.authors: Zejun Wang; Jiawen Zhou; Yiheng Zhang; Weiya Zhu; Yuan Li
summary.executive_summary: The authors design and synthesize a series of star-shaped aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs) to address the instability of open-shell radicals and the limited availability of high-performance organic-small-molecule photothermal conversion materials. Most open-shell radicals are thermodynamically or kinetically unstable in air due to incomplete valency; the authors argue that aromatic nitric acid radicals exhibit high electrochemical and thermal stability because their resonance structures include both closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide structures with unpaired electrons delocalized in conjugated backbones. They prepared these materials via facile demethylation and consequent oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl precursors in air. The resulting ANARs exhibit extremely high spin concentration and highly enhanced nonradiative decay, making them strong photothermal conversion candidates. Among the four synthesized materials—TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8—TPA-TPA-O6 exhibited the highest photothermal conversion performance and negligible photobleaching in seawater desalination. Under 1 sun irradiation, the water evaporation efficiency of TPA-TPA-O6 was 89.41% with a water evaporation rate of 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹, representing top performance for pure organic small-molecule photothermal materials. The study uses CV, UV-vis-NIR spectroscopy, ESR, and photothermal tests to characterize the materials. TPA-TPA-O6 was established as an interface heating evaporation system on white polyurethane (PU) foam, achieving an equilibrium temperature of 81.2 °C under continuous irradiation (2.0 cm diameter foam with 30 mg loading). The study emphasizes the low-cost, easy-synthesis nature of the ANARs versus expensive alternatives like CR-TPE-T. Seawater desalination was verified with reductions in all four primary ions (Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, K⁺). The paper frames this as a novel strategy for stable high-spin radical materials applicable in solar-driven water evaporation, photothermal therapy, photothermal catalysis, organic electronics, spintronics, and magnetic devices. The supporting information is available free of charge at the ACS URL, but the bibliography is not provided in the source, necessitating empty citations.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The authors design and synthesize a series of star-shaped aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs) to address the instability of open-shell radicals and the limited availability of high-performance organic-small-molecule photothermal conversion materials. Most open-shell radicals are thermodynamically or kinetically unstable in air due to incomplete valency; the authors argue that aromatic nitric acid radicals exhibit high electrochemical and thermal stability because their resonance structures include both closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide structures with unpaired electrons delocalized in conjugated backbones. They prepared these materials via facile demethylation and consequent oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl precursors in air. The resulting ANARs exhibit extremely high spin concentration and highly enhanced nonradiative decay, making them strong photothermal conversion candidates. Among the four synthesized materials—TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8—TPA-TPA-O6 exhibited the highest photothermal conversion performance and negligible photobleaching in seawater desalination. Under 1 sun irradiation, the water evaporation efficiency of TPA-TPA-O6 was 89.41% with a water evaporation rate of 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹, representing top performance for pure organic small-molecule photothermal materials. The study uses CV, UV-vis-NIR spectroscopy, ESR, and photothermal tests to characterize the materials. TPA-TPA-O6 was established as an interface heating evaporation system on white polyurethane (PU) foam, achieving an equilibrium temperature of 81.2 °C under continuous irradiation (2.0 cm diameter foam with 30 mg loading). The study emphasizes the low-cost, easy-synthesis nature of the ANARs versus expensive alternatives like CR-TPE-T. Seawater desalination was verified with reductions in all four primary ions (Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, K⁺). The paper frames this as a novel strategy for stable high-spin radical materials applicable in solar-driven water evaporation, photothermal therapy, photothermal catalysis, organic electronics, spintronics, and magnetic devices. The supporting information is available free of charge at the ACS URL, but the bibliography is not provided in the source, necessitating empty citations.

Research Context
Open-shell radicals are usually thermodynamically or kinetically unstable in air because of incompletely satisfied valency. Phenol radicals without steric hindrance protection, aromatic nitric acid radicals exhibit high electrochemical and thermal stability. Compared to inorganic materials, organic two-dimensional frameworks and conjugated polymers, organic small molecules are relatively overlooked in photothermal conversion. Organic small molecules have excellent structural definiteness and convenient preparation, but their open-shell radicals are rarely reported. Preparing stable neutral radicals is the prerequisite for realization of multifunctional application.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can aromatic nitric acid radicals be prepared without steric hindrance protecting groups and be stable enough for air-stable photothermal application? The hypothesis is that star-shaped ANARs will exhibit high spin concentration and enhanced nonradiative decay due to their unique radical character. It is predicted that TPA-TPA-O6 will exhibit the highest photothermal conversion and lowest PLQY among the four variants. The authors expected that the radical species would be purified, show high stability, and enable NIR-to-heat conversion via nonradiative decay.

Methodological Details
Four star-shaped ANAR materials were synthesized by introducing triphenylamine, triazine, pyrene, and spiro fluorene cores. Preparation involved facile demethylation and consequent oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl precursors in air. The precursors were demethylated and their products obtained by oxidation. The demethylation used phenolic methoxy precursors dissolved in dichloromethane. Cyclic voltammetry curves were measured for 15 cycles in dichloromethane with 0.1 M nBu4NPF6 supporting electrolyte. The scan rate for CV was 0.1 V/s. Precursors were dissolved at 5 mg/mL in dichloromethane before film coating on carbon-glass electrodes. Potential values used the saturated calomel electrode with Fc⁺/Fc couple (0.27 V) as internal standard. HOMO and LUMO energy levels were calculated based on CV curves and listed in Table S1. ESR was applied at 0.02 mmol test amount to characterize radical spin signal and concentration. Photoluminescence and PLQY tests were performed in solution and film. PLQY values were recorded for the four demethylated counterparts. Photothermal properties were evaluated by monitoring temperature under IR thermal camera with 808 nm laser at 0.8 W cm⁻².

Procedures And Architectures
The four materials are TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8 with different cores. Characterization was done by cyclic voltammetry, UV-vis-NIR spectroscopy, and electron spin resonance. CV curves were recorded in dichloromethane with a supporting electrolyte. HOMO energy levels were calculated from CV data. ESR signals were compared after demethylation. Photoluminescence quantum yields were measured for all precursors and products. UV-vis-NIR spectra were obtained for solution and film. The photothermal test used an 808 nm laser. A commercially available white polyurethane foam was loaded with TPA-TPA-O6. TPA-TPA-O6 was impregnated into PU foam and dried under 80 °C. The foam used was 2.0 cm diameter with 30 mg TPA-TPA-O6 loading. The system was floated on water. Water evaporation efficiency was calculated as 89.41% under 1 sun. Seawater desalination was verified with ion measurements after desalination.

Key Results
The PLQYs of the radical products were significantly reduced to lower than 1% after demethylation. All demethylated counterparts exhibited highly reversible CV curves with negligible change after 15 cycles. HOMO energy levels of the demethylated radicals were recorded as -4.90, -4.81, -4.97, and -4.84 eV. The HOMO levels were obviously enhanced compared to methoxy precursors. Demethylated TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8 had PLQY values of 0.1%, 0.9%, 1.0%, and 0.3%. TPA-TPA-O6 showed high broadband light absorption covering 300 to 2000 nm in powder state. Under 808 nm laser, TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 rose from 25 °C to about 40 °C within 60 s. TPA-TPA-O6 temperature rose rapidly from 25 °C to about 210 °C within 60 s. Increasing the laser power to 1.0 W cm⁻² raised TPA-TPA-O6 to about 250 °C within 60 s. TPA-TPA-O6 exhibited excellent stability for ten cycles of laser irradiation on and off. PU+ TPA-TPA-O6 foam reached 81.2 °C under 600 s continuous irradiation. The PU foam itself showed a surface temperature of 36 °C under the same condition. The PU+ TPA-TPA-O6 foam reached 45 °C after 1 sun illumination for 1 h. The evaporation rate was 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ with 89.41% water evaporation efficiency. TPA-TPA-O6 displayed wider near-infrared absorption and higher photothermal conversion efficiency. All four primary ions were significantly reduced after desalination.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The black color and long red-shifted tail indicate typical radical character in the solid state. High spin concentration and low PLQY indicate highly nonradiative decay, boosting photothermal conversion. Strong donor-acceptor conjugation reduced the optical bandgap and determined paramagnetic properties. Lower bandgap and more radical character enhanced TPA-TPA-O6 and Spiro-O8 relative to triazine and pyrene cores. Low radical spin in triazine and pyrene cores limited their photothermal conversion and made them prone to protonation. The radical-promoted nonradiative decay explains the superior photothermal conversion performance. These radicals provide a low-cost strategy for stable organic-small-molecule photothermal materials.

Contradictions And Limitations
TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 reached only ~40 °C and may be partially protonated to form hydroxyl groups. The study reports the top performance as 89.41% and 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ but lacks direct comparison metrics for competing materials. The supporting information is available free of charge but contains characterization details not in the main text. The main text does not report the specific water concentration used for evaporation calculations. The exact random seed for simulation or error bar for efficiency is not specified. Seawater desalination was demonstrated but the exact final ion concentrations are not reported in the main text.

Claims
TPA-TPA-O6 is the best organic photothermal converter because of wide absorption and nonradiative decay. The evaporation rate was 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ with 89.41% efficiency. Its absorption was extended from 300 to 2000 nm in powder state. The temperature rose from 25 °C to about 210 °C within 60 s. Its PLQY was 0.1%. The exact ion reduction values are omitted from the main text. Competing organic systems were only mentioned by name, not benchmarked numerically. It opens a strategy for stable organic-small-molecule photothermal materials. It can be applied in photothermal therapy, catalysis, and spintronics.
Open-shell nitric acid radicals are air-stable due to their closed-shell nitro and open-shell nitroxide structures. The ANARs showed negligible change after scanning for 15 cycles. They exhibit high thermal and electrochemical stability. The HOMO energy levels were comparable to methoxy precursors. TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 were only partially protonated. It validates the radical design strategy for stable photothermal conversion.

Data And Code Availability
Supporting information is available free of charge at the ACS website. The detailed synthetic scheme and characterization products are provided in the SI. Table S1 lists CV, PLQY, and HOMO/LUMO energy level values. No computational code or raw data was reported in the main text.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Different cores were compared, showing triphenylamine was best. The black color was consistent with wide absorption across the visible region. The temperature rises regularly with laser power intensity. Ten cycles of laser irradiation proved outstanding photothermal stability.

Ethical Considerations
No explicit ethical statement was reported in the paper. The study concerns in vitro and material materials, not human or animal subjects.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the four star-shaped ANAR structures with different cores. Figure 2 shows the solution and film absorption spectra for all materials. Figure 3 shows the cyclic voltammetry curves after 15 cycles. Figure 4 shows PLQY and ESR spin signal and concentration. Figure 4D shows the PLQY comparison for the four radicals. Figure 5A shows the temperature change under 808 nm laser. Figure 6B shows the broadband light absorption of TPA-TPA-O6. Figure 6C shows the temperature rise against laser power. Figure 6D shows the comparison of materials. Figure 6E shows the temperature of PU foam versus PU+TPA-TPA-O6 foam. Figure 6F shows the mass change curves for evaporation efficiency. Figure 6G shows the desalination performance. Figure 6H shows the ion reductions. Figure 6I shows the competitive organic material comparison.

Three Takeaways
The core contribution is the design of air-stable star-shaped ANAR radicals with extreme photothermal efficiency. The strongest evidence is TPA-TPA-O6 reaching 89.41% evaporation efficiency and 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ rate. The future path involves developing ANARs with enhanced planarity for organic electronics and spintronics.

summary.title: Metal-Free Photocatalysis at Charged Aqueous Interface: Boosting the Photocatalytic Oxidative Coupling of Arylamines to Azoaromatics under Ambient Conditions †
summary.authors: Shivendra Singh; Vidhi Agarwal; Tridib K Sarma; Tushar Kanti Mukherjee
summary.executive_summary:
This study reports a metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics performed at the charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) of micelles under ambient air. Azoaromatics are valuable functional organic molecules with applications in optical storage, molecular switches, and industrial uses, but their synthesis traditionally relies on metal catalysis or diazotization methods that produce unstable diazonium intermediates and waste. The authors address the limitation of previous photocatalytic oxidative coupling (POC) methods, which used Ir-based photocatalysts, suffered from slow kinetics, moderate yields, high catalyst doses, and organic solvents. They formulated a method using Eosin Y (EY) as a common, low-cost organic photocatalyst and K3PO4 as base at the CAI of CTAB (cetyltrimethylammonium bromide) micelles. 

The micellar surface acts as a scaffold hosting both EY and arylamines, enabling non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET) with a time constant of 0.3 ps. Optimized conditions—p-anisidine to 1,2-bis(4-methoxyphenyl)diazene, green light (525 nm), 40 mM CTAB, 0.6 mol% EY, 2 equiv. K3PO4, and 40 mM CTAB—achieve 100% conversion within 4 h of reaction under ambient air, with 100% selectivity. This outperforms previous reports (64% conversion after 24 h in bulk acetonitrile) and achieves an 8.3-fold lower EY dose. Fluorescence studies show EY associates strongly with CTAB, exhibiting enhanced fluorescence (2.4-fold) near the critical micellar concentration (CMC), bathochromic shifts of 9 nm (CTAB) and 16 nm (TX-100), and a fluorescence lifetime increase from 1.17 ns to 2.74 ns upon micellization. K3PO4 stabilizes EY@CTAB but disassembles EY@TX-100. 

Stern-Volmer quenching of EY@CTAB by p-anisidine yields a rate constant of 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1, indicative of non-diffusive bimolecular quenching; p-nitroaniline shows no quenching. Fluorescence up-conversion yields a 0.3 ps time constant. Radical trapping with BHT yields an adduct of 342.2399 g/mol and negligible azo formation (~5.0%). Atmospheric O2 acts as a sacrificial oxidant, regenerating EY and forming H2O2 (detected by color-changing strips). The broad scope includes electron-rich (100% conversion within 4 h) and -deficient amines, plus aniline. The authors attribute the boost to non-diffusive PET and redox potential modulation at the CAI. No bibliography or code/data availability is reported.
