judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports a metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics performed at the charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) of micelles under ambient air. Azoaromatics are valuable functional organic molecules with applications in optical storage, molecular switches, and industrial uses, but their synthesis traditionally relies on metal catalysis or diazotization methods that produce unstable diazonium intermediates and waste. The authors address the limitation of previous photocatalytic oxidative coupling (POC) methods, which used Ir-based photocatalysts, suffered from slow kinetics, moderate yields, high catalyst doses, and organic solvents. They formulated a method using Eosin Y (EY) as a common, low-cost organic photocatalyst and K3PO4 as base at the CAI of CTAB (cetyltrimethylammonium bromide) micelles. 

The micellar surface acts as a scaffold hosting both EY and arylamines, enabling non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET) with a time constant of 0.3 ps. Optimized conditions—p-anisidine to 1,2-bis(4-methoxyphenyl)diazene, green light (525 nm), 40 mM CTAB, 0.6 mol% EY, 2 equiv. K3PO4, and 40 mM CTAB—achieve 100% conversion within 4 h of reaction under ambient air, with 100% selectivity. This outperforms previous reports (64% conversion after 24 h in bulk acetonitrile) and achieves an 8.3-fold lower EY dose. Fluorescence studies show EY associates strongly with CTAB, exhibiting enhanced fluorescence (2.4-fold) near the critical micellar concentration (CMC), bathochromic shifts of 9 nm (CTAB) and 16 nm (TX-100), and a fluorescence lifetime increase from 1.17 ns to 2.74 ns upon micellization. K3PO4 stabilizes EY@CTAB but disassembles EY@TX-100. 

Stern-Volmer quenching of EY@CTAB by p-anisidine yields a rate constant of 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1, indicative of non-diffusive bimolecular quenching; p-nitroaniline shows no quenching. Fluorescence up-conversion yields a 0.3 ps time constant. Radical trapping with BHT yields an adduct of 342.2399 g/mol and negligible azo formation (~5.0%). Atmospheric O2 acts as a sacrificial oxidant, regenerating EY and forming H2O2 (detected by color-changing strips). The broad scope includes electron-rich (100% conversion within 4 h) and -deficient amines, plus aniline. The authors attribute the boost to non-diffusive PET and redox potential modulation at the CAI. No bibliography or code/data availability is reported.

Research Context
Azoaromatics are functional organic molecules with optical storage and industrial applications. Traditional synthesis uses diazotization with nitrile salts, creating unstable intermediates. Metal catalysis produces azo compounds from anilines and nitroaromatics. Photocatalytic reductive coupling of nitrobenzenes needs inert atmosphere and lacks selectivity. Photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines uses Ir catalysts with moderate yields. Earlier reports used organic solvents because amines are poorly soluble in water.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can azoaromatics be synthesized efficiently in an aqueous medium at ambient conditions? Can Eosin Y at micellar charged aqueous interfaces host both PC and substrates? Hypothesis: The micellar scaffold facilitates non-diffusive PET with fast kinetics and low catalyst loading. Hypothesis: The boost arises from non-diffusive PET and redox potential modulation. The authors predict 100% yields and 100% selectivity under ambient air.

Methodological Details
The study compares Eosin Y behavior with CTAB, SDS, and TX-100. The EY absorption peak in water is 516 nm. The CTAB shift is 9 nm; the TX-100 shift is 16 nm. The fluorescence enhancement is 2.4-fold near the CMC (0.75-1.0 mM). EY has two negative charges at pH 7. Fluorescence lifetime in water is 1.17 ns; upon micellization 2.74 ns. The catalyst loading is 0.6 mol% EY with 2 equiv. K3PO4. Micelles are formed at 40 mM CTAB. Reaction products were analyzed by GC-MS and NMR. The substrate tested was p-anisidine. The base checked includes K3PO4 and KOH.

Procedures And Architectures
The reaction was triggered by green light at 525 nm. Light irradiation lasted for 4 h. Spherical micelles were confirmed by HR-TEM. Proton abstraction was identified as a critical step requiring a base. The electron acceptor in the regeneration cycle reduces aerial O2 to H2O2. H2O2 was detected using color-changing sensing strips. The PET time constant was measured by fluorescence up-conversion. Radical trapping added 1 equivalent of BHT after 5 min irradiation. The PC was regenerated via reduction of aerial O2.

Key Results
100% conversion of p-anisidine to the azo product was achieved in 4 h. The catalyst loading was 0.6 mol% EY, an 8.3-fold lower dose than previous. The quenching rate constant is 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1. The PET time constant is 0.3 ps. Electron-rich amines showed 100% conversion within 4 h. Aniline reached 100% conversion under standard conditions. p-chloroaniline and p-bromoaniline reached 98% and 95% conversion. p-nitroaniline showed no fluorescence quenching. The BHT adduct weight is 342.2399 g/mol. With BHT, azo formation was ~5.0%. Blue light (previous) required 6 h for 100% conversion.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The boosting is attributed to non-diffusive PET and CAI redox modulation. The CAI provides an electric field aligning probe dipoles for selectivity. The CAI solubilizes both hydrophilic and hydrophobic probes. The Stern layer hosts the substrate while the aqueous bulk is less favorable. PET precedes proton abstraction. Atmospheric O2 is a sacrificial oxidant regenerating the PC via H2O2. The work is the first report on aqueous phase azo synthesis.

Contradictions And Limitations
No bibliography or references are provided in the text. No raw data tables are presented; results reference tables not included. No code or data availability statement is reported. There is no mention of a random seed, train/test split, or demographics. The abstract uses a † symbol indicating unreviewed content on ChemRxiv. Ablations are limited to radical trapping and base checks.

Claims
Micellar charged aqueous interfaces boost arylamine-to-azoaromatic POC efficacy and selectivity in water. 100% conversion of p-anisidine was achieved in 4 h with 100% selectivity. The boosting is attributed to non-diffusive PET at the CAI. The PET time constant is only 0.3 ps. The quench rate constant is 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1. No fluorescence quenching was observed with p-nitroaniline. The work is not peer-reviewed on ChemRxiv. This enables sustainable, aqueous azo synthesis without metal or organic solvents. Lower catalyst loading makes it greener.
Eosin Y strongly associates and functions at the CTAB micelle interface but is unstable with TX-100. EY bears two negative charges at pH 7. EY@CTAB is stable with K3PO4 but EY@TX-100 disassembles. Fluorescence lifetime increases from 1.17 ns to 2.74 ns. The EY peak shifts 9 nm with CTAB and 16 nm with TX-100. SDS shows no spectral changes, meaning no interaction. The choice of micelle is critical for PC solubilization and stability.
The mechanism proceeds via non-diffusive PET followed by proton abstraction, producing an amine radical. The BHT adduct weighs 342.2399 g/mol. Azo formation dropped to ~5.0% with BHT. PET precedes proton abstraction. BHT conversion is ~5.0% after 4 h, not zero. The radical intermediates are the key mechanistic intermediates.

Data And Code Availability
No data availability statement is provided.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Radical trapping with BHT yielded an adduct of 342.2399 g/mol. Azo conversion dropped to ~5.0% with BHT. Base effects show DABCO gives lower yields than inorganic bases. SDS showed no interaction with EY. Only EY@CTAB was used for POC studies.

Ethical Considerations
The study uses non-toxic organic photocatalysts and is performed under ambient conditions. The license is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. No human subjects or animals were used.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 lists the optimized reaction conditions and conversion percentages. Figure 1a shows the bathochromic shifts; 1b and S1 show quenching; 1c shows aggregation; 1d shows lifetime. Figure 2b shows SV plots; 2c shows SV plots; 2d shows up-conversion; 2e not present. Figure S13 shows EY@CTAB fluorescence quenching. Figure S14 shows K3PO4 effect on SV plots. Figure S6 shows H2O2 detection by color-changing strips. Figure S15 shows the BHT adduct HR-MS peak.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: A metal-free, ambient-air POC of arylamines to azoaromatics in water via micellar CAIs. 2. The strongest evidence: 100% conversion of p-anisidine in 4 h at 0.6 mol% EY, an 8.3-fold lower dose than previously. 3. The future path: Applying this aqueous, CAI-based POC to a broader range of amines and azo synthesis.

summary.title: Spontaneous crystal fluctuation in hydrocarbon polymer-coated monolayer MoS2 , MoSe2 , WS2 , and WSe2 with strong photoluminescence enhancement
summary.authors: Takahiro Nakahara; Takashi Kobayashi; Tetsuji Dohi; Takeshi Yoshimura; Norifumi Fujimura; Daisuke Kiriya
summary.field_subfield: Transition metal dichalcogenides; photonics; 2D materials; monolayer semiconductors
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental materials science and condensed matter physics study
summary.executive_summary:
Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), denoted MX2 (M = Mo, W; X = S, Se), have attracted attention due to their thin crystal structure with a layer-thickness of only three atoms and excellent mechanical robustness. Monolayer TMDCs exhibit a direct band gap at the K and K prime points in the Brillouin zone, making them applicable to optical transistors, light-emitting diodes, and solar cells, among others. However, a drawback of the optical behavior in monolayer TMDCs is their poor photoluminescence (PL) intensity, caused by factors such as over-carrier concentrations, strains, and defects in the crystalline lattice. For the n-type materials MoS2 and WS2, p-type doping with chemicals such as 2,3,5,6-tetrafluoro-7,7,8,8-tetracycanoquinodimethane (F4TCNQ) and tetrafluoro-1,4benzoquinone enhances PL intensity. The p-dopant enhances exciton-dominant emission by decreasing the probability of generating trion emission. Another chemical treatment for MoS2 and WS2 is the superacid bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (TFSI), which can produce PL enhancement of hundreds of times. In contrast, these methods are not effective for the selenium-based TMDCs MoSe2 and WSe2, although oleic acid treatments and hydrohalic acid treatment on MoSe2 succeeded in enhancing PL intensity, and defect repair in the crystalline lattice has been suggested for MoSe2 but not reported for WSe2. For WSe2, the reported methods separate a monolayer WSe2 from substrates by floating or inserting ions, which removes the substrate effect. As shown above, there are different strategies for improving the optical property of different TMDCs, and no universal strategy has been found for improving the optical behavior of a large variety of two-dimensional semiconductor materials.

In this study, the authors developed a method that enhances PL intensity in the sulfur-based TMDCs of MoS2 and WS2 that is also applicable for selenium-based TMDCs of MoSe2 and WSe2 through coating with a simple hydrocarbon, paraffin. The factor of PL enhancement is remarkable: MoS2, WS2, WSe2, and MoSe2 show factors of enhancement of 215-, 55-, 9-, and 50-fold from the as-exfoliated flakes, respectively. The paraffin coating was revealed to induce gradual spontaneous fluctuation and eventual desorption of the monolayer from the substrates. The deformation to a shrunk bundled structure is the result of the desorption if the monolayer is not surrounded by bulk flakes, which is due to stress at the interface with paraffin. The spontaneous fluctuation and desorption remove the substrate effect, which is the key factor in enhancing PL intensity in the monolayers. Because of the large thermal coefficient of paraffin, the strain is effectively applied to the TMDCs in the coating process, leading to spontaneous fluctuation of the paraffin-coated monolayer TMDCs. In an extreme case, the fluctuation forms the shape of a bundle. The method is due to applying the strain by the large thermal expansion coefficient in paraffin; therefore, the underlining science is applicable to other 2D layered materials. Moreover, paraffin is insulative, flexible, and transparent, making it suitable for packaging flexible light-emitting displays and solar cells.

The mechanism of PL enhancement is explained as the penetration of paraffin underneath each monolayer TMDC, which removes the substrate effect from the TMDCs. Raman spectra confirm that the E prime peak shifts in the negative direction and the A prime peak shifts in the positive direction after paraffin coating. Specifically, the E prime peak shifted by about -0.72 cm-1 on average and the A prime peak shifted by 1.03 cm-1. These spectroscopic behaviors can also be explained by the penetration of paraffin between the monolayer MoS2 and the substrate, thus reducing the substrate effect (electron doping from the substrate), and then decreasing the electron concentration in the monolayer TMDCs. The PL enhancement is due to a combination of strain induced by the volume change caused by the high thermal expansion coefficient of the paraffin and the subsequent desorption of the monolayer TMDC flakes from the substrate. This engineering method of hydrocarbon-coating is useful for straining thin 2D materials and for generating transparent and flexible optoelectronic devices.

The PL enhancement is due to strain induced by the volume change of the paraffin. The large thermal expansion coefficient of the paraffin drives the deformation and desorption. The method is useful for straining thin 2D materials. The method is applicable for transparent and flexible optoelectronic devices.

Traditional chemical treatment methods are not effective for selenium-based TMDCs. Defect repair has not been reported for enhancing PL in WSe2. A thick paraffin film produced by simple casting is not transparent. The PL mapping showed nonuniform PL enhancement across the monolayer plane. The paraffin science could apply to other 2D layered materials. The reported method separates WSe2 from substrates but is not universal. Data availability and code are not reported in the paper. The PL enhancement mechanism is suggested by Raman and PL spectra.

Data availability and code are not reported in the paper.

A monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes on the three sides prevents bending and bundling. A thick paraffin film produced by simple casting is not transparent. No ethical considerations or participant information are reported in the paper.

summary.title: Atmospheric pressure continuous flow methane oxidation to methanol and acetic acid using H 2 O 2 over Au-Fe catalyst
summary.authors: Anuradha V Jagtap; Pawan Kumar; Sharad Gupta; N Abharana; S N Jha; D Bhattacharyya; T G Ajithkumar; C P Vinod
summary.field_subfield: Heterogeneous catalysis / inorganic materials chemistry / methane oxidation
summary.executive_summary: Methane to methanol (M2M) by partial oxidation or acetic acid through C insertion is considered one of catalysis's most enterprising chemical transformations. The authors tackle the continuous partial oxidation of methane to methanol and acetic acid at atmospheric pressure using a hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) oxidant over an Au-Fe catalyst. The key material is an Au-Fe bimetallic catalyst supported on modified hydrophobic silica. Synthesis used a modified deposition precipitation (DP) method to disperse Fe atomic clusters. ICP-OES confirmed optimum metal loadings of 0.46 wt % Fe and 0.23 wt % Au. Hydrophobic silica was used because it helps bring H2O2 close to active sites and facilitates methanol desorption, while hydrophilic conditions block sites with moisture and enlarge Au particles. Catalytic activity was initially screened in a 10 bar batch reactor at 0.5 wt % Fe and 0.2 wt % Au. The Fe-HS catalyst gave 285 mmol/gFe with 82% methanol selectivity, while the Au-Fe HS catalyst gave 1666 mmol/gFe+Au with 95% selectivity. Co-feeding CO with methane switched selectivity to acetic acid, producing 3403 µmol/gcat acetic acid with 60% selectivity in the batch reactor. The continuous flow process was extended to a fixed-bed reactor at atmospheric pressure for up to 7 h. At 4 h, the product reached 157 µmol, with AuFeHS giving 224 mmol/gFe+Au of methanol and 648 µmol/gcat of acetic acid with CO. The methanol yield was 422 µmolh -1 gcat -1 (0.42 molmethanol kgcatalyst -1 h -1) for 4 h. Compared to benchmarks, the AuFeHS catalyst gave 224 mmol/gFe+Au versus the 0.081 molProduct kgcatalyst -1 h -1 reported by Hutchings under 20 bar H2O2 pressure. Characterization via ICP-OES, XPS, XANES, EXAFS, HRTEM, IR, and CD4 labeling supported atomic Fe dispersion, the presence of low-valent Fe 3-δ+ species, and synergistic Au interaction. The paper highlights that the continuous process under atmospheric conditions is the best reported, surpassing high-pressure batch processes, and concludes with commercialization potential for M2O technologies.

summary.title: A Workflow for Identifying Viable Crystal Structures with Partially Occupied Sites Applied to Solid Electrolyte: Cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12
summary.authors: Julian Holland; Tom Demeyere; Arihant Bhandari; Felix Hanke; Victor Milman; Chris-Kriton Skylaris
summary.field_subfield: Solid electrolytes and solid-state lithium-ion battery materials
summary.type_of_paper: Computational materials science / Workflow and methodology paper
summary.executive_summary:
This computational study introduces a workflow for identifying and energetically ordering all crystallographically predicted configurations of cubic Li7 La3 Zr2 O12 (c-LLZO), a prominent solid-state lithium-ion battery electrolyte whose ground-state configuration has not been definitively established experimentally or theoretically. The authors address the limitation that existing computational models often use a single experimental occupancy as an idealized starting point, potentially introducing systematic bias into the calculated properties.

The methodological workflow begins by restricting the configuration space: they impose a minimal Li-Li distance of 1.7 Å, which is less than twice the ionic radius of Li and smaller than the minimum distance in the tetragonal phase (2.56 Å), thereby limiting the possible 24d : 96h occupancy ratios. From the ≈ 7.4 × 10^34 ways to arrange 56 Li atoms on 120 sites, they generate all structures and reduce the dataset to approximately 2 × 10^6 unique configurations by discarding symmetry-equivalent duplicates using local sensitive hashing (LSH) symmetry-checker. The LSH approach improves the pairwise comparison scaling from O(N²) to O(N), enabling symmetry checks on over 100 million structures within reasonable time and memory limits.

An energetic ordering was performed via a multiple linear regression (MLR) model fit using 1235 single-point DFT calculations with the ONETEP code, employing the PBE functional with an 830 eV kinetic energy cutoff. The descriptors were frequency occurrence lists of all possible Li-Li interactions, and the model achieved a correlation of 0.9996 on the test set. The lowest-energy structures were found at the 8:48 ratio, with four configurations within 0.026 eV of the ground state; geometry relaxations of 20 structures confirmed that movement from original crystallographic sites lowers energy, but movement to other sites is not necessary.

The authors highlight that a large proportion of reported literature structures may not be reflective of a real system and provide all generated structures in a freely accessible database to improve future accuracy and reproducibility. The method could be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals.

The authors highlight that a large proportion of reported literature structures may not be reflective of a real system and provide all generated structures in a freely accessible database to improve future accuracy and reproducibility. The method could be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals.

Research Context
Solid electrolytes for Li-ion batteries promise higher energy density, improved safety, longer lifetimes, and reduced production costs compared to current liquid cells. Dendrite formation through the electrolyte causing batteries to short-circuit has been reported even for the most stable solid electrolytes. Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (LLZO) has the best interfacial stability of all popular fast ion conducting solid electrolytes against metallic Li. Experimental and theoretical works have, to date, been unable to uncover the ground state configuration of prominent solid electrolyte candidate cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (c-LLZO). Computational studies rely on an initial low-energy structure as a reference point to obtain an idealised unit cell. The range of predicted structures in the literature indicates some disagreement about the ground state. There is no consensus of c-LLZO's Li occupancy, and predicted properties may not be well described. Previous computational studies often use one of the experimental values in Figure 1 as a starting point.

The system studied is cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (c-LLZO). The c-LLZO Hermann-Maguin space group is Ia 3d with Li partially occupying the 24d and 96h sites. All DFT calculations were performed with the ONETEP code. The computational cost scales linearly with the number of atoms. The PBE GGA exchange correlation functional was used. summary.executive_summary: GUIDEMOL is a Python computer program based on the RDKit software to process molecular structures and calculate molecular descriptors with a graphical user interface using the tkinter package. It can calculate descriptors already implemented in RDKit as well as grid representations of 3D molecular structures using the electrostatic potential or voxels. The GUIDEMOL app provides easy access to RDKit tools for chemoinformatics users with no programming skills and can be adapted to calculate other descriptors or to trigger other procedures. A CLI is also provided for the calculation of grid representations. The source code is available at https://github.com/jairesdesousa/guidemol under the three-clause Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) license. Molecular descriptors are central to the QSPR/QSAR methodology, used by scientists from different areas with varying levels of computer skills, making such software for teaching required in chemistry, biology and material science degrees. Prior GUI-based descriptor calculators include the open-source CDK-based PaDEL and the CDK Descriptor Calculator GUI by Guha, alongside the Mordred Python package. The representation of molecules in 3D grids of voxels encoding their atoms has been used to train deep learning neural networks, while electrostatic potentials have long since been used in 3D-QSAR to establish relationships with molecular properties and to assess molecular similarity. 3D representations of molecules can be used for data sets of pre-aligned structures, such as relative to a reference or after docking to a receptor, and can be processed by convolutional neural networks. GUIDEMOL implements RDKit 3D descriptors including RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA and SMR_VSA, plus the exact molecular weight. For 3D grid representation, users can specify coordinates, the grid center, side size, cube size, and the cutoff distance or sigma parameter, and grid electrostatic potential is generated via Gasteiger or MMFF partial charges. For some molecules, particularly GETAWAY, MORSE and WHIM descriptors, different values were obtained with the same RDKit version (2022.9.5) in different runs or in different operating systems, as seen for the 3D structure generated for COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br. No empirical validation or performance metrics were reported, and no formal ethics statement was included.

Research Context
Molecular descriptors are at the core of the QSPR/QSAR methodology, used by a range of scientists from different areas and with varying levels of computer skills. Such software for teaching is required as QSPR/QSAR is gradually permeating the curricula of chemistry, biology and material science degrees. Prior GUI-based descriptor calculators include the open-source CDK-based PaDEL and the CDK Descriptor Calculator GUI by Guha. Mordred is a Python package designed to calculate molecular descriptors with RDKit wrappers. The representation of molecules in 3D grids of voxels encoding their atoms has been used to train deep learning neural networks. Electrostatic potentials have long since been used in 3D-QSAR to establish relationships with molecular properties and assess molecular similarity.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study asks whether a minimalist interface can facilitate the access to RDKit tools for chemoinformatics users with no programming skills. The hypothesis is that a graphical user interface can make RDKit descriptors accessible to scientists and students. The prediction is that both a GUI and a CLI can calculate molecular descriptors with a graphical user interface and command-line access. Furthermore, 3D grid representations of molecules are hypothesized to be useful for processing by complex artificial intelligence algorithms.

Methodological Details
The application is a Python computer program based on the RDKit software to process molecular structures and calculate molecular descriptors. It provides a graphical user interface using the tkinter package to calculate RDKit descriptors and 3D grid representations of molecules using the electrostatic potential or voxels. The source code is hosted on GitHub under the three-clause Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) license. Calculations were performed using RDKit version (2022.9.5), a Python open-source software used in machine learning projects. Descriptors are selected from the RDKit rdMolDescriptors module and the exact molecular weight can also be chosen. The grid electrostatic potential is generated via Gasteiger or MMFF partial charges, and the exact molecular weight can also be chosen. Molecular descriptors are saved in a csv output file, containing the molecule name and molecule ID number.

Procedures And Architectures
The GUI was built with various types of tkinter widgets controlled by its grid geometry manager. Input and output file selection is implemented with the tkinter.filedialog module. 3D molecular models are obtained with the RDKit function MMFFOptimizeMolecule and the arguments mmffVariant='MMFF94' and maxIters=5000. Pre-generation options include the MetalDisconnector to remove metals and the LargestFragmentChooser(preferOrganic=True) to keep the largest fragment. Hydrogen atoms are added using Chem.AddHs() with the argument addCoords=True when coordinates are calculated without changing the other atoms. For some molecules and descriptors, different values were obtained with the same RDKit version (2022.9.5) in different runs or in different operating systems. A log file is created in the same directory to register the successful processing of each molecule, as well as failures.

Key Results
The GUI provides access to 3D descriptors such as RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA and SMR_VSA. The exact molecular weight can also be chosen as a descriptor. The grid of electrostatic potential is generated via Gasteiger or MMFF partial charges. For some molecules and descriptors, different values were obtained with the same RDKit version (2022.9.5) in different runs or in different operating systems. Grid calculation is available via the tkinter GUI or the command-line for input file sdf. ChemDes integrates several available packages to calculate 3679 molecular descriptors. BlueDesc converts an MDL SDFile into ARFF and LIBSVM formats with up to 174 descriptors.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Voxels encoding their atoms have been used to train deep learning neural networks for molecules. Direct 3D representations can be used for pre-aligned structures, such as relative to a reference or after docking to a receptor. Electrostatic potentials have long since been used to establish relationships with molecular properties in 3D-QSAR and to assess molecular similarity.

Different values were obtained with the same RDKit version for some molecules and some GETAWAY, MORSE and WHIM descriptors. The 3D grid representation can be used to train deep learning neural networks. The representations can be processed by complex artificial intelligence algorithms. Direct 3D representations establish relationships with molecular properties in 3D-QSAR.

The source code is hosted on GitHub. The source code is released under the three-clause BSD license.

An option is available to remove metals before generation. An option is available to keep the largest fragment. Hydrogen atoms are added without changing the coordinates of the other atoms. Hydrogen atoms are added with the argument addCoords=True.

    research_context:
    1. Molecular descriptors are central to QSPR/QSAR methodology, used by a range of scientists from different areas and with varying levels of computer skills.

    5. The representation of molecules in 3D grids of voxels encoding their atoms has been used to train deep learning neural networks.
    6. Electrostatic potentials have long since been used in 3D-QSAR to establish relationships with molecular properties.

    research_question_and_hypothesis:
    1. The study asks whether a minimalist interface can facilitate the access to RDKit tools for chemoinformatics users with no programming skills.
    2. The hypothesis is that a graphical user interface can make RDKit descriptors accessible to scientists and students.
    3. The prediction is that both a GUI and a CLI can calculate molecular descriptors with a graphical user interface and command-line access.
    4. Furthermore, 3D grid representations of molecules are hypothesized to be useful for processing by complex artificial intelligence algorithms.

    methodological_details:
    1. The application is a Python computer program based on the RDKit software to process molecular structures and calculate molecular descriptors.
    2. It provides a graphical user interface using the tkinter package to calculate RDKit descriptors and 3D grid representations of molecules using the electrostatic potential or voxels.
    3. The source code is available at https://github.com/jairesdesousa/guidemol under the three-clause Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) license.
    4. Calculations were performed using RDKit version (2022.9.5), which is a Python open-source software much used in machine learning projects.
    5. Descriptors are selected from the RDKit rdMolDescriptors module and the exact molecular weight can also be chosen.
    6. The grid electrostatic potential is generated via Gasteiger or MMFF partial charges, and the exact molecular weight can also be chosen.
    7. Molecular descriptors are saved in a csv output file, containing the molecule name and molecule ID number.

    procedures_and_architectures:
    1. The GUI was built with various types of tkinter widgets controlled by its grid geometry manager.
    2. Input and output file selection is implemented with the tkinter.filedialog module.
    3. 3D molecular models are obtained with the RDKit function MMFFOptimizeMolecule and the arguments mmffVariant='MMFF94' and maxIters=5000.
    4. Pre-generation options include the MetalDisconnector to remove metals and the LargestFragmentChooser(preferOrganic=True) to keep the largest fragment.
    5. Hydrogen atoms are added using Chem.AddHs() with the argument addCoords=True when coordinates are calculated without changing the other atoms.
    6. For some molecules and descriptors, different values were obtained with the same RDKit version (2022.9.5) in different runs or in different operating systems.
    7. A log file is created in the same directory to register the successful processing of each molecule, as well as failures.

    key_results:
    1. The GUI provides access to 3D descriptors such as RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA and SMR_VSA.
    2. The exact molecular weight can also be chosen as a descriptor.
    3. The grid of electrostatic potential is generated via Gasteiger or MMFF partial charges.
    4. For some molecules and descriptors, different values were obtained with the same RDKit version (2022.9.5) in different runs or in different operating systems.
    5. Grid calculation is available via the tkinter GUI or the command-line for input file sdf.

    interpretation_and_theoretical_implications:

    This note presents GUIDEMOL, a minimalist Python graphical user interface (GUI) built using the tkinter package and the RDKit software to make molecular descriptor calculation accessible to chemoinformatics users without programming skills. GUIDEMOL implements a suite of RDKit-based 3D descriptors, including RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, and SMR_VSA, along with the exact molecular weight. It also calculates 3D grid representations of molecules using electrostatic potential or voxel encoding, enabling the direct processing of 3D molecular structures by deep learning neural networks and 3D-QSAR algorithms. A command-line interface is also provided for grid representation calculation. The application supports pre-processing steps such as removing metals via the MetalDisconnector class, keeping the largest fragment with LargestFragmentChooser(preferOrganic=True), neutralizing structures with Uncharger, and adding hydrogen atoms via Chem.AddHs(addCoords=True) without altering the coordinates of existing atoms. Users can specify coordinates, the grid center, side size, cube size, and cutoff distance or sigma parameter for voxelization. Descriptors and grid results are exported to a CSV file including the molecule name and ID number. A log file records successful molecules and failures in the same directory. The source code is released under the three-clause Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) license on GitHub. The study reports that for some molecules and descriptors, particularly GETAWAY, MORSE and WHIM, different values were obtained with RDKit version 2022.9.5 across different runs or operating systems, exemplified by the structure generated for COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br. No empirical validation or performance metrics were reported beyond the software's functionality, and no formal ethics statement was included.

summary.authors: Jing Fang; Tianzuo Li; Jiyeon Lee; Dahye Lim; Lianjie Xu; Yajie Liu; Jongcheol Seo; Wen-Bin Zhang
summary.executive_summary: This paper reports the first single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase, designed and synthesized in cells. A single-domain protein catenane comprises two mechanically interlocked polypeptide rings that fold synergistically into a compact and integrated structure, a topology extremely rare in nature. The authors designed the catenane (cat-DHFR) by rewiring the connectivity between secondary motifs of dihydrofolate reductase to introduce artificial entanglement, and synthesis was achieved via a series of programmed streamlined post-translational processing events in Escherichia coli, requiring no additional in vitro reactions. The target molecule contains few exogenous motifs and was thoroughly characterized using LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry. Compared to the linear control, cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability but exhibits enhanced stability against thermal or chemical denaturation due to conformational restriction. The key molecular design strategy identified a cleavage point at the position between residues 88 and 89 to produce two highly intertwined segments, forming two rings from residues 1-88 and 89-159. Circular permutation was used to relocate the split-intein motifs and position the cyclization reaction on the opposite side of the DHFR fold, accompanied by the embedding of a Tobacco Etch Virus (TEV) protease recognition site within the first ring for topological confirmation via proteolytic digestion. The design was informed by the Gaussian linking number (GLN) matrix of wild-type DHFR (PDB 4KJJ), which enabled identification of splitting positions with the largest GLN to capture the entangling core, yielding a cat-DHFR with a GLN of +1.120. The linear control, bearing extra amino acids at the N- and C-termini, served as the baseline for all comparisons. The design and synthesis relied on the assumption that single-domain topologies would isolate the effect of chemical topology on the structure-property relationship, avoiding the interference of multiple domains. The resulting catenane retained ~15% of the full-length enzymatic activity, interpreted by the authors as a retention of function despite substantial structural engineering. Further, mechanical interlocking preserved 87% activity in 5% DMSO compared to 74% for the linear control. These findings collectively argue that topology can confer elevated stability while preserving function, establishing a modular scaffold that extends beyond the linear backbone of ribosomal polymerization.

Executive Summary
This paper reports the first single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase, designed and synthesized in cells. A single-domain protein catenane comprises two mechanically interlocked polypeptide rings that fold synergistically into a compact and integrated structure, a topology extremely rare in nature. The authors designed the catenane (cat-DHFR) by rewiring the connectivity between secondary motifs of dihydrofolate reductase to introduce artificial entanglement, and synthesis was achieved via a series of programmed streamlined post-translational processing events in Escherichia coli, requiring no additional in vitro reactions. The target molecule contains few exogenous motifs and was thoroughly characterized using LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry. Compared to the linear control, cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability but exhibits enhanced stability against thermal or chemical denaturation due to conformational restriction. The key molecular design strategy identified a cleavage point at the position between residues 88 and 89 to produce two highly intertwined segments, forming two rings from residues 1-88 and 89-159. Circular permutation was used to relocate the split-intein motifs and position the cyclization reaction on the opposite side of the DHFR fold, accompanied by the embedding of a Tobacco Etch Virus (TEV) protease recognition site within the first ring for topological confirmation via proteolytic digestion. The design was informed by the Gaussian linking number (GLN) matrix of wild-type DHFR (PDB 4KJJ), which enabled identification of splitting positions with the largest GLN to capture the entangling core, yielding a cat-DHFR with a GLN of +1.120. The linear control, bearing extra amino acids at the N- and C-termini, served as the baseline for all comparisons. The design and synthesis relied on the assumption that single-domain topologies would isolate the effect of chemical topology on the structure-property relationship, avoiding the interference of multiple domains. The resulting catenane retained ~15% of the full-length enzymatic activity, interpreted by the authors as a retention of function despite substantial structural engineering. Further, mechanical interlocking preserved 87% activity in 5% DMSO compared to 74% for the linear control. These findings collectively argue that topology can confer elevated stability while preserving function, establishing a modular scaffold that extends beyond the linear backbone of ribosomal polymerization.

Research Context
Nature uses protein domains as modules to tailor functions. Linear proteins have limited topological diversity. Topology is a unique dimension for protein engineering. The assembly-reaction synergy advances topological protein synthesis. Single-domain proteins isolate the effect of chemical topology. Preparing such single-domain topological proteins remains challenging. DHFR is a model enzyme from Escherichia coli.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is if catenane can be made without an exogenous entangling motif. The authors convert a model enzyme into a single-domain catenane. The designs are of identical composition to the linear wild-type. Changing chemical topology can profoundly alter properties without collapsing the fold. Reduced activity may be restored by directed evolution.

Methodological Details
Design begins by rewiring the wild-type DHFR structure. Splitting M loops out of a total of N. Combinatorics give N!/[(N-M)!*M!] different ways of splitting. Entanglement is assessed by the Gaussian linking number matrix. The reference structure is PDB entry 4KJJ. Cleavage occurs between residues 88 and 89. Ring I spans residues 1-88. Ring II spans residues 89-159. The catenane has a final GLN of +1.120. Synthesis uses two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs. Plasmids are pMCSG19 and pET21a vectors. The host is E.coli BL21(DE3) competent cells. Protein is expressed at 16 o C for 20 h. Purification uses Ni-NTA affinity chromatography. Size exclusion chromatography yields a further purified product. Two DHFR segments serve as the entangling template. A TEV protease recognition sequence is in the first ring. The linear control bears identical amino acid composition.

Procedures And Architectures
The design follows a retrosynthetic analysis. Ring I was circularly permutated to generate new termini. New termini are between residues 23 and 24. The rewired loops are at least 16residues long. Sequence info is in the SI. The most efficient site is between residues 23 and 24. Innocent flexible linkers with embedded elements are used. Linker L2 of ring II is varied. The design is in Figure 1b. The gene cassette is in Figure 1c. GLN splitting is in Figure S1a. The catenane GLN is in Figure S1b. The entangling core is in Figure 1d. Split-intein pairs are orthogonal. The side-product control is in Figure S3a. Site efficiency is in Figure 3b-d. Linker effects are in Figure S4. Topology is characterized by ion mobility spectrometry (IMS). Ion mobility uses collision-induced dissociation (CID). GLN matrices are in Figure S1.

Key Results
SDS-PAGE shows a single band of approximately 22 kDa for l-DHFR. SDS-PAGE shows a major band of less than 20 kDa for cat-DHFR. Purified products show a single band at a molecular weight. cat-DHFR migrates faster than the linear form. SEC shows cat-DHFR elutes as a broader peak at a slightly larger retention volume. The retention volume is slightly larger than l-DHFR. LC-MS confirmed the accurate molecular weights. The far-UV CD spectra show a folded catenane. Reduced intensities of both positive peak at ~200 nm. A positive peak at ~200 nm. Negative peak ellipticity between 210 nm and 230 nm. The near-UV CD shows positive ellipticity at ~290 nm. The near-UV CD spectrum is in Figure S2. No crystal structure was obtained. The catenane shows ~5 U/mg of activity. The linear control shows ~14 U/mg of activity. Assays were monitored at 340 nm at 25 o C. The catenane retained ~15% of the enzymatic activity. The Km of cat-DHFR is approximately 5-fold that of l-DHFR. The kcat is about 38% that of l-DHFR. Catalytic efficiency is reduced by an order of magnitude. The DHF KD is ~173-fold larger. The NADPH KD is ~14-fold larger. The THF KD increased by ~3.6-fold. Cat-DHFR retained 87% activity in 5% DMSO. l-DHFR retained 74% activity in 5% DMSO.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Conformational restriction stabilizes the catenane. Topology enhances stability against thermal or chemical denaturation. Linear proteins may be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts. Function is preserved and stability is elevated. This represents an entirely new horizon. Topology can bring in profound changes in properties.

Contradictions And Limitations
No crystal structure was obtained for cat-DHFR. Crystals failed due to unsatisfactory purity. Circular permutation is necessary due to steric hindrance. One-side ligation yielded ~33% side products. The Km of cat-DHFR is only 5-fold that of l-DHFR. Enzymatic activity was reduced. Catalytic efficiency is reduced by an order of magnitude.

Claims
A single-domain protein catenane of DHFR can be designed by rewiring the wild-type fold and synthesized in cells without an exogenous entangling motif. Design rewires the wild-type DHFR fold. Synthesis uses orthogonal split-intein pairs. The first ring carries the TEV protease site. The catenane retains catalytic capability. No crystal structure was obtained. Side products comprised ~33% of the form. The catenane Km is only 5-fold higher. Topology isolates the effect of chemical topology. The scaffold provides unusual support for engineering. It extends beyond the linear backbone.
The catenane retains a significant portion of enzymatic activity despite extensive topological engineering. Cat-DHFR retains ~15% of the activity. Cat-DHFR activity is ~5 U/mg. l-DHFR activity is ~14 U/mg. Rethreaded DHFR shows no activity. Catalytic efficiency is reduced by an order of magnitude. Km is approximately 5-fold higher. Catalytic efficiency is lowered an order of magnitude. Fold tolerance allows topological variation. The scaffold could be evolved for better activity.
Mechanical interlocking enhances the thermal and chemical resilience of the enzyme. Cat-DHFR retains 87% activity in 5% DMSO. l-DHFR retains 74% activity in 5% DMSO. Conformational restriction stabilizes the catenane. No DMSO-specific tolerance quantified. DMSO effects are not contrasted. Topology confers elevated stability. This is a new horizon in protein science.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Linker length affects catenane yield. The shortest linker yields only about one-fifth. Short linkers increase monocyclic by-products.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows the design of cat-DHFR. Figure 1b shows the gene cassette design. Figure 2a shows SDS-PAGE bands of the products. Figure 2c shows the LC-MS confirmation. Table 1 lists the kinetic and binding parameters. Figure 4c shows the catalytic activity curves.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first single-domain protein catenane of DHFR made by rewiring the wild-type fold. 2. The strongest evidence is that mechanical interlocking preserved 87% activity in 5% DMSO versus 74% for l-DHFR. 3. The future path is to use directed evolution to restore catenane activity to match the linear control.

summary.executive_summary:
This work presents the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by predicted energy, produced via a machine learning force field (MLFF) developed for lithium-ion battery materials.

The solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) is a critical but poorly understood passivating layer formed at the lithium anode; its amorphous or crystalline nature and Li+ transport mechanisms remain unanswered. No existing method can fully simulate such a complex system spanning long length and time scales with both organic and inorganic components. Traditional pure DFT underestimates reaction barriers and hybrid functionals like wB97X-D3BJ are too computationally expensive for the periodic systems necessary. The authors address this gap by training a QRNN-based MLFF using multitask learning, which labels both pure and hybrid DFT datasets simultaneously.

They selected wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD for non-periodic and PBE-D3 plane wave for periodic systems, using GFN1-xTB to generate charge labels. Data was generated via multiple rounds of active learning, including AFIR and NEB sampling on the QRNN potential energy surface, and augmented with the SPICE dataset (H, Li, C, O, F, P) with GFN1-xTB labels. They used a new Schrodinger SEI Simulator (OPLS4 MD) to generate initial 1M LiPF6 in EC geometries with 700 EC molecules plus 52 Li+ and PF 6 ions each, totaling 7416 atoms per box, across four lithiation levels (5, 12, 23, 33 added Li+). The model was trained with 1% validation data, Adamax optimizer, learning rate 2e-3, batch size 64, hidden layers 256/224/192, 1e-3 weight decay, and an exponential moving average (alpha 0.001).

Systems were annealed at 400 K and 1000 atm for 100 ps and ranked by mean potential energy over 20 ps at 300 K and 1 atm. Validation compared the model to available surface reaction energy barriers, not to experimental density, diffusivity, or elastic modulus. Results showed bond correlations: P-F and Li-O associated with more stable structures, C-O and Li-F with less stable ones. The authors argue that multitask QRNN training allows modeling complex SEI redox reactions and that this is the most complex redox reactive system simulated with MLFF. The limitation is the use of only a single electrolyte formulation (1M LiPF6 in EC), and the scope is deemed small relative to what is required for practical SEI chemistry.

Executive Summary
This work presents the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by predicted energy, produced via a machine learning force field (MLFF) developed for lithium-ion battery materials.

Results showed bond correlations: P-F and Li-O associated with more stable structures, C-O and Li-F with less stable ones. The authors argue that multitask QRNN training allows modeling complex SEI redox reactions and that this is the most complex redox reactive system simulated with MLFF. The limitation is the use of only a single electrolyte formulation (1M LiPF6 in EC), and the scope is deemed small relative to what is required for practical SEI chemistry.

Research Context
The SEI is a vital but poorly-understood class of materials combining organic and inorganic components. Key questions such as amorphous or crystalline nature and Li+ movement remain unanswered. No existing method is fully applicable to simulating such a complex system. Existing pure density functionals work well for metallic systems but underestimate reaction barriers. Hybrid functionals struggle with metals and have very poor scaling for periodic systems. MLFFs promise to allow atomistic simulation with DFT accuracy and classical fast sampling. Multitask learning lets us train MLFFs to both pure and hybrid DFT labels. MLFFs can predict the properties of Li metal and organic liquids. Prior work produced ranked SEI candidates for future ML and experimental comparison.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a multitask QRNN MLFF can model complex SEI redox reactions and rank candidates. The hypothesis is that multitask learning plus the SPICE dataset will enable accurate modeling across disparate organic and inorganic chemical space without a heavy cost on model capacity. The hypothesis is that using the SEI Simulator will yield stable dynamics under extreme annealing conditions. The authors predict that the latent space of these MLFF models contains unused capacity for broadening chemical applicability. They predict that lower-energy candidates will correlate with P-F and Li-O bonds associated with more stable structures. They anticipate the resulting candidates will form the first set of SEI structures for future ML applications and experimental comparison.

Methodological Details
Reference theory: wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD for non-periodic and PBE-D3 plane wave for periodic systems. A random subset of non-periodic systems was labeled with PBE-D3 to improve information exchange. Hybrid functionals were not feasible to label periodic datasets due to great expense. GFN1-xTB was used for charge labels because it balanced accuracy and convergence. Data was generated via multiple rounds of active learning to increase accuracy. AFIR and NEB were used on the QRNN potential energy surface. The SPICE dataset of H, Li, C, O, F, and P was added with GFN1-xTB charge labels. PBE-head validation RMSE showed no increase when adding the SPICE data. Hybrid-head RMSE increased by 8% when adding the SPICE data. The width of the hidden layers was doubled to increase capacity. Each batch was sampled half from priority data and half from the rest of the dataset. Decoupled weight norms were used and not included in the optimizer. Initial geometries were generated using the SEI Simulator with OPLS4 MD. Each system started with 700 molecules of EC plus 52 Li+ and PF 6 ions. Each system contained 52 ions each of Li+ and PF 6 ions. Each box contained 52 Li+ and 52 PF 6 ions. Each system had 7416 total atoms (Fig 1). Four lithiation levels used: 5, 12, 23, and 33 added Li+ ions per box. Systems were annealed using the reactive QRNN model at 400 K and 1000 atm for 100 ps each. Candidates were ranked by mean potential energy over 20 ps at 300 K and 1 atm. Only 1% of the data was used as the validation set. Hidden layers were sized 256, 224, and 192 for all elements. The batch size was 64. The learning rate was 2e-3 and the weight decay was 1e-3. An exponential moving average was averaged every 10 batches with alpha = 0.001. The Adamax optimizer was used with decoupled weight decay. Periodic DFT used the PBE functional with a 40 Ry plane wave cutoff. The Brillouin zone used a 3x3x3 k-point mesh for bulk supercells. Gas-phase wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD was performed using Psi4 v1.6.

The model used a QRNN for potential energy and charge labels. The loss was energy and atomic force mean squared error per theory level. The model used four output levels of theory in total for multitask training. First and last output heads were only used to shape the latent space during training. No DFT-generated MD, AFIR, or NEB geometries were used as training inputs. Clusters were capped with hydrogen atoms for cut bonds.

The QRNN models gave stable dynamics under the extreme annealing conditions. P-F and Li-O bonds were associated with more stable structures. C-O and Li-F bonds were associated with less stable ones. Bond counts with respect to total system energy are shown in Fig 4. PBE-head validation RMSE showed no increase when adding SPICE data. Hybrid-head RMSE increased by 8% when adding the SPICE data. Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Multitask training with a QRNN model allows modeling complex SEI redox reactions. This is the most complex redox reactive system simulated using an MLFF. The model is limited to only a single formulation of electrolyte (1M LiPF6 in EC). Comparing formulations will allow calculating Li+ diffusivity and mechanical properties. Future work should include application of other model architectures like Nequip and MACE. The latent space of these MLFF models can be broadened via multitask training. The weight decay of 3e-3 per batch was useful but reduced reaction barrier heights relative to reference. The final model used a conventional weight decay of 1e-3. "This work presents the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by predicted energy, produced via a machine learning force field (MLFF) developed for lithium-ion battery materials. The solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) is a critical but poorly understood passivating layer formed at the lithium anode; its amorphous or crystalline nature and Li+ transport mechanisms remain unanswered. No existing method can fully simulate such a complex system spanning long length and time scales with both organic and inorganic components. Traditional pure DFT underestimates reaction barriers and hybrid functionals like wB97X-D3BJ are too computationally expensive for the periodic systems necessary. The authors address this gap by training a QRNN-based MLFF using multitask learning, which labels both pure and hybrid DFT datasets simultaneously. They selected wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD for non-periodic and PBE-D3 plane wave for periodic systems, using GFN1-xTB to generate charge labels. Data was generated via multiple rounds of active learning, including AFIR and NEB sampling on the QRNN potential energy surface, and augmented with the SPICE dataset (H, Li, C, O, F, P) with GFN1-xTB labels. They used a new Schrodinger SEI Simulator (OPLS4 MD) to generate initial 1M LiPF6 in EC geometries with 700 EC molecules plus 52 ions of Li+ and PF6- each, totaling 7416 atoms per box, across four lithiation levels (5, 12, 23, 33 added Li+). The model was trained with 1% validation data, Adamax optimizer, learning rate 2e-3, batch size 64, hidden layers 256/224/192, 1e-3 weight decay, and an exponential moving average (alpha 0.001). Systems were annealed at 400 K/1000 atm for 100 ps and ranked by mean potential energy over 20 ps at 300 K/1 atm. Validation compared the model to available surface reaction energy barriers, not to experimental density, diffusivity, or elastic modulus. Results showed bond correlations: P-F and Li-O associated with more stable structures, C-O and Li-F with less stable ones. The authors argue that multitask QRNN training allows modeling complex SEI redox reactions and that this is the most complex redox reactive system simulated with MLFF. The limitation is the use of only a single electrolyte formulation (1M LiPF6 in EC), and the scope is deemed small relative to what is required for practical SEI chemistry."

"The fundamental problem is that the lithium anode must be unstable relative to the cathode but stable relative to the electrolyte during discharge. Stabilization has relied on the formation of a solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI), a complex passivating layer separating metallic lithium from organic electrolyte, but fundamental questions about its amorphous or crystalline nature and Li+ transport remain unanswered. No existing method is fully applicable to simulating the SEI's large length and time scales, which involve conductors, insulators, and redox reactions. Existing pure DFT work well for metallic systems but underestimate reaction barriers; hybrid functionals like wB97X improve barriers but struggle with metals and have poor scaling for periodic systems, leaving SEI simulation out of reach. MLFFs offer DFT accuracy with classical force-field sampling, but traditional fixed-functional forms are hard to fit for complex systems. Multitask learning allows training MLFFs on both pure and hybrid DFT labels, and it has predicted Li metal and organic liquid properties. However, prior MLFF works on these systems have not produced a ranked set of SEI candidates for future machine learning and experimental comparison, leaving a gap in quantitatively understanding battery interphases."

(2011) found A. iva ecdysterone at 5 μg/ml reduced fecundity, fertility, and survival of Oligonychus perseae, while commercial 20-hydroxyecdysone had lesser effects. Clerodanes, such as dihydroclerodin and clerodin hemiacetal, showed 100% antifeedant activity at 50 ppm and were deadly to Spodoptera litura (Koul 2016). The authors previously identified high contents of three phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone) and two clerodanes in A. iva from Israel (Taha-Salaime et al. 2019). They hypothesized that a crude leaf extract containing the three phytoecdysteroids, which specifically control molting and antifeedant activities, might be a promising pest-control agent. Results showed 1st instar mortality increased significantly (25, 65, 85%) at 50, 100, and 250 μg/μl compared to 5% control; 3rd instar reduced LWG and RGR (p < 0.001), with RGR decreasing early as 2 days into the experiment (0.05 and 0.20 g/g day on days 6 and 8), and survival reduced after 11 days (none survived more than 8-10 days). Research Context
Spodoptera littoralis is a serious pest of cotton, maize, rice, alfalfa, potato, tomato, ornamentals and orchard trees. It feeds year-round on the leaves of numerous old-and new-world plant species. Insect pests are mainly controlled by insecticides, which constitute a risk to human health and the environment. Many organic insecticides have been derived from plant sources and exhibit high toxicity against a variety of agricultural pests. Phytoecdysteroids are plant-produced steroids that are analogs of the steroid hormones that control molting and metamorphosis in arthropods. They can mimic insect 20-hydroxyecdysteroid, bind insect ecdysone receptors and elicit the same responses. Phytoecdysteroids may cause abnormal larval development, feeding deterrence and ultimately, death. Ecdysteroids are not toxic to mammals because their structure is quite different from mammalian steroids. Most of them possess a cholest-7-en-6-one carbon skeleton (C27) and are synthesized from phytosterols in the cytosol through the mevalonic acid pathway. Phytoecdysteroids are present in 5-6% of plant species.

Research Question And Hypothesis
We hypothesized that crude extract of A. iva leaves that includes the three phytoecdysteroids responsible for metamorphosis and antifeedant activities might be a promising pest-control agent. The authors previously identified high contents of three phytoecdysteroids and two clerodanes in A. iva growing in Israel. The first research question is whether A. iva crude leaf extract affects S. littoralis larvae. The second question is whether phytoecdysteroids isolated from the crude leaf extract and commercial standards have different effects on the larvae. The third question is whether phytoecdysteroids have a direct effect on the larvae's gut.

Methodological Details
Young and mature leaves and stems of fresh plants were collected after blooming (July-November). The leaves and stems were oven-dried at 55 C for 3-4 days then homogenized to a fine powder prior to extraction. The first and third instars of S. littoralis larvae were from Murad Ghanim's laboratory reared on castor bean leaves. For extraction, leaf and stem powder were pooled (24 g) and soaked in 240 ml of 100% MeOH. The extract was homogenized with shaking (2500 rpm) for 1 h then centrifuged at 112 g for 10 min. The final filtered methanol solution was analyzed by liquid chromatography-time of flight-mass spectrometry (LC-TOF-MS). The solution was dried in a chemical vaporizer for 5 days. For purification, leaf and stem powder (100 g) was soaked in 300 ml methanol. The filtered extract was treated with H2O to give 30% aqueous methanol. LC-TOF-MS analysis identified phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes in three concentrations of A. iva crude leaf extract (50, 100 and 250 µg/µl). Extracts (1 µl) were injected into an Agilent 1290 Infinity Series liquid chromatograph coupled with an Agilent 1290 Infinity DAD and Agilent 6224 Accurate Mass TOF mass spectrometer. Thin-layer chromatography (TLC) used silica gel GF-254 plates (0.25 mm; 20 × 20 cm) to separate components. Mature castor bean leaves were smeared with A. iva crude leaf extract (24 g of dried pooled leaves and stems dissolved in 240 ml MeOH, 1:10) and Tween 20 (1.5 mg). Ten first instar S. littoralis larvae were placed on one treated castor bean leaf in a petri dish and allowed to feed for 3 days at 25 C. Control leaves were smeared with double-distilled water (ddH2O) and Tween 20. Larval mortality was compared to that of controls after 3 days of feeding. Data represent the results of 11 replicates (10 larvae/replicate). Differences were reported as percent mortality using a t-test and significance determined by t-test. For the third instars, 1 or 10 larvae were fed on one treated castor bean leaf for 4 or 8 days at 25 C. Four different treatments were tested with reversal of order. A separate experiment tested third instar larvae exposed to 250 µg/µl A. iva crude leaf extract for 4 days. Survival was recorded as (ln W2 -ln W1)/ (t2 -t1) with n = 20 replicates. In each treatment, pupation rate was evaluated for an additional 15 days. Relative growth rates (RGRs) were compared using a mixed-model ANOVA. Survival rates were analyzed using a Friedman test because data did not follow a normal distribution. Larval weight gain (LWG) comparisons used a repeated measures ANOVA. Statistical significance was reported at p < 0.05 and error bars represent the standard error of the mean (SEM). All statistical analyses were performed with IBM SPSS software v.20 for Windows. Gut morphology used DAPI and phalloidin staining after 7 days of treatment. Guts were dissected in phosphate buffered saline (1X PBS) then fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 30 min. Guts were washed in 0.1% Triton X-100 for 30 min then incubated in phalloidin for 30 min. Visualized with a Leica confocal microscope (Leica SP8 and Olympus IX 81 confocal laser scanning microscope).

Procedures And Architectures
Leaf and stem powder were pooled (24 g) and soaked in 240 ml of 100% MeOH. The extract was homogenized with shaking (2500 rpm) for 1 h. The extract was centrifuged (112 g) for 10 min then filtered and concentrated under vacuum. The filtered methanol solution was dried in a chemical vaporizer for 5 days. Leaf and stem powder (100 g) was soaked in 300 ml methanol for purification. The filtered extract was treated with H2O to give 30% aqueous methanol. Extracts (1 µl) were injected into an Agilent 1290 Infinity Series liquid chromatograph. Detection was Agilent 1290 Infinity DAD and Agilent 6224 Accurate Mass TOF mass spectrometer. TLC used silica gel GF-254 plates (0.25 mm; 20 × 20 cm). Castor bean leaves were smeared with crude leaf extract (24 g dissolved in 240 ml MeOH, 1:10) and Tween 20 (1.5 mg). Leaves were dried in a chemical hood for 2 h before placing 10 larvae. Larvae were exposed to three concentrations (50, 100 and 250 µg/µl). For 250 µg/µl: 1.2 g dried extract powder was dissolved in 4.8 ml ddH2O and Tween 20. For 100 µg/µl: 0.83 ml of the high concentration extract was dissolved in 3 ml ddH2O. For 50 µg/µl: 0.67 ml of the 100 µg/µl solution was dissolved in 3 ml ddH2O. 11 replicates (10 larvae/replicate) and a t-test compared mortality. For the third instars 1 or 10 larvae were fed on one treated castor bean leaf. Survival was recorded as (ln W2 -ln W1)/ (t2 -t1) with n = 20 replicates. Pupation was evaluated for an additional 15 days. RGRs were compared using a mixed-model ANOVA. Survival was analyzed using a Friedman test. LWG was measured with 10 replicates and compared using repeated measures ANOVA. IBM SPSS software v.20 for Windows was used for statistical analysis. Guts were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde in 1X PBS and washed in 0.1% Triton X-100. Guts were washed three times in PBS Tween-PBST then incubated in phalloidin for 30 min. Guts were mounted whole in 0.1% DAPI in hybridization buffer. Changes in actin fibers and nuclei were visualized under a Leica confocal microscope.

Key Results
Phytoecdysteroid spots showed Rf values similar to those of the respective commercial ecdysteroids (Fig. 1). First instar larvae showed a significant increase in mortality (25, 65, 85%) at 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl (Fig. 2a). The control showed only 5% mortality after feeding on water-smeared leaves. Third instar larvae fed on crude extract showed reduced LWG (F3.104 = 20.334, 17.246 and 13.007, p < 0.001; Fig. 2b). All concentrations significantly decreased RGR compared to the control (p < 0.001; Fig. 3a). Reduced RGR was recorded as early as 2 days into the experiment. The highest concentration decreased RGR by 0.05 on day 6 and 0.20 on day 8 (F3.16 = 12.641, p < 0.001; Fig. 3a). All concentrations reduced third instar survival after 11 days (X 2 3 = 6.221, p = 0.038; Fig. 3b). None of the treated larvae survived more than 8 days at the highest concentration (Fig. 3b). None of the treated larvae survived more than 10 days at the other concentrations (Fig. 3b). RGR was affected after day 5 when the order of treatments was reversed (F3.16 = 7.310, p < 0.001; Fig. 4a). RGR continued to decrease until the end of the experiment with no surviving larvae (X 2 3 = 9.282, p = 0.021; Fig. 4b). When the order was reversed a significant decrease in RGR was obtained on days 2-4 (Fig. 4c). The purified phytoecdysteroid mixture significantly reduced RGR (F2.20, 18 = 6.172, p = 0.001; Fig. 5a). Few larvae survived on the leaves treated with the purified phytoecdysteroid fraction (X 2 3 = 11.305, p = 0.04; Fig. 5b). Larvae treated with 250 µg/µl crude extract or purified mixture lost weight and stopped growing (Fig. 5a). Larvae treated with 250 µg/µl crude extract for 8 days had smaller nuclei of abnormal shape (Fig. 6d-f). Phalloidin staining showed normal actin filaments in the control treatment (Fig. 6a-c). Treated larvae showed actin filaments that were smaller and their amount reduced (Fig. 6d-i). Treated larvae exposed to the crude extract or its phytoecdysteroid fraction had less actin fibers and smaller nuclei. Larvae treated with 250 µg/µl crude extract or purified mixture for 8 days were unable to complete development and pupate after 15 days (Fig. 7). The dying larvae had short limbs, small heads, and decreased weight (Fig. 7b and c). Only the stomach and chest pupated (considered nonpupation) (Fig. 7b and c). None of them completed their development to adult moths. No significant effect was seen at 100 ppm of the commercial mixture fed for 8 days.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The phytoecdysteroids of A. iva and its fractionated phytoecdysteroids significantly reduce the development and survival of S. littoralis larvae. These effects were pronounced throughout all larval developmental stages, including pupation. Phytoecdysteroids have been shown to reduce the fertility and fecundity of Bemisia tabaci and Oligonychus perseae (Aly et al. 2011). Ecdysteroids inhibited feeding and drinking of lepidopteran and coleopteran pests at concentrations from 5 to 200 mg/kg. In this study, the crude extract was most effective at the highest concentration applied, indicating a dose-dependent effect. In contrast, S. littoralis was not deterred from feeding by 20-hydroxyecdysone at 50-70 mg/kg (Jones and Firn 1978). Cyasterone and turkesterone are the most effective lepidopteran-and coleopteran-specific ecdysteroids (Slama et al. 1993). Ingesting the phytoecdysteroid 20-hydroxyecdysone caused death before and during Bombyx mori molting (Chou and Lu 1980). Based on the results, phytoecdysteroids may affect insects by interfering with their developmental stages, especially during metamorphosis (Chou and Lu 1980). The reduced growth rate suggests that larvae are adversely affected by ingestion of the crude leaf extract. Histological observations showed the larval gut cells showed histolysis with clear signs of apoptosis. The gut epithelium showed massive deterioration, there was destruction of the microvilli of the columnar cells, and formation of vacuoles. The effect on pupation could be a consequence of disruptions in hormonal balance effected by internal levels of ecdysone. Actin microfilaments have been associated with rounding and loss of adhesion that frequently occur with viral infection or transformation. The phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes of A. iva may be useful for the management of economically important insect pests while reducing the risks to human health.

Contradictions And Limitations
In our study, we did not fractionate clerodanes from A. iva crude leaf extract due to the difficulty involved in calibrating the protocol for fractionation. The high cost of commercial clerodane standards made fractionation not feasible. In our study, we only used a few commercial standards because they are very expensive and are not feasible as a control treatment. We could not use them at the same concentrations as the applied treatment. A commercial mixture was used at a maximum concentration of 100 ppm each, which is very low compared to the applied concentrations (250,000 ppm). No significant effect of the mixture on S. littoralis larvae was seen when the 100 ppm mixture was fed for 8 days. Tanaka (1995) reported altered epidermal sensitivity to 20-hydroxyecdysone at 300 ppm, higher than the standard concentration used in our study. In contrast, S. littoralis was not deterred from feeding by 20-hydroxyecdysone at 50-70 mg/kg (Jones and Firn 1978). Commercial standards were not applied at the same concentrations as the crude leaf extract and phytoecdysteroid fraction treatments (250,000 ppm). The study did not replicate the dose-independent effects observed in some previous studies.

Claims
Ajuga iva crude leaf extract reduces the development and survival of S. littoralis larvae in a dose-dependent manner. 1st instar mortality increased significantly (25, 65, 85%) at the three crude extract concentrations. All concentrations significantly decreased larval relative growth rate compared to the control diet. The highest concentration decreased RGR by 0.05 on day 6 and 0.20 on day 8. No treated larvae survived more than 8-10 days at the crude extract concentrations. S. littoralis was not deterred from feeding by 20-hydroxyecdysone at 50-70 mg/kg (Jones and Firn 1978). The commercial standard mixture at 100 ppm showed no significant effect on S. littoralis larvae. The dose-dependent effect indicates that the crude extract's potency scales with application intensity. Such effects could be harnessed for management of economically important insect pests while reducing human health risks.
The effects on S. littoralis are mediated by the three fractionated phytoecdysteroids and are associated with gut histolysis and hormonal imbalance. The purified phytoecdysteroid mixture significantly reduced RGR (F2.20 = 6.172) compared to the control. Treated larvae showed smaller nuclei, reduced actin fibers, and histolysis of the gut cells. The gut cells showed histolysis with clear signs of apoptosis. The gut epithelium showed massive deterioration, destruction of microvilli, and formation of vacuoles. The effect on pupation could be a consequence of disruptions in hormonal balance effected by internal levels of ecdysone. The commercial mixture at 100 ppm showed no significant effect, suggesting threshold-dependent response. Only a few larvae survived on the purified phytoecdysteroid fraction treatment. Gut histolysis suggests that phytoecdysteroids target midgut epithelial cells rather than systemic metabolism. Reduced pupation may reflect a failure to reach the required threshold weight for metamorphosis.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows that Rf values of the phytoecdysteroid spots were similar to the respective commercial ecdysteroids. Figure 2a shows a significant increase in mortality (25, 65, 85%) for the three crude extract concentrations. Figure 2b shows that third instar larvae fed on crude extract showed reduced LWG. Figure 3a shows all concentrations significantly decreased RGR compared to the control diet. Figure 3b shows all concentrations reduced third instar larval survival after 11 days. Figure 4a shows that RGR was affected after day 5 when the order of treatments was reversed. Figure 4b shows no surviving larvae after reversed treatments. Figure 4c shows a significant decrease in RGR on days 2-4 when the treatment order was reversed. Figure 5a shows that the purified phytoecdysteroid mixture significantly reduced RGR compared to the control. Figure 5b shows that few larvae survived on the leaves treated with the purified phytoecdysteroid fraction. Figure 6 shows that actin filaments were smaller and their amount reduced in guts from treated larvae. Figure 7 shows that larvae fed on the crude extract or the purified fraction were unable to complete development and pupate after 15 days. Figure 7b and c show that the dying larvae had short limbs, small heads, decreased weight, and only the stomach and chest pupated.

Three Takeaways
The core contribution is demonstrating that crude A. iva leaf extract and its fractionated phytoecdysteroids significantly reduce S. littoralis development and survival, including pupation. The strongest evidence is the significant, dose-dependent increase in 1st instar mortality (25, 65, 85%) and a sharp reduction in 3rd instar RGR early as 2 days (F3.16 = 12.641, p < 0.001). The future path involves validating the antifeedant and repellent activities of A. iva phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes in IPM programs, while overcoming the cost and calibration barriers to clerodane fractionation.

summary.title: Highly sensitive and full-genome interrogation of SARS-CoV-2 using multiplexed PCR enrichment followed by next-generation sequencing
summary.authors: Chenyu Li, David N Debruyne, Julia Spencer, Vidushi Kapoor, Lily Y Liu, Bo Zhou, Utsav Pandey, Moiz Bootwalla, Dejerianne Ostrow, Dennis T Maglinte, David Ruble, Alex Ryutov, Lishuang Shen, Lucie Lee, Rounak Feigelman, Grayson Burdon, Jeffrey Liu, Alejandra Oliva, Adam Borcherding, Hongdong Tan, Alexander E Urban, Xiaowu Gai, Jennifer Dien Bard, Guoying Liu, Zhitong Liu
summary.field_subfield: Molecular diagnostics; viral genomics; infectious disease surveillance
summary.executive_summary: RT-PCR is the most commonly used method for SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis due to its high sensitivity, yet reports indicate it identifies only 47-59% of true positive cases, leaving 75% of negative results false-negative. These gaps arise from low viral loads, sampling timing, RNA degradation, or primer-binding mutations. This study developed a multiplex-PCR assay with 343 total primer pairs (172 + 171) producing 100bp amplicons across the 29,903bp SARS-CoV-2 genome with a 76±10bp gap. A mathematical model predicts RT-PCR LOD at 4.8 copies at 95% probability (Fig. 1A), while multiplex PCR drops LOD to 1.15 copies (172-pair pool) and 0.29 copies (both pools). Two plasmids carrying the S and N genes were used to validate the method, spiked into cDNA from human total RNA and quantified by droplet-based digital PCR (QX200). 13 nasopharyngeal swabs (viral loads 8–675,885 copies/uL) amplified the full genome on Illumina MiSeq; 98-99% coverage was reached at 100X for most samples, including those with only 8 copies (Fig. 3A). Low sequencing depth was tolerated: 58% coverage at 100X was retained at 50,000 reads/library (Fig. 3B). Mutation thresholding was conservative, requiring >60% empirical frequency for true calls, with intra-host noise filtered below 20%. The panel discriminated SARS-CoV-2 from other human coronaviruses with 0% cross-alignment, supporting expansion to broader respiratory pathogen detection. A parallel metagenomic method using random hexamers achieved 96% S/N gene coverage at ~0.6M reads, with 16% of recovered bases being viral. The authors warn that intra-host mutations should not be inferred with low-copy or low-depth inputs, and low-depth sequencing alone cannot resolve primer dimers without high-resolution electrophoresis.
