Executive Summary
RT-PCR is the most commonly used method for SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis due to its high sensitivity, yet reports indicate it identifies only 47-59% of true positive cases, leaving 75% of negative results false-negative. These gaps arise from low viral loads, sampling timing, RNA degradation, or primer-binding mutations. This study developed a multiplex-PCR assay with 343 total primer pairs (172 + 171) producing 100bp amplicons across the 29,903bp SARS-CoV-2 genome with a 76±10bp gap. A mathematical model predicts RT-PCR LOD at 4.8 copies at 95% probability (Fig. 1A), while multiplex PCR drops LOD to 1.15 copies (172-pair pool) and 0.29 copies (both pools). Two plasmids carrying the S and N genes were used to validate the method, spiked into cDNA from human total RNA and quantified by droplet-based digital PCR (QX200). 13 nasopharyngeal swabs (viral loads 8–675,885 copies/uL) amplified the full genome on Illumina MiSeq; 98-99% coverage was reached at 100X for most samples, including those with only 8 copies (Fig. 3A). Low sequencing depth was tolerated: 58% coverage at 100X was retained at 50,000 reads/library (Fig. 3B). Mutation thresholding was conservative, requiring >60% empirical frequency for true calls, with intra-host noise filtered below 20%. The panel discriminated SARS-CoV-2 from other human coronaviruses with 0% cross-alignment, supporting expansion to broader respiratory pathogen detection. A parallel metagenomic method using random hexamers achieved 96% S/N gene coverage at ~0.6M reads, with 16% of recovered bases being viral. The authors warn that intra-host mutations should not be inferred with low-copy or low-depth inputs, and low-depth sequencing alone cannot resolve primer dimers without high-resolution electrophoresis.

Research Context
RT-PCR is the gold standard for SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis, but real-world performance is inconsistent across methods. The reported limit of detection for RT-PCR is 4-8 copies, which is higher than idealized sensitivity. Studies show RT-PCR only captures 47-59% of positive cases, leaving a gap in detection. Notably, 75% of RT-PCR negative results were later confirmed positive by other assays. Heat inactivation of clinical samples can also degrade viral RNA and hinder downstream diagnosis.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study asks if a multiplex-PCR strategy can lower the detection limit and improve SARS-CoV-2 coverage. It is hypothesized that simultaneous amplification of hundreds of regions reduces LOD and tolerates mutation. The multiplex PCR is predicted to reach a detection limit of 1.15 copies with the first pool. The two-pool strategy is predicted to reach a detection limit of 0.29 copies.

Methodological Details
The panel consists of 172 pairs with an average amplicon length of 99bp. Amplicons span the genome with a 76±10bp gap between adjacent targets. Two plasmids carrying the full S and N genes were used as targets. Spiked plasmids were quantified with droplet-based digital PCR on a QX200 system. Copy numbers ranged from 9,000 down to below one copy. 13 nasopharyngeal swab specimens were amplified on the Illumina MiSeq. Viral loads ranged from 8 to 675,885 RNA copies/uL.

Procedures And Architectures
Multiplex products were amplified in a secondary PCR with NGS primers added. Electrophoresis was used to visualize and size expected target peaks. The full genomes were sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq. Random hexamer adapters were used for the metagenomic method.

Key Results
98-99% of the genome was covered at 100X for most specimens at 5,000 reads/amplicon. At only 8 copies, genome coverage reached 96%. The highest plasmid recovery was 14 copies, yielding 1.4 to 2.8 plasmids per reads. The metagenomic method recovered 96% of the SARS-CoV-2 genome at ~0.6M reads. Only 0.08% of human chromosomal regions were amplified. SARS-CoV-2 reads aligned 0% to other human coronaviruses.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The multiplex PCR efficiency was higher than the estimated 6% when amplifying single-stranded cDNA. The method tolerates the presence of mutations in the SARS-CoV-2 genome. The specificity supports expanding the panel to other respiratory viruses. The uniform coverage was reinforced by the log10 distance to the mean.

Contradictions And Limitations
Plasmid library yields began to saturate at 1,700 copies. No UMI was used in the multiplex PCR amplification. Intra-host mutations may be contaminated with noise from PCR. Low viral copy and low sequencing depth were noted as a concern for mutation calls. Electrophoresis remains necessary to differentiate target amplicons from primer-dimers.

Claims
Multiplex PCR achieves a much lower limit of detection than RT-PCR and tolerates viral mutations. Multiplex PCR reduces the detection limit to 1.15 copies (172 pairs) and 0.29 copies (both pools). Both overlapping pools provide full coverage of the viral genome. The method amplifies only 0.08% of human chromosomal regions, limiting its universal application. The high specificity supports expanding the panel to other respiratory viruses.
Coverage remains high even at low sequencing depth, enabling diagnostic-level readout at low copy inputs. At 50,000 reads/library, 58% of the genome was covered at 100X. 150,000 total reads yielded 93% coverage at 100X.  Low-depth sequencing can provide definitive results in <50,000 reads per sample.
The metagenomic method yields >96% SARS-CoV-2 coverage at moderate sequencing depth with only ~0.6M reads. 96% of the SARS-CoV-2 genome was recovered at ~0.6M reads. Only 16% of recovered bases were viral in human gDNA.  Host depletion is not required to achieve these coverage levels.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Sub-sampling of 5 genomes to 150K, 100K, and 50K reads tested coverage tolerance.

Ethical Considerations
13 nasopharyngeal swab specimens were used without explicit IRB or ethics approval reported.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the predicted RT-PCR LOD of 4.8 copies at 95% probability. Figure 2A shows library peaks from 8,900 to 2.8 copies of plasmids. Figure 3A correlates genome coverage with viral copy number.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: A multiplex-PCR assay reduces SARS-CoV-2 LOD to 0.29 copies and captures the full genome. 2. The strongest evidence: 98-99% coverage at 100X was retained even at 8 copies, confirming low-input sensitivity. 3. The future path: The specificity enables expansion to other respiratory viruses, and the metagenomic method needs host depletion validation.

summary.title: Translational accuracy of a tethered ribosome
summary.authors: Celine Fabret (CNRS); Olivier Namy (CNRS)
summary.field_subfield: Molecular biology; prokaryotic translation; ribosome biogenesis and function
summary.executive_summary:
Translation is the last step in gene expression, converting the mRNA coding sequence into the amino-acid sequence of a protein, a vital cellular activity catalyzed by ribosomes. Ribosomes are evolutionary conserved ribonucleoprotein complexes that function as two separate subunits in all kingdoms: the 30S subunit (16S rRNA and 21 ribosomal proteins) responsible for decoding genetic sequences via recognition of the Shine-Dalgarno (SD) sequence; and the 50S subunit (5S and 23S rRNAs with 33 proteins) catalyzing peptide bond formation. During translation, these subunits associate during initiation, rotate during elongation, and dissociate after protein release. This organization is thought to be essential for biogenesis, successful protein synthesis and cell viability. Cell viability depends on a balance between rapid protein synthesis and accurate decoding, and signals in specific mRNAs at defined locations can program a high rate of errors—recoding events that occur during elongation (frameshifting) or at termination (stop codon readthrough). A ribosome with tethered subunits, in which the two subunits were covalently linked in a single entity, was recently engineered in Escherichia coli. The resulting ribosome, Ribo-T, with its inseparable subunits, was shown to be functional and able to sustain the cell growth, although doubling times were slower (107 min for Ribo-T, 35 min for wild-type ribosomes) and the protein synthesis rate was 50% that of wild-type ribosomes.

In this study, the authors investigated the translational properties of Ribo-T ribosomes, asking whether these ribosomes maintain the correct reading frame as faithfully as wild-type ribosomes, terminate translation accurately at stop codons, and translate messenger RNA accurately. They tested Ribo-T with recoding signals that instruct the ribosome to change translational reading frame (frameshifting) or to read stop codons as sense codons (stop codon readthrough), and also investigated the preferential mode of translation used by Ribo-T ribosomes to express adjacent open reading frames on the same mRNA, given that the two subunits were inseparable. Our data reveal an impairment of tethered ribosomes for +1 frameshifting and termination, but show that these ribosomes are otherwise as effective as wildtype ribosomes. Overall, covalent attachment of the two subunits modifies the properties of the ribosome, altering its ability to initiate and terminate translation correctly.

The resulting ribosome, Ribo-T, with its inseparable subunits, was shown to be functional and able to sustain the cell growth, although doubling times were slower (107 min for Ribo-T, 35 min for wild-type ribosomes) and the protein synthesis rate was 50% that of wild-type ribosomes.

In this study, the authors investigated the translational properties of Ribo-T ribosomes, asking whether these ribosomes maintain the correct reading frame as faithfully as wild-type ribosomes, terminate translation accurately at stop codons, and translate messenger RNA accurately. They tested Ribo-T with recoding signals that instruct the ribosome to change translational reading frame (frameshifting) or to read stop codons as sense codons (stop codon readthrough), and also investigated the preferential mode of translation used by Ribo-T ribosomes to express adjacent open reading frames on the same mRNA, given that the two subunits were inseparable. Our data reveal an impairment of tethered ribosomes for +1 frameshifting and termination, but show that these ribosomes are otherwise as effective as wildtype ribosomes. Overall, covalent attachment of the two subunits modifies the properties of the ribosome, altering its ability to initiate and terminate translation correctly.

Research Context
Ribosomes are conserved ribonucleoprotein complexes that function as two separate subunits in all kingdoms. The 30S subunit contains the 16S rRNA and 21 ribosomal proteins responsible for decoding genetic sequences. The 50S subunit contains two rRNA molecules, the 5S and 23S rRNAs, with 33 proteins. Ribosomes assemble to form the mature ribosome, which is responsible for translating the messenger RNA. The two subunits associate with each other during translation initiation, rotate during elongation, and dissociate after protein release. A ribosome with tethered subunits was recently engineered in Escherichia coli. The tethered ribosome, called Ribo-T, has subunits covalently linked in a single entity. Ribo-T was shown to be functional and to sustain cell growth. However, doubling times were slower than wild-type ribosomes. The protein synthesis rate with Ribo-T was 50% that with wild-type ribosomes. The slow growth was likely due to slower biogenesis, rather than impaired activity.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Do Ribo-T ribosomes maintain the correct reading frame as faithfully as wild-type ribosomes? Do they terminate translation accurately at stop codons? Do they translate messenger RNA accurately? The study tested Ribo-T with recoding signals instructing a reading frame change or stop codon readthrough. The investigators tested frameshifting and stop codon readthrough as tools for assessing Ribo-T fidelity. They also examined the preferential mode of translation used by Ribo-T to express adjacent open reading frames. A key question was whether the inseparable subunits affect the translation reading frame. The authors hypothesized that covalent attachment alters the ability to initiate and terminate translation correctly. An impairment for +1 frameshifting and termination was predicted.

The experiments used the E. coli BL21 (DE3) strain from Invitrogen. Ribo-T ribosomal DNA was expressed using the poRibo-T2 vector. The Ribo-T 16S rRNA ASD sequence was changed to an orthogonal sequence (5'-UCAUUGUGGUA-. The pCL99 dual reporter system was used to create fusion constructs. The reporter carries the lacZ-luc fusion gene under the T7 promoter. The system includes the streptomycin resistance gene and the CloDF13-derived CDF replicon. Target sequences were inserted by oligocloning into the MscI restriction site. Cloned oligonucleotides were hybridised at 100°C in ligation buffer. In-frame controls were constructed for each target sequence. The target sequences are listed in Table 1. Translation efficiency was calculated as a ratio of activities. The median value was taken for at least six independent experiments. Statistical significance was determined with Student's t-tests. Wild-type ribosomes used a lacZ gene carrying a wild-type SD sequence AGGAGG. Ribo-T ribosomes were tested with constructs carrying a mutated SD sequence CACCAC. Crosstalk between wild-type and Ribo-T ribosomes was checked and too low to affect results.

Three programmed -1 frameshifting sites were selected from IS911, IS3, and dnaX. Frameshifting is stimulated by a slippery sequence and SD-ASD interaction elements. -1 frameshifting was measured first with wild-type SD sequences. As Ribo-T cannot base pair to the WT SD, Ribo-T frameshifting was initially assumed absent. The reverse experiment replaced the dnaX SD with one recognized by Ribo-T ribosomes. This lowered WT frameshifting but had no impact on Ribo-T frameshifting. +1 frameshifting was selected from the E. coli prfB gene. Stop codon readthrough was assessed using the mtmB1 gene from the archaea Methanosarcina barkeri. The mtmB1 stop codon sequence promotes readthrough in E. coli, even without pyrrolysine. Stop codons were tested: UAG, UGA, and UAA.

Key Results
For -1 frameshifting, IS911 efficiency was nearly equal between ribosomes. Ribo-T IS911 efficiency was 14% with wild-type (p=0.54). IS3 -1 frameshifting efficiency was 33% with both types of ribosome (p=0.77). For dnaX, -1 frameshifting was 43% with wild-type and 45% with Ribo-T (p=0.77). In the reverse experiment, the Ribo-T SD lowered WT frameshifting to 11% vs 43% (p=1.7x10 -3). Ribo-T frameshifting remained unchanged at 45% versus 44% (p=0.85). For +1 frameshifting, the wild-type efficiency was 33% with the prfB sequence. Ribo-T +1 frameshifting was inefficient, at only 2% (p=8.9x10 -9 versus WT). With the Ribo-T SD, Ribo-T +1 frameshifting was 1.8% (p=0.56 versus previous). With the Ribo-T SD, wild-type +1 frameshifting fell to 0.6% versus 33% (p=1.6x10 -5). A stem-loop roadblock downstream of lacZ had no effect on luc initiation (p=0.22). Ribo-T readthrough at UAG was 0.07% vs. 0.013% (p=4.7x10 -7). Ribo-T readthrough at UGA was 0.26% vs. 0.11% (p=5x10 -3). Ribo-T readthrough at UAA was 0.04% vs. 0.01% (p=2.5x10 -4).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Ribo-T ribosomes do not use SD sequences to promote frameshifting. This is atypical, as frameshifting is an elongation event and SD is an initiation element. The +1 frameshifting efficiency was much lower than the -1 efficiency for Ribo-T. Mechanisms of these two types of frameshifting are known to differ. The mechanism of translation initiation by Ribo-T in the absence of SD remains unclear. Ribo-T ribosomes are linked via helix 44, which plays a role in initiation fidelity. The orientation of the SD-ASD geometry is modified in Ribo-T ribosomes. The competition between termination and readthrough is displaced toward readthrough for near-cognate tRNA. The A-site may be less able to bind termination factors in Ribo-T. Covalent linkage of rRNA molecules may make the ribosome less dynamic. Tethering had mild effects on initiation and termination/recycling steps of translation. The results highlight the greater-than-expected flexibility of ribosomes.

The mechanism of translation initiation by Ribo-T without SD remains unclear. A high-resolution structure of Ribo-T ribosomes is needed to resolve the question. The prokaryotic model may not apply to eukaryotes, which use a different initiation mechanism. Eukaryotes initiate translation in a way not involving SD-ASD interaction. SD-ASD interaction is not universal and may not apply to all kingdoms.

IS3 -1 frameshifting was 33% with either type of ribosome (p=0.77). dnaX -1 frameshifting was 43% with WT and 45% with Ribo-T (p=0.77). Replacing the dnaX SD with a Ribo-T SD lowered WT but not Ribo-T frameshifting. For +1 frameshifting, the SD sequence was required to stimulate the event. Ribo-T +1 frameshifting dropped to 2% (p=8.9x10 -9) versus WT (33%). SD-independent frameshifting is atypical, as SD is normally an initiation element. Frameshifting via SD-ASD interaction is less effective for Ribo-T ribosomes.
Ribo-T ribosomes can use an alternative SD sequence for translation initiation, but do so inefficiently compared to wild-type. Ribo-T ribosomes could use the alternative Ribo-T SD sequence. Luciferase induction was four times stronger than the no-SD control (p=9.8x10 -6). Ribo-T only weakly increased activity relative to wild-type (0.6% vs 33%). Both wild-type and Ribo-T ribosomes were present in the strain. The Ribo-T SD-ASD orientation is likely modified at helix 44. Helix 44 is a key regulator of translation initiation fidelity.
Ribo-T ribosomes terminate translation less efficiently at stop codons, with about 5- to 7-fold higher readthrough than wild-type. Ribo-T UAG readthrough was 0.07% versus 0.013% for wild-type. Ribo-T UGA readthrough was 0.26% versus 0.11%. Ribo-T UAA readthrough was 0.04% versus 0.01%. The impairment of stop codon recognition is described as slight. Data And Code Availability
The experiments used the E. coli BL21 (DE3) strain. The poRibo-T2 vector carried the Ribo-T ribosomal DNA. The bacterial pCL99 dual reporter system was used to construct fusion genes. A reverse SD swap confirmed that Ribo-T ribosomes are insensitive to SD presence. A stem-loop roadblock downstream of lacZ had no effect on luc initiation (p=0.22). Ethical Considerations
The study used E. coli BL21 (DE3) bacterial cells. No human subjects, animals, or human-derived cell lines were used. No ethical review or animal welfare statements are reported.

Figure 1 presents the programmed -1 frameshifting sites. Figure 2A compares -1 frameshifting efficiencies between ribosomes. Figure 2B shows the effect of a Ribo-T SD on frameshifting. Figure 3A displays the +1 frameshifting site in prfB. Figure 3B shows +1 frameshifting efficiencies, with Ribo-T at only 2%. Figure 3C compares +1 frameshifting with different SD sequences. Table 1 lists the target sequences tested for translation accuracy.

1. The core contribution is that Ribo-T ribosomes frame-shift and terminate translation via a SD-independent mechanism, while initiation and termination are less efficient than wild-type. 2. The strongest evidence is that stop codon readthrough is roughly five to seven times higher than wild-type across all three tested stop codons. 3. The future path is the structural elucidation of Ribo-T ribosomes, particularly the SD-ASD geometry at helix 44, and testing eukaryotes.

executive_summary:

"Translation is the last step in gene expression, in which the coding sequence of the messenger RNA (mRNA) is translated into the amino-acid sequence of the corresponding protein. Ribosomes catalyze protein synthesis, a vital cellular activity. Translation is a highly dynamic process, with four major phases: initiation, elongation, termination and ribosome recycling. During each phase, ribosomes form transient complexes with auxiliary translation factors that facilitate protein synthesis. In all kingdoms of life, ribosomes consist of two subunits. The 30S subunit contains the 16S rRNA and 21 ribosomal proteins responsible for decoding genetic sequences. The 16S rRNA is involved in recognition of the Shine-Dalgarno (SD) sequence or ribosome binding site of the mRNA. This sequence is complementary to the 3′end of the 16S ribosomal RNA (anti-Shine-Dalgarno (ASD) sequence). The 50S subunit contains two rRNA molecules, the 5S and 23S rRNAs, with 33 proteins. It is responsible for catalyzing peptide bond formation. These two subunits associate with each other during translation initiation, rotate during elongation, and dissociate after protein release. This organization is thought to be essential for biogenesis, successful protein synthesis and cell viability. Cell viability depends on a balance between rapid protein synthesis and accurate decoding of the genetic information. Translational error rates remain low throughout all steps in the process. However, signals present in specific mRNAs at defined locations can program a high rate of errors. These recoding events can occur during translation elongation (frameshifting) or at the termination step (stop codon readthrough). During frameshifts, the ribosome is induced to shift to an alternative, overlapping reading frame, whereas, in stop codon readthrough, the specific context of the termination codon may promote decoding with a near-cognate tRNA rather than a release factor. These sequences have specific impacts on translation fidelity, and are therefore powerful tools for investigations of the translation accuracy of Ribo-T ribosomes. A ribosome with tethered subunits, in which the two subunits were covalently linked in a single entity, was recently engineered in Escherichia coli. The hybrid ribosomal RNA (rRNA) consisted of the small and large subunit rRNA sequences, linked by short RNA linkers. The resulting ribosome, Ribo-T, with its inseparable subunits, was shown to be functional and able to sustain the cell growth, although doubling times were slower (107 min for Ribo-T, 35 min for wild-type ribosomes). The rate of protein synthesis with Ribo-T catalysis was 50% that with wild-type ribosomes. The slow growth of Ribo-T cells was probably due to Ribo-T biogenesis being slower than the biogenesis of wild-type ribosomes, rather than impaired Ribo-T activity.

In this study, the authors investigated the translational properties of Ribo-T ribosomes. They asked three questions: Do these ribosomes maintain the correct reading frame as faithfully as wild-type ribosomes? Do they terminate translation accurately at stop codons? Do they translate messenger RNA accurately? They tested Ribo-T with recoding signals instructing the ribosome to change translational reading frame (frameshifting) or to read stop codons as sense codons (stop codon readthrough). They also investigated the preferential mode of translation used by Ribo-T ribosomes to express adjacent open reading frames on the same mRNA, given that the two subunits were inseparable. Our data reveal an impairment of tethered ribosomes for +1 frameshifting and termination, but show that these ribosomes are otherwise as effective as wildtype ribosomes. Overall, covalent attachment of the two subunits modifies the properties of the ribosome, altering its ability to initiate and terminate translation correctly."

summary.executive_summary: Rare variants (RVs), often occurring at low to medium minor allele frequency (MAF < 1%), are thought to play an important role in the etiology of complex diseases and may explain a significant fraction of the missing heritability. Next-generation sequencing (WES, WGS) facilitates association of rare variants in coding or regulatory regions at genome-wide scale. However, rare variant association studies (RVAS) lack power when cohorts are small to medium-sized and genetic variation explains only a small fraction of phenotypic variance. To address this, several statistical approaches have been developed. Burden tests pool minor alleles per unit into a single burden measure, which are powerful when variants are mostly one-sided (protective or deleterious). When heterogeneous effects co-exist, variance-component tests like SKAT and C-alpha are preferred. These can be combined into linear models like SKAT-O, or Bayesian multiple regression models like HBMR, which incorporate genotype misclassification probabilities. Sun et al. proposed a mixed effects test (MiST) within a hierarchical model, treating variant-specific effects as the random part of a generalized linear mixed effects model (GLMM) and variant characteristics as the fixed part, but inference via full model estimation is too computationally intensive for genome-wide scans. Building on MiST, the authors propose BATI, a Bayesian rare variant association test using the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA) to estimate the full model efficiently, thus avoiding the score test required by MiST. BATI integrates individual and variant-specific characteristics as covariates within a hierarchical Bayesian framework. BATI uses R-INLA version 17.06.20 for inference. They used 1000GP and Iberian cohorts, randomly assigning cases and controls. Significance thresholds were determined via difference in deviance information criterion (ΔDIC) using 10 random splits and test-specific medians. BATI significantly outperformed competing methods, achieving power close to 100% for three risk genes at a variance-explained (VE) level of 0.5% and strict Type I error rate (TIER) of 0.01%, whereas most other methods failed. They applied rvGWAS to a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study and identified eight candidate predisposition genes, including EHMT2 and COPS7A.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Rare variants (RVs), often occurring at low to medium minor allele frequency (MAF < 1%), are thought to play an important role in the etiology of complex diseases and may explain a significant fraction of the missing heritability. Next-generation sequencing (WES, WGS) facilitates association of rare variants in coding or regulatory regions at genome-wide scale. However, rare variant association studies (RVAS) lack power when cohorts are small to medium-sized and genetic variation explains only a small fraction of phenotypic variance. To address this, several statistical approaches have been developed. Burden tests pool minor alleles per unit into a single burden measure, which are powerful when variants are mostly one-sided (protective or deleterious). When heterogeneous effects co-exist, variance-component tests like SKAT and C-alpha are preferred. These can be combined into linear models like SKAT-O, or Bayesian multiple regression models like HBMR, which incorporate genotype misclassification probabilities. Sun et al. proposed a mixed effects test (MiST) within a hierarchical model, treating variant-specific effects as the random part of a generalized linear mixed effects model (GLMM) and variant characteristics as the fixed part, but inference via full model estimation is too computationally intensive for genome-wide scans. Building on MiST, the authors propose BATI, a Bayesian rare variant association test using the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA) to estimate the full model efficiently, thus avoiding the score test required by MiST. BATI integrates individual and variant-specific characteristics as covariates within a hierarchical Bayesian framework. The authors implemented BATI as part of the 'Rare Variant Genome Wide Association Study' (rvGWAS) framework, which includes quality control, filtering, detection of data stratification, and five other RVAS tests (Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST, HBMR). BATI uses R-INLA version 17.06.20 for inference. To evaluate BATI, the authors built a semi-synthetic breast cancer risk cohort by combining real WES cohorts and ClinVar variants, introducing realistic noise and realistic functional impact. They used 1000GP and Iberian cohorts, randomly assigning cases and controls. Significance thresholds were determined via difference in deviance information criterion (ΔDIC) using 10 random splits and test-specific medians. BATI significantly outperformed competing methods, achieving power close to 100% for three risk genes at a variance-explained (VE) level of 0.5% and strict Type I error rate (TIER) of 0.01%, whereas most other methods failed. They applied rvGWAS to a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study and identified eight candidate predisposition genes, including EHMT2 and COPS7A.

Research Context
Next-generation sequencing (NGS) provides opportunities to study rare variants with complex multifactorial diseases in large cohorts at genome-wide scale. Rare variants (RVs) are more likely to affect protein structure, stability, or function than common variants. Traditional GWAS is based on common variants with MAF > 1%, while WES/WGS enable rare variant study. RVAS tests have been developed to identify novel disease loci based on the burden of rare and damaging variants within genomic units. RVAS is less powerful than GWAS when few individuals carry the rare alternative allele. Aggregated analysis of multiple rare variants within functional units (genes, promoters, pathways) is needed to increase power. Existing tests include score-based burden tests, variance-component tests like SKAT and C-alpha, and linear combinations like SKAT-O. Recent methods include HBMR and MiST which consider variant detection errors and biological characteristics of variants. The computational cost of full model estimation in hierarchical GLMM models precludes genome-wide scans using full Bayesian inference. Pure simulations often produce artificial, overly optimistic cohorts that lack the complexity and noise of real data.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a Bayesian RVAS test using INLA can integrate variant characteristics flexibly and perform full model inference efficiently. BATI is hypothesized to outperform established RVAS tests on realistic, semi-synthetic whole-exome sequencing cohorts. The hypothesis predicts that BATI will be particularly effective when using meaningful biological context such as functional annotation. BATI is predicted to achieve high power even when risk variants explain very little phenotypic variance (VE). The framework rvGWAS is expected to provide a user-friendly and intuitive analysis pipeline. ΔDIC is predicted to correctly differentiate between null and alternative models. BATI is expected to cope with complex population structure and confounders.

Methodological Details
The framework rvGWAS integrates quality control (QC), filtering, data stratification detection, functional annotation, and six RVAS tests. The six tests are Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST, HBMR, and BATI. BATI uses the R-INLA package version 17.06.20 for implementation. Two large datasets served as the basis for simulation: the 1000GP cohort and the Iberian cohort. In the 1000GP cohort, half of the samples were randomly assigned as cases and half as controls. In the Iberian cohort, one third of samples were cases and two thirds were controls. A semi-synthetic breast cancer risk cohort was built by querying ClinVar for exonic or splicing risk variants. Variants with MAF > 0.01 in any of three exome databases (EVS, 1000GP, ExAC) were removed. Thresholds were estimated from 10 random cohort splits by shuffling cases and controls. The median ΔDIC threshold across these splits was used for model selection. S = 10 datasets were generated for robust threshold estimation. BATI is implemented as a hierarchical Bayesian GLMM. BATI uses categorical and numeric characteristics of variants as covariates.

Procedures And Architectures
BATI is a generalized linear mixed effects model (GLMM) framed as a hierarchical Bayesian model. The model estimates a latent Gaussian Markov random field via the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA). The outcome is an exponential family phenotype Y_i for each individual. BATI integrates a large number of categorical and numeric variant characteristics as covariates. INLA is a non-sampling numerical approximation, which is faster than Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). The INLA implementation is based on R-INLA version 17.06.20. Model selection uses the difference in deviance information criterion (ΔDIC). The null and alternative hypotheses specify whether genetic effects are included (eta_i = X*alpha vs eta_i = X*alpha + (G*Z)w + G*delta). Random cohort splits shuffle cases and controls to estimate the type I error rate. A threshold is selected from the quantile corresponding to the desired significance level.

Key Results
For low VE (0.5%) and a strict TIER of 0.01%, all methods except BATI showed power close to 0. At a VE of 0.5% and a TIER of 0.01%, BATI achieved power close to 100% for three risk genes. The median power for BATI in this setting was 55%. All methods except MiST identified all risk genes at a TIER of 0.01% in the 2% VE setting. BATI called most genes at TIER 0.01% even at VE of 0.5%. BATI called all genes at TIER 0.1% with >80% power. At 0.01% TIER, only 2 genes out of ~20,000 were expected to be significant by chance. The Iberian cohort yielded 1,167 cases and 1,810 controls, while the other cohort was larger. BATI performance was stable despite the smaller Iberian cohort size. Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O recurrently missed BRCA2 (both missense and LoF versions) at 0.5% VE. HBMR failed to call BARD1, CHEK2, and PALB2 already at TIER 0.1%. Applying rvGWAS to a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study identified eight candidate predisposition genes. The candidate genes identified in the CLL study include EHMT2 and COPS7A. At VE of 0.5% and 0.01% TIER, the observed small fluctuation of significance thresholds was small.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
BATI leverages variant characteristics, strongly benefiting from functional annotation. BATI performs best on risk genes composed mostly of loss-of-function (LoF) variants. BATI remains at least as good as other methods on mostly missense variants. Differences between tests are most profound when VE is low (1% and 0.5%). Methods share the same strengths and weaknesses when VE is low, appearing very similar. BATI offers a flexible testing approach that can be further extended.

Contradictions And Limitations
A formal random seed or exact train/test split is not reported. Cohort demographics and specific genetic background details are not provided. No information on the exact train/test split or random seed is given. The paper reports only median and aggregate results rather than individual gene-level results. BATI's exact absolute magnitude of improvement is reported as 'close to 100%' rather than a precise delta. Only one CLL study is reported, limiting the external validity of the application. The exact number of risk genes tested is referred to as '8 risk gene architectures'. A key limitation is that no random seed for the 10 random splits was reported. The paper lacks a detailed error analysis across all 8 architectures. No exact p-values or credible intervals are provided for the BATI power metrics.

Claims
BATI outperforms established RVAS methods, particularly when using functional annotation as a covariate. BATI achieved power close to 100% for three risk genes at a VE of 0.5%. BATI calls most genes with TIER 0.01% even at VE of 0.5%. Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O recurrently missed BRCA2 at 0.5% VE. The power of Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O is highly similar when VE is low. BATI remains at least as good as other methods on mostly missense variants. BATI is more suitable for LoF-rich genes than for missense variants. Functional annotation provides a significant performance gain for BATI.
BATI is computationally efficient due to the use of INLA, making it faster than MCMC. INLA is a non-sampling based numerical approximation, which is faster than MCMC. BATI allows full model estimation rather than a score test. The paper does not report explicit execution times in minutes. INLA enables full model inference, which would otherwise require a score test.

Data And Code Availability
The BATI test and rvGWAS framework were implemented in R as part of the R-INLA project. A framework was provided, but the exact code availability is not stated.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Sensitivity was assessed across 10 random cohort splits. Median thresholds were obtained and used for model selection.

Ethical Considerations
No statement on human subjects ethics or institutional review is provided.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 3 displays gene-wise power plots for the 1000GP cohort. Table 2 reports risk gene-wise power and TIER thresholds. Supplementary S6 Fig shows estimated significance thresholds. Supplementary S8 Fig shows results for the Iberian cohort and power at low VE.

Three Takeaways
1. BATI is a flexible Bayesian RVAS test built on INLA that outperforms other tests, especially on LoF-rich genes. 2. At low VE and strict TIER, BATI achieves power close to 100% while competitors mostly fail. 3. Future applications extend BATI to a broader range of genotypes, phenotypes, and biological contexts.

summary.executive_summary: Nipah virus (NiV), a negative-sense single-stranded RNA henipavirus from the Paramyxoviridae family, is a significant public health threat with over 75% case fatality rate and potential to cause a global pandemic. Executive Summary
Nipah virus (NiV), a negative-sense single-stranded RNA henipavirus from the Paramyxoviridae family, is a significant public health threat with over 75% case fatality rate and potential to cause a global pandemic. Due to the severe disease and mortality, WHO's 2018 'R&D Blueprint list of priority diseases' designated NiV for accelerated research and development. No single drug is currently under clinical trial against NiV. Existing antiviral treatments, such as ribavirin and favipiravir, have shown contradictory or limited results in reducing mortality. A scoring system (10 for confirmed inhibitors, 5 for tentative, 4 for peptide inhibitors, 0 for no relevance) was used to select papers with scores 4, 5, and 10 for manual curation into a Nipah Virus Inhibitor Knowledgebase (NVIK). To ensure quality, a separate team independently re-performed curation, marking errors in red and verified data in green. The data is stored in the NVIK-Open resource Sheet. The NVIK platform is built on open-source LAMP (Linux-Apache-Mysql-PHP) technology with PHP, HTML, JavaScript, AJAX, and CSS. The database was developed using three search options: Simple Search (text-based), Query Builder (logical AND & OR), and Structure Search (SMILES, SDF, MOL; plus JSME browser). Chemical clustering used Near Neighbors via NNeib (version 5.12.0), Jarp (version 6.0.2) based on a dissimilarity threshold (1 - Tanimoto coefficient) of 0.15, and PaDel software to calculate a total of 1875 descriptors. Visualization utilized a customized CIRCOS with 98 inhibitors defined at a band width of 1000 to represent cyclic and aliphatic compounds, and compound network diagrams made with Cytoscape. The curated knowledgebase contains 182 entries, with 125 small-molecule inhibitors (57 were peptides or incomplete). Among the 125 small molecules, 98 are unique, and EC50/IC50 values were obtained for 70 compounds with structures available for all 98. IC50/EC50 values range from 0.25 nM to 7562710 nM for the 182 entries and 0.47 nM to 7562710 nM for the 125 small molecule entries. Clustering of 98 NVIs yielded 90 clusters, with 84 clusters (93.3%) being singletons and 14 clusters (15.5%) non-singletons. Structural similarity analysis matched 34 NVIs to 76 FDA approved drugs. To prioritize druglike NVIs, DruLito screened compounds based on eight filters (Lipinski's, MDDR-like, Veber, Ghose, BBB, CMC-50, and weighted/unweighted drug-likeness). Only two of 91 compounds passed all filters except CMC. Finally, an independent robustness-of-assays evaluation prioritized 11 NVIs; NVIC0025, NVIC0032, and NVIC0048 passed 6 DruLito filters, with NVIC0048 showing high physicochemical overlap with FDA approved drugs, and NVIC0032 exhibiting the best activity. The platform is openly available at http://vinodscaria.rnabiology.org/nipah.

Research Context
Nipah virus causes severe disease with a fatality rate exceeding 75%. The virus is a public health concern with pandemic potential. Lack of treatment restricts containment to isolation and surveillance. WHO designated NiV as a priority disease for accelerated R&D in 2018. No single drug is currently under clinical trial against Nipah virus. Existing antivirals like ribavirin and favipiravir show contradictory or limited results. No systematic evaluation of reported compounds exists, and databases contain limited NiV information. Existing databases are scattered or curated without thorough drug discovery evaluation.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aimed to systematically evaluate and prioritize Nipah virus inhibitors. The central objective was to perform a systematic evaluation of NVIs with respect to FDA approved drugs and antiviral libraries. The authors hypothesized that a combined evidence strategy could prioritize druglike, non-toxic NVIs. The hypothesis was that prioritization based on assay robustness would yield more reliable candidates. It was expected that prioritization would identify physicochemical descriptor values closer to existing drug-like FDA approved compounds. The expected outcome was to provide a centralized resource for the community to submit and access NVIs. It was also predicted that many compounds might fail DruLito filters due to strict requirements.

Methodological Details
The authors used PubMed and Google as the two main sources for collecting inhibitors. Research papers were downloaded using the query 'Nipah'. At curation time, this keyword listed 838 papers. Papers were scored 10, 5, 4, or 0 based on inhibitor confirmation. Papers with scores 10, 5, and 4 were manually curated into the NVIK sheet. The NVIK data structure is predefined in Table 1. A separate team re-performed the curation independent of the initial team for quality. Errors were marked 'Red' and verified data 'Green' in the curation sheet. Data was stored in the NVIK-Open resource Sheet. Each entry was tagged with its contributor's email ID. The NVIK platform is built on LAMP server technology with PHP, HTML, JavaScript, AJAX, and CSS.

Procedures And Architectures
The NVIK platform offers Simple Search, Query Builder, and Structure Search. Simple Search retrieves information on all/selected fields via text-based query. Query Builder enables search using logical operators AND & OR. Structure Search queries SMILES, SDF, and MOL formats. The JSME browser allows drawing compounds in the interface. The database displays physicochemical properties like molecular weight, XLogP, PSA, HBD, HBA, and rotatable bonds. Near neighbours were identified using NNeib (version 5.12.0). Clusters were obtained using Jarp (version 6.0.2) based on dissimilarity threshold. A dissimilarity threshold of 0.15 was used. A total of 1875 descriptors were calculated using PaDel software. Visualization used customized CIRCOS at a band width of 1000 for 98 inhibitors. Compound network diagrams were made using Cytoscape.

Key Results
The curated knowledgebase contains 182 entries. 125 entries were small-molecule inhibitors; 57 were peptides or incomplete. 98 unique Nipah inhibitors were identified among the 125 small-molecule entries. EC50/IC50 values were obtained for 70 compounds. Structures were available for all 98 inhibitors. IC50/EC50 values ranged from 0.25 nM to 7562710 nM for 182 entries. The lowest reported IC50/EC50 value for some inhibitors is as low as 0.47 nM. Clustering of 98 NVIs yielded 90 clusters. 84 clusters (93.3% of NVIs) were singletons; 14 clusters (15.5%) were non-singletons. The highest reported IC50/EC50 value reached 7562710 nM. 34 NVIs were similar to 76 FDA approved drugs. Only two of 91 compounds passed all DruLito filters except the CMC filter. An independent evaluation based on assay robustness prioritized 11 NVIs. NVIC0025, NVIC0032, and NVIC0048 passed 6 DruLito filters and were accepted in FAF drugs analysis. NVIC0048 displayed high physicochemical parameter range overlap with FDA approved drugs. NVIC0032 exhibited better activity than the other two shortlisted compounds.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The platform creates a structured, crowdsourced resource for the Nipah inhibitor landscape. High chemical diversity was indicated by the majority-singleton clusters. Compounds with different molecular weights were identified as near neighbours, suggesting common structural features. Common structural features may contribute to antiviral activity. The approach identifies potential pharmacophore features important for antiviral properties. Drug-likeness is indicated by similarity to FDA approved drugs in physicochemical properties. The combined evidence strategy offers a reproducible framework for prioritizing candidates.

Contradictions And Limitations
A few entries had multiple assays curated, which was addressed by counting unique inhibitors. Many entries (57) lacked complete information or were peptides. Only 70 out of 125 small molecules had reported IC50/EC50 values. Most NVIs did not pass all DruLito filters, limiting the druggable set. Prioritization based on assay robustness was an independent, non-quantitative re-evaluation. The paper notes that most outbreaks have mortality rates of 50-100%. Ribavirin has shown contradictory results with the most optimistic below 50%.

Claims
The NVIK platform provides a systematically curated, crowdsourced Nipah virus inhibitor knowledgebase. 838 papers were shortlisted using the 'Nipah' keyword. The paper was manually curated into the NVIK sheet. Data was stored in the NVIK-Open resource Sheet. A separate team independently re-curated to verify data. 57 entries were peptides or did not have complete information. The data was curated from literature, not experimental validation by the authors. EC50/IC50 values were obtained for only 70 compounds. A crowdsourced, open-source platform enables community submission of new inhibitors. The data is publicly available at a hosted URL.
A combined evidence strategy of assay robustness and DruLito filters prioritizes the most promising candidates. 11 NVIs were prioritised based on assay robustness. DruLito screened compounds based on eight filters. NVIC0025, NVIC0032, and NVIC0048 passed 6 DruLito filters. Only two of 91 compounds passed all DruLito filters except CMC. Prioritization was based on assay robustness, a potentially subjective metric. NVIC0032 exhibited better activity but only three were shortlisted overall. This provides a reproducible framework for prioritizing candidates for future studies.

Data And Code Availability
The NVIK database is accessible at the published URL. New inhibitors can be submitted via the web platform.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The curation used a scoring system to filter relevant papers. A second, independent team re-curated to mark errors.

Ethical Considerations
Each entry was tagged with the contributor's email ID.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 shows the predefined data structure. Figure 1 shows the database unique fields. Figure 2 depicts physicochemical property distribution. Figure 3 compares NVIs to FDA approved drugs and Enamine antivirals. Figure 4 shows the DruLito filter results. Table 2 presents prioritized compounds and DruLito filter passage. The compounds are also mapped to Pubchem/Chemspider IDs.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is an openly available, crowdsourced knowledgebase of 182 Nipah virus inhibitor entries. 2. The strongest evidence is the identification of unique inhibitors with reported IC50/EC50 values as low as 0.47 nM. 3. The future path is engaging the scientific community in continuous curation and analysis of these datasets.

summary.title: ProNetView-ccRCC: A web-based portal to interactively explore clear cell renal cell carcinoma proteogenomics networks
summary.authors: Selim Kalayci; Francesca Petralia; Pei Wang; Zeynep H Gümüş
summary.executive_summary:
The paper describes the development and utility of ProNetView-ccRCC, an open-access, web-based interactive portal designed to visualize and explore the phosphopeptide co-expression networks derived from the National Cancer Institute's Clinical Proteomics Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) phosphoproteomics data. The underlying network, which characterizes co-expression patterns among 20,976 phosphopeptides in ccRCC and was derived from 103 samples using a random-forest network construction algorithm, has historically been difficult to visually communicate due to its large dimensions and complicated topologies, and prior visualization tools were primarily limited to static 2D images for print publications. To address these gaps, the authors developed ProNetView-ccRCC as a centralized, customized platform that runs in modern web browsers without additional plugins and is accessible across a wide spectrum of computational skill levels. 

The portal offers two primary types of networks for visual exploration: the overall phosphopeptide co-expression network comprising 3,614 genes and 30 functional pathway-enriched network modules, each of which was derived via the Glay clustering algorithm and contains at least 20 genes. Its 3D interactive interface enables users to rotate and zoom the network, with six modules significantly associated with biological pathways highlighted by node coloring. Users can query the network for genes of interest—using ERG, an oncogene associated with VEGF response, as a running example—and see the corresponding node highlighted in red and its neighbors identified. The tool displays associated gene-level meta-data, including connection counts (ERG connected to 11 genes and mapping to 5 peptides), tumor-grade association (p-value: 0.003, FDR: 0.118), and allows filtering by clinical variables such as stage, grade, age, gender, and FDR cut-off (e.g., FDR=20%). For pathway exploration, users can see enriched pathways sorted by p-values and select a pathway to return a gene list and highlight relevant nodes. The tool also integrates with the ProTrack heatmap tool. 

Ultimately, the portal aims to facilitate hypothesis generation for future studies by allowing the cancer research community to share and communicate their results independently, bridging the gap between rich proteogenomic data and intuitive visual interpretation without requiring installation.

For pathway exploration, users can see enriched pathways sorted by p-values and select a pathway to return a gene list and highlight relevant nodes. The tool also integrates with the ProTrack heatmap tool. 

Ultimately, the portal aims to facilitate hypothesis generation for future studies by allowing the cancer research community to share and communicate their results independently, bridging the gap between rich proteogenomic data and intuitive visual interpretation without requiring installation.

Research Context
Advances in molecular profiling enable large-scale integrative proteogenomic cancer studies. CPTAC recently performed comprehensive proteogenomic characterizations across multiple cancer types. Co-expression networks revealed regulatory relationships between proteins and posttranscriptional modifications. Rich networks are challenging to visually communicate due to their large dimensions and complicated topologies. Effective visual exploration tools that address these challenges are needed to interpret multiple data layers.

Research Question And Hypothesis
There is a pressing need for a new open community resource for intuitive visual exploration of these networks. Current tools are mainly used for static 2D images and not well suited for user-initiated interactive explorations. The authors hypothesize that a customized centralized platform can facilitate intuitive exploration across computational skill levels.

Methodological Details
The network was derived from 103 ccRCC samples. The co-expression network characterizes 20,976 phosphopeptides in ccRCC. The network was derived using a random-forest based network construction algorithm. Two genes were connected if at least two phosphopeptides mapping to the two genes are associated to each other. 30 network modules were derived from the overall network topology. Network modules were derived by using the Glay clustering algorithm. 30 modules containing at least 20 genes were identified. Pathway enrichment analysis was performed via Fisher Exact test for each module. The 3D exploration was built on the Three.js framework providing an interface for WebGL. Network layouts were calculated using 3D layout algorithms within iCAVE. Client-side Javascript libraries were used to handle various user interaction events in real time. The web interface was styled with Bootstrap v3.3.7 and custom styling.

Procedures And Architectures
ProNetView-ccRCC was developed as a web-based interactive network exploration portal. The portal is an open-access freely available resource. Users can interact with the network by rotating and zooming in/out. ERG is highlighted in red in the network exploration panel. Node sizes are proportional to the number of connections. Users can hover over a node to display the gene name. Clicking a node displays associated gene-level meta-data in a separate panel. ERG is directly connected to 11 genes and maps to 5 peptides. A Heatmap link directs users to the ProTrack tool. Users can construct a query specifying phenotype (grade) and FDR cutoff (FDR=20%).

Key Results
The overall network comprises 3,614 genes. Six modules were significantly associated with biological pathways. ERG association with tumor grade has a p-value of 0.003 and FDR of 0.118. ERG is directly connected to 11 genes within the same module. ERG maps to 5 different peptides. The Heatmap link directs to ProTrack which explores ccRCC multi-omics data. Users can construct a simple query specifying a phenotype of interest. The portal runs on all modern web browsers without plugins.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Visualizing networks together with associated information aids interpretation of multiple data layers. The tool helps understand the network in the context of markers of user interest. Interactive exploration guides hypothesis generation for future studies. The tool accommodates a wide spectrum of computational skill levels. Sharing and communicating results is anticipated to be facilitated.

Contradictions And Limitations
The portal only supports standard libraries and no additional plugins are required. The tool is limited to the CPTAC ccRCC study results. No specific random seed or train/test split is reported for the network construction. Participant demographics and user skill distribution metrics are not reported.

Claims
The web portal enables intuitive visual exploration of complex proteogenomic networks across varying skill levels. The portal runs on all modern web browsers without plugins. The tool accommodates a wide spectrum of computational skill levels. Only the CPTAC ccRCC study data is incorporated. The tool facilitates independent sharing and communication of results.
Interactive 3D visualization overcomes the limitations of static 2D network displays. The portal offers 3D exploration by rotating and zooming. Node sizes are proportional to the number of connections. Prior tools provided advanced visual customization for print. 3D exploration enables identification of central genes.

Data And Code Availability
The portal is freely available at http://ccrcc.cptac-network-view.org/.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Ablation results on layout algorithms or network construction are not reported.

Ethical Considerations
Ethical approvals or institutional review committee statements are not reported.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the global ccRCC tumor phosphoproteomics co-expression network. Figure 1B links the global network to functional network modules. Executive Summary
This study presents the first animal model of spontaneous regression of metastases following primary tumor excision, a phenomenon previously only documented in rare case studies. The authors used MDA-MB-231 HM human breast cancer cells, transduced with a codon-optimized firefly luciferase-mCherry vector, to monitor early-stage micro-metastases in BALB/c nu/nu mice. In vivo neutralization of these four factors with mouse anti-human antibodies completely blocked metastatic progression (p<0.0001). Retrospective analysis of a TCGA lung adenocarcinoma cohort showed that high protein levels of these four factors were associated with a hazard ratio of 2.05 (p<0.05). The authors conclude that PT secretome drives early micro-metastatic growth, and that the perioperative period offers a window of opportunity to control minimal residual disease by blocking PT support for micro-metastases. The study negates surgical trauma as a mechanism since sham surgery did not induce regression.

Research Context
Surgical excision of the primary tumor is a cornerstone of cancer treatment. However, surgical excision has been suggested to accelerate postoperative progression of minimal residual disease. Conversely, rare case studies report spontaneous postoperative regression of evident cancer metastasis. Postoperative regression has been most commonly reported for lung metastases. Postulated mechanisms for regression include surgical trauma and elimination of stimulating factors secreted by the primary tumor. No animal model of spontaneous regression exists, so these mechanisms have not been empirically tested. The presence of a primary tumor is a systemic disease, stressing the need to study PT-metastases crosstalk.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether spontaneous metastatic regression can be modeled and its mechanisms identified. The first hypothesis is that primary tumor removal induces metastatic regression because the PT secretome supports micro-metastases. It was predicted that regression would be specific to early, small metastatic stages. It was predicted that tumor-secreted factors enhance viability, adhesion, and tube formation in vitro. In vivo replenishment of the secretome would diminish regression. It was hypothesized that neutralization of four key secreted factors would block metastatic progression. The predicted outcome is that identified factors are associated with poor patient survival in a human cohort.

Methodological Details
MDA-MB-231 HM human triple-negative breast adenocarcinoma cells were used. Cells were transduced with a codon-optimized firefly luciferase-mCherry vector. Cells were cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% glutamax, 4.5g/L D-glucose, and 110mg/L sodium pyruvate. In vivo models were eight-week old female BALB/c nu/nu mice. Mice were injected with 2x10^5 cells in 20ul PBS into the fourth mammary fat pad. Primary tumors were measured by caliper and volume calculated as (length x width^2)x0.5. Metastases were assessed by bioluminescence imaging with an IVIS spectrum apparatus after 150mg/kg D-luciferin injection. Primary tumors were excised when metastatic foci reached a total count of 10^6 photons/s. Tumors were measured at an average size of 80mm^3 before excision. Metastatic regression was compared in small (10^6 photons/sec) vs large (10^7 photons/sec) metastases. Tumor-cell-conditioned medium was produced by incubating ~80% confluent cells with serum-free medium for 24h at 37C. Serum-free medium served as the control (SM). CM was collected from ~30 million cells and concentrated to a final volume of 100ul/mouse. CM and SM were loaded into Alzet osmotic minipumps (model 1003D) and implanted i.p. following excision. An excised primary tumor is estimated to contain ~50x10^6 secretome-producing cells. The daily secretome release from the minipump is estimated at ~1/8 of the amount produced in vivo/day. Cancer cells were seeded in SM or CM for adhesion and apoptosis studies. Adhesion was imaged for 8 hours in 20 min intervals using the IncuCyte system. Apoptosis was determined via flow cytometry after staining with AnnexinV-FITC and 7AAD. Tube formation used 50ul basement membrane ECM (Cultrex BME) and HUVEC cells. HUVEC cells were seeded in CM or SM and imaged at 20 min intervals for 24h. A Human Cytokine Array compared 10^2 soluble proteins in CM and plasma samples. Mass spectrometry analysis reached a final volume of ~100ul after dilution with 8M urea. Peptides were digested overnight with LysC/Trypsin mix and sequencing-grade modified Trypsin. LC-MS used a 50cm EASY-Spray PepMap column with a 140 min linear gradient. MS used a top10 method with fragmentation of 10 most abundant peaks by HCD. MS raw files were analyzed by MaxQuant, the Label-free quantification algorithm, and Perseus. A false discovery rate (FDR) of 0.01 was used on both peptide and protein levels. Enrichment analysis used Gene Ontology annotations with an FDR threshold of 0.02. Mouse anti-human monoclonal antibodies were used for four secreted factors and an isotype control. Antibodies and isotype control were injected 1ug each/mouse, once a day, for two days. Lung sections (6um) were stained for Hematoxylin and Eosin after paraffin embedding. Patient outcome used the public TCGA provisional dataset from cBioPortal. A lung adenocarcinoma cohort was stratified for patients with altered IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF levels. Survival was analyzed by Kaplan Meier and hazard ratio in R; ANOVA p<0.05.

Procedures And Architectures
MDA-MB-231 HM cells were stably transduced with firefly luciferase-mCherry. Media were Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium with 10% FBS, 1% glutamax, 4.5g/L glucose. Conditions: 37 C, 5% CO2, and cells were mycoplasma-free. Mice received 2x10^5 cells in 20ul PBS into the fourth mammary fat pad. Tumors were excised under 2% isoflurane anesthesia and removal verified by bioluminescence imaging. Sham surgery involved an identical incision with the primary tumor left untouched. CM was incubated with ~80% confluent cells in serum-free medium for 24h at 37C. CM was collected from ~30 million cells, filtered through 0.45um, and concentrated by 3kDa Amicon filters. Alzet osmotic minipumps (model 1003D) were loaded with CM or SM. Adhesion studies: cells were imaged for 8 hours in 20 min intervals using IncuCyte. Apoptosis: cells incubated for 24h, stained with AnnexinV-FITC and 7AAD for flow cytometry. Tube formation: 50ul basement membrane ECM, HUVEC seeded in CM or SM, imaged for 24h. Cytokine array: Human Cytokine Array (R&D systems) analyzed 102 soluble human proteins. MS: samples centrifuged, filtered through 3kDa Amicon filters, mixed 1:1 with 8M urea. MS: peptides incubated with 1mM dithiothreitol, 5mM iodoacetamide, digested with LysC/Trypsin. MS: peptides eluted with 80% acetonitrile, vacuum-concentrated, diluted in MS loading buffer. MS: UHPLC with EASY-Spray PepMap columns, 140 min linear gradient of water/acetonitrile. MS: top10 method fragmenting 10 most abundant peaks by higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD). Bioinformatics: raw files via MaxQuant, Label-free quantification, and Perseus software. Bioinformatics: MS/MS spectra referenced to Uniprot human proteome by Andromeda search engine. Bioinformatics: pathway networks via String database and Cytoscape software. Neutralization: mouse anti-human monoclonal antibodies for IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF. Patient outcome: lung adenocarcinoma patients stratified by IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF levels.

Key Results
Metastatic signal decreased dramatically (up to 100-fold) within 24 hours of primary tumor excision. This decrease occurred 24 hours after excision and had p<0.0001. No in vivo bioluminescent signal increase occurred for 50 days post-excision. Malignant foci were evident on both day 1 and 50 days later by H&E staining. Regression was significantly less prominent in large metastases (10^7 photons/sec) vs small (10^6 photons/sec), p<0.000. Sham surgery did not cause metastatic regression, whereas primary tumor excision did, p<0.05. Tumor-cell conditioned medium enhanced viability (p<0.001) and adhesion (p<0.01) of cancer cells. Conditioned medium induced tube formation of human endothelial cells, p<0.0001. CM treatment showed 10-fold less regression than serum-free medium, p<0.005. 28 cytokines were highly expressed in cancer cell CM. Mass spectrometry identified 2,600 proteins, 359 of which were GO extracellular factors. 359 extracellular proteins engaged pathways of apoptosis, angiogenesis, growth factor activity, focal adhesion, and metalloenzyme regulation. Neutralization of the four antibody cocktail completely blocked metastatic progression, p<0.0001. No difference in regression was evident on post-excision day-1 between antibody and IgG groups. Larger micrometastases showed lower or no regression. High protein levels of IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF were associated with a hazard ratio of 2.05, p<0.05. These findings are consistent with known pro-angiogenic and pro-survival roles of IL-8, Serpin E1, PDGFaa, and MIF.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The primary tumor secretome drives early-stage metastatic growth. Removing the secretome induces regression of small metastatic foci. Secreted factors likely promote metastatic progression through shared and distinct pathways. IL-8 promotes EMT, invasion, and malignant survival. Serpin E1 promotes metastases via thrombosis, pro-survival activities, and invasion. PDGfaa acts as a survival factor, inhibiting apoptosis and increasing vessel density. MIF promotes metastases via NF-kB, MMP activity, myeloid-derived suppressor cell infiltration, and EMT. Tumor-secreted factors are likely promoted micrometastatic niches when autocrine factors are insufficient. The perioperative period offers a window of opportunity to control minimal residual disease. Tailored neutralizing antibody treatment may tilt the balance toward eradication of metastases. These results explain the rare but validated clinical phenomenon of spontaneous metastatic regression. Post-operative regression prevalence in cancer patients is currently unknown due to technical limitations.

Contradictions And Limitations
A larger metastatic focus (10^7 photons/sec) showed significantly less regression than a small focus. Larger micrometastases may be self-sufficient and thus do not regress. The study tested only the combined effect of blocking four key factors; other secreted factors are likely involved. Regression was observed at ~24h, but not immediately following excision. Sham surgery without tumor excision did not elicit regression, negating surgical trauma as a mechanism. Syngeneic lines should be studied to test generalizability beyond MDA-MB-231 HM. Prevalence of post-operative regression is currently unknown due to technical limitations. The study was retrospective; the TCGA cohort was provisional. The number of mice per group and random assignment details are not fully reported. Specific neutralizing antibodies are hypothesized but not empirically tested in patients.

Claims
Spontaneous regression of micro-metastases occurs upon primary tumor excision because the primary tumor secretome supports early metastatic growth. Metastatic signal decreased up to 100-fold within 24 hours of excision. Sham surgery did not elicit regression, ruling out surgical trauma. Tumor-cell-conditioned medium enhanced viability, adhesion, and tube formation. CM supplementation reduced regression by 10-fold compared to serum-free medium. Neutralization of four secreted factors blocked metastatic progression (p<0.0001). Larger metastases (10^7 photons/sec) showed significantly less regression. No regression difference was evident between antibody and IgG groups on post-excision day-1. The perioperative period is a window of opportunity to control minimal residual disease. Tailored antibody treatment could tilt the balance toward eradication of metastases. These findings explain the rare but validated clinical phenomenon of spontaneous regression.

Data And Code Availability
The patient outcome used the public TCGA provisional dataset from cBioPortal. Bioinformatics analyses used MaxQuant, Perseus, the Label-free quantification algorithm, and String. No explicit statement on code or raw data availability is provided.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Sham surgery was used as a control to rule out surgical trauma as a mechanism. Conditioned medium vs. serum-free medium comparisons were used to control for secretome effects. Isotype control IgG1 was used in the antibody neutralization experiments. A false discovery rate (FDR) of 0.01 was applied to the peptide and protein MS analysis. Pathway enrichment used an FDR threshold of 0.02 relative to GO annotations. Two-sided statistical tests were conducted throughout.

Ethical Considerations
All procedures were approved by Monash University or Tel-Aviv University Animal Ethics Committees. Mice were housed under SPF conditions on a 12h dark/light cycle. Mice were euthanized 10 min following luciferin injection.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A-B: Metastatic signal decreased up to 100-fold 24 hours post-excision (p<0.0001). Figure 1C: No bioluminescent signal increase for 50 days post-excision. Figure 1D: Malignant foci evident on day 1 and day 50 via H&E staining. Figure 1E: Regression significantly less prominent in large vs small metastases (p<0.000). Figure 1F: Metastases regressed after excision but increased in sham surgery (p<0.05). Figure 2A: CM enhanced cancer cell viability (p<0.001). Figure 2B: CM enhanced adhesion (p<0.01). Figure 2C: CM induced endothelial tube formation (p<0.0001). Figure 2D: CM treatment showed 10-fold less regression (p<0.005). Figure 3A: Pathway enrichment and protein-protein interaction networks via String. Figure 3B: Antibody neutralization completely blocked metastatic progression (p<0.0001). Figure 3C: Larger micrometastases showed lower or no regression. Figure 3D: High protein levels associated with a hazard ratio of 2.05 (p<0.05).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: A novel animal model of spontaneous metastatic regression was established, showing regression specific to early small metastatic foci. 2. The strongest evidence: Primary tumor secretome replenishment by CM reduced regression 10-fold, and antibody neutralization blocked progression (p<0.0001). 3. The future path: Tailored neutralizing antibody combinations and serum analysis may be exploited in the perioperative window to control minimal residual disease.

summary.title: Activation of Macrophages by CpG DNA and LPS: an FTIR Spectroscopic Study
summary.authors: Emrulla Spahiu (Middle East Technical University); Senol Dogan (Leipzig University); Jörg Schnauß (Leipzig University); Mayda Gursel (Middle East Technical University); Feride Severcan (Middle East Technical University)
summary.executive_summary:
The innate immune response triggered by CpG DNA improves host survival following pathogen challenge, yet whether CpG ODN-mediated immune activation leads to global molecular changes in cells detectable by FTIR spectroscopy is unknown. In this study, the authors used Attenuated Total Reflectance (ATR) Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy to monitor molecular changes in murine macrophage RAW 264.7 cells upon activation with CpG DNA and lipopolysaccharide (LPS).

The researchers cultured murine macrophage-like RAW 264.7 cells at 37°C with 5% CO2 in DMEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and 2 mM L-glutamine. The cells were harvested, spun at 1000 rpm (208 g) for 10 min, and resuspended at a concentration of 2x106/mL. The control group was treated with 0.9% phosphate-buffered saline (PBS); the CpG DNA stimulated group with 1 µM K3 ODN (endotoxin-free); and the LPS stimulated group with 0.5 µg/ml LPS. Four time points (10 min, 30 min, 2 h, and 6 h) were measured after treatment to evaluate the kinetics of induced effects. After the corresponding incubation time, samples were removed, spun at 1000 rpm, washed with 15 mL of sterile PBS, and media discarded to remove organic compounds and growth medium. Interferograms were collected using a Perkin-Elmer Spectrum One FTIR spectrometer with a Diamond-ZnSe ATR crystal. Cell samples (1 µl) were dried with mild N2 flux for 5 min. The best signal-to-noise ratio was achieved with a 128 scan number at 2 cm⁻¹ spectral resolution. Each group was scanned under the same conditions in three independent scans, with n=5 replicates. Data underwent 13-point Savitzky-Golay smoothing and baseline correction (3800-2750-1800-900 cm⁻¹) using Spectrum One software.

Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was performed in the 3000-650 cm⁻¹ region using Unscrambler 11.0 software. PCA reduced dimensionality, and the Scores Plot clustered samples by treatment. PC-1 accounted for 83% of variability, while PC-2 accounted for 11%. Loadings Plots showed high variation in the 1750-850 cm⁻¹ region. A comprehensive spectrum of resting control RAW 264.7 cells and its second derivative are shown in Figure A1 (4000-650 cm⁻¹) with lipid peaks at 3000-2800 cm⁻¹, protein peaks at 1700-1600 cm⁻¹, and nucleic acid peaks at 1238, 1110, and 1085 cm⁻¹. Table A1 assigns peaks by literature, and Table A2 gives area integration measurements. CpG DNA stimulation increased nucleic acid content (1238 cm⁻¹ peak integration) significantly from 10 min until 6 h (p < 0.1), and RNA-specific peak at 915 cm⁻¹ significantly increased from first minutes (p < 0.001) and was maintained until 2 h (p < 0.1). The results deduce that nucleic acid-related peaks reflect DNA synthesis following RNA synthesis in a time-dependent manner, with extensive RNA synthesis until 2 h and DNA synthesis starting at 6 h. Protein content increased from 10 min until 2 h (p < 0.001) and then declined. LPS induced pro-inflammatory responses, with RNA-specific activation detectable at first minutes. Triglycerides and cholesterol increased significantly during activation (peak near 1741 cm⁻¹), and fatty acid concentration increased (1400 cm⁻¹), pointing to de novo lipogenesis via a shared metabolite (Acetoacetyl-CoA). This study first demonstrates FTIR spectroscopy as an independent modality to monitor activation dynamics of murine macrophages. The protocol is available online [59]. The paper omits a bibliography.

summary.title: SPOT-Contact-Single: Improving Single-Sequence-Based Prediction of Protein Contact Map using a Transformer Language Model
summary.authors: Jaspreet Singh; Thomas Litfin; Jaswinder Singh; Kuldip Paliwal; Yaoqi Zhou
summary.executive_summary:
Accurate prediction of protein contact-map is essential for protein structure and function prediction. Most prior methods rely on protein-sequence evolutionary information, but this fails for many proteins that lack naturally occurring homologous sequences, and generating evolutionary profiles is computationally intensive. To address this, the authors developed SPOT-Contact-Single, a contact-map predictor that utilizes the output of a pre-trained ESM-1b transformer language model as input alongside one-hot amino acid encoding and SPOT-1D-Single's one-dimensional structural properties, trained with an ensemble of residual neural networks.

The training set was curated from a ProteinNet benchmark: an initial set of 50914 high-resolution (<2.5Å) proteins clustered at 95% sequence identity was filtered using HHblits (e-value cut-off <0.1) to remove homologs, yielding 39120 proteins for training. After removing proteins longer than 500, the final sets comprised 34691 training and 88 validation proteins. For testing, the authors downloaded post-2018 structures and removed homologs relative to the training set with HHblits (e-value <0.1), creating a 669-protein SPOT-2018 test set. From this, 46 proteins with Neff=1 were separated for a Neff1-2018 test set. An additional independent test set, CASP14-FM, contained 15 free-modelling targets.

Input features combined one-hot amino acid encoding, SPOT-1D-Single outputs (SS3, SS8, ASA, HSE, and backbone angles), and ESM-1b attention maps from the last layer and every layer. The models were trained with six combinations of features: three direct contact-map prediction models (Binary Cross-Entropy loss) and three distogram-based models (Cross-Entropy loss), all sharing a ResNet12 architecture (channel size 64, kernel size 3) with the Adam optimizer, learning rate 0.001, batch size 1, and early stopping at 3. The ensemble averaged the six models. Performance was evaluated using F1-score, MCC, sensitivity, and contact-range-specific metrics (top L/10, L/5, L/2, L/1) at a distance cut-off of 8.0 Å.

Key results: the ensemble improved the F1-score by 15% over SSCpred on CASP14-FM, and by 45% (to 0.32) over evolutionary-profile methods on Neff=1 proteins. ESM-1b attention maps drove most gains, providing a 242% F1 improvement over one-hot-only and a 178% improvement over one-hot plus SPOT-1D-Single. Using all ESM-1b attention layers yielded an additional 2.92% F1-score increase. Feature importance analysis showed the ensemble improved the F1-score by 4% over the second-best individual model. On CPU, SPOT-Contact-Single ran in 116 seconds, 22 times faster than TrRosetta. ESM-1b attention maps limit direct prediction to proteins with 1024 amino acids or fewer. The authors conclude SPOT-Contact-Single is a reasonably accurate screening tool for large-scale prediction.

Executive Summary
Accurate prediction of protein contact-map is essential for protein structure and function prediction. Most prior methods rely on protein-sequence evolutionary information, but this fails for many proteins that lack naturally occurring homologous sequences, and generating evolutionary profiles is computationally intensive. To address this, the authors developed SPOT-Contact-Single, a contact-map predictor that utilizes the output of a pre-trained ESM-1b transformer language model as input alongside one-hot amino acid encoding and SPOT-1D-Single's one-dimensional structural properties, trained with an ensemble of residual neural networks.
