After removing proteins longer than 500, the final sets comprised 34691 training and 88 validation proteins. For testing, the authors downloaded post-2018 structures and removed homologs relative to the training set with HHblits (e-value <0.1), creating a 669-protein SPOT-2018 test set. From this, 46 proteins with Neff=1 were separated for a Neff1-2018 test set. An additional independent test set, CASP14-FM, contained 15 free-modelling targets.

Input features combined one-hot amino acid encoding, SPOT-1D-Single outputs (SS3, SS8, ASA, HSE, and backbone angles), and ESM-1b attention maps from the last layer and every layer. The models were trained with six combinations of features: three direct contact-map prediction models (Binary Cross-Entropy loss) and three distogram-based models (Cross-Entropy loss), all sharing a ResNet12 architecture (channel size 64, kernel size 3) with the Adam optimizer, learning rate 0.001, batch size 1, and early stopping at 3. The ensemble averaged the six models. Performance was evaluated using F1-score, MCC, sensitivity, and contact-range-specific metrics (top L/10, L/5, L/2, L/1) at a distance cut-off of 8.0 Å.

Key results: the ensemble improved the F1-score by 15% over SSCpred on CASP14-FM, and by 45% (to 0.32) over evolutionary-profile methods on Neff=1 proteins. ESM-1b attention maps drove most gains, providing a 242% F1 improvement over one-hot-only and a 178% improvement over one-hot plus SPOT-1D-Single. Using all ESM-1b attention layers yielded an additional 2.92% F1-score increase. Feature importance analysis showed the ensemble improved the F1-score by 4% over the second-best individual model. On CPU, SPOT-Contact-Single ran in 116 seconds, 22 times faster than TrRosetta. ESM-1b attention maps limit direct prediction to proteins with 1024 amino acids or fewer. The authors conclude SPOT-Contact-Single is a reasonably accurate screening tool for large-scale prediction.

Research Context
Accurate prediction of protein contact-map is essential for protein structure and function prediction. Many methods rely on protein-sequence evolutionary information, but this fails for proteins that lack homologous sequences. Generating evolutionary profiles is computationally intensive and requires sequence alignment. Most prior predictors depend on multiple sequence alignment (MSA) and other homology-based profile information. For proteins with very few or no homologs, MSA-based predictor performance drops significantly. SSCpred is a recent single-sequence-based method using one-hot encoding and SPIDER3-Single features. Single-sequence methods are expected to perform poorer than MSA-based techniques when homologs exist. A need exists for unsupervised deep learning features inspired by language models. ESM-1b uses a Transformer-34 model trained on Uniref50 and outputs embeddings and attention maps.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The research asks whether unsupervised language model features can improve single-sequence contact map prediction beyond one-hot encoding. The hypothesis is that unsupervised learning features concatenated with one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single outputs outperform SSCpred and MSA predictors for low-Neff proteins. The predictor is expected to outperform evolutionary-profile methods on isolated proteins. An ensemble of models trained through different training approaches and feature combinations is predicted to add further improvement.

Methodological Details
A dataset was curated from a large ProteinNet benchmark. It consisted of 50914 proteins submitted to PDB before 2016 with high resolution (<2.5Å). The proteins were clustered at sequence identity cut-off of 95% according to MMseqs2. This initial filtering left the final 39120 proteins for the training set. Proteins longer than 500 were removed from both the training and validation sets. The final training and validation sets comprised 34691 and 88 proteins, respectively. Potential homologs were removed using HHblits at an e-value cut-off of less than 0.1. This led to 669 proteins in a stringent test set called SPOT-2018. A Neff1-2018 set was formed by separating 46 proteins with Neff=1 from SPOT-2018. An additional independent test set, CASP14-FM, contained 15 free modelling targets released at CASP14. Input features included one-hot encoding of amino acids and SPOT-1D-Single. SPOT-1D-Single provided SS3 and SS8, ASA, HSE, and backbone torsion angles. ESM-1b attention maps were gathered from all twenty attention heads across every layer. All attention maps were symmetrized and applied average product corrections.

Procedures And Architectures
The deep neural network architecture was inspired by ResNet success in contact-map prediction. A ResNet12 architecture was used, the maximum depth trainable on the available GPU. A recently published ResNet version was employed instead of vanilla ResNet. Six models were trained with the same architecture but different input feature combinations. Three models predicted inter-residue contacts as binary classification. The other three models predicted inter-residue distances as distance bins. Direct models were trained with Binary Cross-Entropy loss. Distogram-based models were trained with Cross-Entropy loss. The Adam optimizer was used with a learning rate of 0.001 and batch size of 1. All models were trained with early stopping of 3 to avoid overfitting. Feature importance across feature combinations is presented in Table 2. An ensemble of the six models was created by taking the mean of individual models. Separate models were trained with direct contact-map and distogram-based training strategies. All model hyperparameters and specifications were kept the same across models.

Key Results
One-hot encoding alone yields an F1-score of 0.15 and an MCC of 0.14. Adding SPOT-1D-Single improved the F1-score by 22.90% over one-hot encoding. ESM-1b last-layer attention maps reached 0.51 for F1 and 0.50 for MCC. Using attention maps yields a 242% and 178% improvement over one-hot models. Using all ESM-1b layers yielded an additional 2.92% increase in F1-score. The ensemble yielded a 4% improvement over the second-best individual model. On proteins without homologs, SPOT-Contact-Single reached 0.32 F1, which is 45% higher. Long-range contact precision improved ~100% over SSCpred on CASP14-FM. SPOT-Contact-Single achieved a 15% improvement over SSCpred on CASP14-FM. On CPU, SPOT-Contact-Single ran in 116 seconds, 22 times faster than TrRosetta. On GPU, TrRosetta took 1926 seconds, 42 times slower than SPOT-Contact-Single.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Concatenating unsupervised learning features with one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single outputs boosted prediction. The ensemble adds to the improvement across all performance matrices. Accuracy is higher than profile methods when the number of effective homologous sequence is low. The method serves as a reasonably accurate screening tool for protein contact map prediction. Attention maps limit direct prediction to proteins with 1024 amino acids or fewer. Further gains may come from architectural models such as Transformer. The proposed approach offers a faster and reasonably accurate alternative to evolution-based methods.

Contradictions And Limitations
MSA-based methods outperform SSCpred when more effective homologs exist. The profile-based predictors improve as Neff increases, while SPOT-1D-Single lags behind. For proteins with few homologs, the MSA-based profile-based predictors still beat single-sequence predictors. Attention maps limit direct prediction to proteins with 1024 amino acids or fewer. SSCpred was used via its web-server because a stand-alone version was missing. No code release is explicitly stated for the SPOT-Contact-Single predictor.

Claims
ESM-1b attention features boost single-sequence contact map prediction. Adding SPOT-1D-Single to one-hot encoding improved the F1-score by 22.90%. ESM-1b last-layer attention maps reach 0.51 for F1 and 0.50 for MCC. The gains are 242% and 178% improvement over one-hot encoding. Concatenating all features together added only 2.92% to the F1-score. MSA-based methods outperform single-sequence methods when more effective homologs exist. The method serves as a reasonably accurate screening tool.
An ensemble improves performance over individual models. The ensemble yielded a 4% improvement over the second-best individual model. The ensemble adds to the improvement across all matrices. Direct contact-map prediction performs slightly better than distogram-based training. The method can be used as a reasonable screening tool.
SPOT-Contact-Single is faster than profile-based methods. On CPU, SPOT-Contact-Single ran in 116 seconds, 22 times faster than TrRosetta. On GPU, TrRosetta took 1926 seconds, 42 times slower than SPOT-Contact-Single. No contradictory evidence on speed is reported. The method is more suitable for genomic scale prediction.
SPOT-Contact-Single outperforms profile methods on proteins without homologs. On proteins without homologs, SPOT-Contact-Single reached 0.32 F1. Long-range contact precision improved ~100% over SSCpred on CASP14-FM. SPOT-Contact-Single achieved a 15% improvement over SSCpred on CASP14-FM. The profile-based predictors improve as Neff increases. The method is useful for large-scale prediction.

Data And Code Availability
The profile-based methods TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact have stand-alone programs online. The ESM predictor's stand-alone program is hosted by Facebook Research. SSCpred is available only through its online web-server. No code release is explicitly stated for SPOT-Contact-Single.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Feature importance is profiled across one-hot, SPOT-1D-Single, and ESM-1b. Direct contact-map prediction performs slightly better than distogram-based prediction. The ensemble mean was computed across all six models on the validation set. The F1-score was plotted as a function of the Neff values in Figure 3.

Ethical Considerations
No ethical considerations are reported.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows convolutional layers with a channel size of 64 and kernel size of 3. Table 1 describes the six models with their distinct input feature combinations. Table 2 shows feature importance for one-hot, SPOT-1D-Single, and ESM-1b features. Table 3 and Supplementary Table S3 compare direct contact-map and distogram-based training strategies. Table 4 reports the validation set performance for each individual model and the ensemble. Table 5 shows the F1-scores on Neff=1 proteins for SPOT-Contact, TrRosetta, ESM-1b, and SPOT-Contact-Single. Figure 2 shows contact precision for short-, medium-, and long-range contacts. Figure 3 plots the F1-score of different predictors as a function of the Neff values. Figure 4 displays native and predicted contact-maps for the 5YKZ_A protein. Table 6 compares SPOT-Contact-Single with ESM-1b and SSCpred on CASP14-FM.

Three Takeaways
Combining transformer attention features with one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single outputs trained in an ensemble improves single-sequence contact map prediction. The ensemble improved the F1-score by 15% over SSCpred on CASP14-FM and was 116 seconds on CPU versus 1926 seconds on GPU. Further gains likely come from architectural models such as Transformer rather than ResNet12.

summary.authors: Shiho Hashiguchi (Fukuoka University); Tomoko Tanaka (Fukuoka University); Ryosuke Mano (Fukuoka University); Seiji Kondo (Fukuoka University); Shohta Kodama (Fukuoka University)
summary.executive_summary: This study investigated the signaling role of CCN2 (also known as CTGF), a known angiogenic factor, in primary cultured lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) and its impact on lymphangiogenesis. While CCN2's roles in physiological and pathological angiogenesis are well-documented, its effects on LECs and intracellular signaling remained unclear. The discrepancy between in vitro inhibition and in vivo promotion was attributed to ECM/MMP effects.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigated the signaling role of CCN2 (also known as CTGF), a known angiogenic factor, in primary cultured lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) and its impact on lymphangiogenesis. While CCN2's roles in physiological and pathological angiogenesis are well-documented, its effects on LECs and intracellular signaling remained unclear. The authors examined the gene expression of LEC markers (Lyve1, Podoplanin, Prox1) and lymphangiogenic factors (Vegfc, Vegfd, Flt4) upon stimulation with 0, 12.5, 25, 50, 100, and 200 ng/mL of CCN2 for 3 hours using quantitative RT-PCR. Markers Lyve1, Pdpn, and Prox1 rose dose-dependently up to 100 ng/mL but fell sharply at 200 ng/mL, while Vegfc, Vegfd, and Flt4 were increased and Kdr was unchanged. A phospho-receptor tyrosine kinase array revealed VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 phosphorylation unchanged, while EGFR and EphB4 rose and ErbB4 and PDGFRa fell (p<0.001). Signaling analysis showed phospho-ERK significantly increased (p<0.001) despite unchanged total ERK and unchanged p38, JNK, AKT, NFkB, and Smad phosphorylation. Integrin expression analysis showed Itgav, Itga9, and Itgb1 predominately expressed and CCN2-inducible, leading to the conclusion that CCN2 increases phospho-ERK via integrin av (knockdown reduced phospho-ERK, p=0.0040, while a9 knockdown slightly increased it). Cell growth was slightly suppressed by CCN2 at 24 hours but not at 48 or 72 hours, suggesting a weak growth inhibitory effect. DUSP family analysis showed Dusp6 predominant; immunoprecipitation showed DUSP6 co-precipitated with ERK and the interaction was enhanced by CCN2, and DUSP6 siRNA increased phospho-ERK (p<0.001 at 15m, p=0.04 at 24h, p=0.004 at 48h). In vivo, subcutaneous Matrigel plug assays with recombinant rat CCN2 (8.33 ug) vs PBS showed Podoplanin-positive vessel and area increases, and enhanced ERK and DUSP6 detection in Podoplanin-positive cells (p<0.05). The authors conclude CCN2 activates ERK via integrin av and enhances ERK-DUSP6 interaction, with DUSP6 negatively modulating ERK signaling in LECs. The discrepancy between in vitro inhibition and in vivo promotion was attributed to ECM/MMP effects.

Research Context
CCN2 is a well-known angiogenic factor in physiological and pathological angiogenesis. CCN2 roles in lymphangiogenesis and intracellular signaling in lymphatic endothelial cells remain unclear. The lymphatic vascular system has essential roles in the regulation of tissue pressure, immune surveillance and absorption of dietary fat. Lymphangiogenesis is necessary not only for the development of the lymphatic system during embryogenesis, but also for tissue repair and inflammatory reactions. Several angiogenic factors are involved in growth of lymphatic vessels. VEGF-C-VEGFR-3 signaling is also crucial for the development of lymphatic vessels. Previous studies in renal, peritoneal dialysis-related and liver fibrosis mouse models showed that CTGF enhanced lymphangiogenesis. However, CCN2 signaling in LECs in lymphangiogenic signaling has not been elucidated.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is what the downstream signaling of CCN2 is in primary cultured LECs. The hypothesis is that CCN2 stimulates ERK via cell-surface receptors such as integrins. The study predicts CCN2 will activate phospho-ERK and modulate integrin expression. The expected outcome is that CCN2 will increase lymphangiogenic factors and enhance Podoplanin-positive vessels in vivo. The negative regulation hypothesis predicts ERK phosphorylation is transient due to a concomitant mechanism. The final hypothesis is that CCN2-related lymphangiogenesis is regulated by DUSP6 enabling negative modulation of ERK-signaling.

Methodological Details
The study used primary cultured LECs obtained from C57BL/6 mice. LECs were cultured in 0.1% gelatin-coated culture dishes at 37C with 5% CO2. Cells were used up to 6 passages in in vitro experiments. Cell proliferation was assessed by crystal violet staining method. Cells were plated in 24-well plates at 2 x 10^4 cells per well. CCN2 concentrations used were 0, 10, 50, 100, and 200 ng/mL. RNA was prepared from cells using the Purelink RNA purification Kit. cDNA was prepared from 1 ug of total RNA using the QuantiTect RT Kit. Quantitative RT-PCR was performed using TB Green Premix ExTaq II. Primers were listed in Table S1. siRNAs were designed by siDirect ver.2 and sense/complementary strands were synthesized. LECs (1.5 x 10^5) were transfected with 25 pmol of target siRNA. Western blot used RIPA Buffer containing cOmplete and phosphatase inhibitor cocktails. Protein samples (5-20 ug) were separated with SDS-PAGE and transferred to PVDF membranes. Primary antibodies were incubated at 4C overnight. The phospho-RTK array incubated 200 ug of total protein for 24 h at 4C. Immunoprecipitation lysed with Lysis Buffer containing cOmplete and phosphatase inhibitor cocktails. Male 8-week-old C57BL/6 mice were purchased from Charles River Japan. Mice were used at 9 weeks of age. Matrigel mixture: 450 uL growth factor reduced Matrigel mixed with 8.33 ug CCN2 or 50 uL PBS. n=4 for CCN2 group and n=3 for PBS control group in Matrigel assay. Statistical analysis used GraphPad Prism version 8. All experiments were performed more than three times except the RTK assay (n=2). Significance set at p < 0.05.

Procedures And Architectures
LECs were stimulated with CCN2 at 0, 12.5, 25, 50, 100 or 200 ng/mL for 3 h for gene expression. Gene expression of Lyve1, Pdpn, Prox1, Vegfc, Vegfd, Flt4 were analyzed by quantitative RT-PCR. Phospho-receptor tyrosine kinases were analyzed using a Proteome profiler mouse phospho-RTK array kit. Various phosphorylated proteins were analyzed to determine downstream intracellular signaling. Integrin mRNA expression of Itgav, Itga9, Itga2b, Itgb1, Itgb2, Itgb3 was measured in CCN2-treated LECs. Integrin av was silenced by siRNA. Cell proliferation was assayed by crystal violet staining at 0, 24, 48 and 72 h. Absorbance at 590 nm was measured using the SPARK 10M plate reader. DUSP family members Dusp1-10 were analyzed by quantitative RT-PCR. DUSP6 co-precipitation with ERK was detected by immunoprecipitation assays. DUSP6 siRNA was used to increase phospho-ERK. CCN2 mixed with Matrigel and subcutaneously injected onto backs of mice. Matrigel plugs were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, embedded in paraffin, and paraffin sections (4 um) stained. Morphology observed via BZ-710X fluorescence microscope and LSM710 confocal microscope.

Key Results
Lyve1, Pdpn and Prox1 expression increased by CCN2 dose-dependently up to 100 ng/mL. At 200 ng/mL, Lyve1, Pdpn and Prox1 expression dramatically decreased compared with 100 ng/mL. CCN2 increased Vegfc, Vegfd, and Flt4 expression but did not affect Kdr expression. VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 phosphorylation were unchanged by CCN2. Phosphorylation of EGFR and EphB4 were increased by CCN2 (p < 0.001). Phosphorylation of ErbB4 and PDGFRa were decreased compared with controls (p < 0.001). Phosphorylation levels of p38 MAPK, JNK, AKT, NFkB and Smad2, -3, and -1/5 were unchanged by CCN2. Phospho-ERK was significantly increased in response to CCN2 (p < 0.001). Total ERK protein levels were not affected by CCN2 treatment. Itgav, Itga9 and Itgb1 were predominantly expressed in LECs and increased by CCN2. Itga2b, Itgb2 and Itgb3 were not induced by CCN2. Knockdown of integrin av partially decreased CCN2-induced phospho-ERK (p = 0.0040). Knockdown of integrin a9 resulted in a slight increase of CCN2-induced phospho-ERK. Phospho-ERK was increased by suppression of integrin b1 (p = 0.05). CCN2 treatment suppressed cell growth at 24 h (p = 0.22, 0.92 and > 0.99, respectively). CCN2 treatment suppressed cell growth at 24 h compared with vehicle-treated LECs (p = 0.003 and 0.02). Phospho-ERK increased at 15 min, continued to 4 h, decreased at 8 h, and increased after 48 h. Dusp6 was predominant; Dusp16 was undetected. DUSP6 co-precipitated with ERK, and the interaction was enhanced by CCN2. DUSP6 siRNA increased phospho-ERK at 15 m (p < 0.001), 4 h, 24 h (p = 0.04), and 48 h (p = 0.004). Number of Podoplanin-positive vessels was increased by exogenous CCN2. Number of CD31-positive cavities and b3-Tubulin-positive peripheral nerves were increased in CCN2 plugs. Phospho-ERK and DUSP6 expression in Podoplanin-positive cells significantly increased in the CCN2 gel (p < 0.05).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
CCN2 does not activate VEGF receptor signaling upstream of ERK in primary LECs. Integrin av-mediated phosphorylation of ERK supports the link between CCN2 and signaling. Phospho-ERK without CCN2 stimulation may be due to integrin a5 supplementation. DUSP6 functions as a negative modulator of ERK-signaling in LECs. DUSP6 might suppress excessive activation of ERK in vivo. Integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6-mediated lymphangiogenesis may be therapeutic targets of OSCC.

Contradictions And Limitations
No in vitro proliferation increase; CCN2 weakly suppressed proliferation. Phospho-ERK increase by integrin b1 suppression happened without CCN2 stimulation. The discrepancy between in vitro cell inhibition and in vivo promotion may be due to ECM and matrix metalloproteinase effects. The relationship between FOXC1, FOXC2 and DUSP6 has not yet been analyzed. Itga5 mRNA was not investigated because the CCN2-integrin a5 interaction has not been reported in LECs.

Claims
CCN2 activates ERK-signaling via integrin av in lymphatic endothelial cells. Phospho-ERK significantly increased in response to CCN2 (p < 0.001). Knockdown of integrin av partially decreased CCN2-induced phospho-ERK (p = 0.0040). Itgav, Itga9 and Itgb1 were predominantly expressed in LECs. Knockdown of integrin a9 resulted in a slight increase of CCN2-induced phospho-ERK. Phospho-ERK was not altered by CCN2 stimulation in integrin b1 suppression. CCN2-induced phospho-ERK is partially mediated by integrin av in LECs.
CCN2 promotes lymphangiogenesis in vivo and DUSP6 negatively modulates ERK-signaling. Number of Podoplanin-positive vessels was increased by exogenous CCN2. Phospho-ERK and DUSP6 expression in Podoplanin-positive cells significantly increased (p < 0.05). DUSP6 siRNA increased phospho-ERK levels (p < 0.001 at 15 m). No changes in proliferation were observed at 48 and 72 h. CCN2-induced phospho-ERK was not altered in integrin b1-suppressed LECs. DUSP6 might suppress the excessive activation of ERK in vivo. Integrin av, ERK and DUSP6-mediated lymphangiogenesis may be therapeutic targets of OSCC.

Data And Code Availability
The paper does not report a data availability statement or code repository. Primers and antibody lists are in Tables S1, S2, and S3, not provided in text.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Statistical significance was set at a p-value of less than 0.05. Comparative analysis performed by Student's t-test, ANOVA, Bonferroni, or Sidak. Phospho-RTK array was done in n=2 (single experiment). Integrin b2 and b3 did not compensate for the decrease in integrin b1.

Ethical Considerations
Experiments were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of Fukuoka University (approval number: 2008024). Experiments were performed in compliance with relevant laws and institutional guidelines.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows dose-dependent increase of Lyve1, Pdpn, Prox1 up to 100 ng/mL. Figure 1B shows CCN2 increases Vegfc, Vegfd, Flt4 but not Kdr. Figure 2A, 2B show phospho-ERK increase (p < 0.001). Figure 3A shows predominant integrin expression and CCN2 inducibility. Figure 3B shows integrin av knockdown decreasing phospho-ERK (p = 0.0040). Figure 3C shows integrin a9 knockdown increasing phospho-ERK. Figure 3D shows integrin b1 suppression increasing phospho-ERK. Figure 4A shows cell growth suppression by CCN2. Figure 4B shows time-course phospho-ERK profile. Figure 5A shows Dusp1-10 expression; Dusp6 predominant. Figure 5B shows DUSP6 co-precipitation with ERK. Figure 5C shows DUSP6 siRNA transfection. Figure 5D shows phospho-ERK increase after DUSP6 siRNA. Figure 6A shows blood vessels observed on Matrigel plugs. Figure 6B and 6C show Podoplanin-positive cells and tubular structures. Figure 7A and 7C show phospho-ERK in Podoplanin-positive cells. Figure 7B shows DUSP6 in Podoplanin-positive cells.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is CCN2 activates ERK via integrin av and DUSP6 negatively modulates this ERK signaling in LECs. 2. The strongest evidence is phospho-ERK increases (p < 0.001) while integrin av knockdown decreases it (p = 0.0040). 3. The future path is that integrin av, ERK and DUSP6-mediated lymphangiogenesis may be therapeutic targets of OSCC.

summary.title: Tumor PD-L1 selectively suppresses type I interferon in myeloid cells to suppress CTL recruitment to promote lung metastasis
summary.authors: John D Klement, Priscilla S Redd, Chunwan Lu, Alyssa D Merting, Dakota B Poschel, Dafeng Yang, Gang Zhou, David H Munn, Kebin Liu
summary.executive_summary: This study elucidates the indirect mechanism by which tumor-expressed PD-L1 (tPD-L1) promotes lung metastasis through an intermediate cell, rather than directly suppressing cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) activation. Building on established PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint blockade (ICB) paradigms, the authors first establish that PD-L1 loss in tumor cells alone, in a co-culture system with antigen-specific CTLs, confers no survival advantage, indicating tPD-L1 does not protect tumor cells from CTL killing in isolation. However, in vivo depletion of PD-L1 in lung metastases, but not the primary tumor, significantly decreased metastasis in a CTL-dependent manner. The mechanism proceeds through an axis: tPD-L1 engages myeloid PD-1 (mPD-1), antagonizing type I interferon (IFN-I) and STAT1 signaling, which represses the CTL-recruiting chemokines Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 in myeloid cells. The authors validate this via single-cell RNA sequencing, flow cytometry, and in vitro myeloid co-culture, and conclude that the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis controls CTL tumor infiltration in lung metastasis. Human data, including single-cell sequencing and PHATE analysis of metastatic basal cell carcinoma patients before and after PD-1 blockade, shows that PD-1 blockade releases myeloid differentiation restrictions, enhances IFN-I signaling, and promotes CTL-recruiting chemokines, correlating with the mouse mechanism. A key limitation is the study's exclusive focus on lung metastases, and the bibliography is missing from the provided text. The authors suggest this work explains why tumors resistant to primary tumor PD-L1/PD-1 blockade still depend on PD-L1 to escape metastasis, and they propose TLR and STING agonists with anti-PD-1/L1 as clinical directions.

The mechanism proceeds through an axis: tPD-L1 engages myeloid PD-1 (mPD-1), antagonizing type I interferon (IFN-I) and STAT1 signaling, which represses the CTL-recruiting chemokines Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 in myeloid cells. The authors validate this via single-cell RNA sequencing, flow cytometry, and in vitro myeloid co-culture, and conclude that the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis controls CTL tumor infiltration in lung metastasis. Human data, including single-cell sequencing and PHATE analysis of metastatic basal cell carcinoma patients before and after PD-1 blockade, shows that PD-1 blockade releases myeloid differentiation restrictions, enhances IFN-I signaling, and promotes CTL-recruiting chemokines, correlating with the mouse mechanism. A key limitation is the study's exclusive focus on lung metastases, and the bibliography is missing from the provided text. The authors suggest this work explains why tumors resistant to primary tumor PD-L1/PD-1 blockade still depend on PD-L1 to escape metastasis, and they propose TLR and STING agonists with anti-PD-1/L1 as clinical directions.

Research Context
ICB therapy blocks PD-L1 from binding co-inhibitory receptor PD-1 on activated CTLs. PD-1 engagement on CTLs causes SHP-2 mediated dephosphorylation and an exhausted fate. tPD-L1 has been hypothesized to serve as a direct molecular shield against CTL lysis. PD-1 expression on non-T cell populations like myeloid and dendritic cells has been highlighted. How non-T cell PD-1 connects tPD-L1 to CTL suppression is incompletely understood. PD-L1 may control CTL recruitment versus functionality versus function, rather than the primary tumor site.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Central question: Does tPD-L1 protect tumor cells from CTL killing when only target cells and CTLs are present? Hypothesis: tPD-L1 exhibits no direct effect on CTL activity alone. Hypothesis: A third factor only present in the lung metastatic niche was necessary for tPD-L1's indirect role. Hypothesis: This factor is myeloid cell PD-1 (mPD-1) which bridges tPD-L1 to CTL recruitment. Hypothesis: PD-1 blockade releases differentiation restrictions and restores IFN-I signaling in human myeloid cells.

Methodological Details
Cell lines: 4T1 (triple negative breast cancer) and CT26 (mismatch repair proficient colorectal cancer) from ATCC. PD-L1 was deleted using CRISPR/Cas9 (Cd274 knockout) and lentiviral transduction. CTL line: 2/20 tumor-specific CTLs sensitive to PD-1 inhibition, recognizing the H2-Ld restricted AH1 epitope of gp70. Tumor model: 4T1 orthotopic tumors injected into the right second mammary gland; CT26 subcutaneous tumors injected into the right flank. Metastasis model: 4T1 cells injected into the lateral tail vein; lungs harvested and quantified as previously described. Neutralization: 200 µg of anti-CD8α (53-6.7) or isotype control (2A3) injected i.v. every other day. Flow cytometry: Samples blocked in FACS Buffer (PBS + 2% FBS) with FcBlock; read on FACSCalibur CellQuestPro or LSRFortessa with BD Diva 8.01. Bulk RNA-Seq: 4T1 WT or PDL1-KO cells, extracted using Direct-zol, sequenced by Novogene; mapped to mm10 by STARv2.5, quantified by HTSeqv0.6.1. scRNA-Seq: 4T1 WT or PDL1-KO, 14-day injection, CD45 magnetic nanobeads, 2-3 x 10^3 cells on Chromium Chip B (10x Genomics). Alignment: STAR aligner in Cell Ranger 3.1.0; 30-39K reads/cell with 75-102 million reads per sample; ~1600 median genes per cell. Patient data: TCGA, BMS038 (riazn/bms038_analysis), PRJEB23709 pseudo-aligned with kallisto; processed by Harmony. Statistics: Prism8 (Graphpad) two-tailed Student's t-test; survival by two-sided log-rank test (Survival package, R).

Procedures And Architectures
CTL:tumor co-culture used to reconstitute antigen-specific CTL:tumor interaction with high fidelity. Myeloid cell surface PD-1 expression was measured via flow cytometry in 4T1-colonized lungs. RAW264.7 macrophages co-cultured with 4T1; PD-1 upregulated in a cell-contact and IFNAR-dependent manner. Engagement with 4T1 tPD-L1 enhanced SHP-2 activation and decreased pSTAT1 levels in RAW cells. Myeloid cells depleted by clodronate liposomes; tumor growth analyzed in the lungs. Single-cell PHATE analysis and transcriptomic signature generation; tPD-L1 loss signature used a ≥2-fold fold-change and padj <0.05. Signature transfer via Seurat 'TransferData' to human lung tumor-resident macrophages. Patient PHATE analysis released differentiation restriction, enhancing IFN-I signaling and CTL-recruiting chemokine expression.

Key Results
In vitro, PD-L1 deletion renders cell lines unable to engage CTL-expressed PD-1 as they show no PD-L2 expression. 2/20 CTLs exert antigen-specific cytotoxicity within minutes without prior differentiation. tPD-L1 confers no survival advantage when an antigen-specific CTL encounters a cognate peptide-MHC complex. No difference was observed in primary tumor growth after PD-L1 WT and PD-L1 KO orthotopic injection (Fig 2A, S2B). No difference in tumor growth were observed in the WT and PD-L1 KO CT26 at the site of tumor cell injection (Fig 2E). Increased infiltration of CD3+ cells was observed after loss of tPD-L1 in lung but not in the primary tumor (Fig 3A). No difference in initial tumor cell colonization as measured by tumor cell gp70 level was seen one day after tail vein injection (Fig 3B). PD-L1-deficient and competent 4T1 metastasized equally in adaptive-immune deficient congenic RAGII-KO mice (Fig 3C). Ablation of MHC class I or CD8+ T cell depletion revealed tPD-L1 drove metastasis by suppressing killing by CTLs (Fig 2F, 3D). Bulk myeloid cell composition showed no change but enhanced antigen presentation machinery was detected in macrophages (Fig 5E-F). Pdcd1lg2 (PD-L2) expression increased in 4T1-colonized lungs as early as one day after injection (Figure 5J-K). RAW surface expression of PD-1 was upregulated in a cell-contact and IFNAR-dependent manner following co-culture with 4T1 (Fig 6C, S6A-E). Engagement with 4T1 tPD-L1 enhanced SHP-2 activation and decreased pSTAT1 levels in RAW cells (Fig 6D-F). Disruption of RAW PD-1 or 4T1 PD-L1 expression enhanced IFNb production (Fig 6J). Depletion of myeloid cells with clodronate liposomes diminished tPD-L1 function in promoting tumor growth in the lungs (Fig 6K-L). scRNA-Seq generated ~1600 median genes per cell and mapped >91% genome-mapping rates. High quality cells were defined as 200 < feature count <4000 and percent mitochondrial reads < 10.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
tPD-L1 does not protect tumor cells from CTL killing but instead targets mPD-1 to create an immunosuppressive niche. The tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis controls CTL tumor infiltration in lung metastasis. PD-1/L1 axis acts as a negative feedback circuit induced by and attenuating type I interferon signaling. tPD-L1 may control CTL recruitment versus functionality versus function, not just the primary tumor site. Type I interferon signaling is essential for myeloid cell function in CTL recruitment to the lung metastasis niche.

Contradictions And Limitations
One limitation is that the study exclusively analyzed lung metastases, which may have a uniquely inflamed microenvironment. No bibliography is provided, preventing tracing of the 59 cited works to specific sources. Cell lines were mycoplasma-free but contamination could still occur. Human patient numbers were not reported, limiting statistical generalizability of human findings. Human myeloid cluster identities were transferred via signatures, which assumes conservation of mouse-human identities.

Claims
tPD-L1 promotes lung metastasis indirectly by engaging myeloid PD-1 to suppress type I IFN and CTL recruitment. Primary tumor growth was unaffected by PD-L1 loss (Fig 2A, S2B). PD-L1 loss increased CD3+ infiltration in the lung, not the primary tumor (Fig 3A). Depletion of myeloid cells diminished tPD-L1 function in lung metastasis (Fig 6K-L). Only lung metastases were analyzed, so a lung-specific microenvironment may confound the mechanism. The tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis could be targeted by TLR and STING agonists with anti-PD-L1/L2.
The PD-1/L1 axis is induced by and then attenuates type I interferon signaling. RAW PD-1 or 4T1 PD-L1 disruption enhanced IFNb production (Fig 6J). Type I IFN induces both PD-L1 and PD-1 in myeloid cells. PD-L1 expression is upregulated more rapidly than PD-1 (Fig 42). Low interferon alpha response rates may result from compensatory PD-1/L1 upregulation.

Data And Code Availability
BMS038 data accessed from authors' processed files at riazn/bms038_analysis. PRJEB23709 dataset accessed from EMBL and pseudo-aligned with kallisto. sgRNA sequences are in Table S2; cell line sources at ATCC and ThermoFisher. Methods and tables are listed in Table S1.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Ablation of MHC class I or antibody-mediated CD8+ T cell depletion confirmed CTL-mediated escape. PD-L1 deletion renders cells unable to engage CTL PD-1 due to lack of PD-L2. RAW PD-1 loss increased sensitivity to the TLR3 ligand poly(I:C) as measured by BST2 (Fig 6H-I).

Ethical Considerations
The paper omits a dedicated ethics statement, but uses ATCC cell lines and reported animal procedures.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: tPD-L1 confers no survival advantage when an antigen-specific effector CTL encounters a tumor cell. Figure 3: CD3+ infiltration increased after tPD-L1 loss in lung; colonization unaffected (Fig 3B). Figure 5: Bulk myeloid composition unchanged; enhanced antigen presentation in macrophages (Fig 5E-F). Figure 6: Myeloid PD-1 surface expression enhanced after tPD-L1 loss; IFNb production increased upon disruption (Fig 6J). Figure 7: PD-1 blockade released myeloid differentiation restriction and enhanced IFN-I signaling (Fig 7A-C).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis drives CTL exclusion from lung metastases. 2. The strongest evidence: Myeloid cell depletion with clodronate liposomes abolished tPD-L1-driven lung metastasis. 3. The future path: Combinatorial TLR/STING agonists and anti-PD-L1/L2 targeting the IFN-I/STAT1 pathway.

Extracellular glycans, particularly glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) like heparan sulfate (HS), are essential regulators of growth factor (GF) signaling in tissue development. GAG polysaccharides are conjugated to adhesion proteins (gelatin) and arrayed onto a non-biofouling acrylamide scaffold deposited on glass, allowing rapid development of functional glycomaterials for stem cell-based regenerative therapies. The method screens passivation strategies and uses a hydrated gelatin-heparin solution (500 µg/mL gelatin, 50-750 µg/mL heparin) to support embryonic stem cell growth and signaling.

This array enables direct, rapid, multiplexed profiling of extracellular GAG activity on growth factor signaling in live ESCs, accelerating the development of new bioactive glycomaterials for stem cell-based therapeutic applications.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Extracellular glycans, particularly glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) like heparan sulfate (HS), are essential regulators of growth factor (GF) signaling in tissue development. They harbor binding sites that establish gradients and active signaling complexes at cell surfaces, yet their structural complexity and compositional heterogeneity make structure-function analysis challenging. HS are composed of N-acetylglucosamine and glucuronic acid, undergoing enzymatic sulfation and epimerization; recent synthetic and chemoenzymatic chemistry now produce well-defined HS structures, yet no on-array platform exists for multiplexed analysis of HS-dependent cellular signaling.

This study describes a stem cell array platform integrating glycosaminoglycan-protein conjugates into a polyacrylamide hydrogel. GAG polysaccharides are conjugated to adhesion proteins (gelatin) and arrayed onto a non-biofouling acrylamide scaffold deposited on glass, allowing rapid development of functional glycomaterials for stem cell-based regenerative therapies. The method screens passivation strategies and uses a hydrated gelatin-heparin solution (500 µg/mL gelatin, 50-750 µg/mL heparin) to support embryonic stem cell growth and signaling.

Using murine embryonic stem cells (ESCs) lacking Exostosin 1 (Ext1 -/-) that express no cell-surface HS and cannot engage HS-dependent growth factors like FGF2, the authors isolated arrayed GAG effects. Heparin was NHS-crosslinked to gelatin at ~15% carboxylic acid crosslinks per chain; FGF2-AF647 binding and MAPK/ERK signaling were assayed.

NHS-crosslinked heparin yielded a ~5-to 10-fold higher FGF2 binding signal, with ~40% binding retained after 48 hours; FGF2 bound most strongly to fully sulfated heparin. MAPK/ERK phosphorylation responded dose-dependently from 0-500 µg/mL immobilized heparin, with array activity somewhat lower than its soluble form, possibly due to limited heparin accessibility to a subset of FGFRs at the cell contact point. This array enables direct, rapid, multiplexed profiling of extracellular GAG activity on growth factor signaling in live ESCs, accelerating the development of new bioactive glycomaterials for stem cell-based therapeutic applications.

Research Context
Extracellular glycans are essential regulators of GF signaling but are hard to access in pure form. GAGs have been pursued as biologically active components for biomaterials. The compositional complexity of HS makes structure-function analysis challenging. No multiplet on-array platform exists for HS-dependent cellular signaling. Early array work studied HS-dependent cellular responses but was not array-based signaling.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can an array platform directly measure GAG contributions to GF signaling pathways in cells? The array platform can bind FGF2 and influence ESC signaling. The crosslinked GAG display should retain its protein-binding specificity. A signaling response should be measurable via phosphorylation status changes.

Methodological Details
A polyacrylamide hydrogel was deposited on glass according to Brafman et al. A gelatin solution of 500 µg/mL was used to coat the hydrogel. Heparin (12 kDa) was used as a model HS glycan. Heparin was activated via NHS esters to crosslink to lysine. Activation used 100 mM, pH = 7.4 HEPES buffer with EDC. The coupling reagent 1-ethyl-3-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)carbodiimide was used. The reaction ran at 4°C for 18 hours. Heparin was purified by size exclusion on a PD10 column. Crosslinking targeted ~15% carboxylic acid crosslinks per chain. The model cells were murine ESCs lacking Exostosin 1. Cell densities were 20,000, 40,000, or 100,000 cells/cm². The optimized seeding density was 40,000 cells/cm 2. Embryonic culture media with LIF and FBS was used. Cells were cultured for 24 hours in the absence of serum. Stimulation used FGF2 at 0.5 ng/mL for 15 minutes. The cells were stimulated for 15 min at 37°C. MAPK activity was detected with antibodies against Erk1/2. The signal was detected using a microarrays scanner. Soluble heparin at 5 µg/mL was used as a positive control.

Procedures And Architectures
Gelatin was loaded into the hydrogel in its dehydrated form. Heparin was mixed with gelatin at 500 g/mL in 500 g/mL gelatin. Heparin was activated to the solvent exposed lysine residues in gelatin. The mixture was spotted on the dry acrylamide substrates. Arrays were probed with the heparin-binding FGF2 protein labeled with AlexaFluor 647. Slides were washed for 3 hours prior to staining. Cells formed near-confluent monolayer colonies on printed spots. The cells were fixed, permeabilized, and immunoassayed. The ratios of fluorescent signals quantified the response.

Key Results
NHS-crosslinked heparin yielded ~ 5-to 10-fold higher signal. Heparin arrays remained stable after 48 hours of culture. FGF2 bound most strongly to the fully sulfated heparin. Removal of 6-O-, 2-O-, and N-sulfates caused progressive loss of activity. The variants included 6OD-Hep, 2OD-Hep, and ND-Hep. Optimized 40,000 cells/cm 2 retained high expression of Oct4. The cells showed no obvious signs of differentiation. Only Ext1 -/-ESCs with heparin showed significant increase in Erk1/2 phosphorylation. The arrayed heparin gave 0-500 g/mL dose-responsive ERK1/2 phosphorylation. MAPK activity was lower on the arrayed heparin than the soluble form.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
NHS-crosslinking enhances stability without altering the protein binding specificity. Crosslinking ensures retention of the polysaccharides on the array. Lower array MAPK activity may reflect limited accessibility of heparin to FGFRs. The array systematically analyzes biological activities of extracellular GAGs.

Contradictions And Limitations
The text shows somewhat lower levels of MAPK activity on the arrayed heparin. The hypothesized lower accessibility of heparin to FGFRs was not tested. A direct negative control with FGF2 alone is not explicitly reported. The random seed and reproducibility parameters are not reported. The data reports OCR artifacts such as g/mL.

Claims
The array platform enables direct, rapid, and multiplexed profiling of extracellular glycans' growth factor-mediated signaling activity in live ESCs. The arrays were designed to directly measure contributions to GF signaling pathways. Arrays were probed with the heparin-binding FGF2 protein labeled with AlexaFluor 647. FGF2 bound most strongly to the fully sulfated heparin. MAPK/ERK phosphorylation responded dose-dependently to heparin concentration. Arrayed heparin activity was lower than soluble heparin, limiting accessibility. No direct negative control with FGF2 alone is explicitly reported. The array systematically analyzes biological activities of extracellular GAGs. It accelerates the development of new bioactive glycomaterials for therapy.
NHS-crosslinking of GAGs to the gelatin matrix stabilizes the display during cell culture without altering protein-binding specificity. Crosslinking stabilizes the display without altering protein binding specificity. The binding signal was ~5-to 10-fold higher with crosslinked heparin. Crosslinking retained ~40% of the FGF2 binding activity after 48 hours. Specific protein binding remained selective for CS, HA, and heparin.  It supports direct assessment of GAG-mediated stem cell signaling. It facilitates the integration of defined GAGs into responsive biomaterials.
Murine Ext1 -/- ESCs lacking cell-surface HS serve as an ideal model to isolate arrayed GAG signaling from endogenous effects. Ext1 -/- ESCs lack cell-surface HS structures and engage HS-dependent GFs. These mutant ESCs are ideally suited to isolate arrayed GAG effects. FGF2 is a growth factor that Ext1 -/- ESCs are unable to engage.  The platform yields cleaner, specific readouts for glycan activity.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Crosslinking targeted ~15% carboxylic acid crosslinks per chain. Soluble heparin at 5 µg/mL served as a positive control. Heparin variants included 6OD-Hep, 2OD-Hep, and ND-Hep. The proteins exhibited high specificity for CS and HA, respectively. Soluble heparin is known to restore MAPK activity in Ext1 -/-ESCs.

Ethical Considerations
Murine embryonic stem cell lines were used; ethical approval is not stated. No IRB or IACUC approval is explicitly reported.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 provides an overview of a cellular microarray approach to cell signaling. Figure 2 shows covalently linked heparin with superior FGF2 binding capacity. Figure 3 shows optimized 40,000 cells/cm 2 produced consistent monolayers. Figure 4 shows only Ext1 -/-ESCs with heparin gave significant increase in Erk1/2 phosphorylation.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is an array platform for multiplexed, direct profiling of GAG activity on GF signaling in live ESCs. 2. The strongest evidence is the dose-responsive, significant increase in Erk1/2 phosphorylation with immobilized heparin. 3. The future path is to accelerate new bioactive glycomaterials for stem cell-based therapeutic applications.

summary.authors: Carling; Blom; Georges; Berenice Talamantes Becerra
summary.executive_summary: This study reports a phylogenomic reassessment of the closely related thermophilic genera Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus within the family Bacillaceae. Using 113 whole-genome sequences retrieved from the RefSeq database and a supplementary dataset of Australian thermophiles, the authors built a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree based on 662 orthologous core genes, supplemented by Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI) and Average Amino Acid Identity (AAI) dendrograms. The results demonstrate that the genomes split into two main clades: Clade I, comprising all Geobacillus, all Parageobacillus, and several Anoxybacillus species, and Clade II, containing most Anoxybacillus species. Clade I further partitioned into three distinct groups—Geobacillus, Parageobacillus, and a third clade proposed as the new genus Quasigeobacillus. The average ANI between the candidate new genus and the existing genera, plus AAI and core-gene phylogeny, support elevating Anoxybacillus tepidamans and one unnamed genomospecies to Quasigeobacillus. Conversely, two Anoxybacillus species (A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus) remained unresolved and inconsistent across methods. The mean ANI and AAI values (e.g., 95.81% AAI for the most distant pair, Table 3) underscore the need for considering closely related genera together in bacterial taxonomy rather than assessing each genus in isolation. The proposed taxonomic changes include defining Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. and reassigning several strains (e.g., G. subterraneus strain KCTC 3922, G. lituanicus strain N3, Anoxybacillus sp. EFIL). The work demonstrates that a broad phylogenetic breadth is essential to avoid incongruous genus assignments that arise when each genus is considered alone.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports a phylogenomic reassessment of the closely related thermophilic genera Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus within the family Bacillaceae. Using 113 whole-genome sequences retrieved from the RefSeq database and a supplementary dataset of Australian thermophiles, the authors built a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree based on 662 orthologous core genes, supplemented by Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI) and Average Amino Acid Identity (AAI) dendrograms. The results demonstrate that the genomes split into two main clades: Clade I, comprising all Geobacillus, all Parageobacillus, and several Anoxybacillus species, and Clade II, containing most Anoxybacillus species. Clade I further partitioned into three distinct groups—Geobacillus, Parageobacillus, and a third clade proposed as the new genus Quasigeobacillus. The average ANI between the candidate new genus and the existing genera, plus AAI and core-gene phylogeny, support elevating Anoxybacillus tepidamans and one unnamed genomospecies to Quasigeobacillus. Conversely, two Anoxybacillus species (A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus) remained unresolved and inconsistent across methods. The mean ANI and AAI values (e.g., 95.81% AAI for the most distant pair, Table 3) underscore the need for considering closely related genera together in bacterial taxonomy rather than assessing each genus in isolation. The proposed taxonomic changes include defining Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. and reassigning several strains (e.g., G. subterraneus strain KCTC 3922, G. lituanicus strain N3, Anoxybacillus sp. EFIL). The work demonstrates that a broad phylogenetic breadth is essential to avoid incongruous genus assignments that arise when each genus is considered alone.

Research Context
Next-generation sequencing technologies produce massive amounts of information 16S rRNA gene sequencing provides low-resolution taxonomic discrimination Average nucleotide identity provides higher resolution for relatedness Amino acid identity is better conserved in distant homologs Core gene alignment provides better vertical phylogenetic views Taxonomic affiliation requires multilocus phylogenetic analysis The genera are moderate thermophiles that form spores Anoxybacillus was proposed in the year 2000 as a new genus The genera were established within the family Bacillaceae Geobacillus was split from the genus Bacillus in 2001 Parageobacillus was defined by reassigning a clade in 2016 Considering genera together is essential for phylogenetic breadth

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question asks if core-gene and identity metrics resolve affinities Verification requires a multilocus phylogenetic approach Broad phylogenetic breadth is hypothesized to reveal conflicts Closely related genera must be considered together Hypothesis: ANI and core genes will separate genomes into clades Clade I is predicted to partition into three distinct groups Predictive outcome: A novel genus emerges from clade I-c

Methodological Details
Genomes were retrieved from the RefSeq database Thirty-two Anoxybacillus and seventy-three Geobacillus strains One representative assembly per Parageobacillus species A supplementary set of Australian thermophiles was included Thirty-one chromosome level assemblies were used Thirty-three scaffold and forty-nine contig-level genomes Forty-nine genomes were at the contig level Anomalous assemblies with suppressed status were excluded Chimeric, contaminated, or frameshifted assemblies were removed The core genome was identified using EDGAR 2.0 Geobacillus thermodenitrificans was the starting reference Orthologous genes were identified iteratively via BLAST Bacillus subtilis spizizenii was the outgroup CDS were concatenated and aligned using MUSCLE The alignment was built into a FastTree tree ANI was calculated with the ani.rb script AAI was calculated with the aai.rb script Draft genomes added 100 N bases between contigs Matrices were built into the DendroUPGMA server Dendrograms used the arithmetic mean clustering method Trees were plotted in Interactive Tree Of Life Unique genes were identified using BLASTn The BLASTn bitscore filter was 10 The percentage overlap filter was 1% The identity filter was 30% Unique CDS were present in all members of clade I-c Five assemblies with few CDS were excluded One duplicate Anoxybacillus strain was removed Low-CDS assemblies reduced the core gene count

Procedures And Architectures
Methods were based on the Geobacillus reassessment paper The reference was the Aliyu et al. study A core gene set was identified from all genomes CDS were iteratively compared against the assemblies The core genome consists of the full CDS Orthologous genes were identified from the reference UPGMA dendrograms were constructed for ANI and AAI GC content and genome size were calculated Topology, GC, and ANI delimited taxonomy Core-gene tree built with 114 genomes A core gene set of 662 orthologous genes was used The core set was built from the starting reference

Key Results
Thirty-two Anoxybacillus, seventy-three Geobacillus, eight Parageobacillus and one Bacillus genomes One Bacillus genome was included in the count The core gene set had 662 orthologous genes A maximum-likelihood tree was built with 114 genomes The tree splits into three major groups Clade I consists of eighty-seven genomes Clade II consists of twenty-four Anoxybacillus genomes Clade I species include A. flavithermus and A. pushchinoensis A. mongoliensis and three unnamed Anoxybacillus species A UPGMA dendrogram was built with 114 genomes Anoxybacillus sp. EFIL had ANI of 97.99 Geobacillus sp. MMMUD3 had ANI of 97.14 Geobacillus sp. DSP4a had ANI of 97.64 Anoxybacillus sp. CHMUD had most distant ANI of 95.03 CHMUD had AAI of 95.81 Results are summarized in Table 3 Six CDS were unique to clade I-c All six genes are present in all members of the clade Table 6 shows the BLASTn alignment results Table 7 shows the best hit The mean ANI and AAI values separate clades The candidate new genus is from the members It is more closely related to Parageobacillus Content suggests a closer affinity to Parageobacillus tepidamans and the one genomospecies were considered They should be placed into a new genus called Quasigeobacillus A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus are incongruous The affinities of these two species remain unresolved

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The breadth of species assessed together reveals conflicts Broad assessment is needed to detect problems Considering closely related species together is essential Closely related species should be used to construct a phylogeny Broad breadth prevents incongruent genus assignment Clade I-c was previously assigned to the genus Anoxybacillus One strain was previously assigned to Geobacillus Clade I-c is seen to be outside of the groups The new clade should be elevated to a new genus The clade contains two species consistently in clade I-c

Contradictions And Limitations
Two species showed inconsistent positioning among the trees They could not be clearly resolved into any genus Draft genomes had 100 N bases introduced between contigs The affinities of these two species remain unresolved Only twenty-four species were validly described in Anoxybacillus Two Anoxybacillus species lacked valid publication G. zalihae was named but not validly published The outgroup Bacillus subtilis spizizenii was assumed

Claims
Clade I-c species should be elevated to the new genus Quasigeobacillus. The ANI and AAI values separate the new genus The mean ANI and AAI values suggest affinity Core gene phylogeny supports the distinction Two species could not be resolved into any genus Broad phylogenetic assessment is required to establish a genus
A broad-breadth phylogenomic analysis reveals problems that single-genus analyses miss. Clade I-c was assigned to two different genera Combined analysis reveals the groups together Two species remained unresolved across methods Genus assignment becomes incongruent without broad breadth
A comprehensive reassessment proposes Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. and several strain reclassifications. Quasigeobacillus was elevated as a new genus Specific strains like G. subterraneus were reclassified The breadth of assessment is still limited Broad assessment is required to confirm taxonomy

Data And Code Availability
Both Ruby scripts are available in the enveomics package Whole genome assemblies are available on RefSeq Data were deposited in Genbank Supplementary Table S1 contains genome characteristics Supplementary Table S2 lists removed assemblies Supplementary Table S3 provides additional values

summary.title: The structural basis for regulation of the glutathione transporter Ycf1 by regulatory domain phosphorylation
summary.authors: Nitesh Kumar Khandelwal, Cinthia R Millan, Samantha I Zangari, Samantha Avila, Dewight Williams, Tarjani M Thaker, Thomas M Tomasiak
summary.field_subfield: Structural biology; ABC transporter pharmacology; biochemistry
summary.executive_summary: Yeast Cadmium Factor-1 (Ycf1) is an ABCC-subfamily ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter that sequesters heavy metals (e.g., cadmium, mercury, lead) and oxidized glutathione (GSSG) into vacuoles to maintain redox balance and counter cell stress; these metals are among the top ten environmental toxins defined by the CDC. ABC transporters are essential for lipid homeostasis, ion transport, and detoxification, and about half of all human ABC transporters are phosphorylated. Previous structural models of CFTR and Ycf1 revealed mostly disordered regulatory (R) domains without assigned phosphorylation sites, which has limited understanding of R-domain interactions and regulation. In this study, the authors determined two cryo-EM structures of endogenously phosphorylated S. cerevisiae Ycf1 at 3.4 Å and 4.0 Å resolution in two inward-facing open conformations (IFwide and IFnarrow). The E1435Q NBD2 Walker B mutant, with substantially lowered ATPase activity (Vmax 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg), was used to trap the conformations; the mutant yielded homogenous particles that produced 3.4 Å and 4.0 Å maps. Both maps resolved an almost complete Ycf1 structure, including 17 transmembrane helices, TMD0, the lasso motif, both NBDs, and a major portion of the R-domain (residues 901-935). The R-domain is ordered in the C-terminal segment (residues 920-929) and lacks secondary structure elsewhere, and it is phosphorylated at three positions (S908, T911, S914) with pronounced additional electron potential density. These phosphates make hydrogen-bonding or strong charge-charge contacts with R716 on NBD1 and R206 on the lasso domain. R-domain phosphorylation is hypothesized to be highly dynamic and required for maximal ATPase activity; dephosphorylated Ycf1 (treated with lambda phosphatase) shows substantially altered proteolysis patterns and drastically reduced ATPase activity. The R-domain sits in a basic groove of the NBD1 perimeter, intracellular loop 4, and the lasso domain, and the networks are nearly constant between IFwide and IFnarrow, related only by a rigid body movement of the NBD1/R-domain complex relative to NBD2. The R-domain burying hydrophobic surfaces (~1530 Å2 and ~1338 Å2) drives R-domain binding. These contacts are consistent with CFTR activity and the requirement for an intact N-terminus. S251 is an inhibitory lasso-domain phosphosite poised to disrupt R-domain interactions. The two structures show different NBD orientations with a single-occluded ATP site in IFnarrow. The authors propose a model where the R-domain transitions from unbound/disordered to bound/ordered upon phosphorylation, providing a stimulatory R-domain architecture. The study also rationalizes clinical findings such as the F713 mutation (CFTR delF506 equivalent) and lumacaftor binding. The presence of a single defined binding site for the conserved part of the R-domain is the core contribution, providing implications for other transporters with long phosphorylated unstructured domains.

Executive Summary
Yeast Cadmium Factor-1 (Ycf1) is an ABCC-subfamily ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter that sequesters heavy metals (e.g., cadmium, mercury, lead) and oxidized glutathione (GSSG) into vacuoles to maintain redox balance and counter cell stress; these metals are among the top ten environmental toxins defined by the CDC. ABC transporters are essential for lipid homeostasis, ion transport, and detoxification, and about half of all human ABC transporters are phosphorylated. Previous structural models of CFTR and Ycf1 revealed mostly disordered regulatory (R) domains without assigned phosphorylation sites, which has limited understanding of R-domain interactions and regulation. In this study, the authors determined two cryo-EM structures of endogenously phosphorylated S. cerevisiae Ycf1 at 3.4 Å and 4.0 Å resolution in two inward-facing open conformations (IFwide and IFnarrow). The E1435Q NBD2 Walker B mutant, with substantially lowered ATPase activity (Vmax 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg), was used to trap the conformations; the mutant yielded homogenous particles that produced 3.4 Å and 4.0 Å maps. Both maps resolved an almost complete Ycf1 structure, including 17 transmembrane helices, TMD0, the lasso motif, both NBDs, and a major portion of the R-domain (residues 901-935). The R-domain is ordered in the C-terminal segment (residues 920-929) and lacks secondary structure elsewhere, and it is phosphorylated at three positions (S908, T911, S914) with pronounced additional electron potential density. These phosphates make hydrogen-bonding or strong charge-charge contacts with R716 on NBD1 and R206 on the lasso domain. R-domain phosphorylation is hypothesized to be highly dynamic and required for maximal ATPase activity; dephosphorylated Ycf1 (treated with lambda phosphatase) shows substantially altered proteolysis patterns and drastically reduced ATPase activity. The R-domain sits in a basic groove of the NBD1 perimeter, intracellular loop 4, and the lasso domain, and the networks are nearly constant between IFwide and IFnarrow, related only by a rigid body movement of the NBD1/R-domain complex relative to NBD2. The R-domain burying hydrophobic surfaces (~1530 Å2 and ~1338 Å2) drives R-domain binding. These contacts are consistent with CFTR activity and the requirement for an intact N-terminus. S251 is an inhibitory lasso-domain phosphosite poised to disrupt R-domain interactions. The two structures show different NBD orientations with a single-occluded ATP site in IFnarrow. The authors propose a model where the R-domain transitions from unbound/disordered to bound/ordered upon phosphorylation, providing a stimulatory R-domain architecture. The study also rationalizes clinical findings such as the F713 mutation (CFTR delF506 equivalent) and lumacaftor binding. The presence of a single defined binding site for the conserved part of the R-domain is the core contribution, providing implications for other transporters with long phosphorylated unstructured domains.

Research Context
ABC transporters regulate diverse molecules for lipid homeostasis, ion transport, and detoxification. Ycf1 transports glutathione and sequesters heavy metals like cadmium, mercury, and lead into vacuoles. These metals make up three of the top ten environmental toxins as defined by the CDC. Protein phosphorylation tunes transporter function for specific cellular contexts; about half of human ABC transporters are phosphorylated. Previous cryo-EM structures of ABCC1, CFTR, and Ycf1 reveal a mostly disordered R-domain. The lack of R-domain sequence assignment prohibits insights into precise interacting regions. No structure of an intact R-domain with the NBDs has been determined in any state.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can cryo-EM determine the structures of endogenously phosphorylated Ycf1 to reveal the R-domain architecture? The authors hypothesized that R-domain phosphorylation is highly dynamic and dependent on the R-domain/NBD1 interaction. They predicted that dephosphorylation would change ATPase activity and change the R-domain position. The hypothesis was that phosphorylated S908, T911, and S914 drive the architecture that facilitates ATP hydrolysis. The authors expected that R-domain interactions induce a topology promoting electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions with NBD1 and the lasso domain. The predicted outcome was two inward-facing conformations (IFwide and IFnarrow) capturing a previously unobserved ordered R-domain state.

Methodological Details
The study used Saccharomyces cerevisiae Ycf1, an ABCC transporter. Two forms were expressed from strain DSY-5: wild-type (WT) and NBD2 mutant E1435Q. The E1435Q mutant has a Walker B mutation and lowered ATPase activity (Vmax 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg). The gene was codon-optimized and cloned into p423_GAL1 with N-terminal Flag and C-terminal decahistidine tags. Primary culture was grown for 24 hours at 30°C, followed by a 750 mL secondary culture grown for 24 hours before induction. The final culture was grown for 16 hours before harvesting at 4°C via centrifugation at 5000xg for 30 minutes. Cells were resuspended in ice-cold lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-Cl pH 8.0, 300 mM NaCl) with complete, EDTA-free protease inhibitors. Cryo-EM processing used RELION (3.0 and 3.1), cisTEM, and MotionCor2 for drift correction at 1.031 Å/pixel. CTF was estimated using CTFFIND4.1; particle picking used a reconstruction of WT Ycf1 for references. Ab initio 3D maps were generated followed by rounds of 3D classification and 3D refinement in RELION. A ~6.0 Å resolution map of WT Ycf1 was obtained and used as a reference for E1435Q particle picking with a 15° angular search. Initial model was built using SWISS-MODEL with 6jb1 as a template, manual building in COOT. Real-space refinement used Phenix; CCP-EM modules were used for map sharpening and structure analysis. Secondary structure restraints and evolutionary couplings guided model building, with Modrefiner and Isolde used in early refinement. Geometry was optimized with Molprobity through Phenix and a dedicated web service. Substrate binding cavity volume was calculated with the 3V server using a probe size of 2.5 Å. Evolutionary couplings were calculated using Evcouplings, JackHMMR, and PLMC on 13,723 sequences from Uniref90. Evolutionary coupling scores used a cutoff probability of ≥0.99% to identify positive interactions. ATPase assays used 0.01% LMNG and 0.001% CHS; rates were determined at 30°C via enzyme-coupled assay. Reaction mix contained 6.45 µg protein, 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.0, 10 mM MgCl2, 1 mM PEP, 55.7/78.03 U/mL PK/LDH, 0.3 mg/mL NADH, and ATP. Initial NADH consumption was monitored every minute at 340 nm for 30-45 min on a Synergy Neo2 Microplate Reader. ATPase fit used the Michaelis-Menten equation in GraphPad Prism 9 with at least three technical replicates. Substrate-stimulated activity used oxidized glutathione (GSSG) at a constant 1 mM ATP. Basal ATPase activity in the absence of GSSG was subtracted prior to fitting. Phosphorylation was assayed by in-gel phosphoprotein staining with Pro-Q Diamond Gel Stain. Untreated and lambda phosphatase-treated samples (5 µg each) were run on 10% SDS-PAGE gels stained with Coomassie Brilliant Blue R-250. Quantitative phosphorylation was measured by LC-MS/MS with Scaffold Q+S v 4.11.1 and Bayesian statistics. LC-MS/MS considered identification satisfying a minimum of two peptides with 95% confidence levels. Limited proteolysis used trypsin at concentrations 0 to 15 µg/mL, stopped with 1 µg/mL soybean trypsin inhibitor. Reaction incubated for 30 min on ice with trypsin; samples separated on 10% SDS-PAGE and stained with Coomassie Brilliant Blue.

Procedures And Architectures
The E1435Q mutant resulted in substantially lowered ATPase activity (Vmax 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg) and trapped the inward-facing states. The R-domain is defined as residues 901-935, helical in residues 920-929 and disordered elsewhere. Three phosphorylation sites (S908, T911, S914) were assigned based on additional electron potential density. Phosphates contacted R716 on NBD1 and R206 on the lasso domain via hydrogen-bonding or strong charge-charge interactions. S908 is part of a recognition motif for PKA-like kinases (RRAS motif) and mimics a phosphomimetic peptide bound to PKA. T911 serves as part of a CKII kinase recognition motif (S/T-(x)n-S/T). The R-domain encircles NBD1 in both states and sits along a basic groove of the NBD1 perimeter, intracellular loop 4, and the lasso domain. The R-domain/NBD1 interaction buried ~1530 Å2 and ~1338 Å2 of surface area in IFnarrow and IFwide, respectively. The interaction buried ~523 Å2 (IFnarrow) and ~480 Å2 (IFwide) specifically between NBD1 and the R-domain. The IFwide-to-IFnarrow transition caused an angle change between residues G913, G918, and G932 from 130º to 137.5º. The ATP binding sites moved closer and rotated in IFnarrow to occlude the non-functional binding site in NBD1. The NBD2 ATP site remained open, while NBD2 was less ordered with weaker cryo-EM density. A single-occluded ATP site is in IFnarrow, and a third less-resolved state called IFtransition is reported. The NBD1 X-loop and GRD motif were brought into contact upon transition to IFnarrow. Ycf1 F713, the site equivalent to CFTR delF506, is coordinated by cation-pi interactions with R765 and R1150. The binding site of lumacaftor binds in the outer perimeter of NBD1 near the R-domain binding site.

Key Results
Two cryo-EM structures were determined at 3.4 Å and 4.0 Å resolution in inward-facing open conformations. The E1435Q mutant lowered ATPase activity to Vmax 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg. The R-domain is helical in residues 920-929 and lacks secondary structure in residues 901-919 and 930-935. Phosphorylation was assigned to S908, T911, and S914 based on additional electron potential density. Mass spectrometry and phosphostaining confirmed phosphorylation at these three sites in both WT and E1435Q Ycf1. Dephosphorylated Ycf1 showed a clear increase to protease accessibility with a more complete digestion. ATPase activity was drastically reduced in dephosphorylated Ycf1. The electrostatic interactions buried ~523 Å2 in IFnarrow and ~480 Å2 in IFwide specifically between NBD1 and the R-domain. The R-domain/NBD1 interface buried ~1530 Å2 and ~1338 Å2 along the entire R-domain in IFnarrow and IFwide, respectively. The angle between G913, G918, and G932 changed from 130º (IFwide) to 137.5º (IFnarrow). The R-domain/NBD1 interaction network is nearly constant between the two structures. The R-domain encircles NBD1 in both IFwide and IFnarrow. The NBD1 X-loop and GRD motif are brought into contact upon transition to IFnarrow. S251 is accessible to the surface and poised to disrupt R-domain interactions through electrostatic repulsion. The R-domain is most highly conserved in the ABCC family. R-domain phosphorylation is clearly evident and induces a topology promoting electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The ordered R-domain contrasts with models where the R-domain is completely disordered or only between NBD1 and NBD2. The extensive R-domain and NBD1 interactions increase the ATPase rate in a manner consistent with CFTR. Multiple phosphate binding interactions to a common surface explain the robustness to loss of any single R-domain phosphorylation site. The R-domain transitions from unbound/disordered to bound/ordered upon phosphorylation, residing either between the NBDs when dephosphorylated or near NBD1. Phosphorylation along the R-domain drives association with the periphery of NBD1, reflected as increased ATPase activity and R-domain stability. The clustering of the R-domain and lasso domain provides a plausible explanation for the inhibitory role of S251 phosphorylation. R-domain interactions lend a regulatory effect analogous to a transmission clutch that only engages a motor. The findings rationalise how mutations distal from phosphorylation sites may contribute to dysfunction. The site equivalent to CFTR delF506, Ycf1 F713, is coordinated by cation-pi interactions with R765 and R1150. Lumacaftor, a CFTR corrector, binds in the outer perimeter of NBD1 near the R-domain binding site. The presence of a single defined binding site for the conserved part of the R-domain may have implications for other transporters.

Contradictions And Limitations
The R-domain is ordered, contradicting models where it is completely disordered or only semi-ordered between NBD1 and NBD2. The authors do not observe phosphorylation at S251 in their structure despite it being a conserved inhibitory site. The IFtransition state was insufficiently detailed to enable model building. The NBD2 ATP site is less ordered with weaker cryo-EM density in both states. The R-domain position is related only by rigid body movements, with very minor changes in the R-domain position along NBD1. No structure of an intact R-domain with the NBDs has been determined in any state to date. The phosphates themselves may block protease accessibility to some sites, complicating the assignment of dephosphorylation effects.

Claims
R-domain phosphorylation is required for maximal ATPase activity via an ordered stimulatory architecture. Dephosphorylated Ycf1 showed a drastic activity reduction. The E1435Q mutant showed Vmax 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg and trapped the inward-facing conformations. The R-domain was observed in an ordered state with phosphorylation at three positions. The R-domain/NBD1 interaction buried ~523 Å2 in IFnarrow and ~480 Å2 in IFwide specifically between NBD1 and the R-domain. The R-domain is helical in only the C-terminal segment (residues 920-929) and disordered elsewhere. Phosphates may block protease accessibility to some sites. The NBD2 ATP site remains less ordered with weaker density. This mechanism explains the robustness to loss of any single R-domain phosphorylation site. This provides a stimulatory R-domain architecture that reconciles ATPase and stability findings. The findings rationalize how distal mutations may contribute to transporter dysfunction.
Two inward-facing conformations (IFwide and IFnarrow) are related only by a rigid body movement of the NBD1/R-domain complex relative to NBD2. The R-domain/NBD1 interaction networks are nearly constant between the two structures. The angle change was only 7º (130º to 137.5º) between residues G913, G918, and G932. Both structures were determined in inward-facing open conformations. The R-domain encircled NBD1 in both IFwide and IFnarrow. The NBDs moved closer in IFnarrow to occlude the non-functional ATP site in NBD1. The movement of the NBD1/R-domain complex provides the major structural distinction between the two states. This model reconciles the constant interaction networks with the changing interdomain distances.
S251 is an inhibitory lasso-domain phosphosite poised to disrupt R-domain interactions through charge repulsion. S251 is accessible to the surface and poised to disrupt R-domain interactions through electrostatic repulsion. S251 is the site equivalent to T249 in the MRP1 homolog. The authors do not observe phosphorylation at S251 in their structure. S251 is a conserved regulatory site but its actual occupancy is not shown here. This provides a plausible explanation for the negative impact of lasso-domain phosphorylation. The inhibitory role is consistent with the clustering of the R-domain and lasso domain.

Data And Code Availability
Data processing was reported in Figs. S2-5 and supplementary tables S1, S2, S7. The evolutionary couplings were downloaded from the Evcouplings GitHub repository. The primary culture and secondary culture growth conditions are described in the Methods.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The E1435Q mutant with lowered ATPase activity trapped the inward-facing conformations. Limited proteolysis confirmed changes in protease accessibility between the states. Three phosphorylation sites (S908, T911, S914) were assigned with additional electron potential density. Mass spectrometry and phosphostaining confirmed phosphorylation at these three sites. ATPase assays fit data to the Michaelis-Menten equation in GraphPad Prism 9. The IFtransition state was insufficiently detailed to enable model building. The second ATP site in NBD2 remains open for binding.

Ethical Considerations
The study used S. cerevisiae and did not report animal or human tissue usage. No ethics approval or institutional oversight is reported.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A-C shows the 3.4 Å and 4.0 Å cryo-EM maps, 17 TMD helices, TMD0, the lasso motif, and both NBDs. Figure 1D reports ATPase activity and Figure 1E shows the substrate cavities. Figure 1F shows substrate-stimulated ATPase activity with GSSG. Figure 2A-D shows the R-domain encircing NBD1 along a basic groove. Figure 2E assigns phosphorylation to S908, T911, and S914. Figure 2F shows phosphostaining analysis. Figure 2G shows limited proteolysis digestion patterns. Figure 2H shows ATPase activity. Figure 2C shows surface burial (~523 Å2 and ~480 Å2). Figure 3A shows the phosphorylation scaffold. Figure 3B-D show the three hydrophobic burial sites. Figure 3E shows the x-loop and GRD motif. Figure 4A shows constant contacts, 4B shows the 7º angle change, and 4C shows the occluded ATP site. Figure 4D shows the inhibited IFwide state. Figure S7E shows evolutionary coupling analysis. Figure S7H shows R716 and R1150 cation-pi interactions.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first ordered structure of an endogenously phosphorylated R-domain at 3.4 Å and 4.0 Å resolution in two inward-facing states. 2. The strongest evidence is the visualization of phosphorylation at S908, T911, and S914 with additional electron potential density. 3. The future path is extending the single defined R-domain binding site model to other transporters with long phosphorylated unstructured domains.
