summary.title: Influence of plant growth regulators and nitrogen sources on the production and development of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk Hormonal treatment and fertilization to plant development
summary.authors: Leone Campos Rocha¹; Fábio Andrade; Teixeira 2& (Bahia State University Southwest (UESB)); Márcio Dos; Santos Pedreira (Bahia State University Southwest (UESB)); Daniela Deitos Fries (Bahia State University Southwest (UESB)); Giovanna Evely; Leite Costa (Bahia State University Southwest (UESB)); Ana Cláudia; Maia Soares (Bahia State University Southwest (UESB)); Daniel Lucas; Santos Dias (Bahia State University Southwest (UESB)); Abdias José De Figueiredo (Bahia State University Southwest (UESB)); Angel Amaral; Seixas 4& (Bahia State University Southwest (UESB)); Camile Carvalho Pacheco
summary.executive_summary: The study evaluated the influence of seed treatment with plant growth regulators (PGR) and various nitrogen fertilization methods on the germination, dry matter yield, and physiological composition of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. The experiments were conducted between June and September 2017 at the State University of Southwestern Bahia (UESB), employing two distinct experimental designs. Experiment 1 used a 2 x 4 factorial scheme with two commercial seed types (coated and conventional) and four PGR levels (0, 8, 16, 24 mL.kg-1 seed), applying a combined auxin (0.05 mg.L-1), cytokinin (0.09 mg.L-1), and gibberellin (0.05 mg.L-1) formulation. Germination was assessed under hermetic storage in a Mangelsdorf chamber at a 12h photoperiod and constant 28°C temperature, with pots filled with eight liters or 12 kg of dry soil (0-20 cm depth, 4-mm sieve). Experiment 2 used a 2 x 4 factorial scheme comparing untreated vs. treated seeds with PGR (0 mL.kg-1; 24 mL.kg-1) and four nitrogen fertilization methods: no fertilization, soil fertilization, foliar fertilization, and multiple (soil + foliar), with 32 experimental units. Fertilization used 75 kg.ha-1 N and 3 L.ha-1 for soil and foliar applications, respectively, and a standardized 15 cm residue cut at 30 days after sowing (DAS). Data were analyzed via SAS MIXED procedure, with significance declared at P ≤ 0.05. Key findings: PGR increased germination and root dry mass production (optimal at 10.3 and 12.8 mL.kg-1, respectively); coated seeds outperformed conventional seeds in germination, number of leaves, and tillers; leaf and pseudostem dry mass production interacted with seed type, with optimal levels at 8.85 and 9.57 mL.kg-1; and soil fertilization dominated dry mass production across structures regardless of PGR. Chlorophyll a significantly responded to PGR, and foliar fertilization increased chlorophyll a, b and carotenoids. No bibliography was provided in the source text, so influential citations are not reported. The conclusion recommends lower PGR levels for coated seeds and soil nitrogen fertilization for mass yield and chlorophyll content.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The study evaluated the influence of seed treatment with plant growth regulators (PGR) and various nitrogen fertilization methods on the germination, dry matter yield, and physiological composition of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. The experiments were conducted between June and September 2017 at the State University of Southwestern Bahia (UESB), employing two distinct experimental designs. Experiment 1 used a 2 x 4 factorial scheme with two commercial seed types (coated and conventional) and four PGR levels (0, 8, 16, 24 mL.kg-1 seed), applying a combined auxin (0.05 mg.L-1), cytokinin (0.09 mg.L-1), and gibberellin (0.05 mg.L-1) formulation. Germination was assessed under hermetic storage in a Mangelsdorf chamber at a 12h photoperiod and constant 28°C temperature, with pots filled with eight liters or 12 kg of dry soil (0-20 cm depth, 4-mm sieve). Experiment 2 used a 2 x 4 factorial scheme comparing untreated vs. treated seeds with PGR (0 mL.kg-1; 24 mL.kg-1) and four nitrogen fertilization methods: no fertilization, soil fertilization, foliar fertilization, and multiple (soil + foliar), with 32 experimental units. Fertilization used 75 kg.ha-1 N and 3 L.ha-1 for soil and foliar applications, respectively, and a standardized 15 cm residue cut at 30 days after sowing (DAS). Data were analyzed via SAS MIXED procedure, with significance declared at P ≤ 0.05. Key findings: PGR increased germination and root dry mass production (optimal at 10.3 and 12.8 mL.kg-1, respectively); coated seeds outperformed conventional seeds in germination, number of leaves, and tillers; leaf and pseudostem dry mass production interacted with seed type, with optimal levels at 8.85 and 9.57 mL.kg-1; and soil fertilization dominated dry mass production across structures regardless of PGR. Chlorophyll a significantly responded to PGR, and foliar fertilization increased chlorophyll a, b and carotenoids. No bibliography was provided in the source text, so influential citations are not reported. The conclusion recommends lower PGR levels for coated seeds and soil nitrogen fertilization for mass yield and chlorophyll content.

Research Context
Shortening of soil preparation and planting windows limits the time to recover degraded pastures. Greater seed efficiency in germination and speed of emergence is necessary. Management practices are essential to improve herbage production using favorable climatic conditions. Phytohormones such as auxins, gibberellins, and cytokinins regulate plant homeostasis and activate genes. PGRs can potentiate plant performance in stress-prone environments by acting on biochemical reactions. High concentrations of gibberellins as a pasture management tool are uneconomical with reductions in forage mass. Low concentrations of gibberellin of 5-10 g.ha-1 are sufficient to affect forage yield positively. Growth regulators act on the positive regulation of genes linked to growth and development. Nitrogen expands the plant lifecycle, leading to higher vegetative growth rates. Nitrogen is indispensable in organic compounds and stimulates cell division and elongation. Nitrogen applications to degraded pasture recover areas and increase water use efficiency. The prior gap concerns understanding the optimal hormonal and nitrogen combinations for Brachiaria development.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether seed treatment with PGR and nitrogen fertilization methods influence Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. The study examines the effect through germinative characteristics, dry matter yield, and physiological composition. It is hypothesized that PGR increases germination and mass yields of plant structures in coated seeds. It is predicted that higher germination and root dry mass occur at specific PGR levels. A significant interaction between seed type and growth regulator is predicted for leaf and pseudostem mass. It is hypothesized that soil N-fertilization increases dry mass of all plant structures. Rates of photoassimilate are predicted to increase with both soil fertilization and PGR. The study posits that exogenous hormones act on organogenesis and increase Brachiaria development. It is hypothesized that soil N-fertilization maximizes photosynthetic processes and growth rates.

Methodological Details
Experiments were performed at UESB, Itapetinga -BA, between June and September 2017. Location: Forage and Pasture Research Center, greenhouse, and Laboratory of Anatomy and Ecological Plant Physiology (LAFIEP). Germination used a Mangelsdorf germination chamber (MA-401) with seedling trays. Germination occurred under a 12h photoperiod and at a constant temperature of 28ºC. Growth and development evaluations were performed in a greenhouse. Each pot was filled with eight liters or 12 kg of dry soil. Soil was collected at 0-20 cm depth and grounded to pass through a 4-mm sieve. Analyses were performed at the Department of Agricultural Engineering and Soils of UESB. Fertilization recommendations were based on the Soil Fertility Commission for the State of Minas Gerais, 5th Approximation [8]. Temperatures and relative humidity were recorded using a digital thermo-hygrometer, as shown in Fig 1. Experiment 1: A 2 x 4 factorial scheme in a completely randomized design (CRD). Two commercial seed types (coated and conventional) were compared. Four PGR levels were used: 0, 8, 16, 24 mL.kg-1 of seed. Seeds were imbibed for two hours, then wrapped in filter paper moistened with distilled water. Each replicate used 25 seeds and there were four replicates per treatment. The PGR composition was auxin (0.05 mg.L-1), cytokinin (0.09 mg.L-1), and gibberellin (0.05 mg.L-1). Initial growth (30 DAS) sowing used a seedling tray with 32 cells per replicate. Sterilized coconut residue served as the substrate to maintain constant humidity. Experiment 2: 2 x 4 factorial CRD with untreated and treated seeds (0; 24 mL.kg-1) and four N methods. summary.executive_summary: This prospective, single-center clinical registry investigates the impact of chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesion length on procedural and clinical outcomes in patients treated with percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) using drug-eluting stents (DES). The study was motivated by the observation that while successful CTO PCI significantly improves clinical outcomes compared with failed attempts, it remained unclear whether lesion length modified the angiographic and clinical trajectories of patients in the DES era. The authors hypothesize that long CTO lesions would be associated with worse angiographic and adverse clinical outcomes, given that long coronary artery lesions are established prognostic factors for adverse outcomes after PCI, and that long CTO lesions are associated with worse clinical risk factors such as prior myocardial infarction (MI) and prior PCI. A total of 235 consecutive patients who underwent successful CTO PCI with DES from November 2004 to October 2010 at the Cardiovascular Center of Korea University Guro Hospital in Seoul, South Korea, were enrolled. Patients were divided into a long CTO group (angiographic lesion length ≥30 mm, n=159) and a short CTO group (angiographic lesion length <30 mm, n=76). The study defined CTO as a complete coronary obstruction with TIMI flow grade 0, estimated duration ≥3 months, with or without visible collateral flow, excluding in-stent restenosis (ISR). After successful PCI, all patients received aspirin and clopidogrel maintenance dual antiplatelet therapy, often supplemented with cilostazol at the physician's discretion. The primary angiographic endpoint was the incidence of binary restenosis at 6-12 months. The primary clinical endpoint was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as the composite of total death, recurrent MI, and revascularization. In hospital complications were compared between groups; the authors found intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group. At 6 months, angiographic outcomes were similar between groups, including binary restenosis, ISR, mean diameter stenosis, and minimal luminal diameter. At 2 years, hard clinical endpoints—cardiac death, MI, and MACE—were not significantly different between groups, but the incidence of repeat PCI, primarily target vessel revascularization (TVR), was significantly higher in the long CTO group. Multivariate analysis showed long CTO was an independent predictor for repeat PCI (OR 4.26, CI 1.53-11.9, p=0.006). The authors conclude that while the long CTO lesion with DES remains similarly safe regarding major mortality and ischemic endpoints compared with the short CTO lesion, it carries a higher risk of repeat revascularization. The study emphasizes that despite procedural success, lesion length remains a clinically meaningful discriminator of revascularization risk.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This prospective, single-center clinical registry investigates the impact of chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesion length on procedural and clinical outcomes in patients treated with percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) using drug-eluting stents (DES). The study was motivated by the observation that while successful CTO PCI significantly improves clinical outcomes compared with failed attempts, it remained unclear whether lesion length modified the angiographic and clinical trajectories of patients in the DES era. The authors hypothesize that long CTO lesions would be associated with worse angiographic and adverse clinical outcomes, given that long coronary artery lesions are established prognostic factors for adverse outcomes after PCI, and that long CTO lesions are associated with worse clinical risk factors such as prior myocardial infarction (MI) and prior PCI. A total of 235 consecutive patients who underwent successful CTO PCI with DES from November 2004 to October 2010 at the Cardiovascular Center of Korea University Guro Hospital in Seoul, South Korea, were enrolled. Patients were divided into a long CTO group (angiographic lesion length ≥30 mm, n=159) and a short CTO group (angiographic lesion length <30 mm, n=76). The study defined CTO as a complete coronary obstruction with TIMI flow grade 0, estimated duration ≥3 months, with or without visible collateral flow, excluding in-stent restenosis (ISR). After successful PCI, all patients received aspirin and clopidogrel maintenance dual antiplatelet therapy, often supplemented with cilostazol at the physician's discretion. The primary angiographic endpoint was the incidence of binary restenosis at 6-12 months. The primary clinical endpoint was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as the composite of total death, recurrent MI, and revascularization. In hospital complications were compared between groups; the authors found intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group. At 6 months, angiographic outcomes were similar between groups, including binary restenosis, ISR, mean diameter stenosis, and minimal luminal diameter. At 2 years, hard clinical endpoints—cardiac death, MI, and MACE—were not significantly different between groups, but the incidence of repeat PCI, primarily target vessel revascularization (TVR), was significantly higher in the long CTO group. Multivariate analysis showed long CTO was an independent predictor for repeat PCI (OR 4.26, CI 1.53-11.9, p=0.006). The authors conclude that while the long CTO lesion with DES remains similarly safe regarding major mortality and ischemic endpoints compared with the short CTO lesion, it carries a higher risk of repeat revascularization. The study emphasizes that despite procedural success, lesion length remains a clinically meaningful discriminator of revascularization risk.

Research Context
Successful CTO PCI is associated with improved clinical outcomes compared with failed CTO PCI. It is not clear whether long CTO lesions differ from short CTO lesions in the DES era. Long coronary artery lesions are a worse prognostic factor after PCI. Procedural success rate of CTO patients is still lower than non-CTO patients. Long-term outcome is affected from clinical risk factors and baseline lesion characters.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can CTO lesion length impact six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes? Longer lesions were expected to have more frequent adverse angiographic and clinical outcomes. Hypothesis supported by history of prior MI and PCI in the long CTO group. Predicted worse outcomes due to dominance of older generation stents in the long group. Hypotheses that hard endpoints would not be affected despite higher revascularization.

Methodological Details
A total of 235 consecutive CTO patients were enrolled. Patients underwent successful PCI with DES from November 2004 to October 2010. The long CTO group had lesion length ≥30 mm (n=159). The short CTO group had lesion length <30 mm (n=76). The long CTO group had more frequent prior PCI. The short CTO group had more frequent bifurcation lesions. CTO was complete obstruction with TIMI grade 0. Estimated CTO duration was ≥3 months. Only de novo lesions were included; ISR-due CTO was excluded. All patients received dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin and clopidogrel). Loading doses of clopidogrel (300-600 mg) and aspirin (200-300 mg) before the procedure. Maintenance doses of aspirin (100 mg) and clopidogrel (75 mg) after PCI. Cilostazol was administered by physicians' discretion. PCI was performed with current guidelines using standard techniques. Simple pre-dilation with balloon was mostly performed. All PCI was performed using DES. Procedural success required diameter stenosis <30% and TIMI grade ≥2. The primary angiographic endpoint was binary restenosis at 6-12 months. Secondary angiographic endpoints included ISR, mean DS, MLD, and late loss. The primary clinical endpoint was MACE. MACE was defined as the composite of total death, recurrent MI, and revascularization. Deaths were considered cardiac unless non-cardiac death could be confirmed. Differences were evaluated by Student's t-test for continuous variables. Categorical variables were analyzed with χ2 or Fisher's exact test. Logistic regression adjusted for sex, age, hypertension, diabetes, CKD, prior PCI, and bifurcation lesion. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All analyses were performed using SPSS 20.

Procedures And Architectures
Procedural success was defined by reduction in stenosis and TIMI grade. Standard PCI techniques and devices were used. Simple pre-dilation with balloon achieved adequate luminal diameter. All stents were drug-eluting stents; the type was decided by the operator. Guidewires crossed the CTO lesion; atheroablative devices were not utilized. Adjunctive balloon dilatation was performed when necessary. Follow-up data was collected at 6 months and 2 years. Angiographic data was obtained from 99 long CTO patients (62%). Angiographic data was obtained from 45 short CTO patients (59%). Quantitative coronary angiography parameters were measured and analyzed. Follow-up was by interview, medical record review, and telephone contact. Multivariate analysis estimated repeat PCI risk with adjustments.

Key Results
In hospital complications were similar between the two groups. Intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group. Cardiac death was 1.2% in long vs. 2.6% in short CTO (p=0.45). MI was 1.8% in long vs. 2.6% in short CTO (p=0.71). Total death was 3.1% in long vs. 5.2% in short CTO (p=0.43). MACE was 21.3% in long vs. 13.1% in short CTO (p=0.13). Repeat PCI was higher in the long CTO group (18.8% vs. 7.8%, p < 0.05). Target vessel revascularization (TVR) was 16.3% in long vs. 6.5% in short CTO (p < 0.05). Long CTO was an independent predictor for repeat PCI (OR 4.26, CI 1.53-11.9, p=0.006). Binary restenosis was 19.1% in long vs. 8.8% in short CTO (p=0.118). In-stent restenosis (ISR) was 33.3% in long vs. 26.6% in short CTO (p=0.42). Late loss (LL) was 0.65 ± 0.82 mm in long vs. 0.46 ± 0.56 mm in short CTO (p=0.13). Long CTO was an independent predictor for TVR (OR 4.23, CI 1.52-11.8, p<0.05).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The long CTO lesion is an important independent predictor of repeat PCI and TVR. Hard endpoints (mortality, MI, MACE) did not translate into individual hard endpoints. A difference between hard endpoints and revascularization was previously reported. Less myocardial viability and collateral channels may play important roles in long lesions. Collateral channels could lessen the harmful physiologic effect of restenosis. Vessel size was smaller in the short CTO group (3.11 vs. 2.92 mm). Both groups had large enough vessel diameters for the categorization. Vessel diameter did not affect angiographic and clinical outcomes significantly. Successful DES CTO PCI is similarly safe regardless of lesion length regarding hard endpoints.

Contradictions And Limitations
The present study is not a randomized study but a single-center prospective registry. Baseline clinical and procedural characters slightly differed between the two groups. Newer generation DES were frequent in the short group; older generation stents in the long group. Follow-up angiography was not routinely performed in all patients. Follow-up angiography was determined by physician discretion or ischemic symptoms. The sample size was relatively small. The study did not have strong power to prove a difference in angiographic events. The two-year follow-up period was not long enough for long-term safety. Real-world CTO cohorts were used, but a larger long-term study is required.

Claims
CTO lesion length predicts repeat revascularization but not major hard endpoints. Long CTO was an important independent predictor for repeat PCI. Repeat PCI was significantly higher in the long CTO group. MACE was not significantly different between groups (p=0.13). Hard endpoints were clinically similar despite higher revascularization. Lesion length guides revascularization prognosis in DES-treated CTO patients. Hard safety endpoints appear preserved in long CTO treated with DES.
Angiographic outcomes are statistically similar between long and short CTO at 6 months. Binary restenosis was similar (p=0.118). ISR was not different (p=0.42). Late loss was not different (p=0.13). A numerical higher trend in adverse outcomes was noted. Power may be insufficient to detect angiographic differences. Short-term angiographic safety appears robust in both groups.

Data And Code Availability
Data were presented as a single-center prospective clinical registry, no repository noted. Specific data repository or code sharing was not reported.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
No explicit ablation or sensitivity analyses were reported. The univariate vs multivariate comparisons are the primary robust tests. A p-value < 0.05 was used across all tests.

Ethical Considerations
The protocol was approved by the institutional review board at Korea University Guro Hospital. All patients provided informed consent to participate in the study. Deaths were considered cardiac unless non-cardiac death could be confirmed.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1: Baseline clinical and angiographic characteristics. Table 2: Procedural and in-hospital complications. Table 3: Two-year follow-up clinical outcomes. Table 4: Predictors for repeat PCI and TVR. Table 5: Six-month angiographic outcomes. Figure tables are mentioned but not reproduced in text.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: lesion length predicts revascularization risk, not mortality in DES-treated CTO. 2. The strongest evidence: repeat PCI and TVR were significantly higher in the long group (p<0.05). 3. The future path: a larger long-term study is needed to elucidate the final conclusion.

summary.executive_summary: Diabetes is an emerging metabolic disorder characterized by hyperglycaemia accompanied by carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism disturbance. The number of people with diabetes increased from 108 million in 1980 to 422 million by 2014, and prevalence among people over 18 years old rose from 4.7% to 8.5% in that period. Executive Summary
Diabetes is an emerging metabolic disorder characterized by hyperglycaemia accompanied by carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism disturbance. The number of people with diabetes increased from 108 million in 1980 to 422 million by 2014, and prevalence among people over 18 years old rose from 4.7% to 8.5% in that period. Risk factors include older age, family history, race or ethnicity, obesity and physical inactivity. Management strategies focus on controlling postprandial hyperglycaemia via α-glucosidase inhibitors, such as acarbose, miglitol and voglibose, which delay carbohydrate hydrolysis. Molecular docking studies against α-glucosidase were conducted to provide insights of a new lead scaffold for the development of new clinically effective antidiabetic drugs. They screened compounds in an α-glucosidase inhibitory assay using 100 µg/mL of each compound and Baker's yeast enzyme, performing the assay in triplicate and comparing against acarbose as a positive control. Six compounds (including 6d and 6h) showed average percent inhibition of more than 50%, with 6h exhibiting the highest inhibition and lower IC 50 than acarbose. IC 50 values reached 167.82 µM for compound 3 (60.38% inhibition), 304.13 µM for 2a (50.36%) and 173.83 µM for 2d (57.48%). Molecular docking with Autodock and PDB ID 3W37, with relative standard deviation < 2.34 kcal/mol, showed 6h had the lowest binding energy (-10.56 kcal/mol), stabilized by hydrogen bonds to Ala234, Arg552 and Asp469, and directed by Trp329. The study concluded that aminobridge substitution of the pyrimidine ring at position 4 drives inhibitory activity, offering a new lead scaffold distinct from carbasugars for new clinically effective antidiabetic drugs treating type II diabetes.

Research Context
Diabetes is an emerging metabolic disorder characterized by hyperglycaemia. Number of diabetic people increased to 422 million by 2014. Prevalence rose from 4.7% to 8.5% between 1980 and 2014. Diabetes risk factors include family history and ethnicity. Diabetes involves metabolism disturbance of carbohydrates, fat and protein. Diabetes management targets postprandial hyperglycaemia. α-glucosidase inhibitors such as acarbose are established drugs. α-glucosidase inhibitors delay carbohydrate hydrolysis. α-glucosidase inhibitors have multiple therapeutic applications. Carbasugars like validamine and valienamine are lead compounds. Carbasugars mimic the oxocarbenium ion-like transition state. Side effects like flatulence and diarrhoea reduce compliance. Side effects are the major cause of reduced compliance. New α-glucosidase inhibitors are explored to overcome side effects. Well-accepted scaffolds were chosen for modification. Pyridine, triazole and pyrimidine scaffolds are common.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The objective is to overcome sugar mimetic side effects. Well-accepted scaffolds were chosen for modification. The pyridine, triazole and pyrimidine scaffolds were reused. Two series of phenoxypyrido-triazolo-pyrimidinones were designed. Significant inhibitory activity was predicted for new compounds. IC 50 values lower than acarbose were predicted for two compounds. Molecular docking was used to study binding modes. A new lead scaffold for antidiabetic drugs was sought.

Methodological Details
The study synthesized 25 tricyclic hybrids. Figure 2 illustrates the synthetic route. A hydrazine moiety was added to generate triazoles. A 1,2,4-triazole intermediate was obtained. Alkyl/heteroalkyl halides gave yields between 45-83%. Formation of N-alkylated products was confirmed by spectra. IR spectra showed the C=O group. Compound 3 was obtained in excellent yield. 13 C NMR showed a C=S peak. Compound 6e was obtained in 63% yield. Compounds 6a-d were obtained in 60-68% yields. Compound 6i was obtained in good yield. Hydrazinolysis produced compounds 6g and 6h. NMR showed two consistent spin coupling systems. The main structure of phenoxy-pyrido-triazolopyrimidinone was clear. N-substitution was targeted at position 4. N-substitution yielded activity only for 2a and 2d. Amino-bridged substitutes produced compounds 6a-6i. Six compounds showed inhibition above 50%. Compounds 3, 6c, 6d inhibited above 60%. Compounds 2a and 2d inhibited between 50-60%. All compounds were screened at equal concentration. Tests were repeated three times per compound. The inhibition range was between 30% and 63%.

Procedures And Architectures
Phosphate-buffered saline was prepared. Sodium phosphate monobasic was dissolved. Sodium chloride was dissolved. Potassium chloride was dissolved. Potassium dihydrogen phosphate was dissolved. The solution was adjusted to pH 6.5 at 20 °C. A p-NPG substrate solution was prepared. The enzyme was prepared at a fixed concentration. The enzyme concentration was 0.125 unit/mL. Samples were prepared in 100% DMSO. Serial dilutions were made with 5% DMSO. 10 µL of DMSO was added per well. 10 µL of the stock sample was added. 20 µL of the α-glucosidase enzyme was added. 40 µL of buffer and 20 µL of water were added. The mixture was pre-incubated at 37 °C for 10 min. 10 µL of p-NPG solution was added. Absorbance was measured at 405 nm at 0 min. The reaction was incubated for 30 min at 37 °C. Negative control used 5% DMSO. Experiments were performed in triplicate. Acarbose was used as positive control. Autodock software was used for docking. Protein was downloaded as PDB 3W37. Detailed steps were reported by Abuelizz et al. Relative standard deviation was < 2.34 kcal/mol.

Key Results
All tested compounds inhibited between 30% and 63%. Eight compounds exhibited >50% inhibition. Compound 3 inhibited by 60.38%. Position 4 derivatives showed weak activity. Only two N-alkylated derivatives inhibited >50%. IC 50 of compound 3 was 167.82 µM. IC 50 of 2a and 2d were 304.13 and 173.83 µM. Some derivatives had IC 50 values lower than acarbose. Compounds 6a, 6b, 6c, 6d showed low IC 50. 6d and 6h showed significant inhibitory activity. Compound 6h exhibited the highest inhibition. Compound 6h IC 50 was reported as 104.07 mM. Docked 6h binding energy was the lowest. Relative standard deviation was < 2.34 kcal/mol. Compound 6a had higher stability than 6b. Compound 6b had binding energy = -9.17 kcal/mol. Aminobridge substitution of 6h reduced binding energy to -10.55 kcal/mol. Acarbose can establish 10 hydrogen bonds. Acarbose correlates with established hydrogen bonds. Acarbose forms two hydrophobic interactions. Trp329 forms hydrophobic bonds with 2a and 6h. Three residues appear to interact with 6h. These hydrogen bonds enhance complex stability.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Aminobridge substitution at position 4 drives inhibition. Aminobridge substitution is compared with other N-substitution. Hydrogen bonds correlate with inhibition activity. Acarbose forms 10 hydrogen bonds. Trp329 plays a significant role in directing the ligand. Trp329 forms hydrophobic bonds with 2a and 6h. A new lead scaffold is provided for development. Non-carbasugars could become clinical drugs for type II diabetes.

Contradictions And Limitations
The abstract reports 6h IC 50 as 104.07 mM. The body reports compound 3 IC 50 as 167.82 µM. The abstract mM value is likely a typo. The IC 50 of 6h is reported as lower than acarbose. N-substitution at position 4 showed no activity except for 2a and 2d. Side effects reduce patient compliance to the diabetic treatment. Sugar mimetics require tedious synthesis. No statement on data availability is provided. No statement on raw data deposition is provided. No bibliography is provided with this paper. Docking results have no independent validation.

Claims
New tricyclic hybrids, particularly compound 6h, inhibit α-glucosidase more effectively than acarbose. Compound 6h was the most active. 6d and 6h had lower IC 50 than acarbose. 6h had the lowest binding energy. The abstract lists an improbable mM IC 50. A new lead scaffold was provided for development. It offers a non-carbasugar alternative.
Aminobridge substitution of the pyrimidine ring at position 4 drives strong inhibitory activity. Amino-bridged derivatives showed activity. Compounds 6a-d and 6h inhibited above 50%. N-substitution yielded activity only for 2a and 2d. This informs scaffold modification strategy.
Trp329 directs ligand binding and forms hydrophobic interactions. Trp329 plays a significant role. Trp329 forms hydrophobic bonds. The interaction is not quantified. Docking informs the binding mechanism.

Data And Code Availability
No statement regarding data availability is provided. No raw data deposition is mentioned.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Position 4 substitution ablation showed no activity. Only two N-alkylated derivatives were active. No independent validation of docking is reported.

Ethical Considerations
No statement on ethics approval is provided. No animal or human subjects were used.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 2 shows the synthetic route. Figure 3 compares inhibition of active compounds. Figure 4 lists the IC 50 values. Figure 5 presents the docking results. Table 1 lists binding energies.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the synthesis of 25 tricyclic hybrids, with six showing >50% inhibition and two better than acarbose. 2. The strongest evidence is compound 6h having the lowest binding energy and the lowest IC 50 compared to acarbose. 3. The future path is to transform these non-carbasugar scaffolds into clinical drugs for type II diabetes.

    *Expanded Executive Summary:*
    Diabetes is an emerging metabolic disorder characterized by hyperglycaemia and disturbed metabolism of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins, driven by insufficient or ineffective insulin action. The number of people with diabetes increased from 108 million in 1980 to 422 million by 2014, and prevalence among people over 18 years old rose from 4.7% to 8.5% in the same period. Risk factors include older age, family history, race or ethnicity, obesity, and physical inactivity. Management strategies focus on controlling postprandial hyperglycaemia via α-glucosidase inhibitors, such as acarbose, miglitol, and voglibose, which delay carbohydrate hydrolysis. While effective, these agents—particularly sugar mimetics like validamine and valienamine carbasugars that mimic the oxocarbenium ion-like transition state—require tedious synthesis and cause gastrointestinal side effects like flatulence and diarrhoea, reducing patient compliance. To overcome these side effects, the authors modified well-accepted scaffolds (pyridine, triazole, pyrimidine) to synthesize 25 tricyclic 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-ones hybrids. They screened compounds in an α-glucosidase inhibitory assay using 100 µg/mL of each compound and Baker's yeast enzyme, performing the assay in triplicate and comparing against acarbose as a positive control. Six compounds (including 6d and 6h) showed >50% inhibition, with 6h exhibiting the highest inhibition and lower IC 50 than acarbose. IC 50 values reached 167.82 µM for compound 3 (60.38% inhibition), 304.13 µM for 2a (50.36%), and 173.83 µM for 2d (57.48%). Molecular docking with Autodock and PDB ID 3W37, with relative standard deviation < 2.34 kcal/mol, showed 6h had the lowest binding energy (-10.56 kcal/mol), stabilized by hydrogen bonds to Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469, and directed by Trp329. The study concluded that aminobridge substitution at position 4 drives inhibitory activity, offering a new lead scaffold distinct from carbasugars for new clinically effective antidiabetic drugs treating type II diabetes.

summary.title: Inhibitor of sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase impairs paramyxovirus replication
summary.authors: Naveen Kumar (ICAR-National Research Centre on Equines); Sanjay Barua (ICAR-National Research Centre on Equines); Nitin Khandelwal (ICAR-National Research Centre on Equines); Kundan Kumar Chaubey (ICAR-Central Institute for Research on Goats); Ram Kumar (ICAR-National ResearchCentre on Equines); Krishan Dutt (ICAR-National Research Centre on Equines); Yogesh Chander (ICAR-National Research Centre on Equines); Thachamvally Riyesh (ICAR-National Research Centre on Equines); Vir Shoor Singh (ICAR-Central Institute for Research on Goats); Bhupendra Nath (ICAR-National Research Centre on Equines)
summary.type_of_paper: Primary research - mechanism of action / antiviral host-targeting study
summary.executive_summary: This study demonstrates for the first time that the membrane-bound cytosolic enzyme sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA) regulates paramyxovirus replication, specifically Newcastle disease virus (NDV) and peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV). Viruses depend on host factors, and while host-targeting agents are hypothesized to impose a higher genetic barrier to resistance, SERCA has not been previously characterized in viral replication. To test the hypothesis that SERCA is a proviral host factor, Vero cells were treated with the SERCA-specific inhibitor Thapsigargin (a sesquiterpene lactone) at a nontoxic concentration (0.5 µM). Results showed that Thapsigargin significantly reduced paramyxovirus replication in a concentration-dependent manner, while overexpression of SERCA2 rescued the inhibitory effect, confirming SERCA as a host factor required for infection. Time-of-addition and virus step-specific assays revealed that Thapsigargin specifically impairs viral entry and subcellular localization (causing cytoplasmic foci rather than cell-surface localization) but does not affect attachment, RNA synthesis, or budding. Furthermore, virus infection induced SERCA2 expression, which Thapsigargin blocked. Critically, in long-term passage (70 passages) in the presence of Thapsigargin, NDV acquired partial but incomplete resistance (stable at ~100-fold inhibition at P35, though not complete), while PPRV did not acquire resistance, highlighting virus-specific differences and a rare instance of virus acquiring resistance to a host-targeting agent. The study concludes that SERCA is a promising host-targeting candidate for novel antiviral therapeutics against paramyxoviruses, though the direct interaction between SERCA and viral proteins remains unknown and resistance mechanisms warrant further investigation.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study demonstrates for the first time that the membrane-bound cytosolic enzyme sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA) regulates paramyxovirus replication, specifically Newcastle disease virus (NDV) and peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV). Viruses depend on host factors, and while host-targeting agents are hypothesized to impose a higher genetic barrier to resistance, SERCA has not been previously characterized in viral replication. To test the hypothesis that SERCA is a proviral host factor, Vero cells were treated with the SERCA-specific inhibitor Thapsigargin (a sesquiterpene lactone) at a nontoxic concentration (0.5 µM). Results showed that Thapsigargin significantly reduced paramyxovirus replication in a concentration-dependent manner, while overexpression of SERCA2 rescued the inhibitory effect, confirming SERCA as a host factor required for infection. Time-of-addition and virus step-specific assays revealed that Thapsigargin specifically impairs viral entry and subcellular localization (causing cytoplasmic foci rather than cell-surface localization) but does not affect attachment, RNA synthesis, or budding. Furthermore, virus infection induced SERCA2 expression, which Thapsigargin blocked. Critically, in long-term passage (70 passages) in the presence of Thapsigargin, NDV acquired partial but incomplete resistance (stable at ~100-fold inhibition at P35, though not complete), while PPRV did not acquire resistance, highlighting virus-specific differences and a rare instance of virus acquiring resistance to a host-targeting agent. The study concludes that SERCA is a promising host-targeting candidate for novel antiviral therapeutics against paramyxoviruses, though the direct interaction between SERCA and viral proteins remains unknown and resistance mechanisms warrant further investigation.

Research Context
Classically, antiviral drugs target essential pathogen proteins. Viral high mutation rates lead to drug resistance at target sites. Drug resistance is rising, shifting focus toward host-targeting agents. Viruses are obligate parasites dependent on host cellular machinery. Host factors are either proviral or antiviral in determining disease outcomes. Proviral host factors can serve as antiviral drug targets. P-type Ca2+-ATPases regulate intracellular Ca2+ homeostasis in vertebrates. SERCA transports Ca2+ to the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi. The role of SERCA in virus replication is only beginning to be appreciated. SPCA1 has been shown to support virus replication.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether SERCA regulates paramyxovirus replication. The working hypothesis is that SERCA is a proviral host factor for PPRV and NDV. SERCA inhibition should reduce virus replication and overexpression should rescue it. Thapsigargin is expected to block replication at the entry step. A specific, nontoxic inhibitor dose is required for the assay. Virus infection should induce host SERCA expression. Resistance may emerge in some viruses but not others.

Methodological Details
Host cells were grown in DMEM with 10% heat-inactivated FBS. Four cell types: Vero, 293T, HeLa, and goat kidney. Thapsigargin is a plant-extracted sesquiterpene lactone. Thapsigargin was procured from Sigma (Catalog Number-T9033, Germany). Cytotoxicity was determined by MTT assay. A nontoxic concentration of 0.5 µM was selected for all assays. Antibodies were from Invitrogen and Sigma (Carlsbad and Steinheim). VIRUS STEP-SPECIFIC ASSAYS: attachment, entry, RNA synthesis, and budding. Virus step-specific assays followed previously described methods (24). OVEREXPRESSION: HeLa/goat kidney transfected in 24 well plates in triplicates. Empty vector pCR3 vs. SERCA2 plasmid (pCR3-SERCA2). Lipofectamine 3000 was used for transfection. Viral titers were determined by plaque assay. IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE: Vero cells at ~20% confluency infected with MOI of 5 for 2 h. Cells fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min. Blocked with 1% BSA for 30 min. Stained with primary antibody and 0.2% saponin. Counterstained with DAPI. VIRUS SELECTION: 70 sequential passages in Vero cells. MOI used for selection was 0.25 µM Thapsigargin or 0.05% DMSO. Passage endpoint was CPE in ≥75% cells. MOI used for quantification at each passage was 0.01. Resistance re-evaluated at standardized MOI=0.1 and harvest time 24 h. Selection used 0.5 µM Thapsigargin or 0.05% DMSO.

Procedures And Architectures
Thapsigargin is a non-competitive SERCA inhibitor. Virucidal assay: ~10^6 pfu incubated for 1.5 h at 37 °C. Viruses diluted 10^-3, 10^-4, 10^-5 before plaque assay. Time-of-addition was conducted as previously described. OVEREXPRESSION: NDV harvested at 24 hpi, PPRV at 96 hpi. IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE TIMEPOINTS: Thapsigargin applied at 3 hpi and 10 hpi. Co-immunoprecipitation was attempted and failed. Western blot: Lysates prepared at 16 hpi to probe SERCA2 and GAPDH.

Key Results
Thapsigargin was non-toxic between 0.00064 µM and 2 µM. Thapsigargin was toxic above 2 µM. Thapsigargin significantly inhibited NDV and PPRV replication. Thapsigargin inhibited BHV-1 but not BPXV (DNA viruses). Thapsigargin had no virucidal effect on any prototype virus. Overexpression of SERCA2 facilitated NDV/PPRV replication. Overexpression of SERCA2 rescued Thapsigargin inhibition. PPRV infection enhanced SERCA2 expression. Enhanced SERCA2 expression peaked between 24-72 hpi. GAPDH levels were similar at all time points. Virus-induced SERCA2 expression was blocked by Thapsigargin. NDV inhibition was highest 30 min before infection. NDV inhibition decreased from 1 hpi to 6 hpi. PPRV inhibition was highest 30 min before infection. PPRV inhibition decreased from 4 hpi to 24 hpi. Thapsigargin inhibited no virus replication at 10 hpi in NDV. Thapsigargin did not affect attachment, RNA synthesis or budding. Thapsigargin reduced NDV and PPRV titers in entry assay. Defective cytoplasmic foci in ~70% of Thapsigargin cells versus 10-30%. NDV resistance appeared at ~P25, significant at P35, but incomplete. P35 NDV exhibited ~100-fold inhibition vs ~10,000-fold at zero passage. All PPRVs showed similar sensitivity at P70. Control-passaged viruses showed no resistance.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
SERCA is a host-factor drug target. Host-targeting agents impose a higher genetic barrier. Multiple calcium transporters may facilitate replication. Resistance to host-targeting agents is generally not expected. This is a rare documented example of a paramyxovirus acquiring resistance to a host-targeting agent. The interaction between SERCA and viral proteins is unknown.

Contradictions And Limitations
Complete resistance could not be achieved. NDV resistance was incomplete and fluctuated. PPRV unlikely to develop resistant mutants. No direct protein-protein interaction could be detected. Selection conditions (MOI, harvest time) varied across passages.

Claims
SERCA is a host-factor that facilitates paramyxovirus replication at the entry and localization steps. SERCA inhibitor reduced NDV and PPRV replication. Overexpression of SERCA2 facilitated NDV/PPRV replication. Thapsigargin blocked virus-induced SERCA2 expression. Thapsigargin reduced NDV and PPRV titers in entry assay. No direct SERCA-viral protein interaction could be detected. SERCA is a candidate host-targeting antiviral drug target. Host-targeting drugs may offer broad spectrum inhibition.
NDV acquires incomplete, stable, virus-specific resistance to Thapsigargin after long-term passage. NDV resistance was significant at P35 (~100-fold vs ~10,000-fold). PPRV showed similar sensitivity across all passages. Control-passaged viruses showed no resistance. A completely resistant phenotype was not achieved even at P70. NDV titers and fold inhibition fluctuated across passages. Resistance to host-targeting agents is a rare, virus-specific phenomenon. Resistance may arise via changes in host factor requirements.

Data And Code Availability
Data availability was not explicitly reported. The antibodies were sourced from Invitrogen and Sigma.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A time-of-addition assay assessed the stage of impaired life cycle. Virus step-specific assays (attachment, entry, RNA synthesis, budding) were conducted. Thapsigargin affected no step other than entry and localization. PPRV and NDV replication cycles vary (~10 h vs ~24 h).

Ethical Considerations
No formal animal ethics or human subjects section is reported. The cell lines used are Vero (African green-monkey kidney). No specific animal welfare or IRB statement is provided.

Key Figures Tables
Fig 1a, 1b show SERCA inhibition and toxicity. Fig 1c-f show paramyxovirus and DNA virus inhibition. Fig 1g shows no virucidal effect. Fig 2a, 2b show SERCA2 overexpression rescues Thapsigargin inhibition. Fig 3a shows PPRV enhances SERCA2 expression. Fig 4a, 4b show time-of-addition results. Fig 5a, 5b show entry assay reduction. Fig 6a, 6b show cytoplasmic foci localization. Fig 6c, 6d quantify defective localization (~70% vs 10-30%). Fig 7a shows NDV resistance onset (~P25) and stability at P35. Fig 7b shows P70 Thapsigargin virus lower sensitivity vs P70-Control. Fig 7c shows all PPRVs show similar sensitivity at P70.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is identifying SERCA as a host-factor that regulates paramyxovirus replication. 2. The strongest evidence is SERCA2 overexpression rescuing Thapsigargin inhibition and the step-specific entry impairment. 3. The future path is characterizing the molecular interaction between SERCA and viral proteins and NDV resistance mechanisms.

summary.title: MicroRNA-196a is regulated by ER and is a prognostic biomarker in ER+ Breast Cancer
summary.authors: Michael J G Milevskiy; Udai Gujral; Carolina Del Lama Marques; Andrew Stone; Korinne Northwood; Lez J Burke; Julia M W Gee; Kenneth Nephew; Susan Clark; Melissa A Brown; Mjg Milevskiy
summary.field_subfield: Molecular and cellular oncology; epigenetic regulation; breast cancer epigenetics
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the transcriptional regulation and prognostic utility of microRNA-196a (MIR196A) in breast cancer, specifically within the context of oestrogen receptor (ER)-driven hormone receptor-positive (HR+) disease. MIR196A is transcribed from two genomic loci (MIR196A1 and MIR196A2) and is strongly associated with oncogenic phenotypes, yet its transcriptional regulation remained poorly understood prior to this work. The authors demonstrate that MIR196A expression is dynamic and controlled by long-range transcriptional regulation between promoter and enhancer elements bound by ERα, with expression significantly increased in models of hormone receptor-positive disease resistance. Using a combination of ChIP-Seq, GRO-Seq, ChIA-PET, 3C-qPCR, and methylation analysis, the study reveals that ERα and its pioneer factor FOXA1 bind to putative promoter regions (PP1, PP2, PP3) upstream of MIR196A2. Long-range interactions were identified with a previously described HOTAIR distal enhancer and a novel MIR196A2-enhancer, both of which physically interact with the promoter in MCF7 cells, with the HOTAIR distal enhancer being the most active. Methylation analysis showed that the upstream CpG island is mostly methylated in non-malignant MCF10A and cancerous MCF7 cells but unmethylated in human mammary epithelial cells (HMEC). Clinically, MIR196A is overexpressed in breast tumours and correlates with advanced tumour stage and poor survival in post-menopausal ER+ tumours, while conversely associating with better outcomes in triple-negative breast cancer. In tamoxifen-resistant MCF7 (TAMR) cells, MIR196A expression increases significantly, whereas it is depleted in fulvestrant-resistant (FASR) cells, mirroring changes in DNA methylation at the HOXC10/MIR196A2 promoters. The results suggest a regulatory model where ERα-driven de-repression and over-activation of promoter and enhancer elements contribute to resistance in ER+ tumours, positioning MIR196A as a potential prognostic stratification biomarker.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the transcriptional regulation and prognostic utility of microRNA-196a (MIR196A) in breast cancer, specifically within the context of oestrogen receptor (ER)-driven hormone receptor-positive (HR+) disease. MIR196A is transcribed from two genomic loci (MIR196A1 and MIR196A2) and is strongly associated with oncogenic phenotypes, yet its transcriptional regulation remained poorly understood prior to this work. The authors demonstrate that MIR196A expression is dynamic and controlled by long-range transcriptional regulation between promoter and enhancer elements bound by ERα, with expression significantly increased in models of hormone receptor-positive disease resistance. Using a combination of ChIP-Seq, GRO-Seq, ChIA-PET, 3C-qPCR, and methylation analysis, the study reveals that ERα and its pioneer factor FOXA1 bind to putative promoter regions (PP1, PP2, PP3) upstream of MIR196A2. Long-range interactions were identified with a previously described HOTAIR distal enhancer and a novel MIR196A2-enhancer, both of which physically interact with the promoter in MCF7 cells, with the HOTAIR distal enhancer being the most active. Methylation analysis showed that the upstream CpG island is mostly methylated in non-malignant MCF10A and cancerous MCF7 cells but unmethylated in human mammary epithelial cells (HMEC). Clinically, MIR196A is overexpressed in breast tumours and correlates with advanced tumour stage and poor survival in post-menopausal ER+ tumours, while conversely associating with better outcomes in triple-negative breast cancer. In tamoxifen-resistant MCF7 (TAMR) cells, MIR196A expression increases significantly, whereas it is depleted in fulvestrant-resistant (FASR) cells, mirroring changes in DNA methylation at the HOXC10/MIR196A2 promoters. The results suggest a regulatory model where ERα-driven de-repression and over-activation of promoter and enhancer elements contribute to resistance in ER+ tumours, positioning MIR196A as a potential prognostic stratification biomarker.

Research Context
MicroRNAs are short non-coding RNAs that post-transcriptionally regulate gene expression. MicroRNAs have been implicated in many disease from rare inherited syndromes to cancers. Research has led to identification of clinically useful genetic and epigenetic biomarkers. MicroRNA-196A is transcribed in two genomic locations downstream of HOXC10 and upstream of HOXB9. MIR196A is strongly implicated in cancers primarily as an oncogene. A single nucleotide polymorphism rs116149130 is associated with decreased breast cancer risk. Transcriptional regulation of miR-196a remains poorly understood despite clear importance in cancer. MicroRNA genes are regulated transcriptionally in a similar manner to protein-coding genes. Several instances of miRNA regulation by enhancers have been described but the area is in its infancy.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aimed to characterise the MIR196A expression landscape and the factors regulating its expression. The study explored potential roles of regulatory elements and factors in breast cancer prognostication. The authors hypothesised that MIR196A transcription is controlled by the oestrogen receptor (ER). The hypothesis was that MIR196A2 is controlled by long-range transcriptional regulation mediated by ERα tethered gene looping. The authors tested whether MIR196A expression is a robust prognostic factor for advanced and post-menopausal ER+ disease. The hypothesis suggested that the pathway to resistance involves de-repression and over-activation of promoter and enhancer elements.

Methodological Details
The study used the MCF7 breast cancer cell line. Tamoxifen-resistant (TAMR) and Fulvestrant-resistant (FASR) endocrine resistance sub-lines were used. All cell lines were authenticated by short-tandem repeat (STR) profiling. Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP-Seq) was used to assess ERα binding. Global-run-on sequencing (GRO-Seq) measured nascent RNA. ChIA-PET identified genome-wide chromatin interactions immunoprecipitating with ERα or RNA Polymerase II. Chromosome conformation capture (3C) was used to assess physical interaction of enhancer elements. Luciferase reporter assays were performed using the pGL3-Basic plasmid. 500 ng of modified pGL3 reporter constructs were transfected into MCF7 cells. 20 ng of pRL-TK Renilla transfection control was included. 0.5 μL of Lipofectamine 3000 was used for transfection. Luciferase readings were measured 48 hours post transfection. Cell lysates were prepared using Life Technologies TRIzol® reagent. RNA for miRNA analysis was reverse transcribed using the miScript RT II kit. Assays for all miRNAs were performed with the miScript SYBR Green PCR Kit. Expression data for miRNAs was normalised to the snoRNA RNU6b. All qRT-PCRs were performed on a Corbet Rotorgene-6000. RNA-Seq data was sourced from several public datasets including GSE68815 and Gascard et al. Publicly available accession codes were retrieved from ENCODE and GEO. ChIP-Seq data was mapped with Bowtie and peaks called by MACS. DNA methylation was sourced from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). METABRIC expression and clinical information were sourced from EGAS00000083. Clustering was performed using the Multiple Experiment Viewer (MeV). Genes were correlated within clusters using the CORREL function of Microsoft Excel. Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazard regression analyses used MedCalc for Windows. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and generation of survival curves was done GraphPad Prism. Optimal cutoffs were determined using receiver operator characteristic (ROC) curves. 3C was adapted from Vakoc 2005, Hagege 2007, and Tan-Wong 2008. Cells were grown to 60-80% confluence and fixed with 1% formaldehyde. Libraries were generated using HindIII digestion. GAPDH primers amplified a fragment containing no cut sites for determining efficiency. Primers were designed between 100-250 bp up or downstream of HindIII cut sites.

Procedures And Architectures
The transcriptional landscape was explored by comparing HOXC protein-coding and non-coding genes. The miR-196A expression correlated to HOXC genes, particularly HOXC10. ChIP-Seq showed polymerase binding surrounding the HOXC10 and MIR196A genes depends on oestrogen. Tamoxifen or fulvestrant treatment repressed this polymerase binding. GRO-Seq showed a dramatic increase in RNA production peaking at 40 mins after oestradiol addition. The qRT-PCR and RNA-Seq validated this increase in precursor miRNA from MIR196A2 but not MIR196A1. summary.title: Toxicity of TiO2, SiO2, ZnO, CuO, Au and Ag engineered nanoparticles on hatching and early nauplii of Artemia sp
summary.authors: Ch Lakshmi N Murthy; Mohammed M Idris; Shashi Singh
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles—silver (Ag), gold (Au), copper oxide (CuO), zinc oxide (ZnO), titanium dioxide (TiO2), and silicon (SiO2)—alongside three soluble salts (CuSO4, ZnSO4, AgNO3)—on the hatching rate and nauplii viability of Artemia sp. Brine shrimp are non-selective filter feeders that are robust and cost-effective model organisms for toxicological assays, and their early developmental stages are highly vulnerable to toxic stress. The research addressed the dearth of information regarding the impact of nanoscale objects on aquatic ecosystems and the lack of standardized, efficient hazard identification methodologies. Six different nanoparticles and three soluble salts were characterized by TEM (transmission electron microscopy) and DLS (dynamic light scattering) at the NANOVALID consortium. Silver and gold nanoparticles were obtained from Colorobbia and INMETRO, respectively; copper oxide from Intrinsiq Materials, zinc oxide from Nanogate, silicon from Nanologica AB, and titanium dioxide was synthesized in-house. Hydrated and bleached Artemia cysts were allowed to hatch in continuously aerated, filtered sterile salt water containing the nanoparticles, and hatching of viable nauplii versus total hatchlings were recorded. In parallel, a standard Artemia toxicity test was conducted on the nauplii, with viability recorded at intervals of 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, and 48 hours, using mortality as the endpoint. DCFDA (dichloroflouresciendiacetate) was used for an oxidative stress test by imaging ROS-stressed nauplii with a Zeiss Axiovert imager. The nanoparticles showed reduced size in high salt concentration and visible flocculation for copper and zinc oxide. Brine shrimp normally showed a hatching rate of 74%+5.5, with viability of about 97%. Exposure to nanoparticles caused a sharp, concentration-dependent drop in hatching rate, with the highest effect seen for silver and copper oxide nanoparticles, dropping to approximately 29% and only 50% motile/viable at 100 mg/L. Conversely, silver nitrate and copper sulfate (the ionic forms) also caused high toxicity, with silver nitrate showing 80% nauplii mortality in 24 hours. The LC50 of silver nanoparticles was around 10.12 mg/L at 24 hours. Silver in ionic form was highly toxic. The most toxic nanoparticles were silver and copper oxide, followed by zinc oxide, then gold, titanium dioxide, and silicon. The two tests showed a good inverse correlation with a correlation coefficient of -0.7853, and no significant difference was found in viability means (P=0.683). The study concluded that both hatching rate and nauplii viability could serve as valid, cost-effective hazard assessment assays. This work also established that the added advantage of continuous aeration in the hatching test keeps the particles in suspended form.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles—silver (Ag), gold (Au), copper oxide (CuO), zinc oxide (ZnO), titanium dioxide (TiO2), and silicon (SiO2)—alongside three soluble salts (CuSO4, ZnSO4, AgNO3)—on the hatching rate and nauplii viability of Artemia sp. Brine shrimp are non-selective filter feeders that are robust and cost-effective model organisms for toxicological assays, and their early developmental stages are highly vulnerable to toxic stress. The research addressed the dearth of information regarding the impact of nanoscale objects on aquatic ecosystems and the lack of standardized, efficient hazard identification methodologies. Six different nanoparticles and three soluble salts were characterized by TEM (transmission electron microscopy) and DLS (dynamic light scattering) at the NANOVALID consortium. Silver and gold nanoparticles were obtained from Colorobbia and INMETRO, respectively; copper oxide from Intrinsiq Materials, zinc oxide from Nanogate, silicon from Nanologica AB, and titanium dioxide was synthesized in-house. Hydrated and bleached Artemia cysts were allowed to hatch in continuously aerated, filtered sterile salt water containing the nanoparticles, and hatching of viable nauplii versus total hatchlings were recorded. In parallel, a standard Artemia toxicity test was conducted on the nauplii, with viability recorded at intervals of 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, and 48 hours, using mortality as the endpoint. DCFDA (dichloroflouresciendiacetate) was used for an oxidative stress test by imaging ROS-stressed nauplii with a Zeiss Axiovert imager. The nanoparticles showed reduced size in high salt concentration and visible flocculation for copper and zinc oxide. Brine shrimp normally showed a hatching rate of 74%+5.5, with viability of about 97%. Exposure to nanoparticles caused a sharp, concentration-dependent drop in hatching rate, with the highest effect seen for silver and copper oxide nanoparticles, dropping to approximately 29% and only 50% motile/viable at 100 mg/L. Conversely, silver nitrate and copper sulfate (the ionic forms) also caused high toxicity, with silver nitrate showing 80% nauplii mortality in 24 hours. The LC50 of silver nanoparticles was around 10.12 mg/L at 24 hours. Silver in ionic form was highly toxic. The most toxic nanoparticles were silver and copper oxide, followed by zinc oxide, then gold, titanium dioxide, and silicon. The two tests showed a good inverse correlation with a correlation coefficient of -0.7853, and no significant difference was found in viability means (P=0.683). The study concluded that both hatching rate and nauplii viability could serve as valid, cost-effective hazard assessment assays. This work also established that the added advantage of continuous aeration in the hatching test keeps the particles in suspended form.

Research Context
Nanomaterials pose a risk to environment and human health due to their unique properties. A dearth of information exists regarding the risk of nanoscale objects to the environment. Information on the predictability of nanoparticle behaviour is almost negligible. The behaviour of nanoparticles under various conditions is not clearly known. Hazard identification is an important step for risk assessment of nanomaterials. Aquatic systems are the inevitable receptacles for materials released in the environment. Many assays for ecotoxicology have been tested for nanomaterials in bacteria, fish, copepods and Daphnia. Few studies are reported for nanomaterial toxicity using Artemia sp. Artemia is a robust and cost-effective model organism for toxicological assays. The early developmental stages of Artemia are highly vulnerable to test materials. Hatching of hydrated cysts has not been used as a toxicity endpoint.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study asked whether acute nanoparticle toxicity could be estimated using Artemia hatching rate. It hypothesized that hatching rate and nauplii viability would inversely correlate as toxicity endpoints. Both tests were predicted to show a good inverse correlation in sensitivity to nanoparticles. The nanoparticles and salts were expected to show concentration-dependent toxicity. A new bioassay was hypothesized that could be developed for nanoparticle hazard assessment.

Methodological Details
Nanoparticles were sourced from five commercial suppliers plus in-house TiO2 synthesis. Silver, gold, copper oxide, zinc oxide, and silicon nanoparticles were commercially obtained. The silica, copper oxide, and zinc oxide nanoparticles were supplied by dedicated firms. A suspension of SiO2, TiO2, CuO and ZnO nanoparticles was made at 2 mg/ml and sonicated. Silver nanoparticles were prepared as a 4% suspension with PVP as a stabilizer. Gold nanoparticles were prepared as a 0.006% aqueous suspension. All nanoparticles were characterized by the NANOVALID consortium in a round-robin manner. TEM used a JEOL 2010 instrument at 100KV with a 20µ aperture and GATAN optics. DLS used a Horiba Nanopartica SZ100 for 25µg/ml suspensions in milliQ and salt water. Artemia used the San Francisco Bay strain at 1.0 gram per litre of culture. Cysts were hydrated for 45 minutes and bleached with 20% sodium hypochlorite for 15 minutes. The hatched cysts were washed six times and hatched in 25% salt water at 28°C. The temperature was maintained at 28°C which is the optimum temperature for hatching. Nanoparticles were added to the culture at 100 mg/l and 10 mg/l. Five nanoparticle types were exposed at 100 mg/L and 10 mg/L for 24 hours. The hatching rate, mortality and viability were checked after 24 hours for each flask. Three 100 µl aliquots were taken and counted under a stereo-microscope. The number of hatched, motile, umbrella-stage and unhatched cysts were counted. Hatching rate was expressed as the percent of fully hatched Artemia. The hatching experiment was repeated six times. For the second set, 10 nauplii were transferred to six well plates. Nanoparticles were added at five concentrations from 100 mg/l to 0.01 mg/l. Viability was counted at 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, and 48 hours. Mortality was used as the endpoint. The LC50 was calculated using Graphpad software. DCFDA was used to image ROS-exposed nauplii. DCFDA is a chemiluminescent probe for ROS. Nauplii were imaged on a Zeiss Axiovert imager. The hatching studies were repeated six times. The validity criterion for hatching was low control mortality. For toxicity tests, validity was <10% mortality in 24 hours. Correlation was calculated with Microsoft Excel.

Procedures And Architectures
Titanium dioxide nanoparticles were synthesized in-house using an existing protocol. SiO2, TiO2, CuO and ZnO were suspended at 2 mg/ml and sonicated at 30W with a 50% pulse for 10 minutes. Silver nanoparticles were obtained as a 4% suspension with PVP as a stabilizing agent. Gold nanoparticles were obtained in water at a 0.006% concentration. Working dilutions were made in NaCl salt water for various studies. Round-robin characterization used TEM and DLS at the NANOVALID consortium. TEM used a JEOL 2010 at 100KV with a 20µ aperture and GATAN camera/software. DLS used a Horiba Nanopartica SZ100 for 25µg/ml suspensions in milliQ and salt water. TEM suspension of 50µg/ml was applied to formvar-coated copper grids and air-dried. Cysts were hydrated in distilled water under aeration for 45 minutes. Cysts were bleached with 20% sodium hypochlorite solution for 15 minutes. The bleached cysts were washed six times and hatched in 25% salt water at 28°C. Brine shrimp were allowed to hatch in continuously aerated, filtered sterile salt water. Five nanoparticle types were exposed at 100 mg/L and 10 mg/L for 24 hours. Hatching rate was calculated as the percent of fully hatched Artemia. Ten nauplii were transferred to six well plates, receiving 100, 10, 1, 0.1 and 0.01 mg/L nanoparticles. Viability was recorded at 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 and 48 hours. Mortality was recorded as cessation of swimming or movement. DCFDA was added at 10µM to image ROS and superoxide stress. Particles were centrifuged and resuspended to test NP versus ionic toxicity. Dispersion patterns were monitored in MilliQ and NaCl solution up to 48 hours. Particle sizes were measured in distilled and salt water via TEM and DLS.

Key Results
Brine shrimp normally showed a hatching rate of 74%+5.5 with viability of about 97%. The hatching rate dropped with increasing nanoparticle concentration in salt water. Silver and copper oxide caused the highest drop in hatching rate. At 100 mg/L, silver and copper oxide dropped hatching to about 29%. Of these, only 50% were motile and viable at 100 mg/L. Viability remained high at 85% for silver at 10 mg/L. Copper oxide gave low hatching with viability around 64%. Silver nitrate gave 33% hatching and PVP improved it to 41%. Gold, titanium, silicon, copper and zinc oxide gave 50-60% hatching. ZnO gave 60% hatching but cysts tended to clump together. TiO2 at 100 mg/L gave 41.50% hatching and 67.8% viability. TiO2 at 10 mg/L gave 54% hatching and ~90% viability. SiO2 at 10 mg/L gave hatching and viability equivalent to controls. Ionic silver nitrate killed 80% of nauplii in 24 hours. The silver nanoparticle LC50 was around 10.12 mg/L at 24 hours. ZnO exhibited visible flocculation and sedimentation. The hatching rate was low for most nanoparticles, around 50-60% compared to control. The two tests showed a good inverse correlation. The correlation coefficient was -0.7853. No significant difference was found in viability means, P=0.683. The pH of salt water remained around 6.3-6.5. Particles did not accumulate in dead nauplii fed with silver nanoparticles.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Silver and copper oxide were the most toxic, likely due to ionic species. Centrifugation confirmed that ionic forms contributed to toxicity even after precipitation. Other nanoparticles (gold, TiO2, SiO2) showed lower concentration-dependent toxicity. SiO2 at low concentration actually enhanced hatching compared to control. The LC50 criteria defined 50 per cent dead after 24 hours as the toxicity threshold. The strong inverse correlation suggests hatching can be a valid pre-screening assay. Mortality was likely due to gut clogging, as particles accumulated in the digestive tract. DCFDA staining confirmed ROS and superoxide accumulation especially with silver. Artemia can serve as a model organism to assess nanoparticle behaviour and ecotoxicity. The added advantage of continuous aeration keeps particles suspended during the assay.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study reports only a few prior hatching endpoint toxicity assays, with single exception [14]. Control validity was only stated as low mortality in the control, with no quantitative threshold. The hatching test used only six repeats, which may limit statistical power. The reference [18] protocol was in-house and not standardized in this preprint. Sedimentation of dissolved components was not explicitly quantified across particles. Only short-term acute effects were assessed, with no chronic data reported. No demographics or culture statistics were provided for the brine shrimp. OCR noise and preprint footers contain non-factual, repetitive filler text.

Claims
Both hatching rate and larval viability are valid, cost-effective assays for nanoparticle hazard assessment. The two tests showed a good inverse correlation. A strong inverse correlation coefficient of -0.7853 was found. Viability means did not differ significantly across concentrations, P=0.683. Artemia is a robust and cost-effective model organism for assays. Hatching is a cheap, short-term, and easily repeated assay. The hatching assay is rarely used, with only one prior study cited [14]. Only six repeats of the hatching test were performed. The control validity was only stated as low mortality without a threshold. Hatching assays can be used as pre-screening prior to in vivo studies. Cost-effective screening reduces laboratory maintenance time and space. High-throughput methods may be adopted with a strictly laid out protocol.
Silver is the most toxic nanoparticle, killing 80% of nauplii in 24 hours as an ionic form. Silver caused the highest drop in hatching rate. Ionic silver nitrate killed 80% of nauplii in 24 hours. The silver nanoparticle LC50 was around 10.12 mg/L. Silver nauplii showed the highest ROS and superoxide staining. Only ionic silver nitrate was tested, not all silver salt forms. Viability was high at 10 mg/L for silver, contrary to ionic toxicity. Ionic and NP forms drive toxicity, necessitating centrifugation differentiation. Silver represents a key acute risk among the engineered nanoparticles tested.
The primary toxicity mechanism is gut clogging by ingested nanoparticles, not solubility changes. Particles accumulated in the gut of Artemia. Mortality is likely due to gut clogging by ingested material. Ionic silver precipitated but still affected hatching and viability. DCFDA staining confirmed stress and ROS in still-dead nauplii. The ionic forms (silver nitrate, copper sulfate) also caused high toxicity. Some nanoparticles showed no ROS or superoxide signs. Assay validity depends on particle suspension rather than solubility. Artemia is suitable to assess nanoparticle behaviour and ecotoxicity.

Data And Code Availability
No data or code availability statement is reported in the source.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The hatching versus nauplii toxicity correlation was assessed. Particles were compared in MilliQ and NaCl solutions. NP versus ionic forms were compared by centrifugation. The TiO2 dose-response was compared at 10 and 100 mg/L. Particle stability in seawater was tested up to one week. Control mortality criterion was not quantitatively defined.

Ethical Considerations
No explicit ethical approval or oversight statement is reported.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 reports the concentration-dependent hatching rate drops. Figure 1 shows particle size reduction in high salt water by TEM. Figure 2 shows higher DLS values in salt water and visible flocculation of CuO and ZnO. Figure 3 shows the hatching rate vs. concentration drop for all NPs. Figure 4 reports silver toxicity with 80% mortality and the LC50 of 10.12 mg/L. Figure 5 shows gut accumulation of NPs and ROS staining in still-dead nauplii. Figure 6 reports the strong inverse correlation between the two assays. Figure S1 shows dispersion patterns up to 48 hours in MilliQ and NaCl.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: A cost-effective hatching assay for nanoparticle acute toxicity, validated by correlation with nauplii viability. 2. The strongest evidence: Ag caused 80% mortality as an ion and the NP LC50 was 10.12 mg/L at 24 hours. 3. The future path: Adapt the protocol for high-throughput hazard identification before in vivo validation.

Let me write the executive_summary:

"This study investigates the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles—silver (Ag), gold (Au), copper oxide (CuO), zinc oxide (ZnO), titanium dioxide (TiO2), and silicon (SiO2)—alongside three soluble salts (CuSO4, ZnSO4, AgNO3)—on the hatching rate and nauplii viability of Artemia sp. Brine shrimp are non-selective filter feeders that are robust and cost-effective model organisms for toxicological assays, and their early developmental stages are highly vulnerable to toxic stress. The research addressed the dearth of information regarding the impact of nanoscale objects on aquatic ecosystems and the lack of standardized, efficient hazard identification methodologies. Six different nanoparticles and three soluble salts were characterized by TEM (transmission electron microscopy) and DLS (dynamic light scattering) at the NANOVALID consortium. Silver and gold nanoparticles were obtained from Colorobbia and INMETRO, respectively; copper oxide from Intrinsiq Materials, zinc oxide from Nanogate, silicon from Nanologica AB, and titanium dioxide was synthesized in-house. Hydrated and bleached Artemia cysts were allowed to hatch in continuously aerated, filtered sterile salt water containing the nanoparticles, and hatching of viable nauplii versus total hatchlings were recorded. In parallel, a standard Artemia toxicity test was conducted on the nauplii, with viability recorded at intervals of 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, and 48 hours, using mortality as the endpoint. DCFDA (dichlorofluorescein diacetate) was used for an oxidative stress test by imaging ROS-stressed nauplii with a Zeiss Axiovert imager. The nanoparticles showed reduced size in high salt concentration and visible flocculation for copper and zinc oxide. Brine shrimp normally showed a hatching rate of 74%+5.5, with viability of about 97%. Exposure to nanoparticles caused a sharp, concentration-dependent drop in hatching rate, with the highest effect seen for silver and copper oxide nanoparticles, dropping to approximately 29% and only 50% motile/viable at 100 mg/L. Conversely, silver nitrate and copper sulfate (the ionic forms) also caused high toxicity, with silver nitrate showing 80% nauplii mortality in 24 hours. The LC50 of silver nanoparticles was around 10.12 mg/L at 24 hours. Silver in ionic form was highly toxic. The most toxic nanoparticles were silver and copper oxide, followed by zinc oxide, then gold, titanium dioxide, and silicon. The two tests showed a good inverse correlation with a correlation coefficient of -0.7853, and no significant difference was found in viability means (P=0.683). The study concluded that both hatching rate and nauplii viability could serve as valid, cost-effective hazard assessment assays. This work also established that the added advantage of continuous aeration in the hatching test keeps the particles in suspended form."
